lessons.title: What PostgreSQL is: cluster, client/server, a query's round trip
tldr: PostgreSQL is a **client/server** database: one server instance manages a **cluster** of databases in a single data directory, and every client connection gets its own server process.
Clients send SQL as **plain text** over a small message protocol, and the server parses, plans and executes it and streams rows back, so any language with a socket can talk to it.

visualizer.title: A query's round trip, byte by byte
visualizer.caption: Step from TCP connect to Terminate. Click any message in the wire log to decode its bytes. Every length follows protocol 3.0 framing exactly.

presets.label: Who and where am I?
presets.note: Every session is one backend process with its own PID, connected to exactly one database as one role. `inet_server_addr()` is NULL when the session did not arrive over TCP (a Unix socket, or this in-process sandbox). Uptime counts from the postmaster start.

presets.label: The query from the visualizer
presets.sql: SELECT city, temp_lo FROM weather WHERE temp_lo < 45;
presets.note: Two rows, so the command tag is `SELECT 2`. In the wire protocol each value travels as text.

presets.label: What lives where
presets.note: initdb creates three databases; `template0` refuses connections. Two tablespaces exist from the start: `pg_default` for database files and `pg_global` for the cluster-wide catalogs (roles, the database list). Schemas belong to one database: this list is only `postgres`'s.

presets.label: Tables are files
presets.note: Each table lives in `base/<database oid>/<relfilenode>` under the data directory. Database `postgres` has OID 5.

presets.label: Describe a table without psql
presets.sql:
-- psql's \d is plain SQL over the catalogs; this is the portable version
SELECT column_name, data_type, character_maximum_length AS max_len, is_nullable, column_default
FROM information_schema.columns
WHERE table_schema = 'public' AND table_name = 'weather' ORDER BY ordinal_position;

SELECT c.relname,
       CASE c.relkind WHEN 'r' THEN 'table' WHEN 'i' THEN 'index' WHEN 'S' THEN 'sequence'
                      WHEN 'v' THEN 'view' WHEN 'm' THEN 'materialized view' ELSE c.relkind::text END AS kind,
       c.relpersistence AS persistence, am.amname AS access_method, pg_size_pretty(pg_table_size(c.oid)) AS size
FROM pg_class c JOIN pg_namespace n ON n.oid = c.relnamespace LEFT JOIN pg_am am ON am.oid = c.relam
WHERE n.nspname = 'public' ORDER BY 1;
presets.note: There is no `SHOW TABLES` or `DESCRIBE`: client tools query `information_schema` and `pg_class`. `varchar(80)` reports as `character varying` with max length 80. Each small table is `heap` storage of exactly one 8 kB page; `p` = permanent.

presets.label: One statement, one transaction
presets.note: Outside a block, every statement runs in its own transaction and gets a new xid. Inside BEGIN … COMMIT both reads share one xid.

presets.label: Statement time vs wall clock
presets.note: `now()` is fixed at transaction start. `statement_timestamp()` moves when a new statement arrives. `clock_timestamp()` is the real wall clock.

presets.label: Connection settings
presets.note: `context = postmaster` means the value is fixed at server start. These decide where the postmaster listens and how many backends it may fork.

production.title: The migration that ran against the wrong database
production.context: A team runs schema migrations from CI with a connection string built from environment variables. Staging and production share one cluster with two databases.
production.problem: A migration created its tables in database `postgres` instead of `app_staging`. The connection string had no database name, and libpq defaults the database to the user name. A later run then failed with `relation does not exist` in the right database.
production.solution: Make every migration assert where it is before it changes anything. A connection names exactly one database, and there are no cross-database queries, so check `current_database()` and fail fast. Also set `application_name` so the session is easy to spot in `pg_stat_activity`.
production.outcome: Misrouted runs now stop on the first statement with a clear message, before any DDL. The stray objects in `postgres` were found with `\dt` and dropped.

pitfalls.title: Expecting cross-database joins
pitfalls.symptom: `SELECT … FROM other_db.public.users` fails with `cross-database references are not implemented`.
pitfalls.cause: A connection is bound to one database at startup. Databases in a cluster are isolated; only roles, tablespaces and the database list are shared.
pitfalls.fix: Put related data in one database with several **schemas**. If two databases are truly needed, use `postgres_fdw` or `dblink`.

pitfalls.title: Leaving trust authentication after initdb
pitfalls.symptom: Any local OS user can connect as the superuser without a password.
pitfalls.cause: A fresh cluster can allow `trust` for local connections. `pg_hba.conf` uses the first matching line, so a broad `trust` line at the top wins.
pitfalls.fix: Initialize with `initdb -A scram-sha-256 -W`, or edit `pg_hba.conf` before the first start and reload. Check the result in `pg_hba_file_rules`.
pitfalls.sql:
SELECT rule_number, type, database, user_name, address, auth_method
FROM pg_hba_file_rules ORDER BY rule_number;

pitfalls.title: Remote clients cannot connect
pitfalls.symptom: From another host, `psql -h db1` fails with `Connection refused`; after one fix it fails again with `no pg_hba.conf entry for host …`.
pitfalls.cause: Two separate gates. `listen_addresses` (default `localhost`, restart required) decides which interfaces the postmaster binds; `pg_hba.conf` decides who may then authenticate. Opening `0.0.0.0/0` with `md5` or `trust` fixes the symptom and creates a security hole.
pitfalls.fix: Bind the interface you need, then add the narrowest hba line with `scram-sha-256` and reload.

pitfalls.title: Assuming each line of a script is separate
pitfalls.symptom: A script sent as one string fails on its third statement, and the first two statements are gone too.
pitfalls.cause: Statements in a single simple-query message run as one **implicit transaction**. An error rolls back everything since the start of the string unless explicit COMMITs split it.
pitfalls.fix: Send statements one at a time (psql does this), or wrap intentional units in explicit `BEGIN … COMMIT` blocks.

pitfalls.title: Dropping a database you are connected to
pitfalls.symptom: `DROP DATABASE shop` fails with `cannot drop the currently open database`, or with `is being accessed by other users`.
pitfalls.cause: A database cannot be dropped while any backend is connected to it, including your own.
pitfalls.fix: Connect to another database such as `postgres`, then run `DROP DATABASE shop WITH (FORCE);` to terminate the remaining sessions.

pointers: A **cluster** is one data directory managed by one server instance. initdb creates `postgres`, `template1` and `template0`.
Hierarchy: **cluster → database → schema → object**. Roles and databases are cluster-wide; a connection sees one database.
One **postmaster** listens on port 5432 and forks one **backend** per connection.
Every message is **type byte + Int32 length + payload**. A simple query is `Q` → `T`, `D`…, `C`, `Z`.
Inside the backend a query goes **parse → rewrite → plan → execute**, reading pages through shared buffers.

lessons.title: The postmaster and one process per connection
tldr: The **postmaster** is the first process of an instance: it starts the auxiliary processes, and it **forks one backend process for every client connection**.
Separate processes isolate sessions from each other, so a crashed backend cannot corrupt another one silently, and the postmaster can reset shared memory and restart cleanly.

visualizer.title: A live instance: fork, connect, crash, shut down
visualizer.caption: Connect clients until the slots run out, leave one idle in a transaction, then **kill -9** a backend and watch the postmaster restart everything. Try the three shutdown modes.

playground.setup:
CREATE TABLE accounts (id int PRIMARY KEY, balance numeric NOT NULL);
INSERT INTO accounts SELECT g, 100 FROM generate_series(1, 1000) g;

presets.label: My backend in pg_stat_activity
presets.sql:
SELECT pid, backend_type, datname, usename, application_name, state, backend_start
FROM pg_stat_activity;
presets.note: This sandbox runs the whole server inside one process, so you see a single **standalone backend**. A normal server lists one row per client backend and per auxiliary process here.

presets.label: Label your session, then find slow ones
presets.note: The second query is the long-running query finder: every non-idle backend, oldest first. Set `application_name` in every service so its rows say which pod they belong to. Here the only active backend is this one, running the finder itself.

presets.label: Every backend type
presets.sql: SELECT DISTINCT backend_type FROM pg_stat_io ORDER BY 1;
presets.note: `pg_stat_io` keeps a row for each kind of server process: client backends, background writer, checkpointer, walwriter, autovacuum, the PG18 **io worker**, and more.

presets.label: Idle in transaction
presets.note: Between statements the session is **idle in transaction**: it holds an xid and a `RowExclusiveLock` on `accounts` until COMMIT. Any other session that wants this row waits for it.

presets.label: What a backend costs
presets.note: Each backend owns private memory contexts (catalog caches, plans, sort space). Multiply by the connection count to see why thousands of connections hurt.

presets.label: Which settings need a restart
presets.sql:
SELECT name, setting, context
FROM pg_settings
WHERE name IN ('max_connections', 'superuser_reserved_connections', 'reserved_connections',
               'authentication_timeout', 'idle_in_transaction_session_timeout', 'restart_after_crash', 'statement_timeout')
ORDER BY context, name;
presets.note: `postmaster` context = set at server start only. `max_connections` sizes shared memory, so changing it needs a restart. `user` settings can be changed per session.

presets.label: Cancel vs terminate
presets.note: Cancel stops the current query and keeps the session. Terminate sends SIGTERM and ends the backend. Without a timeout, `true` only means the signal was **sent**; with `timeout` (ms) it means the process actually exited.

presets.label: Wait events catalog
presets.note: An idle backend waits on `ClientRead`: it is blocked reading the socket for the next Query message. Each auxiliary process has its own main-loop wait event.

production.title: Too many clients during an autoscaling event
production.context: An API runs on 40 pods. Each pod keeps a client-side pool of 20 connections, so the fleet can open 800 backends against a server with `max_connections = 500`.
production.problem: During a traffic spike the autoscaler added pods. New pods failed health checks with `FATAL: sorry, too many clients already`. Most existing backends were **idle**, and a few were **idle in transaction**, holding locks.
production.solution: Count backends by state and owner first. Then cap the pool per pod, put a transaction-mode pooler in front of the database, and add server-side timeouts so abandoned transactions cannot pin locks and slots.
production.outcome: With 40 pods sharing a pooler of, say, 120 server connections, the fleet can no longer exceed `max_connections`; abandoned transactions end after 30 seconds, and the superuser reserve stays free for on-call access during incidents.

pitfalls.title: Raising max_connections into the thousands
pitfalls.symptom: After setting `max_connections = 5000` the server needs more shared memory and semaphores, and throughput falls as connections rise.
pitfalls.cause: Every allowed connection reserves shared-memory slots and a semaphore at startup, and every live backend is a full OS process with private caches. Thousands of mostly idle processes cost RAM and lock contention.
pitfalls.fix: Keep `max_connections` in the low hundreds and use a connection pooler. Size pools to the number of CPU cores and disks, not to the number of app threads.

pitfalls.title: Sessions left idle in transaction
pitfalls.symptom: `pg_stat_activity` shows backends `idle in transaction` for minutes. Other writes queue behind their locks and VACUUM cannot clean up.
pitfalls.cause: The client ran `BEGIN` and some statements, then stopped without `COMMIT`: a request handler crashed, or someone left a psql session open.
pitfalls.fix: Set `idle_in_transaction_session_timeout` per role, and find offenders by `xact_start` age.
pitfalls.sql:
SELECT pid, usename, application_name, now() - xact_start AS open_for, query
FROM pg_stat_activity WHERE state = 'idle in transaction' ORDER BY xact_start;

pitfalls.title: Using kill -9 on a backend
pitfalls.symptom: Killing one stuck backend disconnects **every** client, and the server runs crash recovery.
pitfalls.cause: A process that dies without cleanup may have left shared memory inconsistent. The postmaster therefore terminates all other backends, reinitializes shared memory and replays WAL (`restart_after_crash`).
pitfalls.fix: Use `pg_cancel_backend(pid)` to stop the current query, or `pg_terminate_backend(pid)` to end the session cleanly. Never SIGKILL the postmaster itself.

pitfalls.title: pg_terminate_backend returned true, but the session is still there
pitfalls.symptom: A cleanup script terminates the sessions blocking a migration, gets `true` for each, runs `ALTER TABLE` at once, and still waits on a lock.
pitfalls.cause: A common reading is that `true` means the backend is gone. Without a timeout it only means the SIGTERM was delivered; the backend exits at its next interrupt check and must roll back its transaction first.
pitfalls.fix: Pass a timeout so the call waits for the exit, and check the result before the DDL.

pitfalls.title: The Linux OOM killer picks PostgreSQL
pitfalls.symptom: The kernel log shows `Out of Memory: Killed process … (postgres)`, followed by a crash restart or a dead server.
pitfalls.cause: Memory overcommit lets the kernel kill a backend, which triggers a restart, or the postmaster itself, which stops the whole instance.
pitfalls.fix: Lower `work_mem` and `max_connections`, consider `vm.overcommit_memory = 2`, and protect the postmaster with `oom_score_adj = -1000` while `PG_OOM_ADJUST_FILE` resets children to 0.

pointers: **Postmaster** = first process. It forks a **backend** per connection and supervises the **auxiliary** processes.
`max_connections` (default 100) is fixed at start; `superuser_reserved_connections` (3) keeps slots for emergencies.
`pg_stat_activity.state`: **active**, **idle**, **idle in transaction**. The last one holds locks and blocks cleanup.
One backend crash makes the postmaster **terminate everyone and run crash recovery**.
Shutdown modes: **smart** (SIGTERM, wait), **fast** (SIGINT, abort transactions), **immediate** (SIGQUIT, recovery on next start). `pg_ctl restart` = fast stop + start.

lessons.title: Shared memory: buffers, WAL buffers and the commit log
tldr: At startup the postmaster allocates one **shared memory** segment that every process maps: the **shared buffer pool** of 8 kB pages, the **WAL buffers**, the **commit-log (pg_xact) cache** and the lock tables.
Disk is slow and backends are separate processes, so they share one cache of hot pages and pick victims with a cheap **clock-sweep** algorithm instead of each keeping its own copy.

visualizer.title: The buffer pool and its clock sweep
visualizer.caption: Read and update hot pages, then run a large sequential scan with the ring **off** and watch the hot set get evicted. Reset, scan with the ring **on**, and compare. Click a buffer to pin it.

presets.label: Buffer pool summary
presets.note: 16384 buffers of 8 kB = 128 MB. Usage counts run from 0 to **5**. Most buffers are still unused in a fresh instance.

presets.label: First scan: reads from disk
presets.note: The setup evicted `orders`, so all 192 pages are `shared read`. Each page now sits in a buffer with `usagecount = 1`.

presets.label: Second scan: all hits
presets.note: Now `shared hit=192`. Every access bumped `usagecount` by one: this is the credit the clock sweep spends before evicting a page.

presets.label: UPDATE makes pages dirty
presets.note: Changed pages are **dirty** in memory. The table file on disk is not touched yet; the WAL record is what makes the change durable.

presets.label: CHECKPOINT cleans them
presets.note: The checkpoint wrote every dirty buffer. The pages stay cached, now clean, so the next read is still a hit.

presets.label: Evict and look again
presets.note: Eviction drops the pages from shared buffers (a developer tool, new in 18). The next scan reads them back: `shared read` again.

presets.label: Hit ratio, computed honestly
presets.note: The counters are bigint, so `hit / (hit + read)` truncates to **0**; multiply by `100.0` first. `nullif` avoids a division by zero on a table nobody has read yet. `pg_stat_io` shows the same ratio per process type and context.

presets.label: Shared memory map
presets.note: `Buffer Blocks` is the page pool. `XLOG Ctl` holds the 4 MB of WAL buffers (auto = 1/32 of shared_buffers). `transaction` is the pg_xact commit-log cache.

production.title: A nightly report that flushed the cache
production.context: An order service keeps a few GB of hot pages (recent orders, customers) in a 16 GB `shared_buffers`. A nightly job reads a 200 GB archive table.
production.problem: Right after the job started, p95 latency of the order API tripled and `pg_stat_io` showed reads jumping for client backends. The report walked the archive through an **index scan**. Only large sequential scans get the bulk-read ring, so every archive page entered the pool like a normal page and the clock sweep pushed the hot set out.
production.solution: Measure what is cached, make the report scan sequentially (or move it to a replica), and warm the hot set back after the job with `pg_prewarm`, which **loads** a relation into shared buffers. It is a common mistake to call it to clear the cache; eviction is `pg_buffercache_evict_relation()`.
production.outcome: With the report on a replica, the hot set stayed resident on the primary through the night, client-backend reads in `pg_stat_io` stayed flat, and the API latency spike disappeared.

pitfalls.title: Giving shared_buffers most of the RAM
pitfalls.symptom: With `shared_buffers` at 75% of RAM the server swaps, or the OOM killer strikes when many sorts run at once.
pitfalls.cause: PostgreSQL also relies on the OS page cache, and every backend needs private memory for sorts and hashes. Pages cached twice waste RAM.
pitfalls.fix: Start at **25% of RAM** on a dedicated server; going above 40% rarely helps. Raise `max_wal_size` with it, and enable huge pages for large pools.

pitfalls.title: work_mem multiplied by everything
pitfalls.symptom: Setting `work_mem = 1GB` globally looks fine in testing, then production runs out of memory.
pitfalls.cause: `work_mem` is per sort or hash **node**, per backend and per parallel worker. Hash nodes may use `work_mem × hash_mem_multiplier` (2.0). Ten nodes × 100 sessions is 1,000 allocations.
pitfalls.fix: Keep the global value modest and raise it for the one query that needs it: `SET LOCAL work_mem = '256MB'` inside its transaction.

pitfalls.title: Trusting one global hit ratio
pitfalls.symptom: A dashboard shows a 99% buffer hit ratio while one important query is slow from disk reads.
pitfalls.cause: A global ratio averages many cheap hits on hot pages with the few expensive misses that matter. A hit in shared buffers can also be a miss that the OS cache served cheaply, so the ratio does not equal disk I/O.
pitfalls.fix: Look per query with `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)`, per backend type in `pg_stat_io`, and per statement in `pg_stat_statements` (`shared_blks_read`).

pitfalls.title: A hit-ratio query that lies
pitfalls.symptom: A monitoring query reports a hit ratio of exactly 0 (or 100) for every table, or fails with `division by zero` right after a restart or a stats reset.
pitfalls.cause: `pg_statio_*` and `pg_stat_io` counters are bigint, so `hits * 100 / (hits + reads)` is integer division and truncates. A fresh instance has `hits + reads = 0`. Home-grown formulas such as `(hit - read) / hit` are not a ratio at all.
pitfalls.fix: Use `round(100.0 * hit / nullif(hit + read, 0), 1)`, and read it per table or per backend type rather than as one global number.

pitfalls.title: Transparent huge pages
pitfalls.symptom: Random latency stalls on Linux with a large `shared_buffers`.
pitfalls.cause: Transparent huge pages (THP) compaction can stall processes. PostgreSQL only benefits from **explicit** huge pages.
pitfalls.fix: Disable THP, reserve huge pages with `vm.nr_hugepages` from `postgres -C shared_memory_size_in_huge_pages`, and set `huge_pages = on` to fail fast if they are missing.

pointers: `shared_buffers` (default 128MB) is a pool of 8 kB pages shared by all processes. Start at **25% of RAM**.
Each buffer has a descriptor: **tag, refcount (pins), usage_count 0–5, dirty flag**.
**Clock sweep**: skip pinned buffers, decrement usage counts, evict the first unpinned buffer at 0. A dirty victim must be written first.
Large scans, VACUUM and COPY use a small **buffer access strategy ring** so they cannot flush the cache.
Also in shared memory: **WAL buffers** (1/32 of shared_buffers, max 16 MB) and **SLRU caches** such as `pg_xact`. `work_mem` is per backend, not shared.

lessons.title: The background crew
tldr: Next to the client backends, an instance runs a crew of **background processes**: the walwriter, background writer, checkpointer, autovacuum, archiver, logger and, in PostgreSQL 18, **I/O workers**.
They move slow work off the query path, so a commit only waits for one WAL flush while dirty pages, cleanup, statistics and archiving happen later and in bulk.

visualizer.title: Follow one UPDATE through the whole crew
visualizer.caption: Step through an UPDATE from the first read to the archived WAL segment. Each step lights the process that acts and lists the settings and statistics views that belong to it.

presets.label: The crew and its settings
presets.sql:
SELECT name, setting, unit, context FROM pg_settings
WHERE name IN ('bgwriter_delay', 'bgwriter_lru_maxpages', 'bgwriter_lru_multiplier',
               'checkpoint_timeout', 'max_wal_size', 'checkpoint_completion_target',
               'wal_writer_delay', 'autovacuum_naptime', 'autovacuum_max_workers',
               'io_method', 'io_workers', 'archive_mode')
ORDER BY name;
presets.note: The defaults from the visualizer. This sandbox reports `io_method = sync` because the whole server runs in one process; a normal PostgreSQL 18 server defaults to `worker` with 3 `io_workers`.

presets.label: I/O by process type
presets.sql:
SELECT backend_type, object, context, reads, hits, writes, extends
FROM pg_stat_io
WHERE reads > 0 OR writes > 0 OR hits > 0 OR extends > 0
ORDER BY backend_type, object, context;
presets.note: `pg_stat_io` splits I/O by **process type**, object (relation, temp relation, wal) and context (normal, bulkread, bulkwrite, vacuum). Here one standalone backend does every job. The `wal` rows are new in 18.

presets.label: Who is doing I/O right now?
presets.note: `pg_stat_get_backend_io(pid)` (new in 18) gives one backend's own I/O, in operations and in bytes. `io_combine_limit` (16 × 8 kB) caps how many adjacent blocks one read may merge. `pg_aios` lists I/Os in flight; with `sync` it stays empty.

presets.label: Make work for the crew
presets.note: The first read still shows the old value: statistics lag until the backend flushes them. After the flush, 12,000 dead row versions are visible to autovacuum.

presets.label: Would autovacuum run?
presets.sql:
SELECT s.relname, s.n_dead_tup,
       current_setting('autovacuum_vacuum_threshold')::int
         + current_setting('autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor')::float8 * c.reltuples AS vacuum_threshold,
       s.n_dead_tup > current_setting('autovacuum_vacuum_threshold')::int
         + current_setting('autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor')::float8 * c.reltuples AS needs_vacuum
FROM pg_stat_user_tables s JOIN pg_class c ON c.oid = s.relid
WHERE s.relname = 'orders';
presets.note: Threshold = 50 + 0.2 × 50,000 = **10,050**. With 12,000 dead tuples the launcher would start a worker on its next wake-up.

presets.label: Run the checkpointer's job
presets.note: `CHECKPOINT` forces what the checkpointer does on its timer. The new **redo point** is where crash recovery would start.

presets.label: WAL written so far
presets.note: `wal_fpi` counts full-page images: the first change to a page after a checkpoint logs the whole page. `wal_buffers_full` > 0 would mean WAL buffers are too small.

presets.label: Vacuum by hand
presets.note: This is what an autovacuum worker does for you. Afterwards `n_dead_tup` is back to 0 and the freed space is reusable.

production.title: Checkpoint spikes every few minutes
production.context: A write-heavy ingestion service sees write latency jump every two to three minutes, even though `checkpoint_timeout` is the default 5 minutes.
production.problem: `pg_stat_checkpointer` shows `num_requested` far above `num_timed`: checkpoints are triggered by WAL volume, not time. With `max_wal_size = 1GB` the service fills the allowance in about two minutes, and every checkpoint also restarts full-page writes, so WAL grows even faster.
production.solution: Confirm the trigger, then give WAL more room so checkpoints become time-based and spread out. Keep `checkpoint_completion_target` at 0.9 and turn on `log_checkpoints` (on by default since 15) to verify.
production.outcome: Requested checkpoints dropped to near zero, checkpoints ran every 5 minutes, and WAL volume fell because fewer full-page images were written after each checkpoint.

pitfalls.title: Turning autovacuum off
pitfalls.symptom: Tables and indexes bloat, queries slow down, and eventually the server warns about transaction ID wraparound.
pitfalls.cause: Nothing else removes dead row versions or freezes old ones. Disabling autovacuum only postpones the work and makes it larger.
pitfalls.fix: Leave `autovacuum = on`. Tune busy tables with per-table settings such as `ALTER TABLE t SET (autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor = 0.02)`.

pitfalls.title: Backends doing the background writer's job
pitfalls.symptom: `pg_stat_io` shows large `writes` for `client backend` in context `normal`, and queries stall on I/O.
pitfalls.cause: When the clock sweep picks a dirty victim, the backend must write it itself. The bgwriter and checkpointer are not keeping up.
pitfalls.fix: Raise `bgwriter_lru_maxpages` and `bgwriter_lru_multiplier`, check checkpoint frequency, and size `shared_buffers` for the working set.
pitfalls.sql:
SELECT backend_type, writes, writebacks FROM pg_stat_io
WHERE object = 'relation' AND context = 'normal' AND writes > 0;

pitfalls.title: A failing archive_command fills the disk
pitfalls.symptom: `pg_wal` grows without limit and the server finally stops with a disk-full PANIC.
pitfalls.cause: A segment cannot be recycled until it is archived. If `archive_command` keeps failing, every segment since the failure is kept.
pitfalls.fix: Monitor `pg_stat_archiver.failed_count` and `last_failed_wal`, fix the command, and make sure it returns non-zero exit status only on real failure.

pitfalls.title: Expecting asynchronous I/O to speed up writes
pitfalls.symptom: After moving to 18 with `io_method = worker`, a write-heavy job is no faster, while a cold sequential scan on network storage is clearly faster.
pitfalls.cause: A common claim is that AIO makes all I/O asynchronous. In 18 backends queue **read** requests (sequential scans, bitmap heap scans, VACUUM); data and WAL writes take the usual paths. The gain is largest for cold reads from slow storage and small when pages are already cached.
pitfalls.fix: Measure reads, not commits: compare `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)` of a cold scan and `pg_stat_io` read times (`track_io_timing = on`). Tune `effective_io_concurrency` and `io_workers` for read-heavy workloads.

pitfalls.title: Expecting io_method to change on reload
pitfalls.symptom: `ALTER SYSTEM SET io_method = 'io_uring'` plus `pg_reload_conf()` changes nothing.
pitfalls.cause: `io_method` has context `postmaster`: the I/O subsystem is set up at server start. `pending_restart` shows the waiting value.
pitfalls.fix: Restart the server. Check `SELECT name, setting, pending_restart FROM pg_settings WHERE name = 'io_method'` afterwards.

pointers: Auxiliary processes: **checkpointer, background writer, walwriter, autovacuum launcher, archiver, logger, startup, walreceiver, walsummarizer**; plus PG18 **io workers**.
A COMMIT waits only for its **WAL flush**. Data pages are written later by the **bgwriter** and the **checkpointer**.
Checkpoints run every `checkpoint_timeout` (5min) or at `max_wal_size` (1GB), spread over `checkpoint_completion_target` (0.9).
Autovacuum: launcher every `autovacuum_naptime` (1min); VACUUM when dead tuples > **50 + 0.2 × reltuples**.
Watch them with `pg_stat_activity.backend_type`, `pg_stat_io`, `pg_stat_bgwriter`, `pg_stat_checkpointer`, `pg_stat_archiver`.

lessons.title: Databases, schemas, search_path and roles
tldr: A cluster holds isolated **databases**, each database holds **schemas** that act as namespaces, and **roles** are cluster-wide identities whose privileges and memberships decide what a session may touch.
These layers let many applications and teams share one server safely, with `search_path` choosing which schema an unqualified name means and `pg_hba.conf` deciding who may connect at all.

visualizer.title: Name resolution, authentication and membership
visualizer.caption: Resolve names as different roles and search paths, and create a temp table to shadow one. Switch modes to replay connection attempts against `pg_hba.conf`, and to walk the joe / admin / wheel / island membership chain.

presets.label: Databases, templates, per-database settings
presets.note: `CREATE DATABASE` is a file-level copy of `template1` unless told otherwise; `template0` stays pristine and refuses connections. `ALTER DATABASE … SET` stores a default that every **new** session in `shop` picks up. A connection cannot see into `shop` from here.

presets.label: search_path as alice
presets.note: `"$user"` expands to `alice`, which exists, so new tables land there. Since PostgreSQL 15, ordinary roles have **no CREATE on public**: SQLSTATE 42501.

presets.label: Same name, different table, then a temp table
presets.note: alice has no USAGE on `sales`, so it is **silently dropped** from her path and `orders` means `public.orders` (2 rows). bob inherits USAGE from `sales_team` and gets `sales.orders` (5 rows). The temp schema is searched first for relations, so `orders` then hits the empty temp table.

presets.label: The permission ladder: schema, table, sequence
presets.note: Each gate is checked in order: **USAGE** on the schema, then the table privilege. The identity insert works, but the `serial` table also needs **USAGE on its sequence** (42501). In `relacl`, `simon=ar/postgres` reads: simon may a(ppend = INSERT) and r(ead = SELECT), granted by postgres.

presets.label: Grants are snapshots; default privileges are not
presets.note: `ON ALL TABLES` grants on the tables that exist **now**; `customers` was missed. Default privileges apply to tables created later, but only by the role in `for_objects_created_by`. The predefined `pg_read_all_data` covers every table and schema at once.

presets.label: INHERIT vs SET (joe, admin, wheel, island)
presets.note: joe **inherits** admin and island but not wheel (admin→wheel has INHERIT FALSE). joe may **SET ROLE wheel** through the chain, but never island (SET FALSE). `session_user` stays joe while `current_user` changes.

presets.label: Drop a role that owns things
presets.note: The first DROP fails with **2BP01** and the DETAIL lists every dependency: privileges on the schema and table, and the owned table. Both cleanup commands only act on the **current database**, so in production repeat them in each database.

presets.label: Who may connect: pg_hba.conf
presets.note: This sandbox runs with a permissive `trust` file. In production this view is how you test edits before a reload. Schema ACLs: `=U/pg_database_owner` means PUBLIC has USAGE on `public`, but no `C`.

production.title: A read-only reporting role that stays read-only
production.context: An analytics team needs to query a shared production database. Today they log in as the application role, which can write everything.
production.problem: One mistaken `UPDATE` from a notebook changed live data. The application role also owns the tables, so per-table GRANTs drifted every time a migration created a new table.
production.solution: Create a NOLOGIN group with `pg_read_all_data`, give each analyst a LOGIN role that inherits it, pin their search_path, and route them through a dedicated `pg_hba.conf` line that requires SSL.
production.outcome: New tables are readable without any GRANT, writes fail with SQLSTATE 25006 (read-only transaction) or 42501, and the reload-time `pg_hba_file_rules` check showed the `+analysts` line matched before the catch-all reject.

pitfalls.title: CREATE on public in an upgraded database
pitfalls.symptom: Any role can create tables and functions in `public`, so one user can plant a function that captures another user's unqualified calls.
pitfalls.cause: Databases created before PostgreSQL 15 keep the old default: PUBLIC has CREATE on schema `public`. Upgrades do not change it.
pitfalls.fix: Revoke it, and give each application its own schema.
pitfalls.sql: REVOKE CREATE ON SCHEMA public FROM PUBLIC;

pitfalls.title: search_path in SECURITY DEFINER functions
pitfalls.symptom: A privileged function runs a different `lower()` or table than intended when called by an untrusted user.
pitfalls.cause: The function resolves unqualified names with the caller's `search_path`, which the caller controls. Any schema in that path with CREATE for others can shadow names.
pitfalls.fix: Pin the path on the function and schema-qualify names: `ALTER FUNCTION f() SET search_path = pg_catalog, app;`.

pitfalls.title: pg_hba.conf lines in the wrong order
pitfalls.symptom: A new `hostssl … scram-sha-256` line has no effect, or a broad line lets clients in without a password.
pitfalls.cause: Lines are tested top to bottom and the **first** match wins, with no fall-through on failure. A broad line above a narrow one hides it. A common belief is that hba edits need a server restart; a reload re-reads the file, and a restart just adds downtime.
pitfalls.fix: Put narrow, strong lines first and broad `reject` lines last. Check `pg_hba_file_rules.error`, then `SELECT pg_reload_conf()`.

pitfalls.title: New tables are invisible to the read-only role
pitfalls.symptom: Reporting worked for months, then every query on a table added by last week's migration fails with `permission denied for table …`.
pitfalls.cause: `GRANT SELECT ON ALL TABLES IN SCHEMA` is a one-time snapshot of the tables that exist when it runs. `ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES` covers future tables, but only those created by the role it names (by default, the role that ran it).
pitfalls.fix: Set default privileges **for the role that runs migrations**, or grant the predefined `pg_read_all_data`.
pitfalls.sql:
ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES FOR ROLE migrator IN SCHEMA app
  GRANT SELECT ON TABLES TO reporting;

pitfalls.title: Passwords that leak or use MD5
pitfalls.symptom: A plaintext password shows up in `~/.psql_history`, or in the server log after a failed statement; or PostgreSQL 18 prints a deprecation warning while a deploy script sets an MD5 password.
pitfalls.cause: `ALTER ROLE … PASSWORD '…'` ships the literal password in the SQL text. MD5 password authentication is deprecated and slated for removal; `password_encryption` defaults to `scram-sha-256`.
pitfalls.fix: Use psql `\password dana`, which hashes on the client and sends only the SCRAM verifier. Re-set old MD5 passwords so they are stored as SCRAM, and use `scram-sha-256` in `pg_hba.conf`.

pitfalls.title: DROP ROLE fails: role owns objects
pitfalls.symptom: `ERROR: role "dana" cannot be dropped because some objects depend on it`, with a DETAIL such as `privileges for schema accounting; owner of table …`.
pitfalls.cause: Roles are cluster-wide, but owned objects and grants live in each database. `REASSIGN OWNED` and `DROP OWNED` only see the database you are connected to.
pitfalls.fix: In **every** database, run `REASSIGN OWNED BY dana TO app_owner;` then `DROP OWNED BY dana;`. Then `DROP ROLE dana;`. A non-superuser needs CREATEROLE **and** ADMIN OPTION on the role to drop it.

pointers: Cluster → **databases** (isolated, one per connection) → **schemas** (namespaces) → objects. **Roles** are cluster-wide.
`CREATE DATABASE` is a file copy of **template1** (no other session may be connected to the source); use **template0** for a new encoding or locale.
`search_path` default `"$user", public`. `pg_temp` (relations only) and `pg_catalog` are searched implicitly first; schemas without USAGE are **silently skipped**.
Since 15, PUBLIC has **no CREATE on public**. Membership has **INHERIT**, **SET** and **ADMIN** options; LOGIN, SUPERUSER, CREATEDB, CREATEROLE are never inherited.

`pg_hba.conf`: **first matching line wins**, no fall-through, no match = rejected; a reload applies edits. Gates for a query: CONNECT on the database, **USAGE** on the schema, then the object privilege.

lessons.title: Modelling data: normalization and constraints
tldr: **Normalization** splits data into tables so that every fact is stored exactly once, keyed by what determines it, and **constraints** make PostgreSQL enforce that shape on every write.
Duplicated facts drift apart under concurrent updates, so a normalized schema with keys, foreign keys and checks turns whole classes of application bugs into immediate, well-defined errors.

visualizer.title: From a messy spreadsheet to 3NF, column by column
visualizer.caption: Step through the decomposition. Watch each column move to the table of the key it depends on, then see which constraints guard the result. Colours show functional dependencies.

presets.label: The 3NF schema and its constraint names
presets.sql:
SELECT conrelid::regclass AS table_name, conname, contype, pg_get_constraintdef(oid) AS definition
FROM pg_constraint
WHERE conrelid IN ('customers'::regclass, 'products'::regclass, 'orders'::regclass, 'order_items'::regclass)
ORDER BY 1, 3, 2;

SELECT indexrelid::regclass AS index_built_by_a_constraint, indrelid::regclass AS on_table
FROM pg_index
WHERE indrelid IN ('customers'::regclass, 'products'::regclass, 'orders'::regclass, 'order_items'::regclass);
presets.note: Unnamed constraints get predictable names: `<table>_pkey`, `<table>_<col>_key`, `<table>_<col>_check`, `<table>_<col>_fkey`, `<table>_<col>_not_null`. `contype`: p, u, f, c, and **n** (NOT NULL is a catalog row in 18). Only PRIMARY KEY and UNIQUE built an index; the foreign keys did not.

presets.label: Every constraint, fired once
presets.sql:
SELECT label, try(stmt) AS result FROM (VALUES
  ('NOT NULL',        $$INSERT INTO customers (email, name) VALUES ('x@ex.com', 'X')$$),
  ('UNIQUE',          $$INSERT INTO customers (email, name, city) VALUES ('ana@ex.com', 'Ana Two', 'Faro')$$),
  ('CHECK',           $$INSERT INTO order_items (order_id, sku, qty, unit_price) VALUES (1002, 'KB-01', 0, 45)$$),
  ('CHECK (regex)',   $$INSERT INTO products VALUES ('MS-7', 'Mouse', 19)$$),
  ('FOREIGN KEY',     $$INSERT INTO orders VALUES (1004, 99, '2026-03-06')$$),
  ('PRIMARY KEY',     $$INSERT INTO order_items (order_id, sku, qty, unit_price) VALUES (1001, 'KB-01', 1, 49)$$),
  ('IDENTITY ALWAYS', $$INSERT INTO customers (customer_id, email, name, city) VALUES (7, 'z@ex.com', 'Z', 'Goa')$$)
) AS t(label, stmt);
presets.note: Each failure has its own SQLSTATE: **23502** not-null, **23505** unique, **23514** check, **23503** foreign key, **428C9** writing an ALWAYS identity column. The text after `|` is the DETAIL line, which names the offending key or row.

presets.label: Foreign key actions: same data, one clause changed
presets.note: NO ACTION fails with **23503** and names the still-referenced key. SET NULL keeps John and Jane with `client_id` NULL; they now sit at the **end of the heap** (new ctids), because an update writes new row versions. CASCADE deletes David with his client, and the command tag still says `DELETE 1`. RESTRICT fails with **23001**.

presets.label: NULL is not a violation
presets.note: A CHECK passes when its expression is **NULL**, and UNIQUE treats NULLs as distinct by default. `NULLS NOT DISTINCT` makes a second NULL a duplicate.

presets.label: Identity BY DEFAULT and the duplicate-key trap
presets.note: BY DEFAULT accepts a manual id, but the sequence does not see it, so the next default 2 collides (**23505**). The failed `Ox` insert still consumed 3: sequence values are never rolled back. After `setval`, Blue gets 3.

presets.label: Deferred foreign key
presets.note: A deferred constraint is checked at **COMMIT**, so rows can arrive in any order within the transaction. Only UNIQUE, PRIMARY KEY, EXCLUDE and foreign keys can be deferrable.

presets.label: PG18: virtual columns and temporal keys
presets.note: `attgenerated = v`: **virtual**, the default in 18, recomputed on every read and stored nowhere, so it cannot be written or indexed (**0A000**). The temporal key accepts back-to-back periods (`[)` bounds) and rejects an overlap with **23P01**, enforced by a GiST index.

presets.label: Adding rules to live data: NOT VALID
presets.note: `NOT NULL … NOT VALID` guards new rows at once (**23502**) but skips the existing NULLs; VALIDATE fails until the backfill is done. Adding a NOT NULL column without a DEFAULT fails on a populated table. A **NOT ENFORCED** check is never verified at all.

production.title: Customer data that drifted across 4 million order rows
production.context: An e-commerce team stored `customer_email`, `customer_name` and `shipping_city` directly on every row of a wide `orders` table to "avoid joins".
production.problem: Customers who changed their email kept old addresses on older orders. A marketing export de-duplicated by email and found many more "customers" than accounts, and support could not tell which city was current.
production.solution: Normalize: create `customers` with a unique email, backfill it from the latest order per email, and add a `customer_id` column. Add its NOT NULL rule and its foreign key as `NOT VALID` first, so new orders are checked immediately while the old rows are backfilled in batches, then validate both. Index the new column yourself, because a foreign key never creates one.
production.outcome: Each customer fact now lives in one row, so an email change is one UPDATE. The export count matches the account count, the orders table lost three wide text columns, and no step held a long table lock.

pitfalls.title: Foreign keys without an index on the referencing side
pitfalls.symptom: Deleting one customer, or updating a product key, takes seconds and locks many rows.
pitfalls.cause: A common claim is that declaring a foreign key creates an index for it. It does not: PostgreSQL indexes only the **referenced** key (through its PRIMARY KEY or UNIQUE constraint). Each parent DELETE must scan the child table to check or cascade.
pitfalls.fix: Index foreign key columns that are not already the leading column of an index. Find candidates in the catalog.
pitfalls.sql:
SELECT c.conrelid::regclass AS child, a.attname AS fk_column
FROM pg_constraint c JOIN pg_attribute a ON a.attrelid = c.conrelid AND a.attnum = c.conkey[1]
WHERE c.contype = 'f'
  AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM pg_index i WHERE i.indrelid = c.conrelid AND i.indkey[0] = c.conkey[1]);

pitfalls.title: CHECK constraints that let NULL through
pitfalls.symptom: `CHECK (discount BETWEEN 0 AND 50)` is in place, yet reports find rows with no discount at all.
pitfalls.cause: A CHECK fails only when its expression is **false**. NULL makes it unknown, which passes.
pitfalls.fix: Add `NOT NULL` when a value is required, or write the intent explicitly: `CHECK (discount IS NOT NULL AND discount BETWEEN 0 AND 50)`.

pitfalls.title: UNIQUE on a nullable column
pitfalls.symptom: A unique `external_id` column holds many rows with NULL, and an import created duplicates for every record missing an id.
pitfalls.cause: UNIQUE treats NULLs as distinct by default, so any number of NULLs are allowed.
pitfalls.fix: Use `NOT NULL`, or declare `UNIQUE NULLS NOT DISTINCT` when at most one NULL is acceptable.

pitfalls.title: Duplicate key right after a data import
pitfalls.symptom: After loading rows with explicit ids, the application's next INSERT fails with `duplicate key value violates unique constraint "…_pkey"`, and the error repeats on every retry until it suddenly stops.
pitfalls.cause: An identity column `BY DEFAULT` (or a `serial`) accepts manual ids, but its sequence keeps counting from where it was. Each retry burns one value until the sequence passes the imported range.
pitfalls.fix: Move the sequence past the data after every import, or use `GENERATED ALWAYS` so manual ids need an explicit `OVERRIDING SYSTEM VALUE`.
pitfalls.sql: SELECT setval(pg_get_serial_sequence('color', 'color_id'), (SELECT max(color_id) FROM color));

pitfalls.title: SET NOT NULL on a big table blocks it
pitfalls.symptom: `ALTER TABLE … ALTER COLUMN email SET NOT NULL` on a large table freezes all reads and writes until it finishes, or fails at the end because a few NULLs remain.
pitfalls.cause: SET NOT NULL takes an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock and scans every row in one go. A common claim is that NOT NULL constraints are unnamed and invisible in `pg_constraint`; in 18 they are named catalog rows, which is what lets their validation happen later.
pitfalls.fix: Add `NOT NULL col NOT VALID` (instant, guards new rows), backfill in batches, then `VALIDATE CONSTRAINT`.

pitfalls.title: Treating NOT ENFORCED as a safety net
pitfalls.symptom: A `CHECK … NOT ENFORCED` exists, and bad rows still get in.
pitfalls.cause: NOT ENFORCED (new in 18, for CHECK and foreign keys) records the rule in the catalog but PostgreSQL never verifies it, on insert or later.
pitfalls.fix: Use it only for rules enforced elsewhere. For real protection, add the constraint `NOT VALID` and run `VALIDATE CONSTRAINT` once existing data is clean.

pointers: **1NF**: one value per cell. **2NF**: no column depends on part of a composite key. **3NF**: no non-key column depends on another non-key column.
Store each fact once. A historical price on an order line is a different fact from today's list price.
**PRIMARY KEY** = UNIQUE + NOT NULL. **UNIQUE** allows many NULLs unless `NULLS NOT DISTINCT`. **CHECK** passes on NULL.
Foreign keys: NO ACTION (default, deferrable), RESTRICT, CASCADE, SET NULL, SET DEFAULT. Index the referencing columns yourself.

PG18: generated columns default to **VIRTUAL** (computed on read, not indexable), keys can be temporal with **WITHOUT OVERLAPS**, NOT NULL can be added **NOT VALID**, CHECK and FK can be **NOT ENFORCED**.

lessons.title: Primitive types, alignment and padding
tldr: Every column type has a fixed on-disk width (`typlen`) or is variable-length, plus an **alignment** (`typalign`) that forces it to start at a multiple of 1, 2, 4 or 8 bytes.
Alignment lets the CPU read values in place, but it means **column order changes row size**: badly ordered columns leave padding holes in every row of the table.

visualizer.title: Column tetris: how order creates padding
visualizer.caption: Press **Pack columns**, drag columns around, add types or toggle NULLs, and watch padding appear and disappear. The byte map follows the same rules `pg_column_size` applies.

presets.label: typlen & typalign
presets.sql:
SELECT typname, typlen, typalign, typstorage
FROM pg_type
WHERE typname IN ('bool','int2','int4','int8','float4','float8','numeric','text',
                  'date','timestamp','timestamptz','interval','uuid','money')
ORDER BY typlen DESC, typname;
presets.note: `typlen = -1` means variable length (varlena). `typalign` is c/s/i/d = 1/2/4/8 bytes. `timestamp` and `timestamptz` are both 8 bytes: the zone is never stored. `uuid` is 16 bytes but only char-aligned.

presets.label: Size of single values
presets.sql:
SELECT pg_column_size(true) AS bool, pg_column_size(1::int2) AS int2,
       pg_column_size(1::int8) AS int8, pg_column_size(now()) AS timestamptz,
       pg_column_size('1 day'::interval) AS "interval",
       pg_column_size(0::numeric) AS num_0, pg_column_size(123.45::numeric) AS num_123_45,
       pg_column_size(123456789::numeric) AS num_9_digits,
       pg_column_size(repeat('x', 200)) AS text_200;
presets.note: Fixed types are exactly `typlen`. `numeric` is variable: 6, 10 and 12 bytes here, about 2 bytes per group of 4 decimal digits plus a small header. These are in-memory sizes; inside a row, short varlenas shrink to a 1-byte header.

presets.label: Same data, two orders
presets.note: Identical values: **67 bytes** in the bad order, **54 bytes** packed, exactly what the visualizer shows. MAXALIGN rounds them to 72 and 56, so (8192 − 24) / (72 + 4) = **107** rows fit per page against (8192 − 24) / (56 + 4) = **136**.

presets.label: Exact vs inexact
presets.sql:
SELECT 0.1::float8 + 0.2::float8 = 0.3::float8          AS float_equal,
       0.1::numeric + 0.2::numeric = 0.3::numeric       AS numeric_equal,
       (0.0001::float4 + 0.0001::float4 + 0.0001::float4)::text AS float4_drift,
       round(2.5::numeric) AS round_numeric, round(2.5::float8) AS round_float,
       12.5::numeric::money AS as_money, current_setting('lc_monetary') AS lc_monetary;

SELECT interval '1 month' = interval '30 days' AS equal_intervals,
       date '2024-01-31' + interval '1 month'  AS plus_1_month,
       date '2024-01-31' + interval '30 days'  AS plus_30_days;
presets.note: Binary floats drift: three float4 additions of 0.0001 give `0.00029999999`. `numeric` is exact and rounds ties away from zero. `money` formats with `lc_monetary`. An interval stores **months, days and microseconds separately**: they compare as equal (30-day months) but add differently.

presets.label: Casts: what works, what fails
presets.note: `pg_input_error_info` shows the error a cast would raise without aborting: out of range, bad syntax, `numeric(7,5)` overflowing at 100. A quoted literal is `unknown` until context picks a type, `9.99::int` **rounds** to 10, and the same `06/10/2001` is June or October depending on `DateStyle`.

presets.label: Fixed width, byte by byte
presets.note: The integer-to-`bytea` casts are new in PostgreSQL 18. Width depends on the **type**, not the value: 123 is 2, 4 or 8 bytes, negatives are two's complement. The cast prints most significant byte first; on disk (little-endian here) `id = 1` is stored as `0100000000000000`.

presets.label: Enums, domains, composites
presets.note: An **enum** is a 4-byte OID into `pg_enum`, sorted by `enumsortorder`, not alphabetically. A **domain** is its base type plus a CHECK, so it costs the same 4 bytes as `date`. A **composite** is a varlena with its own tuple header inside (41 bytes here).

presets.label: Generated: STORED vs VIRTUAL
presets.note: PostgreSQL 18 adds **VIRTUAL** generated columns, and makes them the default. The STORED `total` occupies 8 bytes in every row (48 B). The VIRTUAL one is only a NULL bit (`t_bits` 1110…), so the row is 40 B, and it is recomputed on every read.

production.title: Reordering a 200 M-row metrics table before launch
production.context: An IoT platform designs `readings(is_valid bool, device_id int8, sensor smallint, ts timestamptz, value float8, seq int4, flags bool)` and expects 200 million rows.
production.problem: Columns were listed in the order the team thought of them. Each `bool` or `smallint` placed before an 8-byte column forces up to 7 padding bytes, so a row with 32 bytes of real data occupies **72 bytes** on the page.
production.solution: Order columns by alignment: 8-byte types first, then 4, 2 and 1-byte types, then variable-length ones. Check the result with `pg_column_size` on a sample row before the table holds data, because changing column order later means rewriting the table.
production.outcome: Each row drops from 72 to 56 bytes (plus its 4-byte line pointer), which is 76 → 60 bytes per row: **21% less heap**, about 15.2 GB → 12.0 GB at 200 M rows. More rows per page also means fewer pages per sequential scan and a larger share of the table in cache.

pitfalls.title: Using float for money
pitfalls.symptom: Totals are off by a cent, and `WHERE amount = 0.3` misses rows that print as 0.3.
pitfalls.cause: `real` and `double precision` are binary IEEE 754 types: most decimal fractions have no exact representation, and comparisons for equality are unreliable.
pitfalls.fix: Use `numeric` (exact) or integer cents in `bigint`, and store the ISO currency code in its own column. Size the precision generously: `numeric(7,5)` cannot hold 100.00. Avoid the `money` type: it has no currency, and its output depends on `lc_monetary`, so dumps can fail to load under another locale.
pitfalls.sql:
SELECT 0.1::float8 + 0.2::float8 = 0.3::float8;          -- false
SELECT pg_input_is_valid('100', 'numeric(7,5)');             -- false: overflow

pitfalls.title: char(n) for codes and names
pitfalls.symptom: Values come back with trailing spaces, and `char(n)` columns compare in surprising ways with `text`.
pitfalls.cause: `character(n)` is blank-padded to n characters and stored that way. It is never faster than `text` or `varchar` and usually the slowest of the three.
pitfalls.fix: Use `text`, or `varchar(n)` when you want a length check. Add a `CHECK (length(code) = 3)` when the length must be exact.

pitfalls.title: Expecting reordering to always save space
pitfalls.symptom: Columns were reordered with a table rewrite, and the table size did not change.
pitfalls.cause: Every row is padded to a multiple of **MAXALIGN** (8 bytes) on the page. If the padding saved is smaller than that rounding, the row still occupies the same slot.
pitfalls.fix: Compute both orders with `pg_column_size(ROW(...))` and round up to 8 before paying for a rewrite. Reordering pays off when it removes 8 or more bytes per row.

pitfalls.title: Choosing int4 keys for a fast-growing table
pitfalls.symptom: Inserts start failing with `integer out of range` (or `nextval: reached maximum value of sequence`) years after launch.
pitfalls.cause: `integer` stops at 2,147,483,647. PostgreSQL raises an error instead of wrapping around.
pitfalls.fix: Use `bigint` for surrogate keys of tables that can grow large. The 4 bytes `int4` saves are often eaten by alignment padding anyway (an `int4` before an 8-byte column is followed by 4 padding bytes), and they are small compared with a table rewrite under pressure.

pitfalls.title: timestamp without time zone for real instants
pitfalls.symptom: Event times shift by hours when a server, client or session moves to another `TimeZone`, or two regions disagree on when something happened.
pitfalls.cause: `timestamp` stores a wall-clock reading with no zone, and silently ignores an offset in the input. `timestamptz` stores a UTC instant (also 8 bytes, no zone stored) and converts on input and output using `TimeZone`. A `timestamp DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP` column also drops the zone of the value it receives.
pitfalls.fix: Use `timestamptz` for anything that happened at an instant. Render in the user's zone with `AT TIME ZONE`, and keep plain `timestamp` for wall-clock values such as "opening hour 09:00".

pitfalls.title: Integer and numeric arithmetic in generated columns
pitfalls.symptom: A calendar table built with `(EXTRACT(month FROM d) - 1) / 3 + 1` puts March in quarter 2 and December in quarter 5.
pitfalls.cause: `EXTRACT` returns `numeric` (since PostgreSQL 14), so the division is exact: March gives 1.67, which an `int` column rounds to 2. A common claim is that EXTRACT returns double precision, or that `/` always truncates. Integer `/` integer truncates, but numeric does not.
pitfalls.fix: Use `EXTRACT(quarter FROM d)`, or cast before dividing: `(EXTRACT(month FROM d)::int - 1) / 3 + 1`. Check `pg_typeof()` of any expression feeding an integer column.

pointers: Fixed widths: **bool 1, int2 2, int4/date/float4 4, int8/float8/timestamptz 8, uuid/interval 16** bytes.
`typalign` c/s/i/d forces a start offset that is a multiple of **1/2/4/8**. Short varlenas (under 127 bytes) are not aligned.
Rows start with a 23-byte header padded to `t_hoff` = 24, and the whole row is padded to **8 bytes** on the page, plus a 4-byte line pointer.
Order columns **8-byte first, then 4, 2, 1, then variable-length** to remove padding; verify with `pg_column_size(ROW(...))`.
Use **numeric** for exact decimals, **float** for measurements, **bigint** for keys that can grow, and **timestamptz** for instants. VIRTUAL generated columns cost no row bytes; STORED ones do.

lessons.title: Arrays
tldr: A PostgreSQL array is one **varlena value** holding a small header (dimensions, lower bounds, element type, optional null bitmap) followed by the aligned elements.
Arrays let you keep a short list inside a row and search it with **GIN**-indexable operators like `@>` and `&&`, without a separate join table.

visualizer.title: An array, byte by byte, and a GIN lookup
visualizer.caption: In **Bytes on disk**, step through five arrays and click each field to see its little-endian bytes. Switch to **GIN lookup** to see how `@>`, `&&` and `= ANY` use, or fail to use, the index.

presets.label: Array sizes
presets.sql:
SELECT pg_column_size('{1,2,3}'::int4[])        AS three_ints,
       pg_column_size('{1,NULL,3}'::int4[])     AS with_null,
       pg_column_size('{{1,2},{3,4}}'::int4[])  AS two_d,
       pg_column_size('{}'::int4[])             AS empty,
       pg_column_size('{1,2,3}'::int8[])        AS three_bigints;
presets.note: The 16-byte header plus 8 bytes per dimension, then the data: 36, 40, 48, 16 and 48 bytes, the numbers in the visualizer.

presets.label: Dimensions & bounds
presets.sql:
SELECT array_dims('{{1,2},{3,4}}'::int[])   AS dims,
       cardinality('{{1,2},{3,4}}'::int[])  AS elements,
       ('{7,8,9}'::int[])[0]                AS index_0_is_null,
       ('[0:2]={7,8,9}'::int[])[1]          AS custom_lower_bound,
       ARRAY[1, 2] || 3                     AS appended,
       array_append(ARRAY[1, 2], NULL)      AS append_null;
presets.note: Arrays are **1-based** and out-of-range reads return NULL instead of an error. A custom lower bound is stored in the header.

presets.label: Operators
presets.sql:
SELECT '{1,2,3}'::int[] @> '{3,1}'  AS contains,
       '{1,2}'::int[] <@ '{1,2,3}'   AS contained,
       '{1,2}'::int[] && '{2,9}'     AS overlaps,
       2 = ANY ('{1,2,3}'::int[])    AS any_match;
presets.note: `@>` ignores order and duplicates. `&&` is true when any element is shared.

presets.label: GIN: @> vs = ANY
presets.sql:
EXPLAIN (COSTS OFF) SELECT count(*) FROM posts WHERE tags @> '{tag7}';

EXPLAIN (COSTS OFF) SELECT count(*) FROM posts WHERE 'tag7' = ANY (tags);
presets.note: The containment query uses a **Bitmap Index Scan** on the GIN index. The `= ANY` form asks for the same rows but can only run as a **Seq Scan**.

presets.label: unnest & array_agg
presets.note: `unnest` turns an array into rows; `WITH ORDINALITY` adds each element's position. `array_agg` folds rows back into an array.

presets.label: Strings to arrays: spot the bug
presets.sql:
SELECT station, cardinality(string_to_array(temps, ',')) AS readings,
       pg_typeof(string_to_array(temps, ',')) AS type
FROM weather_data;

-- hottest and coldest reading per station, first attempt
SELECT station, max(t) AS max_temp, min(t) AS min_temp
FROM weather_data, unnest(string_to_array(temps, ',')) AS t
GROUP BY station ORDER BY station;

-- fixed: cast the array before aggregating
SELECT station, max(t) AS max_temp, min(t) AS min_temp
FROM weather_data, unnest(string_to_array(temps, ',')::int[]) AS t
GROUP BY station ORDER BY station;
presets.note: The first result looks plausible and is wrong: `string_to_array` returns `text[]`, so `max` compares strings and `'9'` beats `'16'`. Station North reports a minimum of -1 instead of **-16**. South happens to be right because all its readings have two digits. Casting to `int[]` fixes the rest.

presets.label: Sort, reverse, compare
presets.note: `array_sort` and `array_reverse` are new in PostgreSQL 18; `array_reverse` flips only the first dimension. Arrays compare **element by element**, left to right, like strings: `{1,3} < {2,1}`, so `min` and `max` pick whole arrays by their first element.

presets.label: The normalized alternative
presets.note: Both models find the same 266 posts. The array needs one GIN lookup; the join table needs `GROUP BY … HAVING count = 2` (one scan, better than one self-join per tag). The join table is larger here but gives foreign keys, per-tag columns and cheap single-tag updates.

production.title: Tag filtering on a content platform
production.context: A publishing team stores article tags as `text[]` and filters a listing page with `WHERE $1 = ANY (tags)`. The table holds 5 M articles.
production.problem: The team added a GIN index on `tags`, but the listing query still did a sequential scan and took seconds. `= ANY` is not an operator in the GIN `array_ops` class, so the index was never considered.
production.solution: Rewrite the predicate as containment, which the GIN index supports, and check the plan.
production.outcome: The plan switched from a Seq Scan to a Bitmap Index Scan, which the playground reproduces on 20k rows. The cost of a GIN lookup grows with the number of matching rows, not with table size, so rare tags become near-instant.

pitfalls.title: Writing = ANY against a GIN index
pitfalls.symptom: A GIN index on an array column exists, but `EXPLAIN` shows a Seq Scan.
pitfalls.cause: GIN `array_ops` supports `@>`, `<@`, `&&` and `=`. `value = ANY (col)` is a scalar comparison and cannot use it.
pitfalls.fix: Write `col @> ARRAY[value]` for "contains this element", or `col && ARRAY[a, b]` for "contains any of".
pitfalls.sql: EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM posts WHERE tags @> '{tag7}';

pitfalls.title: Updating one element rewrites the whole array
pitfalls.symptom: Appending to a large array in a hot row causes heavy WAL volume, table bloat and lock waits.
pitfalls.cause: An array is a single value. Any change writes a new row version containing the whole array (and new TOAST chunks if it is large).
pitfalls.fix: Keep arrays short and mostly read-only. Move growing lists such as event logs or followers into a child table.

pitfalls.title: Concatenating NULL behaves differently from array_append
pitfalls.symptom: `tags || NULL` silently leaves the array unchanged, while `array_append(tags, NULL)` adds a NULL element.
pitfalls.cause: An untyped NULL next to `||` resolves to a NULL array, and concatenating a NULL array is a no-op.
pitfalls.fix: Use `array_append` / `array_prepend` when adding single elements, and add `CHECK (array_position(tags, NULL) IS NULL)` if NULL elements are not allowed.

pitfalls.title: Treating arrays as sets
pitfalls.symptom: Duplicates accumulate (`{a,a,b}`), and uniqueness or referential checks are written by hand in triggers.
pitfalls.cause: Arrays are ordered lists. Searching an array for specific elements is often a sign that the list belongs in a separate table.
pitfalls.fix: Use a join table when you need foreign keys, per-element data or uniqueness. Keep arrays for small ordered values such as tags or coordinates.

pitfalls.title: Aggregating split strings as text
pitfalls.symptom: A report built from comma-separated values says the hottest reading was 9 when the data contains 16, and the coldest was -1 instead of -16.
pitfalls.cause: `string_to_array` and `unnest` return `text`. `max`, `min` and `ORDER BY` then compare strings character by character, so `'9'` > `'16'`. Nothing errors: the result just looks plausible.
pitfalls.fix: Cast at the source: `string_to_array(col, ',')::int[]` or `unnest(...)::int`. Better, store numbers as `int[]` (or rows) so the type is enforced on write.
pitfalls.sql:
SELECT max(t) FROM unnest(string_to_array('2,9,16', ',')) AS t;         -- '9'
SELECT max(t) FROM unnest(string_to_array('2,9,16', ',')::int[]) AS t;  -- 16

pointers: Header: **vl_len, ndim, dataoffset, elemtype** (16 bytes), then 8 bytes per dimension, then an optional null bitmap and the aligned elements.
`dataoffset = 0` means no NULLs. NULL elements cost **one bit**, no data bytes.
Arrays are **1-based**, out-of-range reads return NULL, and declared sizes like `int[3]` are not enforced.
GIN `array_ops` indexes `@>`, `<@`, `&&` and `=`. Rewrite `x = ANY(col)` as `col @> ARRAY[x]`.
Any change rewrites the whole array, so keep growing lists in a child table.

lessons.title: JSON vs JSONB
tldr: `json` stores the exact input text, while `jsonb` parses it once into a **binary tree** that drops whitespace, sorts keys and keeps only the last duplicate key.
Paying that parsing cost on write makes every later read fast and lets **GIN indexes** answer containment and key-existence queries, which makes `jsonb` the right default for most applications.

visualizer.title: One document, two storage formats
visualizer.caption: Pick a sample document and step through what `jsonb` does to it: parse, de-duplicate, sort and store. The last two steps show which items each GIN operator class extracts.

presets.label: Normalization & size
presets.sql:
SELECT '{"user": "ana", "plan": "pro", "user": "ana2"}'::json::text  AS as_json,
       '{"user": "ana", "plan": "pro", "user": "ana2"}'::jsonb::text AS as_jsonb,
       '{"color": "white", "size": ["S", "M", "L"]}'::jsonb::text   AS shorter_key_first,
       '{"reading": 1.230e-5}'::jsonb::text                         AS number_as_numeric;

SELECT round(avg(pg_column_size(raw))) AS avg_json_bytes,
       round(avg(pg_column_size(doc))) AS avg_jsonb_bytes
FROM events;
presets.note: json keeps both `user` keys and the spacing. jsonb keeps the last `user`, puts `size` before `color` (shorter keys first) and prints numbers as `numeric`. For these small documents jsonb is about 40% **larger** (96 vs 134 bytes).

presets.label: -> vs ->>: the quotes tell the type
presets.sql:
SELECT (doc -> 'type')::text AS arrow, pg_typeof(doc -> 'type')  AS arrow_type,
       doc ->> 'type' AS arrow2, pg_typeof(doc ->> 'type') AS arrow2_type,
       (doc -> 'tags' -> 0)::text AS first_tag, doc -> 'tags' ->> -1 AS last_tag,
       doc -> 'tags' -> 5 IS NULL AS past_end_is_null
FROM events WHERE id = 100;

SELECT j -> 'missing' IS NULL       AS missing_key_is_sql_null,
       j -> 'gone' IS NULL          AS json_null_is_sql_null,
       jsonb_typeof(j -> 'gone')    AS json_null_type,
       j ->> 'gone' IS NULL         AS as_text_it_is_null
FROM (SELECT '{"gone": null}'::jsonb AS j) s;
presets.note: `->` returns **jsonb** (`"click"`, with quotes), `->>` returns **text** (`click`). JSON arrays are **0-based** and `-1` counts from the end, unlike SQL arrays. A missing key is SQL NULL, but a JSON `null` is a real jsonb value until `->>` turns it into SQL NULL.

presets.label: Operators
presets.sql:
SELECT doc -> 'user' ->> 'plan'     AS plan_text,
       doc #>> '{user,id}'          AS user_id_text,
       doc ? 'user'                 AS top_level_key,
       doc ? 'plan'                 AS nested_key,
       doc -> 'user' ? 'plan'       AS navigate_first,
       doc @> '{"type": "click"}'   AS is_click,
       ('{"a": {"x": 1, "y": 2}}'::jsonb || '{"a": {"z": 3}}')::text AS shallow_merge
FROM events WHERE id = 1;
presets.note: `?` only sees **top-level** keys: `plan` lives under `user`, so navigate first. `@>` tests containment. `||` is a shallow merge: the right-hand `a` replaces the whole left-hand object.

presets.label: Which queries use GIN?
presets.note: `@>` and `?` use the GIN index. `doc ->> 'type' = …` applies an operator to an *expression*, so it cannot use an index on `doc`.

presets.label: Text is not a number
presets.note: `->>` yields text, so `> '50'` compares strings and `'9.00'` wins: 7,560 rows instead of **12,980**. Cast first, or compare jsonb to jsonb. Comparing `->> 'type'` to text is fine, and a **B-tree expression index** on exactly that expression turns it into an index scan.

presets.label: jsonb_ops vs jsonb_path_ops
presets.note: The path-hash index is smaller, and the planner picks it for `@>`. `?` still needs `events_doc_ops`.

presets.label: jsonb_set: new row, and the NULL trap
presets.note: Changing one key wrote a **whole new row version** at a new ctid. And `jsonb_set(…, NULL)` returns SQL NULL for the entire document: in an UPDATE it wipes the column. `jsonb_set_lax` sets a JSON null or deletes the key instead.

presets.label: jsonpath & JSON_TABLE
presets.sql:
SELECT jsonb_path_query_array(doc, 'lax $.tags[*] ? (@ starts with "t1")')  AS lax_filter,
       jsonb_path_query_array(doc, 'lax $.user.plan[0]')                  AS lax_wraps_scalar,
       jsonb_path_query_array(doc, 'strict $.user.plan[0]', '{}', true)   AS strict_silent
FROM events WHERE id = 12;

SELECT jt.*
FROM events,
     JSON_TABLE(doc, '$' COLUMNS (
        event_type text    PATH '$.type',
        plan       text    PATH '$.user.plan',
        amount     numeric PATH '$.amount',
        NESTED PATH '$.tags[*]' COLUMNS (tag text PATH '$'))) AS jt
WHERE id BETWEEN 1 AND 3;
presets.note: Lax mode (the default) treats a scalar as a one-element array, so `plan[0]` works; strict mode raises an error there, which `silent => true` turns into an empty result. JSON_TABLE turns documents into rows, one per `NESTED PATH` element.

production.title: Making an event-attribute filter indexable
production.context: An analytics product stores event properties in a `jsonb` column and filters dashboards with `WHERE props ->> 'plan' = $1`, on a 40 M-row table.
production.problem: A GIN index on `props` had been created, yet every dashboard query was a sequential scan. The `->>` comparison is not one of the GIN operators: the index only helps `@>`, `?`, `?|`, `?&`, `@?` and `@@` applied to the column itself.
production.solution: Rewrite equality filters as containment so the GIN index is used. For one hot attribute that is sorted or range-filtered, add a B-tree expression index instead.
production.outcome: The playground shows the change on 20k rows: Seq Scan before, Bitmap Index Scan on the GIN index after. In the playground the path-ops index is also about 19% smaller than jsonb_ops (792 kB vs 976 kB).

pitfalls.title: Expecting a GIN index to serve ->> comparisons
pitfalls.symptom: `EXPLAIN` shows a Seq Scan for `WHERE doc ->> 'type' = 'purchase'` despite a GIN index on `doc`.
pitfalls.cause: GIN indexes on `doc` support operators applied directly to `doc` (`@>`, `?`, `@?`, `@@`). `->>` produces a text expression the index knows nothing about.
pitfalls.fix: Write `doc @> '{"type": "purchase"}'`, or create an expression index on `(doc ->> 'type')`.

pitfalls.title: Relying on key order or duplicate keys
pitfalls.symptom: An API returns keys in a different order than they were sent, or a signed payload no longer verifies.
pitfalls.cause: jsonb sorts keys and keeps only the last duplicate. A common claim is that jsonb rejects duplicate keys: it accepts them silently and discards all but the last. The original text is gone after input.
pitfalls.fix: Store payloads that must be reproduced byte for byte (signatures, audit copies) in `json` or `text`, and a parsed `jsonb` copy for querying if needed.

pitfalls.title: Updating one key in a large document
pitfalls.symptom: Frequent `jsonb_set` updates on big documents cause high WAL volume, TOAST churn and row-lock contention.
pitfalls.cause: A jsonb value is one datum. Changing one key writes a whole new row version, and a new TOAST value if the document is large. Any update also locks the entire row.
pitfalls.fix: Keep frequently changing fields in ordinary columns, and keep documents small and mostly immutable.

pitfalls.title: Comparing ->> results to numbers
pitfalls.symptom: `WHERE doc ->> 'amount' > '50'` silently returns the wrong rows, or `WHERE doc ->> 'amount' > 50.0` fails with `operator does not exist: text > numeric`.
pitfalls.cause: `->>` always returns **text**. Against a quoted literal the comparison is a string comparison (`'9.00' > '50'`); against a number there is no such operator.
pitfalls.fix: Cast the extracted value: `(doc ->> 'amount')::numeric > 50`, or compare jsonb to jsonb with `doc -> 'amount' > '50'`. To index it, the index expression must match the cast exactly, and the cast must be immutable (text to `numeric` is; text to `timestamptz` is not).
pitfalls.sql:
CREATE INDEX ON events (((doc ->> 'amount')::numeric));
SELECT count(*) FROM events WHERE (doc ->> 'amount')::numeric > 50;

pitfalls.title: jsonb_set with a NULL value
pitfalls.symptom: After `UPDATE t SET doc = jsonb_set(doc, '{note}', to_jsonb($1))` with a NULL parameter, whole documents are NULL.
pitfalls.cause: `jsonb_set` is strict: if any argument is SQL NULL the result is SQL NULL, and the UPDATE writes it over the entire column.
pitfalls.fix: Use `jsonb_set_lax`, which by default stores a JSON `null` (or can delete the key), or wrap the value in `COALESCE(to_jsonb($1), 'null')`. Add `CHECK (doc IS NOT NULL)` or `NOT NULL` on document columns.
pitfalls.sql:
SELECT jsonb_set('{"a": 1}', '{b}', NULL);      -- NULL: the whole document
SELECT jsonb_set_lax('{"a": 1}', '{b}', NULL);  -- {"a": 1, "b": null}

pitfalls.title: Using jsonb_path_ops for key-existence queries
pitfalls.symptom: `WHERE doc ? 'coupon'` stays slow after switching the index to `jsonb_path_ops`.
pitfalls.cause: `jsonb_path_ops` only indexes hashed values, not bare keys, so it supports `@>`, `@?` and `@@` only.
pitfalls.fix: Keep the default `jsonb_ops` index if you need `?`, `?|` or `?&`, or index the expression `((doc ? 'coupon'))` for a single hot key.

pointers: **json** = exact text, reparsed on every use, no GIN support. **jsonb** = parsed binary tree: no whitespace, keys sorted shorter-first, last duplicate wins.
jsonb is not smaller: small documents are often **larger** than json. Its advantage is speed and indexing.
`->` returns jsonb, `->>` returns **text** (cast before comparing numbers), `#>` / `#>>` take a path, `?` tests top-level keys, `@>` tests containment.
GIN **jsonb_ops** indexes keys and values (supports `?`); **jsonb_path_ops** hashes paths (only `@>`, `@?`, `@@`, smaller).
jsonpath runs in **lax** mode by default (auto-wraps and unwraps arrays); **strict** raises structural errors.

lessons.title: UUIDv4 vs UUIDv7
tldr: A `uuid` is a 16-byte value: **UUIDv4** is 122 random bits, while **UUIDv7** starts with a 48-bit millisecond timestamp, so new values sort after older ones.

Random keys scatter inserts across a B-tree, while time-ordered keys append at its right edge, so PostgreSQL 18 added a native `uuidv7()` that keeps the global uniqueness of UUIDs with the index locality of a sequence.

visualizer.title: Inside a UUID, and what it does to an index
visualizer.caption: Generate UUIDs and click each bit field to see what it encodes. Then switch to **Index locality** and insert v4 vs v7 keys to see which leaf pages every insert has to touch.

presets.label: Generate & decode
presets.sql:
SELECT u, uuid_extract_version(u) AS version, uuid_extract_timestamp(u) AS ts
FROM (VALUES (uuidv7()), (uuidv4()), (gen_random_uuid())) AS t(u);
presets.note: `gen_random_uuid()` is the same as `uuidv4()`. Only v7 (and v1) carry a timestamp; for v4 it is NULL.

presets.label: v7 is ordered
presets.note: Within one millisecond the 4th group counts up (`7000`, `7001`, …): the sub-millisecond field keeps values increasing. Zero of 50,000 neighbours are out of order.

presets.label: Storage size & input forms
presets.note: Native `uuid` is 16 bytes; the same value as `text` is 40. Input is forgiving (upper case, braces, no hyphens) and output is always the canonical lower-case form, so there is no reason to store UUIDs as text.

presets.label: Index size: bigint vs v7 vs v4
presets.sql:
SELECT t AS key_type,
       pg_relation_size(t || '_pkey') / 8192 AS index_pages,
       pg_size_pretty(pg_relation_size(t || '_pkey')) AS index_size
FROM unnest(ARRAY['k_bigint', 'k_v7', 'k_v4']) AS t;
presets.note: Same 50,000 rows. v7 is larger than bigint only because keys are 16 bytes instead of 8. v4 is about **40% larger again** than v7, purely from half-empty pages.

presets.label: Leaf fill
presets.sql:
SELECT t AS key_type, round(avg(100 - s.free_size * 100.0 / 8148), 1) AS avg_leaf_fill_pct
FROM unnest(ARRAY['k_bigint', 'k_v7', 'k_v4']) AS t,
     LATERAL generate_series(1, (pg_relation_size(t || '_pkey') / 8192 - 1)::int) AS b,
     LATERAL bt_page_stats(t || '_pkey', b) AS s
WHERE s.type = 'l'
GROUP BY t ORDER BY 2 DESC;
presets.note: About 90% for bigint and v7 (right-edge appends respect fillfactor 90) versus about 63% for v4 (the exact figure varies a little per run, since the keys are random).

presets.label: WAL after a checkpoint
presets.note: The first change to a page after a checkpoint writes a **full-page image** into WAL. 2,000 v7 keys touch a handful of right-edge leaves; 2,000 v4 keys touch hundreds of different leaves. Expect roughly **4 to 5 times more WAL** for v4 (about 1.7 MB against 0.3 to 0.4 MB; keys are random, so it varies).

presets.label: Shifted timestamps
presets.note: `uuidv7(shift)` moves the embedded timestamp, which is useful for backfilling historical rows. Note that it reveals when a row was created.

production.title: Moving an orders table from UUIDv4 to UUIDv7 keys
production.context: A commerce service generates `uuid` primary keys with `gen_random_uuid()` so that clients can create ids offline. The orders table grows by several million rows a day.
production.problem: As the primary-key index outgrew memory, insert latency rose. Each random key landed on a different leaf page, most of which had to be read from disk, and mid-page splits left leaves about two-thirds full.
production.solution: Switch the default to `uuidv7()` (native in PostgreSQL 18; clients can generate v7 too). Existing v4 keys stay valid because both are the same `uuid` type. New keys append at the right edge of the index. Rebuild the index online later to compact the old part.
production.outcome: On 50,000 rows in the playground, the v4 index has about 275 pages at about 63% leaf fill (it varies slightly per run), the v7 index 194 pages at 90%. At production scale the larger win is that inserts touch one hot leaf instead of thousands of cold ones.

pitfalls.title: Storing UUIDs as text
pitfalls.symptom: Indexes are 2–3 times larger than expected, and comparisons are slow and collation-dependent.
pitfalls.cause: The 36-character text form takes 37–40 bytes per value; the native type takes 16 and compares as raw bytes.
pitfalls.fix: Use the `uuid` type. It accepts upper case, braces and missing hyphens on input and always prints the standard form.
pitfalls.sql: ALTER TABLE t ALTER COLUMN id TYPE uuid USING id::uuid;

pitfalls.title: Leaking creation time through UUIDv7
pitfalls.symptom: Public URLs like `/orders/01a1d827-…` reveal when each order was placed and roughly how many are created per day.
pitfalls.cause: The first 48 bits of a v7 UUID are a readable millisecond timestamp. `uuid_extract_timestamp()` decodes it.
