pitfalls.fix: Keep v7 as the internal primary key, and expose a separate random v4 (or another opaque token) where the creation time must stay private.

pitfalls.title: Assuming v7 values are globally ordered
pitfalls.symptom: Rows inserted by different servers or clients appear slightly out of order when sorted by id.
pitfalls.cause: Ordering is only as good as the clocks. PostgreSQL guarantees increasing values within one session, but separate generators with clock skew interleave.
pitfalls.fix: Use a `timestamptz` column (or a sequence) when you need exact ordering. Treat v7 order as "roughly by creation time", which is all an index needs.

pitfalls.title: Benchmarking v4 vs v7 with buffer statistics
pitfalls.symptom: A comparison based on `pg_statio_user_indexes` (`idx_blks_read`, `idx_blks_hit`) shows little difference, and the team concludes the key type does not matter.
pitfalls.cause: Those counters measure buffer reads, not page splits or fill. On a small test that fits in memory every page is a hit for both key types. A common claim is that these views show page splits; they do not.
pitfalls.fix: Compare what the key type actually changes: index size (`pg_relation_size`), leaf fill (`bt_page_stats`), and WAL volume per insert after a checkpoint (`pg_current_wal_lsn()` before and after).
pitfalls.sql:
SELECT pg_size_pretty(pg_relation_size('k_v4_pkey')) AS v4,
       pg_size_pretty(pg_relation_size('k_v7_pkey')) AS v7;

pointers: `uuid` is **16 bytes**, compared byte by byte. Store it as `uuid`, never as text.
`gen_random_uuid()` = `uuidv4()` (random); `uuidv7([shift])` puts a **48-bit Unix-ms timestamp** first.
Decode with `uuid_extract_version()` and `uuid_extract_timestamp()` (v1 and v7 only).
Random keys scatter writes (more dirty pages, more full-page images in WAL) and leave B-tree leaves about **2/3 full**; v7 keys append at the right edge and fill leaves to **90%**.
v7 still takes **twice the space of bigint** per key: choose UUIDs for distributed id generation, not by default.

lessons.title: The 8 KB slotted page
tldr: Every table and index is an array of fixed **8 KB pages**, each with a 24-byte header, an array of 4-byte **line pointers** growing forward, and tuples growing backward from the end.
The indirection through line pointers lets PostgreSQL move, prune and compact tuples inside a page without changing their address, the **ctid** `(block, item)` that indexes point to.

visualizer.title: Inside a heap page, byte by byte
visualizer.caption: Step through eight operations. Click any line pointer or tuple to inspect its header fields and byte offsets.

presets.label: ctid & system columns
presets.sql: SELECT ctid, xmin, xmax, * FROM accounts;
presets.note: Every row has hidden system columns. `ctid` is (block, line pointer).

presets.label: Page header
presets.sql:
SELECT lower, upper, special, pagesize, version, prune_xid
FROM page_header(get_raw_page('accounts', 0));
presets.note: `upper - lower` is the free space. `special` = 8192 because heap pages have no special space.

presets.label: Line pointers & tuples
presets.note: Offsets decrease as rows are added: tuples are allocated from the end of the page.

presets.label: UPDATE → new version
presets.note: lp 2 keeps its bytes but gets `t_xmax` and `t_ctid = (0,4)`. lp 4 is the new version, flagged `HEAP_ONLY_TUPLE`.

presets.label: DELETE + VACUUM
presets.note: Run after the UPDATE preset. lp 2 becomes `lp_flags = 2` (redirect to lp 4), lp 3 becomes 0 (unused), and the survivors are compacted.

presets.label: Fill a page
presets.note: Each 61-byte row needs 64 bytes plus a 4-byte line pointer, so about **120 rows fit per page**. Files grow in whole pages, so even a one-row table takes 8192 bytes.

presets.label: Heap order is not id order
presets.note: No ORDER BY, so rows come back in **physical order**: 1, 4, 5, 3, 2. Each UPDATE wrote a new version at the next free slot, so 3 and 2 moved behind the others. Updating every row moves all five again, to (0,8)–(0,12), even though nothing was deleted.

presets.label: ctid inside one statement
presets.note: A table with no key can still be de-duplicated: within one statement every row version has a distinct, stable ctid. Keeping the lowest ctid per fruit leaves (0,1), (0,3) and (0,6). Outside a single statement, ctid is not a safe identifier.

production.title: Sizing a 500 M-row events table before it ships
production.context: A team plans an `events(id bigint, user_id bigint, kind smallint, created_at timestamptz)` table and wants a disk and cache estimate.
production.problem: A spreadsheet based on "8 + 8 + 2 + 8 = 26 bytes a row" predicted 13 GB. The real table was **2.3× larger**, and the hot set no longer fit in `shared_buffers`.
production.solution: Do the page arithmetic. Each row costs a 23-byte header rounded up to `t_hoff` = 24, plus aligned data. The `smallint` placed before the `timestamptz` adds 6 padding bytes, so the data takes 32 bytes, the whole row is MAXALIGNed to 56, and each row also needs a 4-byte line pointer. That gives `(8192 - 24) / (56 + 4)` ≈ **136 rows per page**. Confirm on a 100k-row sample with `pg_relation_size` and `pageinspect` before committing to hardware.
production.outcome: The measured ~60 bytes per row predicts about **30 GB** for 500 M rows, against the spreadsheet's 13 GB. The team sized storage and memory from the measured number. Reordering columns would not help here: with the `smallint` last the row is 50 bytes, which still rounds up to 56. Per-row overhead (header + line pointer + alignment) is a fixed cost to budget for, not a rounding error.

pitfalls.title: Expecting rows back in insertion or id order
pitfalls.symptom: A report or export without ORDER BY comes back in a different order after an UPDATE, a VACUUM or an upgrade, and pagination skips or repeats rows.
pitfalls.cause: A heap is unordered. A sequential scan returns tuples in physical (block, line pointer) order, and every UPDATE writes the new version wherever there is room. Synchronized scans can even start mid-table.
pitfalls.fix: Write `ORDER BY` whenever order matters, with a unique tiebreaker such as the primary key. Never rely on the order of a plain `SELECT *`.
pitfalls.sql:
SELECT ctid, id FROM courses;          -- physical order
SELECT ctid, id FROM courses ORDER BY id;  -- the order you meant

pitfalls.title: Using ctid as a row identifier
pitfalls.symptom: An application caches `ctid` values to re-find rows and later updates the **wrong row**, or finds nothing.
pitfalls.cause: A ctid is a *physical* address. Any UPDATE writes a new version with a new ctid, and VACUUM recycles freed slots, so a later INSERT can take an old address. VACUUM FULL and CLUSTER rewrite every address.
pitfalls.fix: Always identify rows by a primary key. Use ctid only inside one statement, for example de-duplicating with `DELETE … WHERE ctid NOT IN (…)`.

pitfalls.title: Expecting DELETE to shrink the file
pitfalls.symptom: After deleting 80% of a table, `pg_relation_size` is unchanged and sequential scans are just as slow.
pitfalls.cause: DELETE only stamps `t_xmax`. VACUUM later reclaims the space *inside* pages for reuse, but only truncates empty pages at the very end of the file.
pitfalls.fix: Plain `VACUUM` makes the space reusable. To return it to the OS, rebuild the table: `VACUUM FULL` takes an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock; `pg_repack` can do it online. Or partition the table and drop whole partitions instead of deleting rows.

pitfalls.title: Assuming the block size can be tuned
pitfalls.symptom: Someone looks for a `block_size` setting to try 16 KB or 32 KB pages on a running cluster.
pitfalls.cause: `block_size` is a read-only preset fixed when the server binaries are compiled. Every page in the cluster uses that one size.
pitfalls.fix: Keep the default 8 KB. A different size means rebuilding PostgreSQL and reloading the data, so tune `fillfactor`, row width and TOAST instead.
pitfalls.sql: SHOW block_size;  -- 8192, read-only

pointers: A page is **24-byte header → line pointers (4 B each, growing up) → free space → tuples (growing down) → special space**.
Free space is exactly **`pd_upper - pd_lower`**. The page is full when they would meet.
A **ctid `(block, lp)`** names a line pointer, not a byte offset, so tuples can move inside the page without breaking index entries.
Each tuple carries a **23-byte header** (`t_xmin`, `t_xmax`, `t_cid`, `t_ctid`, `t_infomask2`, `t_infomask`, `t_hoff`), padded to 24 before the row data.
Line pointer states: **NORMAL**, **REDIRECT** (HOT chain root), **DEAD** (waiting for index cleanup), **UNUSED** (free for reuse).

lessons.title: The heap tuple header: xmin, xmax, ctid, infomask
tldr: Every row version starts with a **23-byte header**: who created it (`t_xmin`), who deleted or locked it (`t_xmax`), where its newer version lives (`t_ctid`), and two flag words, `t_infomask` and `t_infomask2`.
MVCC visibility, row locks, HOT chains and freezing are all decided from these few bytes, and readers cache commit status in them as **hint bits** so later readers can skip the commit log.

visualizer.title: Flip the infomask bits, one statement at a time
visualizer.caption: Step through eleven statements. Bits that change in a step pulse; click any bit for its meaning, or any tuple to inspect it. The values are what `heap_page_items` reports after each statement.

presets.label: Fresh insert
presets.sql: SELECT * FROM hdr;
presets.note: `HEAP_XMAX_INVALID` (not deleted) and `HEAP_HASNULL` with `t_bits = 11100000`: the 4th column is NULL. The view itself was created after the insert, so no reader has hinted the row yet.

presets.label: Read → hint bit
presets.sql:
SELECT * FROM acct;
SELECT lp, t_infomask, flags FROM hdr;
presets.note: After one SELECT, `HEAP_XMIN_COMMITTED` appears. Reading wrote to the page.

presets.label: Aborted insert
presets.note: lp 2 is still physically on the page. The SELECT stamped it `HEAP_XMIN_INVALID`, so nobody will check its xid again.

presets.label: HOT update
presets.sql:
UPDATE acct SET balance = 120 WHERE id = 1;
SELECT lp, t_xmin, t_xmax, t_ctid, flags FROM hdr;
presets.note: The old version points at the new one through `t_ctid` and carries `HEAP_HOT_UPDATED`. The new version is a `HEAP_ONLY_TUPLE`.

presets.label: Row locks live in xmax
presets.note: Inside the transaction, the live version has `t_xmax` = your xid plus `HEAP_XMAX_LOCK_ONLY` and `HEAP_XMAX_EXCL_LOCK`: a lock, not a delete.

presets.label: Null bitmap & t_hoff
presets.note: A NULL costs **one bit** and no data bytes (28 B), while an empty string costs its 1-byte varlena header (29 B): NULL and `''` are different on disk too. With 9 columns and a NULL, the bitmap needs 2 bytes: 23 + 2 = 25, MAXALIGNed to **t_hoff = 32**.

presets.label: No-op updates & upserts
presets.note: An UPDATE that changes nothing still writes a **new version** with a new ctid and xmin. In the upsert, PostgreSQL 18 `RETURNING old/new` says which rows were inserted (`old` is NULL). The older `xmax = 0` trick agrees here because the updated version carries the conflict lock in its xmax, but that is an implementation detail.

presets.label: Freeze
presets.note: Dead versions are gone. The survivors (alice and carol) show `HEAP_XMIN_FROZEN` in `combined_flags`: XMIN_COMMITTED and XMIN_INVALID set together.

production.title: A full-table read that writes gigabytes
production.context: A data team bulk-loads 50 M rows into a reporting table every night with `COPY`, then runs a first `SELECT count(*)` report against it.
production.problem: The first read after the load ran far longer than later identical reads, generated heavy write I/O and WAL on a server with checksums enabled, and the replica lagged behind. Nobody expected a SELECT to write.
production.solution: Every freshly loaded tuple has no hint bits, so the first reader of each row checks the commit log and sets `HEAP_XMIN_COMMITTED`, dirtying every page (and with checksums or `wal_log_hints`, logging full-page images). Run `VACUUM (FREEZE, ANALYZE)` straight after the load: it sets hints, freezes rows, fills the visibility map and gathers statistics in one controlled pass, before users arrive.
production.outcome: The playground shows the mechanism directly: one SELECT changes `t_infomask` from 2051 to 2307. Moving that write to a planned VACUUM makes first-read latency match later reads, and `COPY … FREEZE` skips the extra rewrite entirely.

pitfalls.title: Assuming an UPDATE that changes nothing is free
pitfalls.symptom: A sync job runs `UPDATE t SET col = $1` on every row each night; values rarely change, yet the table bloats, WAL grows and autovacuum runs constantly.
pitfalls.cause: PostgreSQL does not compare old and new values. Every matched row gets a new version, a new ctid and a dead predecessor, and the `UPDATE n` count includes the unchanged rows.
pitfalls.fix: Filter out no-op rows: `UPDATE t SET col = $1 WHERE col IS DISTINCT FROM $1`. For row-by-row writes from applications, the built-in `suppress_redundant_updates_trigger()` can skip them.
pitfalls.sql:
UPDATE acct SET balance = 120
WHERE id = 1 AND balance IS DISTINCT FROM 120;

pitfalls.title: Reading t_xmax as "deleted"
pitfalls.symptom: A monitoring query counts rows with `xmax <> 0` as deleted and reports thousands of phantom deletes.
pitfalls.cause: `t_xmax` is also used for **row locks** (`SELECT … FOR UPDATE / SHARE`, foreign-key checks), marked by `HEAP_XMAX_LOCK_ONLY`. Aborted deleters also leave their xid there.
pitfalls.fix: Never infer liveness from raw xmax. Decode the flags with `heap_tuple_infomask_flags`, or rely on MVCC and count live rows with `count(*)`. For the same reason, prefer `RETURNING old IS NULL` (PostgreSQL 18) or `merge_action()` over the `xmax = 0` trick for telling inserts from updates in an upsert.
pitfalls.sql:
SELECT lp, t_xmax, (heap_tuple_infomask_flags(t_infomask, t_infomask2)).raw_flags
FROM heap_page_items(get_raw_page('acct', 0));

pitfalls.title: Many NULLable columns pushing t_hoff up
pitfalls.symptom: Wide tables with many optional columns take more space per row than the data suggests.
pitfalls.cause: A row with any NULL carries a bitmap of one bit per column. Past 8 columns it no longer fits in the padding byte, and `t_hoff` jumps from 24 to 32 (then 40 past 72 columns).
pitfalls.fix: Keep very wide sparse attributes in a `jsonb` column or a side table, and keep frequently NULL columns out of hot narrow tables.

pitfalls.title: Assuming row locks are cheap to hold
pitfalls.symptom: A job that locks millions of rows with `SELECT … FOR UPDATE` causes huge WAL volume and, with many shared lockers, `pg_multixact` growth.
pitfalls.cause: Row locks are written into each tuple header (`t_xmax`), so locking a row modifies its page. Multiple share-lockers need a **MultiXact** (`HEAP_XMAX_IS_MULTI`).
pitfalls.fix: Lock only the rows you need, in small batches, and prefer `FOR NO KEY UPDATE` when you do not change keys so foreign-key checks are not blocked.

pointers: Header = `t_xmin` 4 + `t_xmax` 4 + `t_cid` 4 + `t_ctid` 6 + `t_infomask2` 2 + `t_infomask` 2 + `t_hoff` 1 = **23 bytes**, data at `t_hoff` (24 without a long null bitmap).
**Hint bits** `XMIN_COMMITTED`, `XMIN_INVALID`, `XMAX_COMMITTED`, `XMAX_INVALID` cache commit-log answers; readers set them, so a SELECT can write.
`t_xmax` means "deleted" only without `XMAX_LOCK_ONLY`; row locks live in the tuple itself.
`t_infomask2` = attribute count (11 bits) + `HOT_UPDATED`, `HEAP_ONLY_TUPLE`, `KEYS_UPDATED`.
**Frozen** = `XMIN_COMMITTED | XMIN_INVALID`: visible to all, safe from xid wraparound.

lessons.title: TOAST: oversized attributes
tldr: **TOAST** (The Oversized-Attribute Storage Technique) compresses large variable-length values and, if they are still too big, slices them into ~2 kB chunks stored in a separate `pg_toast` table.
A row must fit on one 8 KB page, so TOAST is how PostgreSQL stores values of up to 1 GB while keeping the main table narrow and fast to scan.

visualizer.title: Follow a big value through the toaster
visualizer.caption: Pick one of four inserts and step through compression, chunking and the 18-byte pointer that stays behind. Click the pointer bytes to decode them.

presets.label: What happened to each value
presets.sql:
SELECT id, octet_length(body)            AS raw_bytes,
       pg_column_size(body)             AS stored_bytes,
       pg_column_compression(body)      AS compression,
       pg_column_toast_chunk_id(body)   AS toast_chunk_id
FROM docs ORDER BY id;
presets.note: Row 1 is compressed inline (9000 → 122). Row 2 is out of line, uncompressed. Row 3 is untouched. Row 4 is compressed **and** out of line (1.2 MB → 13,745 bytes).

presets.label: The TOAST table
presets.note: Every TOASTed table has its own hidden `pg_toast.pg_toast_<oid>` table. Chunks are at most **1996 bytes**; row 2 needs 5 chunks, row 4 (compressed) needs 7.

presets.label: Main row vs pointer
presets.sql:
SELECT lp, lp_len, encode(substring(t_data FROM 9 FOR 18), 'hex') AS first_18_bytes_of_body
FROM heap_page_items(get_raw_page('docs', 0));
presets.note: Rows 2 and 4 are tiny: `body` is an 18-byte pointer starting `0112` (external, tag 18). Row 1 holds 122 compressed bytes inline.

presets.label: Update without touching TOAST
presets.note: Updating another column **reuses** the same chunk_id: the new row version copies only the 18-byte pointer. Changing `body` writes a whole new TOAST value.

presets.label: Where the bytes live
presets.sql:
SELECT pg_size_pretty(pg_relation_size('docs'))           AS main_heap,
       pg_size_pretty(pg_relation_size(reltoastrelid))     AS toast_heap,
       pg_size_pretty(pg_indexes_size(reltoastrelid))      AS toast_index,
       pg_size_pretty(pg_indexes_size('docs'))             AS docs_indexes,
       pg_size_pretty(pg_table_size('docs'))               AS table_size,
       pg_size_pretty(pg_total_relation_size('docs'))      AS total
FROM pg_class WHERE oid = 'docs'::regclass;
presets.note: The main heap is a single 8 kB page even though it "holds" 1.2 MB of text. `pg_relation_size` counts only the main fork; `pg_table_size` adds TOAST and the FSM/VM forks; `pg_total_relation_size` adds every index, including the TOAST table's own index.

presets.label: bytea vs large objects
presets.note: `bytea` is an ordinary varlena: 3 bytes stay inline, 6,400 bytes are TOASTed with the row. A **large object** lives in `pg_largeobject` as 2,048-byte pages, and the row holds only its OID. Writing that OID into a `bytea` column stores its digits (`3136…` = "16…"), not the file.

presets.label: Storage strategies
presets.note: EXTERNAL stores the 9000 bytes out of line uncompressed. MAIN compresses and keeps it inline, moving out of line only as a last resort.

presets.label: toast_tuple_target
presets.note: Both rows are about 2.4 kB, so the toaster runs. By default it moves one column out until the row fits 2032 bytes; with a target of 256 it keeps going and moves **both** out.

production.title: Wide product descriptions slowing every listing query
production.context: A catalog table stores `description text` (typically 1.5 kB of HTML) next to the columns used by listing pages: name, price and stock.
production.problem: Descriptions just under the 2 kB threshold are never TOASTed, so each row is about 1.6 kB and only 4–5 rows fit per page. Listing queries that never read `description` still scan pages full of it.
production.solution: Lower `toast_tuple_target` so the description is moved out once a row passes the threshold, and, more robustly, move rarely read large columns to a side table. Measure rows per page before and after.
production.outcome: The playground shows the target behaviour: with `toast_tuple_target = 256` a 2.4 kB row moves both columns out of line instead of one. Note that the toaster only starts at about 2 kB, so values under that threshold stay inline whatever the target; for those rows, the side-table split is what improves scan density: a row of name, price and stock is under 80 bytes, so a page holds about 100 of them instead of 4–5.

pitfalls.title: Changing the strategy and expecting old rows to move
pitfalls.symptom: After `ALTER COLUMN … SET STORAGE EXTERNAL` or `SET COMPRESSION`, existing rows look exactly the same.
pitfalls.cause: Storage and compression settings apply to **newly written** values only. Existing tuples keep their format until they are rewritten.
pitfalls.fix: Rewrite the affected rows (`UPDATE t SET col = col || ''` in batches) or the table (`VACUUM FULL`, `pg_repack`) when you need the new format everywhere.

pitfalls.title: Updating a large value in place, frequently
pitfalls.symptom: The TOAST table grows much faster than the main table, and autovacuum spends most of its time there.
pitfalls.cause: Changing a TOASTed column writes a complete new copy of the value as new chunks. The old chunks become dead rows in the TOAST table.
pitfalls.fix: Keep frequently changed fields out of big documents. Unchanged TOASTed columns cost nothing on UPDATE, so put the counters in their own columns.

pitfalls.title: Expecting lz4 everywhere
pitfalls.symptom: `ALTER TABLE … SET COMPRESSION lz4` fails with `compression method lz4 not supported`.
pitfalls.cause: lz4 is only available when PostgreSQL is built with `--with-lz4`. The default `default_toast_compression` is pglz, and some builds (including the one in this playground) have no lz4 at all.
pitfalls.fix: Check `SHOW default_toast_compression;` and test `SET COMPRESSION lz4` on your build. lz4 is usually faster than pglz when available.

pitfalls.title: Storing a large object's OID in a bytea column
pitfalls.symptom: Uploaded files come back as five or six bytes such as `\x3137323730`, and `pg_largeobject` keeps growing even after rows are deleted.
pitfalls.cause: Large objects are a separate store: `lo_create` / `lo_from_bytea` return an **OID**, and the data lives in `pg_largeobject`. Inserting that OID into a `bytea` column stores the ASCII digits of the number. Deleting the row does not delete the object.
pitfalls.fix: Pick one design. Either a `bytea` column (simple, TOASTed, up to 1 GB, deleted with the row), or an `oid` column with the large-object API plus `lo_unlink` (or the `lo_manage` trigger from the `lo` module) when the row goes away.
pitfalls.sql: SELECT encode(convert_to(16450::oid::text, 'UTF8'), 'hex');  -- 3136343530: digits, not data

pitfalls.title: Hitting the 1 GB value limit
pitfalls.symptom: `ERROR: invalid memory alloc request size` or `requested length too large` when building a huge text or bytea.
pitfalls.cause: A single varlena value is limited to **1 GB** (30 length bits), even with TOAST.
pitfalls.fix: Store very large objects outside the row: in object storage with a reference, or chunked across rows yourself.

pointers: TOAST starts when a row exceeds **~2 kB** (2032 bytes) and works until it is under `toast_tuple_target` (default 2032).
Strategies: **PLAIN** (never), **EXTENDED** (compress, then out of line; default), **EXTERNAL** (out of line, no compression), **MAIN** (compress; out of line last).
Out-of-line values become **1996-byte chunks**, 4 per TOAST page, keyed by `(chunk_id, chunk_seq)`; the row keeps an **18-byte pointer**.
UPDATEs that do not change a TOASTed column **reuse** its chunks.
Inspect with `pg_column_size`, `pg_column_compression` and `pg_column_toast_chunk_id`. Max value size is **1 GB**.

lessons.title: Files, forks, the free space map and visibility map
tldr: Each table is a set of files named by its **relfilenode**, split into 1 GB segments, with up to four forks: the **main** data, the **free space map**, the **visibility map** and, for unlogged tables, an **init** fork.
The FSM lets inserts find a page with room without scanning the table, and the VM lets VACUUM skip clean pages and index-only scans skip the heap.

visualizer.title: One table on disk: files, free space and visibility
visualizer.caption: Step through nine statements and watch the fork files, each page's FSM value and VM bits change. Drag the slider under the FSM tree to see how an INSERT finds a page with enough room.

presets.label: Where is the file?
presets.note: The path is `base/<database OID>/<relfilenode>`. The FSM fork already exists; the VM does not, because nothing has been vacuumed.

presets.label: VACUUM builds the VM
presets.note: A VM fork appears with **all_visible** set for every page. `pg_freespace` reports free bytes in steps of 32.

presets.label: DELETE: VM cleared, FSM stale
presets.note: Pages 0, 4 and 5 lose all_visible immediately. Their FSM values do not move: the dead rows still occupy the space until VACUUM.

presets.label: VACUUM updates the FSM
presets.note: Pages 0, 4 and 5 now show thousands of free bytes. FSM block 2 is the leaf page: nodes 4095… are the per-page categories (bytes / 32), lower node numbers are the max-tree above them.

presets.label: Freeze & the all-frozen bit
presets.note: After the freeze every page is all-visible and all-frozen. One UPDATE clears both bits on the page it touches.

presets.label: TRUNCATE gets a new file
presets.note: TRUNCATE swaps in a fresh, empty relfilenode while the table OID stays the same. Never assume filenode = OID.

presets.label: Unlogged: the init fork
presets.note: Unlogged relations get an `_init` fork: empty for the heap, one metapage (8192 bytes) for the B-tree. After a crash it is copied over the main fork, so the table comes back empty.

presets.label: Which ALTERs rewrite the file?
presets.note: A new relfilenode means the whole table was copied under an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock. A constant DEFAULT is kept in the catalog (`attmissingval`), a VIRTUAL column and a longer varchar change only metadata, and DROP COLUMN just marks `attisdropped`. A STORED column and a type change rewrite every row.

production.title: Index-only scans that still read the heap
production.context: A reporting query on an append-heavy `events` table uses a covering index and shows `Index Only Scan` in its plan, yet it reads thousands of heap pages.
production.problem: `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)` reports a high **Heap Fetches** count. Autovacuum triggers on dead tuples, and an insert-only table produces almost none, so recently filled pages never had their **all-visible** bit set. Every row on those pages needed a heap visit.
production.solution: Make sure vacuum runs on insert-heavy tables (PostgreSQL triggers it on inserted rows via `autovacuum_vacuum_insert_threshold` / `_scale_factor`; lower them for this table) and check the VM directly.
production.outcome: After the vacuum the VM covers the table and Heap Fetches drops towards zero, so the query reads only index pages. The VM is tiny (2 bits per heap page: one 8 KB VM page covers about 255 MB of heap), so it stays cached.

pitfalls.title: Assuming the filenode equals the OID
pitfalls.symptom: A script that copies or inspects files by `pg_class.oid` finds the wrong file, or none, after a TRUNCATE or REINDEX.
pitfalls.cause: TRUNCATE, REINDEX, CLUSTER, VACUUM FULL and some ALTER TABLE forms assign a new relfilenode while keeping the OID. Some catalogs have `relfilenode = 0` and use a relation map.
pitfalls.fix: Always ask the server: `SELECT pg_relation_filepath('t');`. Never touch files in the data directory of a running server.

pitfalls.title: Expecting DELETE to free space immediately
pitfalls.symptom: After a large DELETE, new inserts still extend the table instead of reusing space.
pitfalls.cause: Deleted rows still occupy their pages until VACUUM removes them, and the FSM only learns about free space from VACUUM.
pitfalls.fix: Run `VACUUM` (or let autovacuum run) after large deletes. For bulk purges, partition and `DROP` / `DETACH` whole partitions.

pitfalls.title: Treating TRUNCATE as a light, MVCC-safe DELETE
pitfalls.symptom: A nightly `TRUNCATE` of a staging table stalls every reader of that table, or a long report running in REPEATABLE READ suddenly sees the table as empty.
pitfalls.cause: A common claim is that TRUNCATE is fast because it uses lighter locking. It takes an **ACCESS EXCLUSIVE** lock, which blocks even SELECT, and swaps in a new empty relfilenode instead of marking rows dead. Transactions with an older snapshot then see the new, empty file.
pitfalls.fix: Use TRUNCATE for tables nobody reads concurrently, with a short `lock_timeout` so it gives up instead of queueing behind long queries. For tables under live reads, `DELETE` in batches plus VACUUM, or swap partitions.
pitfalls.sql:
SET lock_timeout = '2s';
TRUNCATE ev;

pitfalls.title: Using unlogged tables for data you cannot lose
pitfalls.symptom: After a crash or failover, an unlogged table is suddenly empty, and it never existed on the replica.
pitfalls.cause: Unlogged tables skip WAL. On crash recovery the `_init` fork replaces the main fork, and nothing is replicated.
pitfalls.fix: Use unlogged tables only for caches and staging data you can rebuild. Convert with `ALTER TABLE … SET LOGGED` before the data matters.

pointers: Path = `base/<db OID>/<relfilenode>`, plus `_fsm`, `_vm`, `_init` forks and `.1`, `.2` segments every **1 GB**. Look it up with `pg_relation_filepath()`.
**FSM**: one byte per page (free space / 32), organised as max-trees so a search is a short descent. Updated mainly by **VACUUM**.
**VM**: two bits per heap page, **all-visible** and **all-frozen**; set only by VACUUM, cleared by any change to the page. Indexes have no VM.
All-visible pages let **index-only scans** skip the heap; all-frozen pages let anti-wraparound VACUUM skip them.
TRUNCATE and VACUUM FULL write a **new relfilenode**; unlogged tables restore from the **init fork** after a crash.

lessons.title: INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, MERGE: what really happens
tldr: Every write in PostgreSQL appends or stamps **row versions**: INSERT adds a tuple, DELETE sets its `xmax`, and UPDATE does both, while `RETURNING` hands the affected rows (old and new, in 18) straight back.
Knowing this explains real behaviour you will meet: why updates bloat tables, why an upsert burns sequence values, and why MERGE and `ON CONFLICT` are not interchangeable.

visualizer.title: Eight statements, one heap page
visualizer.caption: Step through real statements and watch row versions, the RETURNING output and the identity sequence. Click a version to inspect its `xmin`/`xmax`. Note the xids: one statement, one transaction, even when MERGE does three different things.

presets.label: UPDATE makes a new version
presets.note: Three tuples for two rows. The old apple (lp 1) has `xmax` set and `t_ctid` pointing at its replacement, lp 3.

presets.label: RETURNING old and new
presets.note: For UPDATE both sides are filled. `SET qty = qty` changes nothing, yet the row moves to a new ctid: every UPDATE writes a version. `WITH (OLD AS o, NEW AS n)` renames the qualifiers, which you need inside trigger functions. For DELETE `new.*` is NULL. Always alias `old.x` and `new.x`: two output columns both named `qty` collide in most clients.

presets.label: Upsert and the sequence gap
presets.note: apple is updated (old values present), fig is inserted. The sequence advanced for both proposed rows, so fig gets a higher id than you might expect: one value was burned on apple. Both paths report `INSERT 0 n`; `old.id IS NOT NULL` tells them apart. Before 18 the usual trick was `xmax = 0`: an inserted row has no xmax, an updated one carries the upsert's lock.

presets.label: MERGE + merge_action()
presets.sql:
MERGE INTO inventory i
USING delivery d ON i.sku = d.sku
WHEN MATCHED AND i.qty + d.qty <= 0 THEN DELETE
WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET qty = i.qty + d.qty
WHEN NOT MATCHED AND d.qty > 0 THEN INSERT (sku, qty) VALUES (d.sku, d.qty)
RETURNING merge_action() AS action, d.sku, old.qty AS old_qty, new.qty AS new_qty;
presets.note: One row per action taken. Rows that match no WHEN clause are silently skipped. After the earlier presets pear is already gone, so it shows up as NOT MATCHED and is skipped (its delta is negative).

presets.label: Cardinality violations
presets.sql:
-- the same key twice in one upsert
SELECT try_sql($q$
  INSERT INTO inventory (sku, qty) VALUES ('kiwi', 1), ('kiwi', 2)
  ON CONFLICT (sku) DO UPDATE SET qty = EXCLUDED.qty $q$) AS upsert;

-- one target row matching two source rows
SELECT try_sql($q$
  MERGE INTO inventory i
  USING (VALUES ('apple', 1), ('apple', 2)) AS d(sku, qty) ON i.sku = d.sku
  WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET qty = i.qty + d.qty $q$) AS merge;
presets.note: Both fail with SQLSTATE `21000`. DO UPDATE and MERGE refuse to change one row twice in a statement. `UPDATE … FROM` would silently apply just one match.

presets.label: One transaction, one xid, one clock
presets.note: A read-only transaction has **no xid** (NULL) until its first write. Both rows share one `xmin`. `now()` is frozen at transaction start, so it repeats exactly in the second statement; only `clock_timestamp()` keeps moving. After ROLLBACK the rows are gone but the ids are not given back, and the failed CHECK insert burns one more.

presets.label: UPDATE … FROM and DELETE … USING
presets.sql:
-- join another table into an UPDATE (FROM) or a DELETE (USING)
UPDATE inventory i SET qty = i.qty + d.qty
FROM delivery d
WHERE d.sku = i.sku AND d.qty > 0
RETURNING i.sku, old.qty AS before, new.qty AS after;

-- the SET target cannot be table-qualified
SELECT try_sql($q$ UPDATE inventory i SET i.qty = 0 FROM delivery d WHERE d.sku = i.sku $q$) AS qualified_set;

DELETE FROM inventory i
USING recalls r
WHERE r.sku = i.sku
RETURNING old.sku, old.qty;
presets.note: FROM and USING are the same idea: extra tables joined into the write. `SET i.qty = …` fails (`42703`) because a qualified name after SET means a field of a composite column; write `SET qty = …`. Rows with no match in the joined table are not touched. Forgetting the join condition would pair every target row with every source row.

presets.label: Move rows with a CTE
presets.note: DELETE and INSERT run in **one statement and one transaction**. The archive only ever receives what RETURNING passed along.

production.title: Idempotent stock ingestion for a warehouse feed
production.context: A warehouse system receives a CSV of stock deltas every five minutes. It loads them into a staging table with `COPY`, then applies them to `inventory(sku PK, qty)`.
production.problem: The first version ran SELECT, then INSERT or UPDATE, row by row. Two overlapping runs both saw "no row" for a new SKU and one failed with a unique violation. Feeds with the same SKU twice also crashed an `ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE` rewrite with `ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE command cannot affect row a second time`.
production.solution: Aggregate the staging rows per SKU first, so each key appears once, then apply them with one atomic upsert. Use RETURNING to write an audit row with the before and after quantities in the same statement.
production.outcome: One statement per batch, no read-then-write race (ON CONFLICT guarantees an atomic insert-or-update), and a complete audit trail. Expect gaps in `inventory.id`: every conflicting row still consumed a sequence value. That is harmless for a surrogate key.

pitfalls.title: Expecting gapless ids from a sequence
pitfalls.symptom: Invoice numbers jump from 1041 to 1043 and auditors ask where 1042 went.
pitfalls.cause: `nextval` is never rolled back. Aborted transactions, failed constraint checks, upserts that hit a conflict and crashes all consume values.
pitfalls.fix: Use identity/sequence values only as surrogate keys. If you need a gapless business number, allocate it from a counter row updated inside the same transaction (`UPDATE counters SET n = n + 1 … RETURNING n`), and accept that this serializes writers.

pitfalls.title: UPDATE … FROM silently picks one match
pitfalls.symptom: A price sync from a feed with duplicate SKUs leaves random prices: re-running it gives different results.
pitfalls.cause: When a target row joins to several FROM rows, UPDATE applies **one** of them, and which one is not predictable. No error is raised.
pitfalls.fix: Deduplicate the source first (`DISTINCT ON (sku) … ORDER BY sku, updated_at DESC`), or use MERGE, which raises a cardinality violation instead of guessing.

pitfalls.title: One huge UPDATE bloats the table
pitfalls.symptom: After `UPDATE events SET processed = true` on 50 M rows, the table doubles in size and replicas lag for an hour.
pitfalls.cause: Every updated row writes a **new version**, and the old ones stay until VACUUM. One statement also holds its row locks to the end.
pitfalls.fix: Batch it: a CTE selects `ctid`s with `ORDER BY … FOR UPDATE LIMIT 5000`, the UPDATE joins on `ctid`, and the loop repeats with VACUUM between batches.
pitfalls.sql:
WITH batch AS (
  SELECT ctid FROM events WHERE NOT processed
  ORDER BY id FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED LIMIT 5000)
UPDATE events e SET processed = true
FROM batch WHERE e.ctid = batch.ctid;

pitfalls.title: UPDATE or DELETE without WHERE
pitfalls.symptom: A one-row fix reports `UPDATE 4` (or `UPDATE 50000`) and every row now has the same value.
pitfalls.cause: Without WHERE the statement applies to every row. The command tag is the only warning, and with autocommit the change is already committed when you read it.
pitfalls.fix: Run ad-hoc fixes inside `BEGIN`, check the tag (and `RETURNING`), then COMMIT or ROLLBACK. Write the WHERE clause first.

pitfalls.title: Get-or-create with a no-op DO UPDATE
pitfalls.symptom: A "find or insert" endpoint makes a hot table bloat, although almost every call finds an existing row.
pitfalls.cause: `ON CONFLICT (email) DO UPDATE SET email = EXCLUDED.email RETURNING id` returns the row, but every call writes a **new row version** (new ctid, a dead tuple, WAL, maybe index entries) and burns a sequence value.
pitfalls.fix: Use `DO NOTHING RETURNING id` and fall back to a SELECT when nothing came back. Under concurrency the fallback SELECT can miss a row committed after the statement's snapshot, so retry once.
pitfalls.sql:
WITH ins AS (
  INSERT INTO users (email) VALUES ($1)
  ON CONFLICT (email) DO NOTHING RETURNING id)
SELECT id FROM ins
UNION ALL
SELECT id FROM users WHERE email = $1 AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM ins);

pitfalls.title: Treating MERGE as a concurrency-safe upsert
pitfalls.symptom: Two sessions MERGE the same new key at once and one fails with a unique violation.
pitfalls.cause: A common claim is that MERGE and upsert are equivalent. They are not under concurrency. MERGE follows the normal isolation rules: both sessions see NOT MATCHED and both INSERT. Only `INSERT … ON CONFLICT` re-checks the arbiter index and switches to UPDATE.
pitfalls.fix: Use `INSERT … ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE` for concurrent upserts. Use MERGE for batch synchronisation, where you need DELETE or `NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE`.

pointers: INSERT writes a tuple, DELETE sets its **xmax**, UPDATE does both: the old version stays until VACUUM.
`RETURNING` works on all four commands; PostgreSQL 18 adds `old.*` and `new.*` (old is NULL for INSERT, new is NULL for DELETE).
`ON CONFLICT (cols)` infers its **arbiter** unique index; `EXCLUDED` is the proposed row; DO UPDATE never touches one row twice.
MERGE gives each candidate row one status and runs the **first** matching WHEN clause; `merge_action()` tells you which.
Sequences are **not gapless**: upserts, failed inserts and rollbacks all burn values.

lessons.title: Joins, visualized
tldr: A join pairs rows from two inputs wherever the **join condition is true**, and outer joins then add back the unmatched rows **NULL-extended**, while semi- and anti-joins only ask whether a match exists.
Joins are how a normalized schema is read back, and the exact rules (NULL never equals NULL, ON filters before the join and WHERE after it) decide whether a report is right or silently wrong.

visualizer.title: The join matcher
visualizer.caption: Pick a join type and a filter placement, then step through each left row. Badges show the ON condition in three-valued logic. Compare **LEFT + ON filter** (4 rows) with **LEFT + WHERE filter** (2 rows).

presets.label: Row counts per join type
presets.sql:
SELECT 'inner' AS join_type, count(*) FROM teams t JOIN players p ON p.team_id = t.id
UNION ALL SELECT 'left',  count(*) FROM teams t LEFT JOIN  players p ON p.team_id = t.id
UNION ALL SELECT 'right', count(*) FROM teams t RIGHT JOIN players p ON p.team_id = t.id
UNION ALL SELECT 'full',  count(*) FROM teams t FULL JOIN  players p ON p.team_id = t.id
UNION ALL SELECT 'cross', count(*) FROM teams t CROSS JOIN players p;
presets.note: 3, 5, 5, 7, 20: the same numbers the visualizer ends on. Dee and Eli (team_id NULL) never match, because `NULL = 1` is NULL, not true.

presets.label: ON vs WHERE
presets.sql:
SELECT t.name, p.name AS player
FROM teams t LEFT JOIN players p ON p.team_id = t.id AND p.active
ORDER BY t.id;

SELECT t.name, p.name AS player
FROM teams t LEFT JOIN players p ON p.team_id = t.id
WHERE p.active
ORDER BY t.id;
presets.note: First query: 4 rows, Bears and Wolves kept with NULL players. Second: 2 rows. A WHERE test on the nullable side throws away the NULL-extended rows.

presets.label: Anti-join: find orphans
presets.note: Both return Bears and Wolves, and the second plans as a **Hash Right Anti Join** (an anti-join that hashes the left side). Test a NOT NULL column (`p.id`) for IS NULL, never a nullable one.

presets.label: USING vs NATURAL
presets.note: `USING (player_id)` prints the join column once. `NATURAL JOIN` joins on **every** same-named column: here `id = id AND name = name`, which never holds, so 0 rows. A column added later can change any NATURAL join silently.

presets.label: Self-join: mentors and teammates
presets.note: The same table appears twice under two **aliases**. LEFT keeps Ana and Eli, who have no mentor. For pairs, `a.id <> b.id` returns (Ana, Ben) and (Ben, Ana); `a.id < b.id` keeps one of each.

presets.label: Fan-out double counting
presets.sql:
-- WRONG: joining two child tables multiplies rows
SELECT t.name, count(p.id) AS players, count(g.player_id) AS goals
FROM teams t
LEFT JOIN players p ON p.team_id = t.id
LEFT JOIN goals g ON g.player_id = p.id
GROUP BY t.name ORDER BY t.name;

-- RIGHT: aggregate each child before joining
SELECT t.name,
       (SELECT count(*) FROM players p WHERE p.team_id = t.id) AS players,
       (SELECT count(*) FROM goals g JOIN players p ON p.id = g.player_id WHERE p.team_id = t.id) AS goals
FROM teams t ORDER BY t.name;
presets.note: The first query says Lions have 4 players: Ana is counted once per goal. The second gives 2 players and 3 goals.

presets.label: Diff two tables: EXCEPT vs FULL JOIN
presets.sql:
-- rows present on one side only (parentheses matter, see pitfalls)
(SELECT 'only in 2025' AS side, * FROM squad_2025
 EXCEPT SELECT 'only in 2025', * FROM squad_2026)
UNION ALL
(SELECT 'only in 2026', * FROM squad_2026
 EXCEPT SELECT 'only in 2026', * FROM squad_2025)
ORDER BY id, side;

-- FULL JOIN on the key says what kind of change it is
SELECT coalesce(a.id, b.id) AS id, a.position AS was, b.position AS now,
       CASE WHEN a.id IS NULL THEN 'added'
            WHEN b.id IS NULL THEN 'removed' ELSE 'changed' END AS change
FROM squad_2025 a FULL JOIN squad_2026 b ON b.id = a.id
WHERE a.id IS NULL OR b.id IS NULL
   OR (a.name, a.position) IS DISTINCT FROM (b.name, b.position)
ORDER BY 1;

-- joining on every column: NULL never matches, so Dee looks changed
SELECT id, name, position
FROM squad_2025 FULL JOIN squad_2026 USING (id, name, position)
WHERE squad_2025.id IS NULL OR squad_2026.id IS NULL ORDER BY id;
presets.note: EXCEPT compares whole rows and treats NULLs as **equal**: 4 rows (Ben's old and new version, Cy, Fay), and Dee (position NULL in both years) is not reported. The keyed FULL JOIN returns 3 rows: Ben changed, Cy removed, Fay added. Joining on all columns reports Dee twice, because `NULL = NULL` is not true. Only `IS DISTINCT FROM` compares NULLs the way EXCEPT does.

production.title: A churn report that lost every quiet customer
production.context: A subscription team reports customers and their orders this month: `customers LEFT JOIN orders`, so customers with no orders should show 0.
production.problem: Someone added `WHERE o.created_at >= date_trunc('month', now())` to restrict the month. The report dropped from 12,400 customers to 8,100. The 4,300 missing customers were exactly the ones with no orders, the at-risk group the report existed to find.
production.solution: Move the restriction on the nullable side into the ON clause, so it decides which orders match instead of filtering joined rows. Count a column from the right side, so unmatched customers count 0.
production.sql:
SELECT c.id, c.name, count(o.id) AS orders_this_month
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o
  ON o.customer_id = c.id
 AND o.created_at >= date_trunc('month', now())
GROUP BY c.id, c.name;
production.outcome: Every customer appears again, with 0 for the quiet ones. The rule to remember: a WHERE predicate that is not true for NULL turns a LEFT JOIN into an inner join.

pitfalls.title: Filtering the nullable side in WHERE
pitfalls.symptom: A LEFT JOIN returns exactly the same rows as an inner join.
pitfalls.cause: WHERE runs after the join. NULL-extended rows have NULL in every right-side column, and `NULL = x` or `NULL > x` is not true, so they are removed.
pitfalls.fix: Put right-side restrictions in the `ON` clause. Keep `WHERE` for left-side filters and for deliberate `IS NULL` anti-join tests.

pitfalls.title: NATURAL JOIN after a schema change
pitfalls.symptom: A report that worked for years suddenly returns zero rows after a migration added `updated_at` to two tables.
pitfalls.cause: `NATURAL` joins on **all** same-named columns, so the new column became part of the join condition.
pitfalls.fix: Write `USING (col)` or an explicit `ON`. Both survive unrelated column additions.

pitfalls.title: Fan-out inflates aggregates
pitfalls.symptom: Revenue per customer is 3× too high after joining orders and support tickets in one query.
pitfalls.cause: Joining one parent to two independent child tables produces every combination of child rows (m × n per parent).
pitfalls.fix: Aggregate each child in a subquery or LATERAL first, then join the totals. Or use `count(DISTINCT …)` when that is truly what you mean.

pitfalls.title: Expecting NULL keys to match
pitfalls.symptom: Rows with a NULL `region` vanish from a join that compares `a.region = b.region`.
pitfalls.cause: NULL compared with anything, NULL included, is NULL. Join conditions keep only true pairs.
pitfalls.fix: Use `a.region IS NOT DISTINCT FROM b.region` if NULLs should pair up, knowing it cannot use a plain hash or merge join as efficiently.

pitfalls.title: Set operators without parentheses
pitfalls.symptom: A "differences in both directions" query built from EXCEPT and UNION misses or keeps the wrong rows.
pitfalls.cause: `UNION` and `EXCEPT` have the **same precedence** and group left to right (`INTERSECT` binds tighter). `A EXCEPT B UNION C EXCEPT D` means `((A EXCEPT B) UNION C) EXCEPT D`.
pitfalls.fix: Parenthesize each side: `(A EXCEPT B) UNION ALL (C EXCEPT D)`. Use UNION ALL when the two halves cannot overlap.
pitfalls.sql:
SELECT 'x' UNION SELECT 'y' EXCEPT SELECT 'x';    -- y
SELECT 'x' UNION (SELECT 'y' EXCEPT SELECT 'x');  -- x, y

pitfalls.title: A self-join that lists every pair twice
pitfalls.symptom: A "duplicate customers" report shows (A, B) and (B, A), and its count is double the real number.
pitfalls.cause: `ON a.id <> b.id` is true in both directions, so each unordered pair appears twice.
pitfalls.fix: Use `ON a.id < b.id` to keep each pair once (and never pair a row with itself).

pointers: INNER keeps pairs where ON is **true**; LEFT/RIGHT/FULL add unmatched rows **NULL-extended**; CROSS is N × M.
ON decides *matching*; WHERE filters *after* the join. They differ only for outer joins.
`NULL = NULL` is NULL, so NULL keys never join. Use `IS NOT DISTINCT FROM` deliberately.
`EXISTS` / `NOT EXISTS` are **semi- and anti-joins**: they never duplicate the left row.
Prefer `USING` or `ON` over `NATURAL`; join algorithms (nested loop, hash, merge) are covered in m4.

lessons.title: Subqueries: scalar, IN, EXISTS, ANY/ALL
tldr: A subquery is a query nested inside another: a **scalar** subquery yields one value, while `IN`, `EXISTS`, `ANY` and `ALL` turn a whole row set into a true, false or NULL test.

They let you ask "is there a matching row?" directly, and the planner rewrites most of them into semi- and anti-joins, except `NOT IN`, whose NULL rules make it both slower and a classic source of empty results.

visualizer.title: NOT IN vs NOT EXISTS, one row at a time
visualizer.caption: Pick an operator and step through the customers. Each comparison is shown in three-valued logic. Start with **NOT IN** and the NULL present, then flip to **NOT EXISTS**.

presets.label: The NOT IN trap
presets.note: 0 vs 1,713. One refund row with a NULL `customer_id` makes every NOT IN test NULL. Filtering the NULLs out, or using NOT EXISTS, gives the right answer.

presets.label: Three-valued truth table
presets.sql:
SELECT 1 IN (2, NULL)         AS in_null,
       2 IN (2, NULL)         AS in_hit,
       1 NOT IN (2, NULL)     AS not_in_null,
       2 NOT IN (2, NULL)     AS not_in_hit,
       NULL IN (SELECT 1 WHERE false)     AS null_in_empty,
       5 > ALL (SELECT 1 WHERE false)     AS all_empty,
       5 > ANY (SELECT 1 WHERE false)     AS any_empty,
       EXISTS (SELECT NULL)               AS exists_null_row;
presets.note: NULL when nothing matches and a NULL is present; true or false when a match decides it. Against an empty set, IN and ANY are false and ALL is true, even for a NULL left side. EXISTS is true for a row of NULLs.

presets.label: Plans: semi, anti, SubPlan
presets.note: IN becomes a **Semi Join**, NOT EXISTS an **Anti Join**. NOT IN stays a Filter with a hashed SubPlan, which the planner cannot reorder.

presets.label: Scalar subqueries
presets.sql:
-- correlated scalar subquery: one value per outer row
SELECT c.name,
       (SELECT sum(amount) FROM refunds r WHERE r.customer_id = c.id) AS refunded
FROM customers c WHERE c.id <= 4 ORDER BY c.id;

-- more than one row is a runtime error; zero rows is NULL
SELECT try_sql('SELECT (SELECT customer_id FROM refunds WHERE amount > 10)') AS too_many,
       (SELECT customer_id FROM refunds WHERE amount > 1000) AS zero_rows;
presets.note: Ava gets NULL (no rows, not 0). A scalar subquery that returns 2+ rows fails with SQLSTATE `21000` only when it runs, so it can pass tests on small data.

presets.label: ANY / ALL with arrays
presets.note: `= ANY(array)` is the parameter-friendly form of IN: one bind parameter instead of a list. `>= ALL` finds the rows that are at least every value.

presets.label: ANY / ALL are min / max in disguise
presets.sql:
SELECT min(salary) AS lowest_manager, max(salary) AS highest_manager FROM managers;

SELECT '> ALL' AS test, string_agg(name, ', ' ORDER BY salary DESC) AS staff
FROM staff WHERE salary > ALL (SELECT salary FROM managers)
UNION ALL
SELECT '> ANY', string_agg(name, ', ' ORDER BY salary DESC)
FROM staff WHERE salary > ANY (SELECT salary FROM managers)
UNION ALL
SELECT '= ANY', string_agg(name, ', ')
FROM staff WHERE salary = ANY (SELECT salary FROM managers)
UNION ALL
SELECT '< ALL', count(*)::text FROM staff WHERE salary < ALL (SELECT salary FROM managers)
UNION ALL
SELECT '< ANY', count(*)::text FROM staff WHERE salary < ANY (SELECT salary FROM managers);
presets.note: Managers earn 55,000 to 60,000. `> ALL` means above the **highest** (only Bob). `> ANY` means above the **lowest** (Bob, Liam, Jack). `= ANY` is IN (Charlie). `< ALL` is below the lowest (8 people), `< ANY` below the highest (11). `SOME` is a synonym for ANY.

presets.label: Correlated subquery vs window
presets.sql:
-- refunds above their customer's country average: a SubPlan per row
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, COSTS OFF, TIMING OFF, BUFFERS OFF, SUMMARY OFF)
SELECT r.id, r.amount FROM refunds r JOIN customers c ON c.id = r.customer_id
WHERE r.amount > (SELECT avg(r2.amount) FROM refunds r2
                  JOIN customers c2 ON c2.id = r2.customer_id
                  WHERE c2.country = c.country);

-- the same answer from one pass
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, COSTS OFF, TIMING OFF, BUFFERS OFF, SUMMARY OFF)
SELECT id, amount FROM (
  SELECT r.id, r.amount, avg(r.amount) OVER (PARTITION BY c.country) AS country_avg
  FROM refunds r JOIN customers c ON c.id = r.customer_id) x
WHERE amount > country_avg;
presets.note: The first plan shows `SubPlan 1` with `loops=287`, one per joined refund: the inner join and average run again for every row. The window version joins once, sorts once and computes every country average in one **WindowAgg**. Both return the same 143 rows.

presets.label: Subquery in FROM
presets.sql:
SELECT country, round(avg(total), 2) AS avg_refunded
FROM (SELECT c.country, sum(r.amount) AS total
      FROM customers c JOIN refunds r ON r.customer_id = c.id
      GROUP BY c.id, c.country) AS per_customer
GROUP BY country ORDER BY country;
presets.note: A derived table: aggregate per customer first, then average per country. The planner may flatten simple FROM subqueries into the outer query.

production.title: A suppression list that suppressed everyone
production.context: A marketing job emails customers who are **not** on an unsubscribe list: `WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT customer_id FROM unsubscribes)`.
production.problem: One day the campaign sent zero emails. A new import path had written a single unsubscribe row with `customer_id` NULL (the address could not be linked). From then on every `NOT IN` test was NULL, and the query returned nothing. No error and no warning.
production.solution: Rewrite as NOT EXISTS, which only asks whether an equal row exists, and constrain the column so the bad row cannot be written again.
production.outcome: Correct results whatever the list contains. The plan changes from a filter with a hashed SubPlan to a Hash Anti Join, which the planner can reorder and which does not degrade to a per-row SubPlan when the list outgrows `work_mem`. With 2,000 customers and one NULL row in the list, the old query returns 0 rows and the new one 1,713.

pitfalls.title: NOT IN with a nullable column
pitfalls.symptom: An exclusion query suddenly returns zero rows, with no error.
pitfalls.cause: `x NOT IN (…)` is `x <> v1 AND x <> v2 AND …`. If any value is NULL and nothing equals x, the result is NULL, and WHERE drops the row.
pitfalls.fix: Use `NOT EXISTS`, or add `WHERE col IS NOT NULL` inside the subquery, and declare the column NOT NULL if NULL has no meaning.

pitfalls.title: Scalar subquery returning several rows
pitfalls.symptom: `ERROR: more than one row returned by a subquery used as an expression` in production, never in tests.
pitfalls.cause: A scalar subquery must return at most one row. The check happens at run time, so it only fails once the data has duplicates.
pitfalls.fix: Make the subquery provably single-row (aggregate, `LIMIT 1` with an `ORDER BY`, or a unique key in the WHERE), or turn it into a join or LATERAL.

pitfalls.title: Correlated subquery in the select list on a big table
pitfalls.symptom: A report with `(SELECT sum(…) WHERE r.customer_id = c.id)` per row runs for minutes.
pitfalls.cause: A common belief is that a subquery runs once, before the outer query. That holds only for an uncorrelated one (an **InitPlan**). A correlated scalar subquery is a **SubPlan** that runs once per outer row, and the planner does not turn it into a join.
pitfalls.fix: Aggregate once and join (`LEFT JOIN (SELECT customer_id, sum(amount) … GROUP BY 1)`), use a window function (`avg(x) OVER (PARTITION BY key)`), or index the correlation column. Check `loops=` in EXPLAIN ANALYZE.

pitfalls.title: Side effects inside EXISTS
pitfalls.symptom: A `nextval()` or logging function inside an EXISTS subquery runs a different number of times than expected.
pitfalls.cause: EXISTS stops at the **first** row, and the planner may turn it into a join. How often the inner expressions run is not defined.
pitfalls.fix: Keep subqueries side-effect free. Do writes in data-modifying CTEs or separate statements.

pointers: `EXISTS` is true if at least one row comes back and is **never NULL**; the select list inside it does not matter.
`IN` = `= ANY`, `NOT IN` = `<> ALL`. With a NULL in the list and no match, both give **NULL**.
Empty subquery: `IN`/`ANY` → false, `NOT IN`/`ALL` → true.
A scalar subquery with 0 rows is NULL; with 2+ rows it is an **error**.
IN/EXISTS plan as **semi-joins**, NOT EXISTS as an **anti-join**; NOT IN stays a SubPlan filter.

lessons.title: CTEs: inlined vs MATERIALIZED
tldr: A **common table expression** (`WITH name AS (…)`) names a subquery for one statement, and since PostgreSQL 12 the planner **inlines** it when it is referenced once and has no side effects, otherwise it **materializes** it once.

CTEs exist to make complex queries readable and to chain data-modifying steps in one statement, and the `MATERIALIZED` / `NOT MATERIALIZED` keywords let you decide when the planner may see through them.

visualizer.title: One CTE, five plans
visualizer.caption: Step through the same CTE planned five ways, then a data-modifying CTE. Watch rows read and shared buffers per plan: the same 20,000-row table, five very different amounts of work.

presets.label: Inlined (default)
presets.note: No CTE node at all: the plan is a Bitmap Index Scan, exactly as if you wrote `SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 42`.

presets.label: MATERIALIZED fence
presets.note: A `CTE c` subplan scans all 20,000 rows into a tuplestore (`Storage: Memory`), then `CTE Scan` filters. Shared hits go from about 42 to 128.

presets.label: Two references
presets.note: Default: CTE Scan twice over a materialized copy (128 buffers). NOT MATERIALIZED: a Nested Loop of two primary-key Index Scans (6 buffers).

presets.label: When materializing wins
presets.sql:
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, COSTS OFF, TIMING OFF)
WITH totals AS MATERIALIZED (
  SELECT customer_id, sum(amount) AS total FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id)
SELECT a.customer_id, a.total
FROM totals a JOIN totals b ON b.total = a.total AND b.customer_id <> a.customer_id
ORDER BY 1 LIMIT 5;
presets.note: The expensive aggregate runs **once** (one HashAggregate over 20,000 rows) and both references read the 500-row result. Inlining would aggregate twice.

presets.label: Same snapshot
presets.note: Inside the statement the table still shows 1.99, RETURNING shows 3.98, and the next statement sees 3.98. Sub-statements cannot see each other's writes.

presets.label: Move rows atomically
presets.note: DELETE and INSERT commit together or not at all. Seven days of orders move: 468 rows, leaving 19,532.

presets.label: Parent and children in one statement
presets.sql:
-- an invoice for Mary plus two line items: no id round trip
WITH new_invoice AS (
  INSERT INTO invoices (customer_id)
  SELECT customer_id FROM customers WHERE name = 'Mary'
  RETURNING invoice_id
)
INSERT INTO items (invoice_id, name)
SELECT ni.invoice_id, v.name
FROM new_invoice ni
CROSS JOIN (VALUES ('Purple Automobile'), ('Yellow Automobile')) AS v(name)
RETURNING invoice_id, item_id, name;

-- three levels deep: a new customer, an invoice, an item
WITH c AS (INSERT INTO customers (name) VALUES ('Ann') RETURNING customer_id),
     inv AS (INSERT INTO invoices (customer_id) SELECT customer_id FROM c RETURNING invoice_id)
INSERT INTO items (invoice_id, name)
SELECT invoice_id, 'Red Train' FROM inv
RETURNING *;

SELECT c.name, count(DISTINCT i.invoice_id) AS invoices, count(it.item_id) AS items
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN invoices i USING (customer_id)
LEFT JOIN items it USING (invoice_id)
GROUP BY c.name ORDER BY c.name;
presets.note: The generated `invoice_id` flows from one INSERT to the next through RETURNING, never back to the client. The foreign keys are checked at the end of the statement, so the child rows may reference a parent inserted in a sibling CTE. If any part fails, nothing is written.

production.title: Removing CTE fences from a multi-tenant dashboard
production.context: A reporting service wrote every query as a chain of CTEs, then filtered the last one by tenant: `WITH base AS (SELECT … FROM events) … SELECT … FROM base WHERE tenant_id = $1`.
production.problem: On PostgreSQL 11 every CTE was an optimization fence. Each request scanned and materialized all tenants' events, then threw away 99% of them. Someone had also added `MATERIALIZED` everywhere "for safety" while preparing the upgrade, which kept the old behaviour.
production.solution: Remove the blanket `MATERIALIZED`. Single-reference CTEs are then inlined, so the tenant filter is pushed into the scan and uses the `(tenant_id, created_at)` index. Keep `MATERIALIZED` only on the one CTE that is referenced several times and is expensive, and check each plan with EXPLAIN.
production.outcome: At 20,000 rows the gap is already 42 shared buffers inlined vs 128 materialized for one customer. The materialized cost grows with the whole table while the inlined cost grows only with one tenant's rows, so the saving grows with the number of tenants in the table.

pitfalls.title: Using a CTE as a "temporary table" for speed
pitfalls.symptom: Moving a subquery into a CTE "so it is computed once" makes no difference, or makes it slower.
pitfalls.cause: A common claim is that a CTE is calculated once and reused. Since PostgreSQL 12 a single-reference CTE is simply inlined: it is not computed separately at all. Materializing only happens with 2+ references, side effects, recursion or `MATERIALIZED`.
pitfalls.fix: Decide with EXPLAIN. If you need computed-once semantics for an expensive or volatile expression, write `AS MATERIALIZED` explicitly.

pitfalls.title: A fence left behind by an old query
pitfalls.symptom: A query filters a CTE by a selective key but the plan shows `CTE Scan` with a huge `Rows Removed by Filter`.
pitfalls.cause: The CTE is referenced twice, is `MATERIALIZED`, or calls a volatile function, so the filter cannot be pushed down into it.
pitfalls.fix: Use `AS NOT MATERIALIZED` (if duplicated work is cheap), move the filter inside the CTE, or remove the volatile call.

pitfalls.title: Reading your own writes inside one statement
pitfalls.symptom: A query updates rows in one CTE and reads the table in another part of the statement, and sees the old values.
pitfalls.cause: All sub-statements run with **one snapshot**. Changes made by a data-modifying CTE are invisible to the rest of the statement, except through RETURNING.
pitfalls.fix: Pass data along with `RETURNING` and select from the CTE name, not from the table. Never modify the same row in two sub-statements: which change wins is unspecified.

pitfalls.title: ORDER BY inside the CTE
pitfalls.symptom: A report sorted inside `WITH ranked AS (… ORDER BY total DESC)` comes back unsorted after a harmless change, such as a join added to the outer query.
pitfalls.cause: Only the outermost ORDER BY defines the order of a result. An ORDER BY inside a CTE or subquery orders the rows that one step produces; a join, aggregate or parallel plan above it can reorder them.
pitfalls.fix: Sort in the outer query. Keep ORDER BY inside a CTE only where it feeds `LIMIT` or an order-sensitive step in that same CTE.

pointers: Default: a side-effect-free, non-recursive CTE referenced **once** is **inlined**; referenced 2+ times it is **materialized** once.
`AS MATERIALIZED` forces a fence; `AS NOT MATERIALIZED` forces inlining of every reference.
Volatile functions, data-modifying statements and recursion always materialize.
Data-modifying CTEs run once, to completion, on the **same snapshot**; use RETURNING to pass rows on.
In EXPLAIN, a `CTE Scan` node means materialized; no CTE node means inlined.

lessons.title: Recursive CTEs
tldr: A `WITH RECURSIVE` query is a non-recursive term `UNION [ALL]` a recursive term, evaluated **iteratively**: each pass feeds only the previous pass's new rows (the **working table**) back into the recursive term until no new rows appear.
It is how SQL walks trees and graphs of unknown depth (org charts, bills of materials, routes) in one statement, and the `CYCLE` and `SEARCH` clauses make loops and ordering explicit.

visualizer.title: Working table, intermediate table, result
visualizer.caption: Step through the algorithm one pass at a time. Start with the org chart, then switch to the graph and compare **UNION ALL** (runs forever), **UNION** and the **CYCLE** clause.

presets.label: Everyone under Raj
presets.sql:
WITH RECURSIVE sub AS (
  SELECT id, name, manager_id, 0 AS depth FROM employees WHERE id = 2
  UNION ALL            -- recursive term:
  SELECT e.id, e.name, e.manager_id, s.depth + 1
  FROM employees e JOIN sub s ON e.manager_id = s.id
)
SELECT * FROM sub;
presets.note: 6 rows in four passes: Raj (depth 0), Omar and Ivy, Zoe and Kai, then Noor. The fifth pass finds nobody and the loop stops.

presets.label: Self-join: one level per join
presets.sql:
-- a self-join reaches exactly as deep as you write joins
SELECT m.name AS manager, e.name AS direct, e2.name AS second_level
FROM employees m
JOIN employees e ON e.manager_id = m.id
LEFT JOIN employees e2 ON e2.manager_id = e.id
WHERE m.name = 'Raj';

-- recursion reaches every level; count what each pass added
WITH RECURSIVE sub AS (
  SELECT id, name, 0 AS depth FROM employees WHERE id = 2
  UNION ALL
  SELECT e.id, e.name, s.depth + 1 FROM employees e JOIN sub s ON e.manager_id = s.id
)
SELECT depth AS pass, count(*) AS rows_added, string_agg(name, ', ' ORDER BY name) AS who
FROM sub GROUP BY depth ORDER BY depth;

EXPLAIN (COSTS OFF)
WITH RECURSIVE sub AS (
  SELECT id, name FROM employees WHERE id = 2
  UNION ALL
  SELECT e.id, e.name FROM employees e JOIN sub s ON e.manager_id = s.id
)
SELECT * FROM sub;
presets.note: Two joins find Omar, Ivy, Zoe and Kai, and miss Noor on level 3. The recursive version adds 1, 2, 2, 1 rows per pass and stops when a pass adds nothing. In the plan, **Recursive Union** runs the recursive term against a **WorkTable Scan**: the previous pass's rows only.

presets.label: Path to the top
presets.sql:
WITH RECURSIVE up AS (
  SELECT id, name, manager_id, name::text AS chain FROM employees WHERE name = 'Noor'
  UNION ALL
  SELECT m.id, m.name, m.manager_id, up.chain || ' → ' || m.name
  FROM employees m JOIN up ON m.id = up.manager_id
)
SELECT chain FROM up WHERE manager_id IS NULL;
presets.note: Walking **upwards** is the same algorithm with the join reversed: Noor → Zoe → Omar → Raj → Maya.

presets.label: SEARCH DEPTH / BREADTH FIRST
presets.note: `SEARCH DEPTH FIRST` adds an `ord` column (the path of ids) to sort by, giving an indented outline. Use `SEARCH BREADTH FIRST` to order level by level. Never rely on the natural output order.

presets.label: CYCLE detection
presets.note: 5 rows. The row that returns to A has `is_cycle = true` and is not expanded. Without the CYCLE clause this query never terminates.

presets.label: UNION vs UNION ALL
presets.note: With only `node`, UNION discards the repeat of A and stops after 4 rows. Add `hops` and no row ever repeats, so UNION no longer protects you. The LIMIT works only because the outer query stops fetching.

presets.label: A calendar without gaps
presets.note: A counter with a stop condition in WHERE. For plain series, `generate_series` is simpler and faster.

production.title: Expanding a bill of materials for a manufacturer
production.context: A manufacturing app stores `parts(assembly_id, component_id, quantity)`: a bike has wheels, a wheel has spokes. Purchasing needs the total of every leaf component for an order of 50 bikes.
production.problem: The application walked the tree with one query per level. A deep product took 9 round trips, and a data-entry error that made an assembly contain itself sent the loop spinning until the request timed out.
production.solution: One recursive CTE multiplies quantities down the tree, and `CYCLE` turns a bad self-reference into a flagged row instead of an infinite loop.
production.sql:
WITH RECURSIVE bom AS (
  SELECT component_id, quantity * 50 AS qty
  FROM parts WHERE assembly_id = 'bike'
  UNION ALL
  SELECT p.component_id, p.quantity * b.qty
  FROM parts p JOIN bom b ON p.assembly_id = b.component_id
) CYCLE component_id SET is_cycle USING path
SELECT component_id, sum(qty) AS total
FROM bom WHERE NOT is_cycle
GROUP BY component_id;
production.outcome: One round trip whatever the depth, and a cyclic definition terminates with `is_cycle = true` rows that a check can alert on. Add an index on `parts(assembly_id)`: the recursive term joins the working table to it once per level.

pitfalls.title: Infinite recursion on cyclic data
pitfalls.symptom: A recursive query on a graph never returns and memory or temp files keep growing.
pitfalls.cause: With UNION ALL, or with a column like depth or path that makes every row unique, the working table never empties.
pitfalls.fix: Add `CYCLE col SET is_cycle USING path`, or a depth limit in the recursive term (`WHERE depth < 20`). Do not rely on a LIMIT in the outer query: it stops working as soon as the outer query sorts or joins.

pitfalls.title: Relying on breadth-first output order
pitfalls.symptom: An indented tree prints in the right order in tests and scrambled in production.
pitfalls.cause: The algorithm happens to emit rows level by level, but that is an implementation detail, not a guarantee, and order within a level is undefined.
pitfalls.fix: Add `SEARCH DEPTH FIRST BY id SET ord` (or BREADTH FIRST) and `ORDER BY ord` in the outer query.

pitfalls.title: Expecting UNION to stop a loop
pitfalls.symptom: Switching UNION ALL to UNION did not fix the runaway query.
pitfalls.cause: UNION only discards rows that are **entirely** duplicates. A hops or path column makes each lap a new row.
pitfalls.fix: Track visited nodes explicitly with `CYCLE`, or keep the CTE's columns to the node key only when that is all you need.

pitfalls.title: Anchor and recursive term with columns in a different order
pitfalls.symptom: A recursive query returns plausible-looking but wrong rows, or never terminates.
pitfalls.cause: The two terms are combined like a UNION: columns match by **position**, not by name or alias. If the recursive term lists `(manager_id, id)` while the anchor lists `(id, manager_id)`, the values swap on every pass. When the types agree there is no error.
pitfalls.fix: Name the CTE columns once (`WITH RECURSIVE sub(id, manager_id) AS …`) and list them in the same order in both terms.
pitfalls.sql:
-- swapped: returns (2,1), (2,4), (2,5): Raj three times, nobody below him
WITH RECURSIVE sub(id, boss) AS (
  SELECT id, manager_id FROM employees WHERE id = 2
  UNION
  SELECT e.manager_id, e.id FROM employees e JOIN sub s ON e.manager_id = s.id)
SELECT * FROM sub;

pointers: Shape: **non-recursive term** `UNION [ALL]` **recursive term**; only the recursive term may reference the CTE, once.
Each pass reads only the **working table** (last pass's new rows); recursion ends when a pass produces nothing.
UNION drops rows that duplicate **any earlier row**; UNION ALL keeps everything.
`CYCLE col SET is_cycle USING path` stops loops; `SEARCH DEPTH|BREADTH FIRST BY col SET ord` gives a sortable order.
Recursive CTEs are always materialized; data-modifying statements cannot be recursive.

lessons.title: Window functions and frames
tldr: A **window function** computes a value for every row from a set of related rows (its partition, and for aggregates and value functions a **frame** inside it), without collapsing rows the way GROUP BY does.

It answers "compared with its neighbours" questions in one pass: rankings, running totals, moving averages, previous-row deltas and top-N per group, where a self-join or correlated subquery would be slower and harder to read.

visualizer.title: The window frame explorer
visualizer.caption: Click a row to make it current, then change mode, bounds, offset and EXCLUDE. Start with **Default frame** on Sony VAIO (a three-way tie at 700), then compare **Running total**.

presets.label: Rows stay, unlike GROUP BY
presets.sql:
SELECT group_name, round(avg(price), 2) AS avg_price
FROM products JOIN product_groups USING (group_id)
GROUP BY group_name ORDER BY group_name;

SELECT product_name, group_name, price,
       round(avg(price) OVER (PARTITION BY group_name), 2) AS group_avg
FROM products JOIN product_groups USING (group_id)
ORDER BY group_name, price;
presets.note: GROUP BY returns 3 rows. The window version returns all 11, each with its group's average attached (Laptop 850, Smartphone 500, Tablet 350).

presets.label: Ranking with ties
presets.sql:
SELECT product_name, price,
       row_number() OVER w, rank() OVER w, dense_rank() OVER w,
       round((percent_rank() OVER w)::numeric, 2) AS pct_rank,
       round((cume_dist() OVER w)::numeric, 2) AS cume_dist,
       ntile(3) OVER w
FROM products JOIN product_groups USING (group_id)
WHERE group_name = 'Laptop'
WINDOW w AS (ORDER BY price);
presets.note: Lenovo and Sony tie at 700: row_number 1,2 (arbitrary order), rank 1,1,3,4 (gap), dense_rank 1,1,2,3 (no gap). `percent_rank` = (rank − 1) / (rows − 1), so the first row is always 0. `cume_dist` = rows up to the last peer / rows: 0.5 for both 700s. `ntile(3)` over 4 rows makes buckets of 2, 1, 1: bigger buckets come first.

presets.label: The default frame trap
presets.sql:
SELECT product_name, price,
       sum(price) OVER (ORDER BY price) AS range_default,
       sum(price) OVER (ORDER BY price ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING) AS rows_running,
       last_value(product_name) OVER (ORDER BY price) AS last_default,
       last_value(product_name) OVER (ORDER BY price
         ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING) AS last_whole
FROM products ORDER BY price, product_id;
presets.note: All three 700 rows show `range_default` = 3550 (peers share the frame end), while `rows_running` differs across them, in an order PostgreSQL does not guarantee. `last_default` is just the current row's last peer; `last_whole` is HP Elite everywhere.

presets.label: Cheapest per group
presets.sql:
SELECT group_name, product_name, price
FROM (
  SELECT g.group_name, p.product_name, p.price,
         dense_rank() OVER (PARTITION BY g.group_name ORDER BY p.price) AS r
  FROM products p JOIN product_groups g USING (group_id)
) ranked
WHERE r = 1
ORDER BY group_name, product_name;
presets.note: Window functions run after WHERE, so filtering on the rank needs a subquery. dense_rank keeps **both** 700s in Laptop; row_number would silently pick one.

presets.label: LAG: year over year
presets.sql:
SELECT year, group_id, amount,
       lag(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY group_id ORDER BY year) AS prev,
       amount - lag(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY group_id ORDER BY year) AS delta
FROM sales ORDER BY group_id, year;
presets.note: The first year of each group has no previous row, so `lag` returns NULL (pass a third argument for a default). `lag` and `lead` ignore the frame. They look at the previous **row**, not the previous year: if 2019 were missing, 2020 would be compared with 2018. And with `ORDER BY year DESC`, `lag` returns the following year.

presets.label: Percent of total in one pass
presets.sql:
SELECT band, name, earnings,
       round(100 * earnings / sum(earnings) OVER (), 1) AS pct_of_all,
       round(100 * earnings / sum(earnings) OVER (PARTITION BY band), 1) AS pct_of_band
FROM musicians ORDER BY band, earnings DESC;

-- window over grouped rows: the inner sum is the aggregate, the outer one the window
SELECT band, sum(earnings) AS band_total,
       round(100 * sum(earnings) / sum(sum(earnings)) OVER (), 1) AS pct_of_all
FROM musicians GROUP BY band ORDER BY band;
presets.note: `sum(…) OVER ()` puts the grand total (20.8) on every row, so no CROSS JOIN to a total subquery is needed. Changing only the window to `PARTITION BY band` switches the denominator to the band total: Stills is 30.3% of all earnings but 48.5% of CSNY. The second query works because windows run **after** GROUP BY: CSNY 62.5%, PPM 37.5%.

presets.label: Fill gaps: last known value
presets.sql:
SELECT ts, temperature, grp,
       first_value(temperature) OVER (PARTITION BY sensor_id, grp ORDER BY ts) AS filled,
       lag(temperature) OVER (ORDER BY ts) AS naive_lag
FROM (
  SELECT *, count(temperature) OVER (PARTITION BY sensor_id ORDER BY ts) AS grp
  FROM sensor_readings
) s
ORDER BY ts;
presets.note: `count(temperature)` skips NULLs, so the running count only rises on a real reading: every NULL row inherits the group of the last reading. `first_value` within that group carries 22.50 forward twice and 23.10 once. A plain `lag` is no fix: after two NULLs in a row it returns NULL.

presets.label: Moving window: ROWS vs RANGE
presets.sql:
SELECT product_name, price,
       sum(price) OVER (ORDER BY price ROWS BETWEEN 1 PRECEDING AND 1 FOLLOWING) AS rows_1,
       sum(price) OVER (ORDER BY price RANGE BETWEEN 100 PRECEDING AND 100 FOLLOWING) AS range_100,
       sum(price) OVER (ORDER BY price GROUPS BETWEEN 1 PRECEDING AND 1 FOLLOWING EXCLUDE TIES) AS groups_1
FROM products ORDER BY price, product_id;
presets.note: Compare with the explorer's presets: ROWS counts rows, RANGE compares price values, GROUPS counts distinct prices.

production.title: Deduplicating a change-data feed: latest row per key
production.context: An analytics team receives a CDC feed into `customer_changes(customer_id, changed_at, payload)`, many rows per customer, and needs the current state of each customer every hour.
production.problem: The first query used a correlated subquery `WHERE changed_at = (SELECT max(changed_at) … WHERE customer_id = c.customer_id)`. It ran one subquery per row, and returned two rows when two changes shared a timestamp.
production.solution: Number the rows per customer with `row_number()` ordered by time and a tie-breaker, then keep number 1. One sort, one pass, exactly one row per key.
production.sql:
SELECT customer_id, changed_at, payload
FROM (
  SELECT *, row_number() OVER (
           PARTITION BY customer_id
           ORDER BY changed_at DESC, change_id DESC) AS rn
  FROM customer_changes
) x
WHERE rn = 1;
production.outcome: One scan and one sort instead of one subquery per row, and a deterministic answer when timestamps tie, thanks to the `change_id` tie-breaker. An index on `(customer_id, changed_at DESC, change_id DESC)` can provide the order and skip the sort.

pitfalls.title: last_value returns the current row
pitfalls.symptom: `last_value(price) OVER (PARTITION BY g ORDER BY price)` returns each row's own price instead of the group maximum.
pitfalls.cause: With ORDER BY, the default frame is `RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW`: it ends at the current row's last peer.
pitfalls.fix: Add `ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING`, or use `first_value(…)` with the ORDER BY reversed.

pitfalls.title: Running totals that jump on ties
pitfalls.symptom: A running balance shows the same total on two rows, then skips ahead.
pitfalls.cause: The default RANGE frame includes all **peers**, so rows with an equal ORDER BY value get the same sum.
pitfalls.fix: Use `ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING` and add a unique tie-breaker to the ORDER BY (`ORDER BY booked_at, id`) so the order is deterministic.

pitfalls.title: Filtering on a window function in WHERE
pitfalls.symptom: `ERROR: window functions are not allowed in WHERE`.
pitfalls.cause: Window functions are computed after WHERE, GROUP BY and HAVING, just before the final ORDER BY and LIMIT.
pitfalls.fix: Compute the window function in a subquery or CTE, then filter in the outer query.

pitfalls.title: A ROWS window treated as a time window
