pitfalls.symptom: A "7-day moving average" over daily rows is wrong after days with no data.
pitfalls.cause: `ROWS 6 PRECEDING` means six **rows**. Missing days silently stretch the window.
pitfalls.fix: Use `RANGE BETWEEN interval '6 days' PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW` on a date column, or fill the gaps with `generate_series` first.

pitfalls.title: DISTINCT does not deduplicate a row_number()
pitfalls.symptom: `SELECT DISTINCT price, row_number() OVER (ORDER BY price)` still returns every duplicate price.
pitfalls.cause: Window functions run **before** DISTINCT, and every row gets a different number, so no two output rows are equal.
pitfalls.fix: Deduplicate first, then number: `SELECT price, row_number() OVER (ORDER BY price) FROM (SELECT DISTINCT price FROM products) p` (8 rows instead of 11). Or use `dense_rank()`, which gives equal values the same number.

pitfalls.title: Top-N with LIMIT on a tie
pitfalls.symptom: "Top 4 products by price" shows Lenovo on one run and Sony or iPad on the next.
pitfalls.cause: Three products tie at 700 for the fourth place. `ORDER BY price DESC LIMIT 4` returns some 4 rows that satisfy the order; which tied row makes the cut is not defined.
pitfalls.fix: Add a unique tie-breaker (`ORDER BY price DESC, product_id`), or include every tie with `FETCH FIRST 4 ROWS WITH TIES` (6 rows here) or `rank() <= 4`.

pointers: Window functions run **after** WHERE/GROUP BY/HAVING and never collapse rows.
**Peers** are rows equal under the window ORDER BY; rank functions give peers the same value.
Default frame with ORDER BY: `RANGE UNBOUNDED PRECEDING` to the current row's **last peer**; without ORDER BY: the whole partition.
`ROWS` counts rows, `RANGE` compares values (one ORDER BY column for offsets), `GROUPS` counts peer groups; `EXCLUDE` trims the result.
Frames matter for aggregates and `first_value`/`last_value`/`nth_value`, not for `row_number`, `rank`, `lag` or `lead`.

lessons.title: LATERAL joins
tldr: A `LATERAL` subquery in FROM may reference columns of the FROM items to its left, so it is evaluated **once per outer row**, like the body of a for-each loop.
It exists for questions a plain join cannot express, such as "the latest N rows for each parent" or "expand this row's array", and with the right index it is often the fastest top-N-per-group plan.

visualizer.title: LATERAL as a for-each loop
visualizer.caption: Step through the outer rows and watch the subquery re-run with each `a.id`. Compare **CROSS JOIN LATERAL** (5 rows) with **LEFT JOIN LATERAL … ON true** (6 rows), and try the plain JOIN to see the error.

presets.label: Without LATERAL: an error
presets.sql:
SELECT try_sql($q$
  SELECT a.name, p.item
  FROM accounts a
  JOIN (SELECT * FROM purchases WHERE account_id = a.id) p ON true
$q$) AS result;
presets.note: `42P01: invalid reference to FROM-clause entry for table "a"`. A plain FROM subquery cannot see its neighbours.

presets.label: Latest 2 per account
presets.sql:
SELECT a.name, p.item, p.created_at
FROM accounts a
CROSS JOIN LATERAL (
  SELECT item, created_at FROM purchases
  WHERE account_id = a.id
  ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 2
) p
ORDER BY a.id, p.created_at DESC;
presets.note: 5 rows. Umbrella has no purchases, so CROSS JOIN LATERAL drops it.

presets.label: Keep empty parents
presets.sql:
SELECT a.name, p.item, p.created_at
FROM accounts a
LEFT JOIN LATERAL (
  SELECT item, created_at FROM purchases
  WHERE account_id = a.id
  ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 2
) p ON true
ORDER BY a.id, p.created_at DESC;
presets.note: 6 rows: Umbrella appears with NULLs. `ON true` is required syntax for LEFT JOIN; the real condition lives inside the subquery.

presets.label: loops=4 and the index
presets.note: A **Nested Loop** whose inner side shows `loops=4`. With the index the inner side is an Index Scan that reads at most 2 entries per account, no sort.

presets.label: Functions are implicitly lateral
presets.note: A set-returning function in FROM may always reference earlier items, with or without the keyword. `WITH ORDINALITY` adds a bigint position column. Initech has no tags: dropped by the comma form, kept by LEFT JOIN.

presets.label: Split a CSV column (and the text trap)
presets.sql:
-- hourly readings stored as one comma-separated string per station
SELECT w.station, max(t) AS max_reading, min(t) AS min_reading
FROM weather_data w, unnest(string_to_array(w.temps, ',')) AS t
GROUP BY w.station ORDER BY 1;

-- cast before comparing
SELECT w.station, max(t) AS max_temp, min(t) AS min_temp, count(*) AS readings
FROM weather_data w, unnest(string_to_array(w.temps, ',')::int[]) AS t
GROUP BY w.station ORDER BY 1;

-- the hottest hour per station: ordinality + LATERAL top-1
SELECT w.station, h.hour, h.temp
FROM weather_data w
CROSS JOIN LATERAL (
  SELECT hour, temp
  FROM unnest(string_to_array(w.temps, ',')::int[]) WITH ORDINALITY AS u(temp, hour)
  ORDER BY temp DESC LIMIT 1
) h ORDER BY 1;
presets.note: `string_to_array` returns `text[]`, so the first query compares **strings**: North's minimum is '-1' (true value −16) and West's maximum is '9' (true 16). Casting to `int[]` fixes it. The last query numbers each reading with `WITH ORDINALITY` and keeps the top one per station: hour 8 at West (16°), hour 7 at South (33°).

presets.label: LATERAL vs a window function
presets.sql:
SELECT name, item, created_at
FROM (
  SELECT a.name, p.item, p.created_at,
         row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY a.id ORDER BY p.created_at DESC) AS rn
  FROM accounts a JOIN purchases p ON p.account_id = a.id
) x
WHERE rn <= 2
ORDER BY name, created_at DESC;
presets.note: Same 5 rows. The window version numbers **every** purchase and then filters; LATERAL + LIMIT with an index reads only the rows it returns. With few parents and many children per parent, LATERAL wins.

production.title: An activity feed: latest 3 events per followed user
production.context: A social app shows each user the 3 newest posts from every account they follow. `posts` has 400 M rows; a typical user follows 200 accounts.
production.problem: The original query ranked all posts of all followed accounts with `row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY author_id ORDER BY created_at DESC)` and then filtered `rn <= 3`. For a user following prolific accounts it sorted hundreds of thousands of rows to return 600.
production.solution: Drive the query from the follow list and fetch each author's newest 3 with LATERAL, backed by an index whose order matches the subquery.
production.outcome: The plan becomes a Nested Loop with an Index Scan inside, `loops` = number of followed accounts, and at most 3 index entries read per loop: about 600 rows touched instead of every post of those authors.

pitfalls.title: CROSS JOIN LATERAL silently drops parents
pitfalls.symptom: Accounts with no purchases are missing from a "latest purchase per account" report.
pitfalls.cause: With comma or CROSS JOIN LATERAL, an outer row whose subquery returns zero rows produces no output, just like an inner join.
pitfalls.fix: Use `LEFT JOIN LATERAL (…) p ON true` to keep every outer row, NULL-extended.

pitfalls.title: LATERAL without a supporting index
pitfalls.symptom: A LATERAL top-N query is slower than the window-function version.
pitfalls.cause: The subquery runs once per outer row. Without an index matching `WHERE … ORDER BY`, each run scans and sorts the inner table.
pitfalls.fix: Create an index on `(correlation_column, sort_column DESC)` so each loop is a short index scan, and check `loops=` in EXPLAIN ANALYZE.

pitfalls.title: Referencing the right side from a RIGHT/FULL join
pitfalls.symptom: `ERROR: invalid reference to FROM-clause entry` even though LATERAL is written.
pitfalls.cause: A LATERAL item may only reference items that are INNER or LEFT joined to it. In `X RIGHT JOIN LATERAL Y`, Y cannot reference X.
pitfalls.fix: Rewrite with the LATERAL item on the right side of an inner or LEFT join.

pitfalls.title: Max-then-join-back for "latest per group"
pitfalls.symptom: A "latest purchase per account" query built as `GROUP BY account_id` + `max(created_at)`, joined back on both columns, returns two rows for some accounts.
pitfalls.cause: The join back matches every row with that timestamp, so a tie on `created_at` returns all tied rows. It also reads the table twice. A common claim is that this GROUP BY form always beats LATERAL at scale; with an index on `(account_id, created_at DESC)` the LATERAL plan reads one index entry per account.
pitfalls.fix: Use LATERAL with `ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT 1`, or `DISTINCT ON (account_id) … ORDER BY account_id, created_at DESC, id DESC`. Both return exactly one row per key, with a deterministic tie-breaker.

pointers: `LATERAL` lets a FROM subquery reference columns of FROM items **to its left**; it runs once per outer row.
Set-returning functions in FROM are **implicitly lateral**; the keyword is optional there.
CROSS JOIN / comma LATERAL drops rows with an empty result; `LEFT JOIN LATERAL … ON true` keeps them.
Top-N per group: LATERAL + `ORDER BY … LIMIT n` + index on `(key, sort DESC)` → Nested Loop with Index Scan.
`WITH ORDINALITY` numbers the rows of a function in FROM (bigint, from 1).

lessons.title: Aggregates, FILTER and GROUPING SETS
tldr: An **aggregate** folds many input rows into one value per group, and `FILTER`, ordered-set aggregates and `GROUPING SETS` / `ROLLUP` / `CUBE` control which rows feed it and which groupings are produced.

Together they turn a dozen report queries (totals, subtotals, conditional counts, medians) into one pass over the data, provided you respect the NULL rules that make `count(col)` differ from `count(*)` and `sum` of nothing NULL.

visualizer.title: Grouping sets, one set at a time
visualizer.caption: Pick ROLLUP, CUBE or your own GROUPING SETS and step through each set. Watch which input rows fold together, and how `grouping()` tells a subtotal's NULL from Baz's real NULL size.

presets.label: CUBE and grouping()
presets.sql:
SELECT brand, size, sum(sales), grouping(brand, size) AS g
FROM items_sold
GROUP BY CUBE (brand, size)
ORDER BY g, brand, size;
presets.note: 12 rows. Two rows read `NULL, NULL`: sum 8 with g = 2 (Baz's real NULL size, grouped by size) and sum 58 with g = 3 (the grand total).

presets.label: Four queries, or one GROUPING SETS
presets.sql:
-- four GROUP BYs glued together: four scans
EXPLAIN (COSTS OFF)
SELECT brand, size, sum(sales) FROM items_sold GROUP BY brand, size
UNION ALL SELECT brand, NULL, sum(sales) FROM items_sold GROUP BY brand
UNION ALL SELECT NULL, size, sum(sales) FROM items_sold GROUP BY size
UNION ALL SELECT NULL, NULL, sum(sales) FROM items_sold;

-- the same 12 rows from one scan
SELECT brand, size, sum(sales)
FROM items_sold
GROUP BY GROUPING SETS ((brand, size), (brand), (size), ())
ORDER BY brand, size;

EXPLAIN (COSTS OFF)
SELECT brand, size, sum(sales) FROM items_sold
GROUP BY GROUPING SETS ((brand, size), (brand), (size), ());
presets.note: The UNION ALL plan is an **Append** of four aggregates, each over its own Seq Scan. GROUPING SETS returns the same 12 rows from one **MixedAggregate** (one Hash Key per set, `Group Key: ()` for the total) over a single scan. `CUBE (brand, size)` is shorthand for exactly these four sets.

presets.label: ROLLUP with labels
presets.sql:
SELECT CASE WHEN grouping(brand) = 1 THEN 'ALL brands' ELSE brand END AS brand,
       CASE WHEN grouping(size) = 1 THEN 'all sizes' ELSE coalesce(size, '(none)') END AS size,
       sum(sales)
FROM items_sold
GROUP BY ROLLUP (brand, size)
ORDER BY grouping(brand), brand, grouping(size), size;

EXPLAIN (COSTS OFF)
SELECT brand, size, sum(sales) FROM items_sold GROUP BY ROLLUP (brand, size);
presets.note: ROLLUP gives detail rows, a subtotal per brand and a grand total. The plan is one **MixedAggregate** with a Hash Key per set: a single scan.

presets.label: count(*) vs count(col)
presets.sql:
SELECT count(*)               AS all_rows,
       count(amount)          AS with_amount,
       count(coupon)          AS with_coupon,
       count(DISTINCT region) AS regions,
       sum(amount)            AS total,
       round(avg(amount), 2)  AS avg_amount,
       round(sum(amount) / count(*), 2) AS naive_avg
FROM orders;

SELECT sum(amount) AS sum_of_nothing, count(*) AS count_of_nothing,
       coalesce(sum(amount), 0) AS fixed
FROM orders WHERE false;
presets.note: `count(*)` counts rows, `count(col)` skips NULLs (40 orders have no amount, so `avg` ignores them: 104.63). Dividing `sum` by `count(*)` counts those 40 rows as zeros and gives 102.54. Over zero rows `sum` is **NULL**, not 0; only count returns 0.

presets.label: FILTER: one pass, many counts
presets.sql:
SELECT region,
       count(*)                                    AS orders,
       count(*)    FILTER (WHERE status = 'paid')     AS paid,
       sum(amount) FILTER (WHERE status = 'refunded') AS refunded,
       round(100.0 * count(*) FILTER (WHERE coupon IS NOT NULL) / count(*), 1) AS coupon_pct
FROM orders
GROUP BY region ORDER BY region;
presets.note: Each aggregate sees only the rows its FILTER allows, all in a single scan. Clearer than `sum(CASE WHEN … THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)`, and it works with any aggregate: `array_agg(x) FILTER (…)` skips rows, while the CASE trick would collect NULLs. FILTER is standard SQL, not a PostgreSQL extension.

presets.label: Median and mode
presets.sql:
SELECT region,
       percentile_cont(0.5) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY amount) AS median_cont,
       percentile_disc(0.5) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY amount) AS median_disc,
       mode() WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY status)              AS most_common_status
FROM orders GROUP BY region ORDER BY region;
presets.note: Ordered-set aggregates sort their input. `percentile_cont` interpolates between the two middle values; `percentile_disc` returns an actual input value. There is no separate `median()`: `percentile_cont(0.5)` is the median.

presets.label: WHERE vs HAVING
presets.note: Aggregates are not allowed in WHERE (`42803`): WHERE filters input rows, HAVING filters groups after aggregation. HAVING cannot use the output alias `total` either (`42703`), because the SELECT list is computed after HAVING. Logical order: FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, SELECT, DISTINCT, ORDER BY, LIMIT. ORDER BY can use output names, and so can GROUP BY as a PostgreSQL extension; WHERE and HAVING cannot.

presets.label: DISTINCT ON: first row per key
presets.sql:
SELECT DISTINCT ON (region) region, id, amount, created_at
FROM orders
WHERE amount IS NOT NULL
ORDER BY region, amount DESC, id;
presets.note: One row per region: the first after sorting, here the largest order. The DISTINCT ON expressions must lead the ORDER BY; add a tie-breaker (`id`) for a deterministic pick.

production.title: A finance dashboard: from 9 queries to 1
production.context: A finance dashboard shows revenue by region and month, subtotals per region, per month, a grand total, and for each cell the refunded amount and the share of coupon orders.
production.problem: It ran 9 separate queries (one per breakdown and metric), each scanning the orders table, and the page took seconds. Subtotal rows were found with `WHERE month IS NULL`, which also caught orders whose month column was legitimately NULL.
production.solution: One `GROUP BY CUBE` with FILTER clauses, and `grouping()` to label the subtotal rows.
production.sql:
SELECT region, date_trunc('month', created_at) AS month,
       grouping(region, date_trunc('month', created_at)) AS level,
       sum(amount) FILTER (WHERE status = 'paid')     AS revenue,
       sum(amount) FILTER (WHERE status = 'refunded') AS refunded,
       round(100.0 * count(*) FILTER (WHERE coupon IS NOT NULL) / count(*), 1) AS coupon_pct
FROM orders
GROUP BY CUBE (region, date_trunc('month', created_at));
production.outcome: One scan feeding one MixedAggregate instead of nine scans. For 4 regions and 2 months that is 4 × 2 + 4 + 2 + 1 = 15 rows. Subtotal rows are identified by `level`, so a real NULL can never be mistaken for a total.

pitfalls.title: sum() of no rows is NULL
pitfalls.symptom: A balance shows blank (or the app crashes on null) for a customer with no transactions.
pitfalls.cause: Every aggregate except `count` returns **NULL** on an empty input: `sum`, `avg`, `max`, even `array_agg`.
pitfalls.fix: Wrap it: `coalesce(sum(amount), 0)`. For arrays, `coalesce(array_agg(x), '{}')`. The same applies to FILTER: a month with no matching rows gives `sum(x) FILTER (…)` = NULL, so a CASE or FILTER rewrite of a report that used to print 0 needs the COALESCE back.

pitfalls.title: count(col) where count(*) was meant
pitfalls.symptom: A conversion rate is too high: the denominator is smaller than the number of visits.
pitfalls.cause: `count(col)` counts only non-NULL values. If the column is nullable, rows silently drop out.
pitfalls.fix: Use `count(*)` to count rows; use `count(col)` only when "rows with a value" is what you mean.

pitfalls.title: Telling subtotals apart with IS NULL
pitfalls.symptom: A ROLLUP report shows two "Total" lines for one region.
pitfalls.cause: Grouping sets fill ungrouped columns with NULL, which is indistinguishable from a real NULL in the data.
pitfalls.fix: Use `grouping(col)`: 1 means the NULL is a subtotal placeholder, 0 means it is data.

pitfalls.title: Order-sensitive aggregates without ORDER BY
pitfalls.symptom: `string_agg(name, ', ')` lists names in a different order on each run.
pitfalls.cause: Aggregate input order is unspecified. A sorted subquery usually works but is not guaranteed once the plan changes.
pitfalls.fix: Put the order inside the call: `string_agg(name, ', ' ORDER BY name)`, `array_agg(x ORDER BY ts)`.

pitfalls.title: BETWEEN on a timestamp drops the last day
pitfalls.symptom: An October report built with `WHERE created_at BETWEEN '2026-10-01' AND '2026-10-31'` is missing most of October 31.
pitfalls.cause: BETWEEN is inclusive on both ends, and `'2026-10-31'` on a timestamp means midnight at the **start** of the 31st. Hourly rows for October: 721 instead of 744. In adjacent BETWEEN buckets the boundary row lands in both.
pitfalls.fix: Use a half-open range: `created_at >= '2026-10-01' AND created_at < '2026-11-01'`. It is exact for dates and timestamps, never double-counts, and an index can use it.

pitfalls.title: Integer division in ratios
pitfalls.symptom: A conversion rate prints 0 for every row, or a share prints 33 instead of 33.3.
pitfalls.cause: `count(*)` returns bigint, and integer / integer truncates: `2 / 3` is 0. A zero denominator raises `division by zero`.
pitfalls.fix: Make one operand numeric first (`100.0 * count(*) FILTER (…) / count(*)`) and guard the denominator with `NULLIF(count(*), 0)`, which turns 0 into NULL so the ratio is NULL instead of an error.

pointers: `count(*)` counts rows; `count(col)` counts non-NULL values; every other aggregate returns **NULL** on no rows.
`agg(...) FILTER (WHERE ...)` restricts one aggregate's input; WHERE restricts all rows; HAVING filters groups.
`ROLLUP (a, b)` = (a,b), (a), (); `CUBE (a, b)` = all 4 subsets; all sets run in one scan.
`grouping(a, b)` is a bitmask: bit = 1 when that column is **not** grouped in the current row's set.
Ordered-set aggregates: `percentile_cont` interpolates, `percentile_disc` picks a value, `mode()` returns the most frequent.

lessons.title: From SQL text to rows: parse, analyze, rewrite, plan, execute
tldr: Every statement passes through five stages: a **parser** that knows only grammar, **analysis** that resolves names against the catalogs, a **rewriter** that expands views and rules, a **planner** that costs alternative paths, and an **executor** that pulls rows up a plan tree.
Splitting the work this way lets PostgreSQL parse transaction commands without a transaction, reuse analyzed statements through **PREPARE**, and pick among many equivalent plans by estimated cost.

visualizer.title: Follow one query through the backend
visualizer.caption: Step through a join against a view, from characters to tokens, trees, costed paths and finally rows pulled up the plan. Switch modes to watch the plan cache decide between custom and generic plans.

presets.label: The view is a rule
presets.sql:
SELECT rulename, ev_type FROM pg_rewrite WHERE ev_class = 'big_orders'::regclass;

SELECT pg_get_viewdef('big_orders');
presets.note: A view is stored as a `_RETURN` rule (`ev_type` 1 = SELECT). The rewriter pastes this definition into every query that names the view.

presets.label: The view disappears
presets.sql:
EXPLAIN VERBOSE
SELECT c.name, b.amount
FROM big_orders b JOIN customers c ON c.id = b.customer_id
WHERE c.region = 'north';
presets.note: The plan scans `public.orders` directly with the view's `amount > 900` filter. After rewriting and subquery pull-up, `big_orders` no longer exists.

presets.label: Three join paths
presets.note: Disabling the winner reveals the runner-up paths the planner costed: merge join (about 2788), then nested loop with Memoize (about 3528). The hash join (about 2022) won.

presets.label: Demand-pull counts
presets.sql:
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, TIMING OFF)
SELECT c.name, b.amount
FROM big_orders b JOIN customers c ON c.id = b.customer_id
WHERE c.region = 'north';
presets.note: Each node reports the rows it handed to its parent: customers 1250 (3750 removed), orders 9700 (90300 removed), join 2425.

presets.label: Subqueries become joins
presets.note: The planner rewrites EXISTS into a join: here a Hash Join over the de-duplicated customer ids. NOT EXISTS becomes a **Hash Right Anti Join** estimated at 3974 rows. NOT IN cannot become an anti join, because one NULL in the subquery would make every row unknown. It stays a `hashed SubPlan` filter, with a blind 2500-row guess.

presets.label: CTE: inlined or materialized
presets.note: A plain CTE used once is **inlined**: the outer filter joins it, and a BitmapAnd of two indexes finds 1 row (cost about 21). `MATERIALIZED` computes all 1027 pending rows first, then filters a `CTE Scan` (cost about 155).

presets.label: Custom → generic
presets.note: Five custom plans, then the generic plan wins: `generic_plans = 1`. EXPLAIN shows `customer_id = $1`, a plan built without knowing the value.

presets.label: Skew keeps it custom
presets.note: The generic plan assumes 50000 matching rows and costs far more than the custom plans, so `generic_plans` stays 0.

production.title: A prepared statement that turned slow on the sixth call
production.context: A ticketing service used a driver that prepares every query. The hot query was `SELECT … FROM tickets WHERE tenant_id = $1 AND state = $2 ORDER BY created_at LIMIT 50`. One tenant owned most of the rows.
production.problem: Latency for small tenants jumped after a connection had served a few requests. The first five executions got custom plans. Then the cached **generic plan** won the cost comparison, and it was tuned for an average tenant, so it walked the big tenant's part of the index for everyone.
production.solution: Confirm with `EXPLAIN EXECUTE` and `pg_prepared_statements.generic_plans`. Then force replanning for the role that runs this query, or send that one query unprepared. Planning costs well under a millisecond here, which is much cheaper than a bad plan.
production.outcome: Every execution is planned with the real tenant id, so small tenants get an index scan on their own rows again. The cost is one planning pass per call, which `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE)` reports as Planning Time (about 0.1 to 0.9 ms in the playground).

pitfalls.title: Generic plans on skewed parameters
pitfalls.symptom: A prepared query is fast for its first five calls on a connection, then slow for some parameter values only.
pitfalls.cause: With `plan_cache_mode = auto`, the sixth execution may switch to a **generic plan** whose estimates use average selectivity instead of the actual value.
pitfalls.fix: Check `generic_plans` in `pg_prepared_statements` and compare `EXPLAIN EXECUTE` with `EXPLAIN (GENERIC_PLAN)`. Set `plan_cache_mode = force_custom_plan` for that workload.
pitfalls.sql: SET plan_cache_mode = force_custom_plan;

pitfalls.title: Expecting a view to be cached
pitfalls.symptom: A view over an expensive aggregate is as slow as the query itself, every time.
pitfalls.cause: A view is a rewrite **rule**: its definition is pasted into each query. Nothing is stored or reused.
pitfalls.fix: Use a **materialized view** (refreshed explicitly) or a summary table when you need the result stored.

pitfalls.title: Big joins switch to GEQO
pitfalls.symptom: A report joining a dozen tables gets different, sometimes much worse plans after unrelated changes.
pitfalls.cause: At `geqo_threshold` (12) FROM items the planner stops near-exhaustive search and uses the **genetic optimizer**, which samples join orders randomly.
pitfalls.fix: Reduce the join count (pre-aggregate, split the query), or write joins in a good order and set `join_collapse_limit = 1` for that query. `geqo_seed` makes the choice repeatable.

pitfalls.title: Using a CTE as an optimization fence, or as a cache
pitfalls.symptom: A query was split into a WITH clause "so it is computed once", yet the plan shows the CTE merged into the outer query. Or a CTE that used to isolate an expensive step now changes the plan.
pitfalls.cause: A common claim is that a CTE is always evaluated once and its result reused. Since PostgreSQL 12, a non-recursive, side-effect-free CTE that is referenced **once** is inlined like a subquery. Only a CTE referenced twice, a recursive or data-modifying CTE, or one marked `MATERIALIZED` is computed separately.
pitfalls.fix: Write `AS MATERIALIZED` when you really want compute-once or a fence, and `AS NOT MATERIALIZED` to allow inlining of a CTE that is referenced several times. Check the plan for a `CTE Scan` node.

pitfalls.title: NOT IN over a nullable subquery
pitfalls.symptom: `WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT ref FROM t)` suddenly returns no rows at all, or runs far slower than the equivalent NOT EXISTS.
pitfalls.cause: If the subquery yields one NULL, `x NOT IN (…)` is never true. Because of that rule the planner cannot turn NOT IN into an anti join, so it uses a hashed SubPlan, or a plain SubPlan rescanned per row when the result does not fit in `work_mem`.
pitfalls.fix: Write `NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM t WHERE t.ref = x.id)`. It is NULL-safe and becomes an Anti Join.

pointers: Stages: **parser** (grammar only, no catalogs) → **analysis** (names, types, operators) → **rewriter** (views, rules) → **planner** (paths, costs) → **executor**.
The rewriter turns query trees into query trees. A view is a `_RETURN` rule expanded like a macro, then usually flattened into the outer query.
The planner costs **paths** for each relation, then join pairs, keeping the cheapest. Above `geqo_threshold` = 12 FROM items it switches to GEQO.
The executor is **demand-pull**: each node returns one row per call, or NULL when done. Hash and Sort must drain their input first.
**PREPARE** caches the analyzed tree. Five custom plans, then a generic plan if its cost is not much higher (`plan_cache_mode`).

lessons.title: The cost model
tldr: The planner prices every candidate plan in abstract **cost units**, where reading one page sequentially costs `seq_page_cost` = 1.0 and every random page, row, index entry and operator call has its own relative price.
Comparing those totals is how PostgreSQL decides between a sequential scan, an index scan and a bitmap scan, so the constants (and the statistics they multiply) decide which plan you get.

visualizer.title: Where the sequential scan starts to win
visualizer.caption: Drag the predicate wider and watch three real cost curves cross. Then make the column scattered, shrink the cache, and lower `random_page_cost` to see each factor move the crossover.

presets.label: Seq scan formula
presets.note: 935 pages × 1.0 + 100000 rows × 0.01 = **1935**. Adding one filter adds 100000 × `cpu_operator_cost` 0.0025 = 250, giving **2185**.

presets.label: Cost constants
presets.sql:
SELECT name, setting, short_desc FROM pg_settings
WHERE name IN ('seq_page_cost', 'random_page_cost', 'cpu_tuple_cost', 'cpu_index_tuple_cost',
               'cpu_operator_cost', 'effective_cache_size', 'parallel_setup_cost', 'parallel_tuple_cost')
ORDER BY name;
presets.note: Defaults: random 4.0, tuple 0.01, index tuple 0.005, operator 0.0025. `effective_cache_size` is a hint for costing only: it allocates nothing.

presets.label: Correlation matters
presets.note: Same 5% of rows. The correlated column gets a cheap Index Scan (about 193). The scattered one gets a Bitmap Heap Scan (about 1090), because those rows are spread over almost every page.

presets.label: Scattered rows, every page
presets.sql:
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS, TIMING OFF)
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE rnd_k < 2000;
presets.note: `Heap Blocks: exact=934`: only 2% of the rows, but they live on 934 of the 935 pages. That is why the bitmap scan is nearly as expensive as a full scan.

presets.label: Tiny table, index ignored
presets.note: 200 rows fit in **2 pages**. Reading both and testing 200 rows costs 2 + 2 + 0.5 = **4.50**. The index path costs 8.16, because it reads index pages and then a random heap page. At 20000 rows the same query switches to the Index Scan (8.30). An unused index on a tiny table is the planner working correctly.

presets.label: Startup cost and LIMIT
presets.sql:
EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM orders ORDER BY note;
EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM orders ORDER BY seq_k LIMIT 5;
presets.note: A Sort has a large **startup cost**: it must read everything before returning a row. The index scan under LIMIT starts at 0.29 and the Limit node charges only a fraction of the total.

presets.label: SSD pricing
presets.note: At 1.1 the random heap fetches look almost as cheap as sequential ones, so the plan cost drops and index plans win over a wider range.

presets.label: enable_* only discourages
presets.note: There is no index on `note`, so a seq scan is the only path and it is still used. PostgreSQL 18 marks it `Disabled: true`.

production.title: Moving a reporting database to NVMe without telling the planner
production.context: An analytics team migrated a 400 GB database to NVMe storage with a much larger RAM cache. Configuration was copied from the old spinning-disk server, including `random_page_cost = 4` and `effective_cache_size = 4GB`.
production.problem: Dashboards filtering on scattered columns kept choosing full sequential scans of large tables, even when the filter matched well under 1% of rows. The planner was still pricing every random read at four sequential reads and assumed almost nothing was cached.
production.solution: Tell the planner what the hardware now is, then verify plan by plan. Lower `random_page_cost` to about 1.1 (random reads on flash cost about the same as sequential ones), and set `effective_cache_size` to roughly shared_buffers plus the OS page cache. Both can be set per database or per tablespace, so test on one first.
production.outcome: On the playground table, at 1.1 the 1% scattered-column bitmap plan drops from cost 999 to 661, plain index scans win at 40–50% of the table, and the seq scan wins only from 70% instead of 50%. On a large table the same shift turns many seq scans into index plans. Check the slow queries with `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)` before and after.

pitfalls.title: Testing plans with enable_seqscan = off
pitfalls.symptom: An index plan looks great in a session with `enable_seqscan = off`, but production keeps choosing the seq scan.
pitfalls.cause: The `enable_*` flags do not forbid a node. They add a huge penalty, so the comparison is no longer the one the planner makes. A plan you forced is not evidence that it is cheaper.
pitfalls.fix: Use the flag only to see the alternative's cost. Then fix the inputs: statistics (`ANALYZE`, a higher statistics target) or cost constants. Compare `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)` runs, not costs alone.

pitfalls.title: Comparing cost numbers across queries
pitfalls.symptom: A team ranks queries by EXPLAIN cost and is surprised when the "cheapest" one is the slowest in production.
pitfalls.cause: Costs are arbitrary units built on estimates. They are only meaningful for choosing between plans for **the same query**. Wrong row estimates make them wrong in any case.
pitfalls.fix: Rank queries by measured time and buffers (`pg_stat_statements`, `EXPLAIN ANALYZE`). Use costs to understand why one plan beat another.

pitfalls.title: Leaving random_page_cost at the spinning-disk default
pitfalls.symptom: On SSD or a fully cached database, selective queries on scattered columns still get sequential scans or bitmap scans when an index scan would be faster.
pitfalls.cause: The default 4.0 assumes random reads are expensive and that about 90% of them hit cache. On flash, a random read costs about the same as a sequential one.
pitfalls.fix: Set `random_page_cost` close to `seq_page_cost` (1.1 is common for SSD) and size `effective_cache_size` honestly. Change one setting at a time and re-check key plans.
pitfalls.sql:
ALTER SYSTEM SET random_page_cost = 1.1;
SELECT pg_reload_conf();

pointers: Unit: one sequential page = `seq_page_cost` **1.0**. Defaults: random page **4.0**, row **0.01**, index entry **0.005**, operator **0.0025**.
Seq scan = **pages × seq_page_cost + rows × cpu_tuple_cost**, plus `cpu_operator_cost` per qual per row. It does not depend on selectivity.
Index scans cost heap fetches between "sequential" and "random" depending on **correlation**. Bitmap scans read each heap page once, in physical order.
Every plan shows **startup..total** cost. LIMIT and EXISTS favour low startup cost.
`enable_*` flags only discourage a node (`Disabled: true`). `effective_cache_size` is a costing hint, not an allocation.

lessons.title: Planner statistics
tldr: `ANALYZE` samples each table and stores per-column **statistics** (null fraction, distinct count, most common values, an equal-frequency histogram and physical correlation) that the planner turns into row-count estimates.
Every cost in a plan is multiplied by those estimates, so knowing how `eqsel` and `scalarltsel` read `pg_stats` (and where their independence assumption breaks) explains most bad plans.

visualizer.title: Estimate rows from a real pg_stats row
visualizer.caption: Drag the constant and watch the MCV list and histogram produce the estimate, matched against PostgreSQL's own number and the true count. The third mode shows correlated columns and extended statistics.

presets.label: Before the first ANALYZE
presets.note: Never analyzed: `reltuples = -1`, and the plan guesses **rows=8 width=240**. The width comes from the declared `varchar(50)` sizes, and the row count from a default selectivity. After ANALYZE: rows=25, width=15, and the real count is 25.

presets.label: Read pg_stats
presets.sql:
SELECT attname, null_frac, n_distinct, most_common_vals, most_common_freqs, histogram_bounds, correlation
FROM pg_stats WHERE tablename = 'trips' AND attname IN ('zone', 'id');
presets.note: `zone` (target 10): 10 MCVs covering 48.5% of rows and 11 histogram bounds. `id`: `n_distinct = -1` means "unique", and the histogram has 101 bounds at the default target of 100.

presets.label: Under the hood: pg_statistic
presets.sql:
SELECT a.attname, s.stanullfrac, s.stadistinct, s.stawidth,
       s.stakind1, s.stakind2, s.stakind3,
       s.stanumbers1[1:3] AS first_freqs
FROM pg_statistic s
JOIN pg_attribute a ON a.attrelid = s.starelid AND a.attnum = s.staattnum
WHERE s.starelid = 'trips'::regclass
ORDER BY a.attnum;
presets.note: `pg_stats` is a readable view over this catalog. Each column has five slots; `stakind` says what a slot holds: **1** = most common values (frequencies in `stanumbers`), **2** = histogram bounds, **3** = correlation. A unique column has no MCV slot, so it starts with the histogram.

presets.label: Equality: MCV vs not
presets.note: zone 7 is an MCV with frequency 0.2214, so the estimate is 4428. zone 99 is not, so it gets (1 − 0.48515) / 490 × 20000 = **21** rows.

presets.label: Range: MCV + histogram
presets.sql:
EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM trips WHERE zone < 60;
SELECT count(*) FROM trips WHERE zone < 60;
presets.note: MCVs 7, 3, 12 and 40 contribute 0.4753 exactly. The histogram adds one full bucket plus 9/54 of bucket 51–105, times the non-MCV share 0.515. Estimate **10686**, actual 10706.

presets.label: Independence assumption
presets.note: zip determines city, but the planner multiplies their selectivities: **5** rows estimated vs 100 real, and 2000 groups vs 200.

presets.label: Extended statistics
presets.note: `{"4 => 5": 1.000000}`: column 4 (zip) fully determines column 5 (city). Estimates become 100 rows and 200 groups. CREATE STATISTICS collects nothing until ANALYZE runs.

presets.label: Statistics target
presets.note: With target 100 the MCV list grows to 100 entries and the histogram gets more bounds, so more values get exact frequencies instead of the uniform guess.

production.title: A nested loop over 50,000 "one row" matches
production.context: A logistics app filtered shipments with `WHERE carrier_id = $1 AND service_code = $2`. Each service code belongs to exactly one carrier, so the two columns are perfectly correlated.
production.problem: The planner multiplied the two selectivities and estimated a handful of rows. It chose a nested loop that probed another large table once per row. The real count was tens of thousands, and the query ran for seconds.
production.solution: Teach the planner about the correlation with extended statistics, then re-analyze. Use `dependencies` for equality filters and `ndistinct` for GROUP BY on the pair. Check `pg_stats_ext` to confirm the dependency degree is close to 1.
production.outcome: In the playground's version of the same shape, the estimate goes from 5 rows to 100 (actual 100) and GROUP BY from 2000 groups to 200 (actual 200). With correct estimates the planner switches to a hash join on the real workload.

pitfalls.title: No statistics after a bulk load
pitfalls.symptom: Right after loading or creating a table, queries get absurd estimates and plans until autovacuum catches up.
pitfalls.cause: Statistics are only collected by `ANALYZE` (manual, autovacuum, or VACUUM ANALYZE). A fresh table has none, and the planner falls back to fixed default selectivities.
pitfalls.fix: Run `ANALYZE` as the last step of every bulk load or migration, and after creating an **expression index** (its expression gets its own statistics).
pitfalls.sql: ANALYZE trips;

pitfalls.title: Correlated columns
pitfalls.symptom: Estimated rows are orders of magnitude below actual rows for filters on two related columns (city and zip, tenant and account).
pitfalls.cause: The planner assumes predicates are **independent** and multiplies their selectivities.
pitfalls.fix: Create extended statistics (`dependencies`, `ndistinct` or `mcv`) on the column group, then ANALYZE. Use `mcv` when value combinations matter or when filters are not plain equality.

pitfalls.title: n_distinct badly estimated from the sample
pitfalls.symptom: GROUP BY or join estimates are far off on a large table with a skewed column, even right after ANALYZE.
pitfalls.cause: ANALYZE reads a sample of 300 × statistics target rows. Distinct counts are hard to extrapolate from a sample.
pitfalls.fix: Raise the target for that column, or pin the value: `ALTER TABLE t ALTER COLUMN c SET (n_distinct = -0.05)` (negative means a fraction of rows), then ANALYZE.

pointers: `pg_stats`: **null_frac**, **n_distinct** (positive count, negative fraction, −1 unique), **most_common_vals/freqs**, **histogram_bounds**, **correlation**.
`=` on an MCV uses its frequency. Otherwise **(1 − Σ mcv freqs − null_frac) / (n_distinct − #MCVs)**.
`<` sums matching MCV freqs exactly, then adds histogram buckets (linear inside a bucket) scaled by the non-MCV fraction.
ANDed predicates are **multiplied**. Correlated columns need `CREATE STATISTICS` (dependencies, ndistinct, mcv) plus ANALYZE.
`default_statistics_target` = **100** caps MCVs and histogram buckets. ANALYZE samples 300 × the largest target rows.

lessons.title: B-Tree internals: splits, high keys and right-links
tldr: PostgreSQL's default index is a **B+tree** whose pages are sibling-linked on every level, and every page except the rightmost carries a **high key**, the upper bound of the keys it may hold.

Those two additions, from **Lehman & Yao**, let readers descend without locking parents: a reader that lands on a page split behind its back notices its key exceeds the high key and simply **moves right**.

visualizer.title: Grow a B-Tree, one key at a time
visualizer.caption: Insert keys and watch descents and page splits. Then reset, switch to **random keys**, and compare page count and leaf fill. That gap is the UUIDv4 vs UUIDv7 story.

presets.label: Metapage
presets.sql:
SELECT root, level, fastroot, fastlevel, allequalimage
FROM bt_metap('seq_pkey');
presets.note: Block 0 is the **metapage**. `level` is the root height (0 = the root is a leaf). `allequalimage` = true means deduplication is safe.

presets.label: A leaf page
presets.note: `btpo_prev`/`btpo_next` are the sibling links. **Item 1 is the high key**: it is the first key of the right sibling, not a row on this page.

presets.label: Root & downlinks
presets.note: On internal pages, `ctid` holds `(child block, …)`: a downlink, not a heap row. The first item has no key and covers "minus infinity".

presets.label: v4 vs v7 vs bigint
presets.sql:
SELECT t AS key_type,
       pg_relation_size(t || '_pkey') / 8192 AS index_pages,
       pg_size_pretty(pg_relation_size(t || '_pkey')) AS size
FROM unnest(ARRAY['seq', 'v7', 'v4']) AS t;
presets.note: Same row count. Random UUIDv4 keys split pages all over the index (about 23% more pages here). UUIDv7 and bigint append at the right edge and pack leaves to about 90%.

presets.label: Leaf fill %
presets.sql:
SELECT t AS key_type, round(avg(100 - s.free_size * 100.0 / 8148), 1) AS avg_leaf_fill_pct, count(*) AS leaf_pages
FROM unnest(ARRAY['seq', 'v7', 'v4']) AS t,
     LATERAL generate_series(1, (pg_relation_size(t || '_pkey') / 8192 - 1)::int) AS b,
     LATERAL bt_page_stats(t || '_pkey', b) AS s
WHERE s.type = 'l'
GROUP BY t ORDER BY 2 DESC;
presets.note: Walks every leaf with `bt_page_stats`. Expect about 90% for sequential keys and about 70% for random ones. Random fill keeps drifting lower as the index grows.

presets.label: Index scan buffers
presets.sql:
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS, COSTS OFF)
SELECT * FROM seq WHERE id = 12345;
presets.note: An equality lookup touches only a handful of buffers (metapage, root, leaf, heap page). `Index Searches: 1` (new in 18) counts descents of the tree.

production.title: Switching primary keys from UUIDv4 to UUIDv7
production.context: An orders service generated `uuid` primary keys client-side with v4 (fully random). At 300 M rows, insert latency crept up and the index outgrew RAM.
production.problem: Every insert landed on a **random leaf**. With the index larger than cache, most inserts first had to read a cold leaf from disk, and full leaves split down the middle, leaving pages about 65% full at scale. Checkpoints also had to write a full-page image for every scattered leaf they touched.
production.solution: Generate **UUIDv7** keys, natively `uuidv7()` in PostgreSQL 18. The leading 48 bits are a millisecond timestamp, so new keys arrive in roughly ascending order and hit the rightmost leaf. Appends at the right edge fill leaves to `fillfactor` (90), and the hot leaf stays in cache.
production.outcome: UUIDv4 needs 23% more index pages than UUIDv7 at 20k rows and 39% more at 100k rows (64.7% vs 89.8% leaf fill). In production the bigger win is locality: inserts touch one hot leaf instead of thousands of cold ones, so fewer reads and less full-page-image WAL.

pitfalls.title: Random keys on a large, write-heavy table
pitfalls.symptom: Insert throughput falls as the table grows, `shared_buffers` hit ratio drops, and WAL volume rises after each checkpoint.
pitfalls.cause: UUIDv4 (or hash-like) keys scatter inserts across all leaves. Each touched leaf must be read in, splits leave half-empty pages, and the first change to each page after a checkpoint writes a full-page image.
pitfalls.fix: Use time-ordered keys (`bigint` identity or `uuidv7()`). If a random id must be exposed externally, keep it as a secondary unique column and leave the primary key sequential.

pitfalls.title: Indexing values that are too large
pitfalls.symptom: `ERROR: index row size … exceeds btree version 4 maximum 2704 for index …` when inserting a long text value.
pitfalls.cause: A B-Tree entry must fit in about **one third of a page**, so a page can always hold at least three items and split safely.
pitfalls.fix: Index a hash or prefix instead: `CREATE INDEX ON docs (md5(body))` for equality lookups, a trigram GIN index for search, or a `left(col, 100)` expression index.

pitfalls.title: Bloat after mass deletes
pitfalls.symptom: The index stays large and range scans stay slow after deleting most of the rows.
pitfalls.cause: VACUUM can only recycle a B-Tree page once it is **completely empty**. Sparse pages stay allocated, and the index never shrinks on its own.
pitfalls.fix: Run `REINDEX INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx;` (no long write lock), then check the size with `pg_relation_size`. For time-based purges, partition and drop whole partitions instead.

pointers: Block 0 is the **metapage**. The **root** can move up as the tree grows. Leaf and internal pages on each level form a **doubly-linked list**.
Every non-rightmost page stores a **high key**. If a reader's key is greater than it, the reader follows the **right-link**: that is the Lehman & Yao move-right rule.
When a page is full: try **deleting dead entries**, then **deduplicate** into posting lists, and only then **split**. Splits cascade upward, and a root split adds a level.
Appending new largest keys fills leaves to **fillfactor 90**; random keys split pages in half, leaving leaves only about 65–72% full.
Entries max out at about **1/3 page** (2704 bytes); index a hash or prefix of big values.

lessons.title: Hash indexes
tldr: A hash index stores only a **4-byte hash code** per row, grouped into **buckets** that a lookup reaches directly from the metapage, without descending a tree.
That makes it compact for long keys and cheap for pure equality lookups, at the price of no ranges, no ordering, no uniqueness and no multicolumn support.

visualizer.title: Linear hashing, one bucket split at a time
visualizer.caption: Insert keys and follow each hash code through the masks into a bucket. Watch exactly one bucket split when the fill factor is exceeded, then insert a duplicate key until it grows an overflow chain.

presets.label: Empty metapage
presets.note: An empty int4 hash index already has **8 buckets** (`maxbucket` 7, `highmask` 15, `lowmask` 7), 10 pages counting the metapage and bitmap page. `ffactor` 307 is the target tuples per bucket.

presets.label: One bucket split
presets.note: 2456 = 307 × 8 tuples fit. Row 2457 crosses the threshold, so `maxbucket` goes 7 → 8: exactly **one** bucket split.

presets.label: Page types
presets.sql:
SELECT b AS block, hash_page_type(get_raw_page('h_idx', b)) AS type
FROM generate_series(0, (pg_relation_size('h_idx') / 8192 - 1)::int) b;
presets.note: Block 0 is the **metapage**, then primary **bucket** pages, a **bitmap** page that tracks free overflow pages, and more buckets added in batches as the index grows.

presets.label: Only the hash is stored
presets.note: Each item is a heap `ctid` plus a 32-bit hash code, sorted by hash within the page. The key itself is not stored, so every match is rechecked against the heap.

presets.label: Duplicates → overflow
presets.note: 800 copies of one key all land in one bucket. Its primary page overflows into a chain of 2 overflow pages, and the Bitmap Index Scan reads all 3 pages of that bucket.

presets.label: Long keys: hash vs B-tree
presets.note: For ~90-byte URLs the hash index is smaller than the B-tree (about 2.0 MB vs 2.4 MB) and a lookup reads about 3 buffers. For a 16-byte uuid the opposite happens: hash 1040 kB vs B-tree 632 kB at 20000 rows.

production.title: Deduplicating long URLs in a crawler
production.context: A crawler stores every fetched URL (often 200+ characters) and checks "seen before?" with `WHERE url = $1` millions of times a day. Nothing ever queries URL ranges or sorts by URL.
production.problem: A B-tree on `url` stored every full string, so the index was nearly as large as the table and lookups touched more pages than necessary. Very long URLs also risked the B-tree entry limit of about a third of a page.
production.solution: Replace the B-tree with a hash index. It stores 4 bytes per row no matter how long the URL is, and an equality lookup goes straight to one bucket. Keep a B-tree only if something needs uniqueness, because hash indexes cannot enforce it.
production.outcome: In the playground, 20000 URLs of about 90 bytes give a 2.0 MB hash index against 2.4 MB for the B-tree, and a lookup reads 3 buffers. The gap grows with key length, because hash entries never get wider.

pitfalls.title: Many duplicates in one key
pitfalls.symptom: Lookups on a few popular values are slow, and the index has many `overflow` pages.
pitfalls.cause: All rows with the same value hash to the **same bucket**. When its primary page fills, overflow pages are chained on, and every scan of that bucket reads the whole chain.
pitfalls.fix: Use hash indexes for unique or nearly unique columns. Exclude the hot values with a partial index (`WHERE status <> 'done'`), or use a B-tree, which deduplicates.

pitfalls.title: Expecting it to shrink or to be smaller
pitfalls.symptom: After deleting most rows the hash index stays the same size, and for small keys like uuid it is larger than the B-tree.
pitfalls.cause: Bucket pages are allocated in batches and are **never released**. Freed overflow pages are reused, never returned to the OS. Small keys gain nothing from storing a hash instead.
pitfalls.fix: Rebuild with `REINDEX INDEX CONCURRENTLY`. Measure with `pg_relation_size` before choosing hash over B-tree for short keys.

pitfalls.title: Using it for anything but =
pitfalls.symptom: A hash index exists but `ORDER BY`, `<`, `BETWEEN`, `IN` with ranges or a unique constraint still need a B-tree.
pitfalls.cause: A hash index supports only the `=` operator, single columns, and no uniqueness checking. Hash order says nothing about value order.
pitfalls.fix: Keep hash indexes for equality-only access paths. Everything else needs a B-tree.

pointers: Stores a **4-byte hash** per row, sorted by hash within each page. Every match is **lossy** and rechecked against the heap.
bucket = **hash & highmask**, folded with **lowmask** if above `maxbucket`. The masks live in the metapage, cached by each backend.
Growth is **linear hashing**: when `ntuples > ffactor × buckets`, exactly one bucket splits, in the foreground.
Page kinds: **metapage**, **bucket**, **overflow** (chained duplicates), **bitmap** (free overflow pages).
`=` only, single column, no UNIQUE, never shrinks without REINDEX. Best for long, nearly unique keys.

lessons.title: GIN: inverted indexes
tldr: A GIN index stores each **key** that occurs inside a composite value (array element, jsonb path, text-search lexeme) exactly once, with a sorted **posting list** of the rows that contain it.
That inverted layout makes "which rows contain these elements?" fast, and the **pending list** exists because a single row insert would otherwise touch one entry per element.

visualizer.title: Inside a GIN index on tags
visualizer.caption: Insert rows and watch them queue in the pending list, then overflow it or VACUUM it into the entry tree. Popular keys outgrow their posting list into a posting tree. Run the search to see posting lists intersected and the pending list scanned.

presets.label: Entries and pages
presets.note: 5000 rows but only **29 keys** (t0–t19, c0–c6, rare, common). `common` occurs in 4950 rows, too many for a posting list, so it has a **posting tree**: the `{data,leaf,compressed}` page.

presets.label: Containment search
presets.sql:
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, COSTS OFF, TIMING OFF)
SELECT id FROM docs WHERE tags @> ARRAY['rare', 't0'];
presets.note: GIN finds both keys and intersects their posting lists. GIN only supports **bitmap scans**, so a Bitmap Heap Scan rechecks the rows. The index part reads **5 buffers**.

presets.label: Pending list fills
presets.note: 300 new rows sit in **2 pending pages**, not in the entry tree. The same search now also reads the pending pages: index buffers go from 5 to **7**.

presets.label: Flush the pending list
presets.note: `gin_clean_pending_list` (or VACUUM, or autovacuum's analyze) moves pending entries into the main structure in one bulk pass and returns the number of pages flushed.

presets.label: jsonb_ops vs jsonb_path_ops
presets.note: `jsonb_path_ops` hashes whole paths, so it is smaller but supports only `@>`, `@?` and `@@`. Neither GIN index helps `->> =`: that is a plain equality on an expression and needs a B-tree expression index.

presets.label: Fix ->> with a B-tree
presets.note: Three ways to ask for one SKU. `->> =` is a Seq Scan (cost 172.50). Rewritten as containment it uses the GIN index (about 17). A **B-tree expression index** on `attrs ->> 'sku'` serves the original query as an Index Scan (8.30), and at 128 kB it is less than half the size of the `jsonb_path_ops` index.

presets.label: Substring search with trigrams
presets.note: pg_trgm splits text into 3-character keys, so a GIN index can answer `LIKE '%…%'`, which no B-tree can. The bitmap scan rechecks rows because trigram matches are only candidates.

production.title: A product catalog with p99 insert spikes
production.context: A marketplace indexed `attributes jsonb` with GIN for faceted search. Sellers bulk-upload products through an API, a few hundred rows per request, all day.
production.problem: Most inserts were fast, but every so often one API call took seconds. Those were the inserts that pushed the **pending list** past `gin_pending_list_limit` (4MB) and had to merge it in the foreground. Searches also slowed down between autovacuum runs, because every search scanned the whole pending list.
production.solution: Keep fastupdate, but make cleanup happen in the background and keep the list short: run autovacuum on this table more often (lower its analyze/vacuum insert thresholds) and keep the per-index limit modest. For a one-off bulk import, drop the index and recreate it afterwards, which is much faster than incremental maintenance.
production.outcome: Cleanup moves from user requests into autovacuum, so the occasional multi-second insert goes away and searches read a short pending list. In the playground, 300 pending rows add 2 buffer reads to every search (5 → 7) until the list is flushed.

pitfalls.title: Expecting GIN to speed up ->> equality
pitfalls.symptom: `WHERE data->>'email' = $1` still does a sequential scan although the jsonb column has a GIN index.
pitfalls.cause: GIN opclasses for jsonb support containment and existence (`@>`, `?`, `@?`, `@@`). `->>` returns text, and equality on that expression is not a GIN operator.
pitfalls.fix: Either rewrite the filter as containment (`data @> '{"email": "x"}'`) or add a B-tree expression index.
pitfalls.sql: CREATE INDEX ON customers ((data ->> 'email'));

pitfalls.title: Reaching for GIN on range columns
pitfalls.symptom: `CREATE INDEX … USING gin (during)` on a `tstzrange` column fails with `data type tstzrange has no default operator class for access method "gin"`.
pitfalls.cause: A common claim lists range types among the things GIN indexes. PostgreSQL ships no GIN operator class for ranges. Built-in GIN covers arrays, `jsonb`, `tsvector`, and (with extensions) `hstore` and trigrams.
pitfalls.fix: Index ranges with GiST (`USING gist (during)`) or SP-GiST. Both support `&&`, `@>` and `<@`, and GiST also backs exclusion constraints and `WITHOUT OVERLAPS` keys.

pitfalls.title: Occasional very slow inserts
pitfalls.symptom: Insert latency is normally low with rare spikes of seconds on a table with a GIN index.
pitfalls.cause: With `fastupdate` on, the insert that overflows `gin_pending_list_limit` flushes the whole pending list itself.
pitfalls.fix: Make autovacuum visit the table more often, lower the per-index limit, or set `fastupdate = off` when steady latency matters more than insert throughput.

pitfalls.title: Building GIN indexes slowly
pitfalls.symptom: CREATE INDEX for a GIN index on a large table takes far longer than a B-tree build, or a bulk load into an indexed table crawls.
pitfalls.cause: GIN build time is very sensitive to `maintenance_work_mem`, and incremental inserts touch one entry per extracted key.
pitfalls.fix: Raise `maintenance_work_mem` for the build session. For bulk loads, drop the GIN index, load, then recreate it.
pitfalls.sql:
SET maintenance_work_mem = '1GB';
CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY docs_tags ON docs USING gin (tags);

pointers: GIN = an **entry tree** (B-tree over keys) whose leaf entries hold a **posting list** of TIDs, or point to a **posting tree** when the list is too big.
Each key is stored **once**, so repeated elements compress well. GIN supports only **bitmap scans** and never index-only scans.
**fastupdate** (default on) appends new entries to an unsorted **pending list**. VACUUM, autoanalyze, `gin_clean_pending_list()` or exceeding `gin_pending_list_limit` (4MB) merges it.
Every search also scans the pending list. A big list slows reads, and the insert that overflows it pays for the merge.
Opclasses decide the keys: `array_ops`, `jsonb_ops` (default), `jsonb_path_ops` (smaller, `@>` only), `tsvector_ops`, `gin_trgm_ops`.

lessons.title: GiST and SP-GiST
tldr: **GiST** is a balanced tree whose entries are predicates such as bounding boxes, and **SP-GiST** is an unbalanced tree that splits space into non-overlapping parts such as quadrants, k-d halves or string prefixes.

Both are frameworks where an operator class supplies the geometry, so one access method can serve overlap, containment, range, nearest-neighbour `<->` and exclusion-constraint queries that a B-tree cannot express.

visualizer.title: Nearest-neighbour search, box by box
visualizer.caption: Step a 3-nearest-neighbour search through a GiST R-tree, then through an SP-GiST quad-tree over the same points. Click anywhere to move the query point and compare how many nodes each visits.

presets.label: KNN with GiST
presets.note: `Order By: (loc <-> …)` inside the Index Scan: the index returns rows nearest-first, so 5 neighbours out of 50000 cost about **8 buffers**, with no sort.

presets.label: Box containment
presets.sql:
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, COSTS OFF, TIMING OFF)
SELECT count(*) FROM shops WHERE loc <@ box '((40,40),(45,45))';
presets.note: The `consistent` function prunes every subtree whose bounding box cannot intersect the query box. The bitmap scan reads only a handful of index pages.

presets.label: SP-GiST quad-tree
presets.note: `quad_point_ops` is the default SP-GiST opclass for `point`. Same KNN plan shape; here it reads about 14 buffers, and the index is smaller (about 2.3 MB vs 3.3 MB for GiST).

presets.label: Exclusion constraint
presets.note: No two rows may have equal `room` **and** overlapping `during`. `btree_gist` supplies GiST support for `=` on int. Back-to-back bookings are fine because `[)` ranges do not overlap. Try inserting 101 at 10:30 to see the conflict error.

presets.label: Temporal primary key (18)
presets.note: PostgreSQL 18 `WITHOUT OVERLAPS` turns the primary key into "no two rows for the same product whose periods overlap". The backing index is a **GiST** index (`USING gist (product_id, valid)`), the same machinery as an exclusion constraint. Try `INSERT INTO prices VALUES (1, tstzrange('2025-06-01', '2025-09-01'), 31);`: it fails with SQLSTATE **23P01**, an exclusion violation, not 23505.

presets.label: Operator classes
presets.sql:
SELECT am.amname, opc.opcname, opc.opcdefault
FROM pg_opclass opc JOIN pg_am am ON am.oid = opc.opcmethod
WHERE opc.opcintype = 'point'::regtype
ORDER BY 1, 2;
presets.note: For `point`: GiST `point_ops`, SP-GiST `quad_point_ops` (default) and `kd_point_ops`. Choosing an opclass chooses the tree shape.

production.title: Double-booked meeting rooms
production.context: A workplace app stores room reservations as `(room_id, starts_at, ends_at)`. It checked for overlaps in application code before inserting.
production.problem: Two users clicking "book" at the same moment both passed the check, because neither saw the other's uncommitted row. The result was a few double bookings every week and support tickets to fix them by hand.
production.solution: Move the rule into the database with an **exclusion constraint**. A GiST index on `(room_id, tstzrange)` lets PostgreSQL find any conflicting row atomically at insert time, including rows from concurrent uncommitted transactions (the second inserter waits, then fails).
production.outcome: Overlapping inserts now fail with SQLSTATE `23P01` (exclusion_violation), which the app turns into a "slot just taken" message. The same index also speeds up "what is booked in this room this week" queries.

pitfalls.title: Ordering by distance without the index operator
pitfalls.symptom: `ORDER BY ST_Distance(…)` or `ORDER BY point_distance(a, b) LIMIT 10` sorts the whole table.
pitfalls.cause: Only an **ordering operator** of the opclass (`<->`) can be pushed into a GiST or SP-GiST scan. A function call is just an expression to evaluate per row.
pitfalls.fix: Write `ORDER BY loc <-> $1 LIMIT k` so EXPLAIN shows `Order By:` inside the index scan.

pitfalls.title: Missing btree_gist for mixed exclusion constraints
pitfalls.symptom: `EXCLUDE USING gist (room WITH =, during WITH &&)` fails with "data type integer has no default operator class for access method "gist"".
pitfalls.cause: Core GiST has no opclass for scalar equality on int, text or uuid.
pitfalls.fix: `CREATE EXTENSION btree_gist;` then create the constraint.

pitfalls.title: Catching 23505 for a temporal or exclusion key
pitfalls.symptom: Application code that turns duplicate keys into a friendly "already booked" message lets overlap errors through as 500s after a table moves to `WITHOUT OVERLAPS` or an EXCLUDE constraint.
pitfalls.cause: These constraints are enforced by a GiST index with exclusion semantics. A conflict raises `exclusion_violation`, SQLSTATE **23P01**, not `unique_violation` (23505), even when it is declared as a PRIMARY KEY.
pitfalls.fix: Handle both codes. In PL/pgSQL, catch `exclusion_violation` alongside `unique_violation`. Temporal keys also reject empty ranges, so validate input ranges before inserting.

pitfalls.title: Assuming GiST behaves like a B-tree
pitfalls.symptom: A GiST index on a column with few distinct values or heavy overlap is slow even for selective queries.
pitfalls.cause: GiST boxes can **overlap**, so a search may descend several subtrees. Index quality depends on the opclass's `penalty` and `picksplit`, and large unsorted builds can produce poorer trees.
pitfalls.fix: For point data that is partitioned naturally, try SP-GiST (no overlap). Compare buffers with `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)` and rebuild with REINDEX after heavy churn.

pointers: **GiST**: balanced, entries are predicates (e.g. bounding boxes). Support functions: `consistent`, `union`, `penalty`, `picksplit`, `same`, plus optional `distance` for KNN.
**SP-GiST**: unbalanced space partitioning (quad-tree, k-d tree, radix tree). Regions never overlap. `quad_point_ops` is the default for point.
KNN: `ORDER BY col <-> value LIMIT k` walks the tree best-first with lower-bound distances, so it never sorts the table.
Exclusion constraints (`EXCLUDE USING gist (… WITH &&)`) generalise UNIQUE to "no two rows overlap". `btree_gist` adds `=` for scalars.
Both are lossy per opclass: `Recheck Cond` and `Rows Removed by Index Recheck` show rows re-tested against the heap.

lessons.title: BRIN for huge append-only tables
tldr: A BRIN index stores one tiny **summary** (such as the min and max value) per **block range** of consecutive heap pages, so it stays a few kilobytes even for a table of gigabytes.
When a column follows the physical row order, as timestamps do in an append-only log, those summaries let a scan skip almost every block for the cost of reading a handful of index pages.

visualizer.title: Block ranges, summaries and what a query must read
visualizer.caption: Slide the query window and watch which ranges are consistent with it. Then add outliers, shuffle the rows, change `pages_per_range`, append unsummarized blocks, and compare minmax with minmax-multi.

presets.label: Tiny index
presets.note: 1082 heap pages need only **68** range summaries (16 pages each): 24 kB of BRIN against about 4.4 MB of B-tree. `correlation` is 1 for `readings` and close to 0 for `shuffled`.

presets.label: Read the summaries
presets.note: Each tuple covers 16 blocks starting at `blknum`. In `readings` each summary spans about 8 hours. In `shuffled` every summary spans the whole 23 days, so it can never exclude anything.

presets.label: Lossy bitmap scan
presets.note: `Heap Blocks: lossy=16`: one matching range, all 16 of its pages read. `Rows Removed by Index Recheck: 2600` are the rows on those pages outside the hour. About 21 buffers in total.

presets.label: Uncorrelated: useless
presets.note: Same query, same index type, shuffled rows: every range matches, so the planner does a **Seq Scan** of all 1088 pages.

presets.label: New rows: unsummarized
presets.note: Pages appended after the index was built have no summary until VACUUM, `autosummarize`, or `brin_summarize_new_values()` processes them. Until then every scan must read them. Here 68 summaries become **75**.

presets.label: minmax-multi and bloom
presets.note: **minmax-multi** stores several intervals per range (good with outliers). **bloom** stores a Bloom filter for equality on values that are not ordered. Both are still lossy.

production.title: Indexing a 2-billion-row sensor table without doubling its size
production.context: An IoT platform appends about 3,000 readings per second to `readings(ts, device_id, value)`. Almost every query asks for a time window: the last hour, yesterday, one week last March.
production.problem: A B-tree on `ts` was larger than a fifth of the table, every insert had to update it, and it no longer fit in memory. Dropping it made window queries scan the whole table.
production.solution: Rows arrive in time order, so `ts` is almost perfectly correlated with physical position. Replace the B-tree with a BRIN index and turn on `autosummarize` so each filled range is summarized by autovacuum soon after it fills.
production.outcome: In the playground the BRIN index is 24 kB against 4.4 MB for a B-tree on the same 200000 rows (about 180× smaller), and a one-hour query reads 21 buffers instead of 1088. Inserts barely touch the index, because a range's summary changes only when a new value widens it.

pitfalls.title: BRIN on a column that does not follow physical order
pitfalls.symptom: The BRIN index exists, but EXPLAIN shows a seq scan or a bitmap scan reading nearly every block.
pitfalls.cause: If values are scattered across the table, every range's min..max covers almost the full domain. Updates make this worse over time, because moved rows land wherever there is space.
pitfalls.fix: Check `correlation` in `pg_stats` (close to ±1 is good). Use BRIN only for append-mostly data, or physically order the table first (`CLUSTER` with a B-tree, then switch).
pitfalls.sql: SELECT attname, correlation FROM pg_stats WHERE tablename = 'readings';

pitfalls.title: Freshly inserted ranges are never skipped
pitfalls.symptom: Queries for the most recent data read more and more blocks until the next VACUUM.
pitfalls.cause: New pages beyond the last summarized range have no summary. `autosummarize` is **off** by default, so they wait for VACUUM.
pitfalls.fix: Create the index `WITH (autosummarize = on)` or call `brin_summarize_new_values()` from your loader.

pitfalls.title: Outliers and backfills widen ranges
pitfalls.symptom: After a backfill of old data or a few bad timestamps, BRIN scans read many more blocks than before.
pitfalls.cause: A **minmax** summary only ever widens. One far-off value makes its whole range match almost every query.
pitfalls.fix: Use `minmax-multi` opclasses, or `brin_desummarize_range()` plus re-summarize after fixing the data.

pointers: One index tuple per **block range** (`pages_per_range`, default **128** pages). Index size ≈ table pages / pages_per_range.
BRIN scans are always **bitmap** and always **lossy**: every page of a matching range is read and every row rechecked.
Useful only when values follow **physical order** (`pg_stats.correlation` near ±1): append-only logs, time series, IoT.
Opclass kinds: **minmax**, **minmax-multi** (outliers), **inclusion** (ranges, boxes, inet), **bloom** (equality).
New ranges stay unsummarized until VACUUM, `autosummarize = on` (default off) or `brin_summarize_new_values()`.

lessons.title: Designing indexes: multicolumn, partial, expression, covering
tldr: A good index matches how one important query filters and sorts: **equality columns first and the range column last**, a **predicate** for the rows you actually query, the **same expression** the WHERE clause uses, and **INCLUDE** columns so the heap is never read.
Each extra index slows every write and can block HOT updates, so the goal is the smallest set of indexes that turns your hot queries into short, ordered index reads.

visualizer.title: Pick the index: five real queries
visualizer.caption: For each query, choose one of three candidate indexes. The answer shows the real plan, buffers and index size PostgreSQL 18 produced for that index alone.

presets.label: Equality first, range last
presets.note: Both conditions appear in `Index Cond`, and the scan reads only user 42's February entries: about 5 buffers.

presets.label: Skip scan (18)
presets.note: Run 1 uses `(region, category, sale_date)` without any condition on `region`. That is a **skip scan**, new in PostgreSQL 18, and it shows `Index Searches: 7`. Run 2 names the three regions and needs only 3 searches. Run 3, with an index that leads with the filtered columns, needs 1. Skip scan rescues an index whose leading column has few distinct values. It does not replace the right column order.

presets.label: Partial index
presets.note: 32 kB, ordered, and only pending rows. The planner uses it only when the query's WHERE **implies** the predicate: the `status = 'done'` query cannot use it.

presets.label: Expression index
presets.note: Before: Seq Scan with a `lower()` Filter. After creating the index and running ANALYZE (which collects statistics for the expression), the row estimate is right and the index is used.

presets.label: A cast hides the index
presets.note: `int = bigint` still uses the index, because both types belong to the same B-tree operator family. `42.0` is `numeric`, so PostgreSQL casts the **column**: `Filter: ((user_id)::numeric = 42.0)` and a Seq Scan costing 2531 instead of 76. Casting the column to text does the same thing. Match the literal to the column type.

presets.label: INCLUDE and heap fetches
presets.note: First run: `Heap Fetches: 0`, 15 buffers. The UPDATE clears the all-visible bits of the pages it touched, so the second run visits the heap: **4120 heap fetches**, more than the 4020 rows, because the non-HOT update left old index entries pointing at dead versions. VACUUM fixes both.

presets.label: NULLS NOT DISTINCT
presets.note: By default NULLs are distinct, so two `(1, NULL)` rows are allowed. With `NULLS NOT DISTINCT` a second `(1, NULL)` would violate the index. Try inserting it again.

presets.label: Unused indexes
presets.note: Statistics are flushed lazily; the first call forces it. `idx_scan = 0` over a long period means the index costs write time and space without serving reads. Check replicas too before dropping it. The second query is the usual "index usage %" check. It needs `NULLIF` against division by zero, and `coalesce` because `idx_scan` is NULL for a table with no indexes. Only trust it on large tables: seq scans on tiny tables are correct.

production.title: A job queue that slowed down as it grew
production.context: A background-job table kept every job ever run: about 40 million rows, of which a few thousand are `queued` at any moment. Workers poll with `WHERE state = 'queued' ORDER BY run_at LIMIT 10 FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`.
production.problem: The only index was on `state`. Each poll found all queued rows, fetched them from the heap and sorted them to keep ten. A full index on `run_at` alone would have walked millions of finished jobs before finding queued ones.
production.solution: Index exactly the rows the workers want, in the order they want them. A partial index on `run_at WHERE state = 'queued'` stays tiny because finished jobs leave it, and it returns the next ten jobs without a sort. Build it without blocking writes, and drop the old index once the new one is used.
production.outcome: In the playground's smaller version (500 pending of 100000 rows) the same change cuts the poll from 503 buffers with a sort to 12 buffers without one, using a 32 kB index instead of 700 kB.

pitfalls.title: Range column first in a composite index
pitfalls.symptom: A two-column index is used, but the query still reads many index pages and gets slower as data accumulates.
pitfalls.cause: Only equality on leading columns plus a range on the **first** non-equality column limits the scanned part of a B-tree. Columns after the range are filtered entry by entry.
pitfalls.fix: Order key columns as: equality columns, then at most one range or ORDER BY column. Verify with buffers in `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)`.

pitfalls.title: Partial index never chosen with parameters
pitfalls.symptom: A partial index `WHERE status = 'pending'` works in psql but not from the application.
pitfalls.cause: Predicate matching happens at **plan time**. With a generic prepared plan, `status = $1` cannot be proven to imply the predicate.
pitfalls.fix: Write the predicate as a literal in the query (`WHERE status = 'pending'`), or use custom plans (`plan_cache_mode = force_custom_plan`).

pitfalls.title: CREATE INDEX on a busy table
pitfalls.symptom: Writes stall for minutes while an index builds. Or a `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` fails halfway and leaves an index marked INVALID that slows writes but is never used.
pitfalls.cause: Plain CREATE INDEX takes a SHARE lock that blocks INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE. CONCURRENTLY avoids that with two table scans, but any error leaves the half-built index behind. A common claim has this backwards: a failed **plain** CREATE INDEX rolls back completely, and only the CONCURRENTLY forms leave an INVALID index. CONCURRENTLY is also not lock-free: it holds SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE, which blocks other DDL and VACUUM on the table.
pitfalls.fix: Use `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` outside a transaction block. On failure, `DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY` the invalid index or `REINDEX INDEX CONCURRENTLY` it.
pitfalls.sql: SELECT indexrelid::regclass, indisvalid FROM pg_index WHERE NOT indisvalid;

pitfalls.title: Indexes that block HOT updates
pitfalls.symptom: After adding an index on a frequently updated column, update throughput drops and every index bloats.
pitfalls.cause: An UPDATE can be **HOT** (no index changes) only if no indexed column changes. Indexing a hot column, even as an INCLUDE column, turns every update into new entries in every index.
pitfalls.fix: Avoid indexing columns that change constantly (counters, `updated_at`) unless a key query needs them. Watch `n_tup_hot_upd` in `pg_stat_user_tables`.

pitfalls.title: Assuming foreign keys are indexed
pitfalls.symptom: Deleting one parent row, or joining child to parent, is slow. EXPLAIN ANALYZE of the DELETE shows the time inside `Trigger for constraint …_fkey`.
pitfalls.cause: A common claim is that PostgreSQL indexes foreign keys automatically. It does not. Only PRIMARY KEY, UNIQUE and EXCLUDE constraints create indexes. Without an index on the **referencing** column, every parent DELETE or key UPDATE scans the child table.
pitfalls.fix: Index the referencing columns of every foreign key that sees parent deletes or joins. This catalog query lists foreign keys whose first column leads no index.
pitfalls.sql:
SELECT c.conrelid::regclass AS child_table, c.conname, a.attname
FROM pg_constraint c
JOIN pg_attribute a ON a.attrelid = c.conrelid AND a.attnum = c.conkey[1]
WHERE c.contype = 'f'
  AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM pg_index i
                  WHERE i.indrelid = c.conrelid AND i.indkey[0] = c.conkey[1]);

pitfalls.title: Expression index on a cast that is not immutable
pitfalls.symptom: `ERROR: functions in index expression must be marked IMMUTABLE` when indexing `((doc->>'ts')::timestamptz)` or `lower(col)` through a custom function.
pitfalls.cause: An index expression must give the same result forever. Text-to-`timestamptz` and text-to-`date` casts depend on the `DateStyle` and `TimeZone` settings, so they are only STABLE.
pitfalls.fix: Store the value in a real `timestamptz` column written by the application or a trigger (a generated column has the same immutability rule), or store an immutable form such as epoch seconds and index `((doc->>'ts')::float8)`. Then write the query with exactly the same expression.

pointers: B-tree rule: **equality on leading columns + one range** on the next column bound the scan. PostgreSQL 18 **skip scan** helps when a leading column has few distinct values.
**Partial** indexes need the query to imply the predicate at plan time. Great for queues, soft deletes and rare states.
**Expression** indexes match only the identical expression. Run ANALYZE after creating one.
**INCLUDE** columns enable index-only scans (needs all-visible pages, i.e. VACUUM). INCLUDE indexes are never deduplicated.
Unique indexes treat NULLs as distinct unless `NULLS NOT DISTINCT`. Build with `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` and check for INVALID leftovers.

lessons.title: Reading EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
tldr: `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` runs the query and prints the plan tree with each node's **estimated** cost and rows next to its **actual** time, rows, loops and (by default in PostgreSQL 18) **buffers**.
Reading it bottom-up shows where time and I/O really go, and the gaps between estimates and reality point straight at the statistics, indexes or memory settings to fix.

visualizer.title: Click through seven real plans
visualizer.caption: Pick a scenario and click any node, or press Next node to tour the tree. Compare the in-memory and spilled sort, 1 and 2 hash batches, and an index-only scan before and after VACUUM.

presets.label: Node anatomy
presets.sql:
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE)
SELECT c.region, count(*), sum(o.amount)
FROM orders o JOIN customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id
GROUP BY c.region;
presets.note: Read bottom-up: two scans feed a Hash Join, which feeds HashAggregate. Each line shows `(cost=… rows=…)` then `(actual time=… rows=… loops=…)`. Buffers appear without asking: BUFFERS is on by default with ANALYZE in 18.

presets.label: Filter becomes Index Cond
presets.note: Before: `Seq Scan`, `Filter`, `Rows Removed by Filter: 4999`, cost 94.50 and 32 buffers. After: `Index Scan`, `Index Cond`, cost 8.30 and 3 buffers. A **Filter** is checked on every row after it is read. An **Index Cond** decides which rows are read at all. The IN list shows `Index Searches: 3`.

presets.label: Sort spill
