presets.note: `Sort Method: external merge  Disk: 2128kB` with `temp read/written` buffers, versus `quicksort  Memory: 5174kB`. The fix is memory for that query, not an index.

presets.label: Hash batches
presets.note: `Batches: 2` on the Hash node: the inner side did not fit in `work_mem × hash_mem_multiplier` (2.0), so it went to temp files and was processed in two passes.

presets.label: Loops multiply
presets.sql:
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE)
SELECT c.name, o.id, o.amount
FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
WHERE c.id <= 3;
presets.note: The inner Bitmap Heap Scan shows `rows=20.00 loops=3`: 60 rows in total. `Index Searches: 3` counts one descent per loop.

presets.label: Heap fetches → 0
presets.note: Before VACUUM: `Heap Fetches: 6020` and about 6028 buffers. After VACUUM sets the visibility map: `Heap Fetches: 0` and 9 buffers. Same plan shape, a 600× difference in I/O.

presets.label: Misestimate
presets.sql:
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS OFF)
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE amount::int % 10 = 0 AND customer_id < 100;
presets.note: An expression the planner has no statistics for gets a default selectivity, here **10 rows estimated, 199 actual**. Compare the two `rows=` values on each line first: everything above a misestimate is planned on wrong numbers.

presets.label: JSON and settings
presets.note: `SETTINGS` lists planner-relevant settings that differ from defaults: `work_mem`, and also `max_parallel_workers_per_gather = 0`, which is why the playground never shows parallel plans. `FORMAT JSON` is what plan visualizers parse. The `Sort Method` is `top-N heapsort`: LIMIT keeps only 10 rows, so no spill.

production.title: A nightly report that took 40 minutes
production.context: A finance team's nightly job joined invoices to line items and sorted the result for export. It ran for 40 minutes and got slower every month.
production.problem: `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)` showed a Hash node with **Batches: 64** and gigabytes of temp writes, then a Sort with **external merge**. The server ran with the default `work_mem` of 4MB, so every hash and sort spilled to disk.
production.solution: Give this one job more memory instead of raising it globally (each sort or hash node in every session may use `work_mem`, and hashes up to `hash_mem_multiplier` times that). Set it in the job's transaction, rerun EXPLAIN, and confirm `Batches: 1` and an in-memory sort.
production.outcome: In the playground the same effect is visible at small scale: the sort goes from external merge with 1636 temp blocks to an in-memory quicksort, and the hash join from 2 batches to 1. Spill-free plans also stop competing for disk with daytime traffic.

pitfalls.title: Reading per-loop numbers as totals
pitfalls.symptom: A nested-loop inner node shows `actual time=0.014 rows=20` and looks cheap, yet the query is slow.
pitfalls.cause: Actual time and rows are **averages per loop**. With `loops=50000` that node ran 50000 times.
pitfalls.fix: Multiply time and rows by `loops`. Look for the node whose time × loops dominates. Buffers, unlike rows, are already totals.

pitfalls.title: Running EXPLAIN ANALYZE on writes
pitfalls.symptom: Someone "just explains" a DELETE in production and the rows are gone.
pitfalls.cause: ANALYZE really **executes** the statement, side effects included.
pitfalls.fix: Wrap it in a transaction and roll back.

pitfalls.title: Blaming the wrong node
pitfalls.symptom: Tuning effort goes into the top node because it shows the largest time.
pitfalls.cause: A node's actual time **includes its children**. The top node is always the slowest.
pitfalls.fix: Subtract children's times to find each node's own work, or use a visualizer that does it. Start from the deepest node whose estimate first diverges from actual rows.

pitfalls.title: Index-only scans that are not
pitfalls.symptom: `Index Only Scan` with a large `Heap Fetches` count is barely faster than an index scan.
pitfalls.cause: Index entries carry no visibility information. Pages not marked all-visible in the visibility map force a heap visit per row.
pitfalls.fix: VACUUM the table (or tune autovacuum for insert-heavy tables with `autovacuum_vacuum_insert_scale_factor`) so pages become all-visible.

pitfalls.title: Looking for EXPLAIN options that do not exist
pitfalls.symptom: `ERROR: unrecognized EXPLAIN option "io"`, or a search through `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, VERBOSE)` output for CPU figures that never appear.
pitfalls.cause: Common claims say PostgreSQL 18 added an `IO` option and that VERBOSE reports CPU usage. Neither is true. The options are ANALYZE, VERBOSE, COSTS, SETTINGS, GENERIC_PLAN, BUFFERS, SERIALIZE, WAL, TIMING, SUMMARY, MEMORY and FORMAT. The CPU, WAL and read statistics added in 18 appear in `VACUUM (VERBOSE)` and `ANALYZE (VERBOSE)` output.
pitfalls.fix: For I/O, read the `Buffers:` lines (automatic with ANALYZE in 18), and set `track_io_timing = on` to add `I/O Timings`. Use `BUFFERS OFF` to hide them. For CPU time, compare `actual time` with the I/O timings.
pitfalls.sql:
SET track_io_timing = on;
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE) SELECT count(*) FROM orders;

pointers: Each node: `(cost=startup..total rows= width=)` estimated, then `(actual time=first..last rows= loops=)` measured. **Compare the two rows values first.**
Actual rows and time are **per loop**; multiply by `loops`. A node's time includes its children.
**Buffers** (default with ANALYZE in 18): shared hit = cached, read = from OS, temp = spills. They include child nodes.
Red flags: `external merge Disk`, `Batches` > 1, `Heap Fetches` > 0, big `Rows Removed by Filter`, `lossy` heap blocks.
Not shown in the playground but common in production: `Gather` with `Workers Planned/Launched` for parallel query, and a `JIT:` block when the plan cost exceeds `jit_above_cost`.

lessons.title: ACID and transactions
tldr: A **transaction** groups statements so they commit or vanish together, and PostgreSQL implements that by stamping every row version with an **xid** and recording one 2-bit status per xid in the commit log.
Because rollback and crash recovery only have to flip or ignore that status, an abort is instant and PostgreSQL needs **no undo log**.

visualizer.title: A transfer with a savepoint, xid by xid
visualizer.caption: Step through BEGIN, two UPDATEs, a SAVEPOINT and a ROLLBACK TO. Switch the ending to compare a clean COMMIT, a crash, and an error followed by COMMIT.

presets.label: Virtual vs real xid
presets.note: Before the UPDATE the xid is **NULL**: only a virtual xid exists. After it, a `transactionid` lock on the new xid appears, held in the main lock table (`fastpath = false`).

presets.label: Savepoint = subtransaction
presets.note: Two `transactionid` locks: the top xid and a **subxid** one higher. Bob's new version has `cmin = 1`. After `ROLLBACK TO`, bob's surviving row shows `xmax` = the aborted subxid, which readers ignore.

presets.label: Transfer: all or nothing
presets.note: The first CALL commits inside the procedure: alice **70**, bob **80**. The negative transfer fails on the credit (**23514**) and alice's debit vanishes with it. Inside a transaction block the procedure may not COMMIT, so CALL fails with **2D000** `invalid transaction termination`.

presets.label: Transactional DDL
presets.note: The third ALTER fails (**23502**: existing rows have no postal code), and the first two columns are rolled back with it: `new_columns = 0`. Schema changes are ordinary transactional writes to the catalogs.

presets.label: Read the commit log
presets.sql:
SELECT lp, t_ctid, t_xmin, t_xmax,
       pg_xact_status(t_xmin::text::xid8) AS xmin_status,
       CASE WHEN t_xmax::text <> '0' THEN pg_xact_status(t_xmax::text::xid8) END AS xmax_status
FROM heap_page_items(get_raw_page('acct', 0));
presets.note: Every version ever written is still on the page. `pg_xact_status` reads `pg_xact`: versions whose xmin is **aborted** are invisible forever, and an aborted xmax deletes nothing.

presets.label: Sequences ignore ROLLBACK
presets.note: The rollback did not give back 1 and 2, and the failed INSERT used up **3** before its CHECK fired, so the first real invoice is number **4**. Sequences are non-transactional by design, which is what lets concurrent sessions take values without waiting.

presets.label: Cost of subtransactions
presets.note: Each `BEGIN … EXCEPTION` block is a subtransaction, and each one that writes burns a **subxid**: the 500-row loop advances the counter by about 500. The set-based UPDATE uses one xid.

presets.label: Implicit transactions & 2PC
presets.note: A plain read gets no xid (**NULL**). `txid_current()` forces one, and outside BEGIN each statement is its own transaction, so the two values differ by one. `max_prepared_transactions = 0` disables `PREPARE TRANSACTION`; production 2PC needs it raised.

production.title: A nightly job that burned half a million xids
production.context: A billing job applies late fees row by row in a PL/pgSQL loop. Each row update sits in its own `BEGIN … EXCEPTION` block so a bad row is logged and skipped.
production.problem: Every exception block is a **subtransaction**, and every one that writes gets its own subxid. One run over 500 k accounts assigns about 500 k subxids inside one top-level transaction. Past **64 cached subxids** per backend, other sessions' visibility checks must consult `pg_subtrans`, and the xid counter races toward the freeze thresholds.
production.solution: Validate first, then write in one set-based statement. Move the bad-row filter into the WHERE clause, and use a separate rejects table for rows that fail validation. Keep exception blocks for genuinely unexpected errors, outside the per-row loop.
production.outcome: On 500 rows the per-row exception loop advances the xid counter by **502**, the set-based UPDATE by **1**. The subxid cache can no longer overflow, and xid consumption drops by the row count.

pitfalls.title: Idle in transaction
pitfalls.symptom: `pg_stat_activity` shows sessions in state `idle in transaction` for minutes; table bloat grows and DDL queues behind them.
pitfalls.cause: An open transaction keeps its locks until it ends and holds back the xmin horizon, so VACUUM cannot remove rows that died after it started. Drivers with autocommit off send BEGIN before the first statement, so one SELECT on a pooled connection that never commits is enough.
pitfalls.fix: Commit or roll back after every unit of work (reads included), and set a server-side guard.
pitfalls.sql: ALTER ROLE app SET idle_in_transaction_session_timeout = '30s';

pitfalls.title: Subtransaction overflow
pitfalls.symptom: Throughput collapses under concurrency and wait events show `SubtransSLRU` / `SubtransBuffer` when one transaction uses many savepoints or exception blocks.
pitfalls.cause: Only 64 subxids per backend are cached in shared memory. Beyond that, every snapshot check for that transaction's rows has to look in `pg_subtrans`.
pitfalls.fix: Avoid per-row savepoints (ORM "nested transactions", PL/pgSQL EXCEPTION inside loops). Batch the work set-based, or commit in smaller transactions.

pitfalls.title: Carrying on after an error
pitfalls.symptom: Every statement after a failed one returns `ERROR: current transaction is aborted, commands ignored until end of transaction block` (25P02), and the final COMMIT replies `ROLLBACK`. Rows written before the error are gone.
pitfalls.cause: Any error puts the whole transaction block into the aborted state. Nothing more can run in it, and COMMIT on an aborted transaction performs a rollback. A common belief is that COMMIT saves the statements that succeeded; it never does.
pitfalls.fix: Check every statement result and ROLLBACK on error, then retry the unit of work. To survive an expected failure inside one transaction, set a SAVEPOINT before it and `ROLLBACK TO` it on error.

pitfalls.title: A procedure that COMMITs, called inside BEGIN
pitfalls.symptom: `CALL transfer(…)` works from psql but fails from the application with `ERROR: invalid transaction termination` (2D000).
pitfalls.cause: A procedure may only COMMIT or ROLLBACK when CALL runs in its own transaction. The driver or framework wrapped the CALL in BEGIN … COMMIT, or a function sits between the caller and the procedure.
pitfalls.fix: Run such procedures in autocommit mode, as a top-level CALL. If the caller must own the transaction, remove COMMIT from the procedure and let the caller commit.

pitfalls.title: Expecting ROLLBACK to undo everything
pitfalls.symptom: Invoice numbers have gaps after rollbacks, failed INSERTs and upserts, and a session-level advisory lock is still held after a rollback.
pitfalls.cause: Sequence increments and session-level advisory locks are deliberately non-transactional. An INSERT draws its default value before constraints are checked, so a failed or conflicting INSERT still consumes a number.
pitfalls.fix: Never use a sequence as a gap-free counter. Use `pg_advisory_xact_lock` when the lock should end with the transaction.

pitfalls.title: Forgotten prepared transactions
pitfalls.symptom: After a coordinator crash, locks are held forever and `age(datfrozenxid)` keeps rising even with no sessions connected.
pitfalls.cause: A `PREPARE TRANSACTION` survives restarts and keeps its locks and its xid until someone runs `COMMIT PREPARED` or `ROLLBACK PREPARED`.
pitfalls.fix: Leave `max_prepared_transactions = 0` unless you run a transaction manager, and alert on old rows in `pg_prepared_xacts`.
pitfalls.sql: SELECT gid, prepared, age(transaction) FROM pg_prepared_xacts ORDER BY prepared;

pointers: Every transaction has a **virtual xid**. A real **xid** (32-bit, wraps; `xid8` adds the epoch) is assigned only at the first write.
Commit and abort are a **2-bit status** per xid in `pg_xact`. Rows are never undone: aborted xmins are invisible and aborted xmaxes are ignored.
**SAVEPOINT** and PL/pgSQL **EXCEPTION** blocks are subtransactions with their own **subxids**. Only 64 are cached per backend.
Locks are held to **transaction end**, except those taken after a savepoint that is rolled back to.
**2PC**: `PREPARE TRANSACTION` → `COMMIT PREPARED` / `ROLLBACK PREPARED`; inspect `pg_prepared_xacts`.

lessons.title: Snapshots and tuple visibility
tldr: A **snapshot** is three numbers, `xmin:xmax:xip`, that classify every xid as finished, in progress, or not yet started, and a row version is visible when its inserting xid counts and its deleting xid does not.
Snapshots let readers and writers work on the same rows at once without blocking, because each reader just ignores the versions its snapshot cannot see.

visualizer.title: Two sessions, one row, two isolation levels
visualizer.caption: Step the timeline, then flip A to Repeatable Read and replay it. Below, edit a snapshot and click xids to see the visibility rule decide.

presets.label: Your snapshot
presets.sql:
SELECT pg_current_snapshot() AS snap,
       pg_snapshot_xmin(pg_current_snapshot()) AS xmin,
       pg_snapshot_xmax(pg_current_snapshot()) AS xmax,
       pg_current_xact_id_if_assigned() AS my_xid;
presets.note: With only one session, nothing is in progress: `xmin = xmax` and `xip` is empty. `my_xid` is NULL because this read-only statement never needed an xid.

presets.label: UPDATE writes a new version
presets.note: `SET price = price` changes nothing, yet a new version is written: `old` is the version at **(0,1)** that just received an `xmax`, `new` is the one at **(0,3)**. A SELECT without ORDER BY returns heap order, so the desk now comes back after the chair.

presets.label: Own xid vs own snapshot
presets.note: The function says your own xid is **not** visible (it equals xmax), yet the SELECT shows price 11. Own changes are visible through a separate rule, by command id.

presets.label: Save a snapshot, then write
presets.note: A `pg_snapshot` is an ordinary value: we stored the snapshot from before three later transactions. The next preset judges every version against it.

presets.label: Time travel with the rule
presets.sql:
WITH s AS (SELECT snap FROM saved WHERE label = 't0'),
v AS (
  SELECT lp, t_xmin::text::xid8 AS xmin8, NULLIF(t_xmax::text, '0')::xid8 AS xmax8,
         get_byte(t_attrs[1], 0) AS id
  FROM heap_page_item_attrs(get_raw_page('item', 0), 'item'::regclass)
  WHERE lp_flags = 1)
SELECT lp, id, xmin8 AS xmin, xmax8 AS xmax,
  pg_visible_in_snapshot(xmin8, s.snap) AND pg_xact_status(xmin8) = 'committed'
  AND NOT coalesce(pg_visible_in_snapshot(xmax8, s.snap)
                   AND pg_xact_status(xmax8) = 'committed', false) AS t0_sees,
  pg_visible_in_snapshot(xmin8, pg_current_snapshot()) AND pg_xact_status(xmin8) = 'committed'
  AND NOT coalesce(pg_visible_in_snapshot(xmax8, pg_current_snapshot())
                   AND pg_xact_status(xmax8) = 'committed', false) AS now_sees
FROM v, s ORDER BY lp;
presets.note: The visibility rule in SQL. The **t0** snapshot still sees the old desk price and the chair; **now** sees the new desk and the lamp. Every version is still on the page until VACUUM.

presets.label: Hint bits
presets.note: Right after the INSERT the tuple has no `HEAP_XMIN_COMMITTED`. The next reader looks up `pg_xact`, then caches the answer as a **hint bit** (and dirties the page).

presets.label: Repeatable Read snapshot
presets.note: The transaction snapshot is taken at the **first statement** and reused. With concurrent writers, `later_stmt` would still equal `first_stmt` under RR, but would move under Read Committed.

production.title: One forgotten transaction bloats every table
production.context: A reporting tool opens a REPEATABLE READ transaction, runs a query, and then leaves the connection idle in transaction while a user looks at a dashboard for hours.
production.problem: That transaction's snapshot has an old **xmin**. Every row version deleted after it might still be visible to it, so VACUUM on every table in the database must keep them. Hot tables bloat, and index scans slow down as they wade through dead versions.
production.solution: Find the oldest snapshot holders by `backend_xmin`, end them, and put timeouts in place so it cannot recur.
production.outcome: VACUUM can again remove versions older than the next-oldest snapshot. `n_dead_tup` in `pg_stat_user_tables` falls on the next autovacuum pass, and a recurring offender is cut off after 5 minutes.

pitfalls.title: Long snapshots block cleanup everywhere
pitfalls.symptom: VACUUM VERBOSE reports "dead row versions cannot be removed yet" and tables keep growing.
pitfalls.cause: Any open snapshot pins the xmin horizon for the whole database, including one held by a replication slot, by standby feedback, or by a driver connection with autocommit off that ran one SELECT and went idle.
pitfalls.fix: Monitor `age(backend_xmin)` in `pg_stat_activity` and `pg_replication_slots.xmin`; set `idle_in_transaction_session_timeout` and `transaction_timeout`.

pitfalls.title: Relying on the order rows come back in
pitfalls.symptom: A list that always came back in insertion order suddenly shows an edited row at the end, or a paginated API skips and repeats rows.
pitfalls.cause: Without ORDER BY, a sequential scan returns rows in **heap order**. Every UPDATE writes a new version wherever there is free space, so editing a row (or an `ON DELETE SET NULL` rewriting child rows) moves it. The old version stays behind until VACUUM.
pitfalls.fix: Always add `ORDER BY` with a unique tiebreaker when order matters. Never read meaning into `ctid`: it changes on every update and after VACUUM FULL.

pitfalls.title: TRUNCATE empties the table for old snapshots
pitfalls.symptom: A Repeatable Read export sees an empty table, although its snapshot was taken before the table was truncated and refilled.
pitfalls.cause: TRUNCATE is **not MVCC-safe**: it swaps in a new empty file instead of stamping `xmax` on each row. A transaction whose snapshot predates the TRUNCATE, but which had not yet touched that table, finds no old versions to read.
pitfalls.fix: Use DELETE when concurrent snapshot readers must see the old rows, or touch every table the export needs at its start, so the TRUNCATE waits for its ACCESS SHARE lock to go.

pitfalls.title: Read Committed reports that do not add up
pitfalls.symptom: A multi-query report shows totals that disagree with its own detail rows.
pitfalls.cause: Each statement in Read Committed takes a **new snapshot**, so later queries see commits that earlier ones did not.
pitfalls.fix: Run multi-statement reports as `BEGIN ISOLATION LEVEL REPEATABLE READ READ ONLY`, so every query shares one snapshot.

pitfalls.title: Comparing xid values directly
pitfalls.symptom: A query using `xmin` to find "rows changed after transaction X" returns garbage after a while.
pitfalls.cause: `xid` is 32-bit and compared modulo 2^32: it has no ordering operator and wraps around. `xid8` (from `pg_current_xact_id()`) does not wrap.
pitfalls.fix: Compare `xid8` values, or better use a `updated_at` column or logical decoding for change tracking.

pointers: Snapshot `xmin:xmax:xip`: below xmin = finished, at or above xmax = not started, xip = in progress.
A version is visible if its **xmin** committed before the snapshot and its **xmax** is 0, aborted, or not yet visible.
**Read Committed**: one snapshot per statement. **Repeatable Read** and Serializable: one per transaction, taken at the first statement.
**Hint bits** cache commit status on the tuple, so the first reader after a write may dirty the page.
Use `pg_current_snapshot()`, `pg_visible_in_snapshot()` and `pg_xact_status()` with **xid8** values.

lessons.title: HOT updates and fillfactor
tldr: A **heap-only tuple (HOT)** update writes the new row version on the same page and chains to it from the old one, so no index entry is added when no indexed column changed.
It exists because every non-HOT update must insert into **every index** on the table, and leaving free space with **fillfactor** is how you make HOT the common case.

visualizer.title: HOT chains vs index churn
visualizer.caption: Step through two HOT updates, a non-HOT update, an index scan and VACUUM. Then pick a fillfactor and a workload to see the HOT rate and index growth it produces.

presets.label: HOT update
presets.note: lp 1 gets `HEAP_HOT_UPDATED` and `t_ctid = (0,4)`; lp 4 is `HEAP_ONLY_TUPLE`. The pkey index still has exactly three entries, all pointing at the original ctids.

presets.label: Chain a second HOT update
presets.note: The chain is now lp 1 → 4 → 5. An index scan for id = 1 enters at lp 1 and walks the chain inside the page.

presets.label: Non-HOT: change an indexed column
presets.note: Both indexes gain an entry pointing at (0,6), even `items_pkey` whose key did not change. The counters show 3 updates, 2 of them HOT.

presets.label: VACUUM: redirects
presets.note: `lp_flags = 2` is a **redirect**: lp 1 now points to lp 5 (its `lp_off` holds the target). lp 2 and lp 4 are unused (0). The pkey entry for (0,2) is gone.

presets.label: fillfactor 100 vs 80
presets.note: Same 2,000 updates. **ff80** does all of them HOT and the primary key stays the same size. **ff100** does none HOT and its primary key index nearly doubles from page splits.

presets.label: An index on the hot column
presets.note: Free space no longer helps: `qty` is now indexed, so `n_tup_hot_upd` does not move. A BRIN index would not block HOT, because BRIN is a *summarizing* index.

presets.label: No-op updates are real writes
presets.note: The first UPDATE changes no value but still moves alice from **(0,1)** to **(0,3)** and leaves a dead version. It is HOT, since no indexed value changed, yet it still costs a tuple, WAL and later VACUUM work. The guarded UPDATE reports **UPDATE 0** and writes nothing.

presets.label: Upsert: DO UPDATE vs DO NOTHING
presets.note: A "no-op" `DO UPDATE` exists only to make RETURNING produce the row, and each run writes a new version: the ctid and xmin move every time. `DO NOTHING` writes nothing and returns no row. All three attempts still drew an identity value, so the sequence moved from 2 to **5**.

production.title: An index on last_seen_at killed HOT on a sessions table
production.context: A web app updates `sessions.last_seen_at` on every request. Someone added an index on `last_seen_at` to speed up an hourly cleanup job.
production.problem: Every request now changes an indexed column, so **no update is HOT**. Each one inserts into all four indexes, and the table and indexes bloat between vacuums. WAL volume and checkpoint I/O rise with them.
production.solution: Drop the index (the cleanup job can scan, or use a BRIN index, which does not block HOT). Lower `fillfactor` so updated rows find room on their own page. Watch the HOT ratio.
production.outcome: On a 10,000-row table updating 20% of rows, fillfactor 100 gave **0% HOT** in the first round and grew the primary key from 30 to 57 pages; fillfactor 80 gave **100% HOT** with zero index growth, at the cost of 25% more heap pages up front.

pitfalls.title: Indexing a frequently updated column
pitfalls.symptom: `n_tup_hot_upd` is near zero and indexes keep growing although the row count is flat.
pitfalls.cause: Changing any column referenced by any non-summarizing index (including expression and partial-index predicates) rules out HOT.
pitfalls.fix: Keep volatile columns out of B-tree indexes, or use BRIN. Check the ratio per table.
pitfalls.sql:
SELECT relname, n_tup_upd, n_tup_hot_upd, n_tup_newpage_upd
FROM pg_stat_user_tables ORDER BY n_tup_upd DESC LIMIT 10;

pitfalls.title: Expecting ALTER TABLE … SET (fillfactor) to fix existing pages
pitfalls.symptom: After lowering fillfactor, the HOT ratio does not improve.
pitfalls.cause: Fillfactor is only honoured when new rows are inserted into pages. Existing full pages stay full.
pitfalls.fix: Rewrite the table once (`VACUUM FULL` or `pg_repack` during a maintenance window), or let churn redistribute rows over time.

pitfalls.title: Believing an unchanged UPDATE is free
pitfalls.symptom: A sync job that "only touches changed rows" generates as much WAL and as many dead tuples as a full rewrite, and `n_tup_upd` climbs on rows whose values never change.
pitfalls.cause: A common belief is that setting a column to its current value costs nothing. Every matched row gets a complete new version (the command tag `UPDATE n` counts them too), and a no-op `ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE` used for get-or-create does the same on every call. A one-key `jsonb_set` likewise writes the whole row, and the whole TOAST value when the document is large.
pitfalls.fix: Filter out unchanged rows with `IS DISTINCT FROM`, or add the built-in `suppress_redundant_updates_trigger()` as a BEFORE UPDATE trigger. For get-or-create, use `ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING` and read the existing row separately.

pitfalls.title: Pruning blocked by old snapshots
pitfalls.symptom: HOT updates still lead to page growth, and HOT chains get long.
pitfalls.cause: Pruning can only remove versions that no snapshot can see. A long-running transaction keeps every intermediate version alive.
pitfalls.fix: Remove long transactions (see `backend_xmin` in `pg_stat_activity`), then pruning and HOT reuse resume on their own.

pointers: HOT needs both: **no indexed column changed** (BRIN excepted) and **room on the same page**.
A HOT update adds **no index entries**; index scans follow the `t_ctid` chain within the page.
Pruning turns the chain root into an **LP_REDIRECT** and frees intermediate versions, even during normal reads.
Tables default to **fillfactor 100**; 70–90 leaves room for HOT on update-heavy tables.
Monitor `n_tup_hot_upd` and `n_tup_newpage_upd` in `pg_stat_user_tables`.

lessons.title: Isolation levels: RC, RR, Serializable (SSI)
tldr: PostgreSQL offers **Read Committed** (a snapshot per statement, re-checking rows changed by others), **Repeatable Read** (one snapshot per transaction) and **Serializable** (Repeatable Read plus conflict tracking with SIRead locks).
Each step up removes a class of anomalies at the cost of **serialization failures** (SQLSTATE `40001`) that the application must answer by retrying the whole transaction.

visualizer.title: Three classic races, replayed
visualizer.caption: Pick a scenario and step through it. Watch wait bars, snapshots and row versions; in the SSI case, watch the rw-conflict edges close into a cycle.

presets.label: Levels you can ask for
presets.note: You may request READ UNCOMMITTED, and it is reported back, but PostgreSQL runs it as **Read Committed**: dirty reads are never possible.

presets.label: Hits example, run serially
presets.note: Run one after the other, the DELETE removes **id 1** (now 10). Run concurrently (the visualizer), the same two statements delete nothing. That gap is the RC anomaly.

presets.label: Race-free upsert
presets.sql:
INSERT INTO website VALUES (2, 1), (3, 1)
ON CONFLICT (id) DO UPDATE SET hits = website.hits + 1
RETURNING id, old.hits AS old_hits, new.hits AS new_hits,
          old.id IS NULL AS inserted,
          (xmax = 0) AS inserted_pre18;
presets.note: id 2 existed and took the UPDATE path (11 → 12), id 3 was inserted. Under Read Committed, a session that meets an uncommitted insert of the same key **waits** for it, then updates the committed row: it never fails with 23505 on the conflict key. `old IS NULL` (PG18) and the older `xmax = 0` trick both tell the two paths apart.

presets.label: SIRead locks: seq scan
presets.note: The tiny table is read by a sequential scan, so the predicate lock covers the **whole relation**: any insert into mytab by another serializable transaction conflicts.

presets.label: SIRead locks: index scan
presets.note: With an index scan the locks are fine-grained: two **tuple** locks on the heap and one **page** lock on `mytab_class_idx`. Fewer false conflicts, fewer needless 40001s.

presets.label: READ ONLY DEFERRABLE
presets.note: A deferrable read-only transaction waits (if needed) for a **safe snapshot**, then reads with **no SIRead locks** and can never fail with 40001. Ideal for long reports.

production.title: On-call scheduling that let everyone go off call
production.context: A rota app enforces "at least one doctor on call per shift" in application code: count on-call doctors, and if the count is above 1, let this one go off call.
production.problem: Two doctors press "go off call" at the same moment. Under Read Committed or Repeatable Read both transactions count **2**, both update their own row, and both commit. Neither update touched a row the other wrote, so no lock ever conflicted: **write skew**, and the shift has nobody.
production.solution: Run the check-and-update as **SERIALIZABLE** and wrap it in a retry loop on SQLSTATE `40001`. SSI sees that each transaction read what the other wrote and aborts one. The retry then counts 1 and refuses.
production.outcome: The invariant holds under any interleaving, with no explicit locks. Retries are rare (only on true overlap); the tradeoff is the SSI bookkeeping overhead and a retry path that every writer must implement.

pitfalls.title: Retrying only the failed statement
pitfalls.symptom: After catching 40001 the app re-sends the last UPDATE and gets `current transaction is aborted, commands ignored until end of transaction block`.
pitfalls.cause: A serialization failure aborts the **whole** transaction. Its reads were made under the old snapshot and are no longer trustworthy.
pitfalls.fix: ROLLBACK and rerun the entire transaction from BEGIN, re-reading everything, with a bounded number of attempts.

pitfalls.title: Assuming Repeatable Read prevents write skew
pitfalls.symptom: Business rules that span several rows ("total ≤ limit", "one on call") are violated under load, with no errors raised.
pitfalls.cause: Repeatable Read is snapshot isolation: it stops lost updates on the **same** row, not anomalies across different rows.
pitfalls.fix: Use SERIALIZABLE for such transactions, or take explicit locks (`SELECT … FOR UPDATE` on the rows the rule depends on).

pitfalls.title: Treating MERGE as an upsert
pitfalls.symptom: Under concurrent load, a MERGE with `WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT` fails now and then with `23505 duplicate key value violates unique constraint`.
pitfalls.cause: A common claim is that MERGE is equivalent to an upsert. Under Read Committed, if another session inserts the same key after MERGE decided "not matched", MERGE does not re-check its MATCHED branches: the INSERT simply hits the unique index. `INSERT … ON CONFLICT` is built for that race.
pitfalls.fix: Use `INSERT … ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE` for single-table upserts. Keep MERGE for multi-action synchronisation, and retry it on 23505.

pitfalls.title: Get-or-create that returns nothing
pitfalls.symptom: A rare request gets zero rows back from a "get or create" query, although the row clearly exists afterwards.
pitfalls.cause: The query is `WITH ins AS (INSERT … ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING RETURNING *) SELECT * FROM ins UNION ALL SELECT … WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM ins)`. When another session inserted the key and committed after this statement took its snapshot, the INSERT sees the conflict and does nothing, and the SELECT cannot see the new row, because every part of a statement shares one snapshot.
pitfalls.fix: When the statement returns no row, run the SELECT again as a new statement (it gets a fresh snapshot in Read Committed), or loop in PL/pgSQL until one of the two paths returns the row.

pitfalls.title: Serializable with sequential scans
pitfalls.symptom: Many 40001 errors between transactions that touch unrelated rows.
pitfalls.cause: A sequential scan takes a **relation-level** SIRead lock, so any write to the table conflicts. Lock promotion under memory pressure has the same effect.
pitfalls.fix: Index the predicates serializable transactions filter on, keep them short, mark read-only ones `READ ONLY`, and raise `max_pred_locks_per_transaction` if promotion is frequent.

pointers: PostgreSQL has three real levels; **READ UNCOMMITTED = READ COMMITTED**, and its Repeatable Read also blocks phantoms.
**Read Committed**: snapshot per statement; a blocked UPDATE/DELETE re-checks its WHERE on the newest row version.
**Repeatable Read**: changing a row updated after your snapshot raises `40001` *could not serialize access due to concurrent update*.
**Serializable** (SSI): SIRead locks never block; a cycle of rw-conflicts aborts one transaction with `40001`.
Always retry the **whole transaction** on 40001 (and 40P01). Read-only transactions under RR never need to.

lessons.title: Heavyweight locks and the conflict matrix
tldr: PostgreSQL has **eight table lock modes** that commands take automatically, and two transactions can hold locks on the same table only if their modes do not conflict.
The modes exist so reads, writes, VACUUM and schema changes can each run alongside exactly the operations that are safe, and the **lock queue** decides who waits when they are not.

visualizer.title: A migration stalls the whole table
visualizer.caption: Step through the lock queue, then switch the migration to `lock_timeout = 2s` and replay it. Below, click cells or two modes in the matrix to test any pair.

presets.label: Locks a SELECT holds
presets.note: **AccessShareLock** on the table and on every index the plan may use, all taken through the **fast path** (`fastpath = true`): weak locks skip the shared lock table.

presets.label: Locks an UPDATE holds
presets.note: **RowExclusiveLock** on the table and its indexes, plus an ExclusiveLock on the new xid. The row lock itself is not in `pg_locks`: it lives in the tuple.

presets.label: ALTER TABLE lock levels
presets.note: ADD COLUMN and ADD CONSTRAINT … NOT VALID take **AccessExclusive** but finish instantly. VALIDATE CONSTRAINT scans the table under the much weaker **ShareUpdateExclusive**, so writes continue. CREATE INDEX takes **Share**, which blocks writes.

presets.label: PG18: NOT NULL in two steps
presets.note: The NOT VALID constraint is added under AccessExclusive but without a scan, and it rejects new NULLs at once (**23502**). VALIDATE fails while 400 old rows are NULL. After the backfill it scans the table under **ShareUpdateExclusive**, so writes keep flowing, and `convalidated` turns true.

presets.label: TRUNCATE vs DELETE
presets.note: DELETE takes **RowExclusive** and stamps `xmax` on each row, so readers and other writers carry on. TRUNCATE takes **AccessExclusive**, which blocks even SELECT, and points the table at a brand-new empty file. It is still transactional: after ROLLBACK the old file and all 1,000 rows are back.

presets.label: A transaction never blocks itself
presets.note: Share and AccessExclusive conflict, but **not with yourself**: both are granted. Strong modes always go to the main lock table (`fastpath = false`).

presets.label: Timeouts and NOWAIT
presets.note: With another session holding a lock, `NOWAIT` would fail at once and `lock_timeout` after 2 s, both with **55P03**. Alone, the lock is granted and nobody blocks us (`{}`).

presets.label: Who is blocking whom
presets.sql:
SELECT pid, state, wait_event_type, wait_event,
       pg_blocking_pids(pid) AS blocked_by,
       now() - xact_start AS xact_age, left(query, 40) AS query
FROM pg_stat_activity
WHERE backend_type = 'client backend' OR pid = pg_backend_pid()
ORDER BY xact_start NULLS LAST;

-- stop sessions idle in a transaction for over 10 minutes
SELECT pid, pg_terminate_backend(pid, 5000) AS gone
FROM pg_stat_activity
WHERE state = 'idle in transaction'
  AND now() - state_change > interval '10 minutes';
SHOW max_locks_per_transaction;
presets.note: A waiting session has `wait_event_type = Lock` and a non-empty `blocked_by`; the oldest transaction is usually the root. `pg_cancel_backend` stops the running query, `pg_terminate_backend` ends the session and rolls back its transaction. With a timeout (ms) terminate returns true only once the process has exited. The lock table is sized by `max_locks_per_transaction` (objects, not rows).

production.title: A one-line migration that took the API down
production.context: A deploy runs `ALTER TABLE orders ADD COLUMN note text` at midday. The statement is metadata-only and normally finishes in milliseconds.
production.problem: An analyst's session had run a SELECT on `orders` and stayed **idle in transaction**. The ALTER queued for ACCESS EXCLUSIVE behind it, and every API query on `orders` queued behind the ALTER. Connection pools filled and the API timed out, though no query was doing any work.
production.solution: Run DDL with a short `lock_timeout` in a retry loop, so the migration gives up instead of becoming the head of a queue. Cap idle transactions so the blocker cannot exist for long.
production.outcome: The worst stall an API query can see from the migration drops from "as long as the oldest open transaction" to the 2-second timeout, and the migration still lands on a later retry.

pitfalls.title: Assuming a waiting DDL is harmless
pitfalls.symptom: A blocked `ALTER TABLE` or `TRUNCATE` is followed by a pile-up of ordinary SELECTs on that table.
pitfalls.cause: Lock requests queue in order: a request that conflicts with a *waiting* ACCESS EXCLUSIVE request waits behind it, even if it is compatible with every granted lock.
pitfalls.fix: Always set `lock_timeout` for DDL, and check for long transactions first.
pitfalls.sql:
SELECT pid, now() - xact_start AS xact_age, state, left(query, 60)
FROM pg_stat_activity WHERE xact_start IS NOT NULL ORDER BY xact_start LIMIT 5;

pitfalls.title: CREATE INDEX blocks writes
pitfalls.symptom: INSERTs and UPDATEs stall for the whole duration of an index build.
pitfalls.cause: Plain `CREATE INDEX` takes **SHARE**, which conflicts with ROW EXCLUSIVE.
pitfalls.fix: Use `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY`. It is not lock-free: it takes SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE (blocking other DDL and VACUUM), waits for every existing transaction that could modify or use the new index, and cannot run inside a transaction block. A failed concurrent build leaves an INVALID index you must drop; a failed plain CREATE INDEX rolls back completely. For a new unique constraint, build `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` first, then `ADD CONSTRAINT … UNIQUE USING INDEX`.

pitfalls.title: Assuming TRUNCATE needs only a light lock
pitfalls.symptom: A nightly `TRUNCATE staging` hangs behind a long report, and every query on that table piles up behind it.
pitfalls.cause: A common claim is that TRUNCATE is fast because it uses lighter locking than DELETE. It takes **ACCESS EXCLUSIVE**, the strongest mode. It is fast because it swaps in a new empty file instead of marking each row, and so leaves no dead tuples to vacuum.
pitfalls.fix: Run TRUNCATE with a short `lock_timeout` and retry. When readers must never block, DELETE in batches instead, or rotate partitions (DETACH, then DROP).

pitfalls.title: SET NOT NULL on a big table
pitfalls.symptom: `ALTER TABLE … ALTER COLUMN email SET NOT NULL` blocks all reads and writes on the table for minutes.
pitfalls.cause: SET NOT NULL scans every row to prove there are no NULLs, while holding ACCESS EXCLUSIVE for the whole scan.
pitfalls.fix: In PostgreSQL 18, add the constraint as `NOT NULL … NOT VALID` (instant), backfill in batches, then `VALIDATE CONSTRAINT`, which scans under SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE while writes continue.

pitfalls.title: Running out of lock table space
pitfalls.symptom: `ERROR: out of shared memory`, `HINT: You might need to increase max_locks_per_transaction`, on queries over many partitions.
pitfalls.cause: Every table and index touched is one lock-table entry, held to transaction end. Thousands of partitions in one transaction can exhaust the shared lock table.
pitfalls.fix: Raise `max_locks_per_transaction` (server restart), and make sure partition pruning removes partitions at plan time.

pointers: Eight modes from **ACCESS SHARE** (SELECT) to **ACCESS EXCLUSIVE** (DROP, TRUNCATE, most ALTER TABLE). Only ACCESS EXCLUSIVE blocks a plain SELECT.
Locks are held to **transaction end**; a transaction never conflicts with its own locks.
Waiters queue in order: a strong waiting request blocks newcomers too. Use `lock_timeout` for DDL.
Find blockers with `pg_blocking_pids(pid)` and `pg_locks.granted = false`.
Weak locks (ACCESS SHARE, ROW SHARE, ROW EXCLUSIVE) use the per-backend **fast path** when nothing conflicts.

lessons.title: Row locks, SKIP LOCKED and advisory locks
tldr: Row locks (`FOR UPDATE`, `FOR NO KEY UPDATE`, `FOR SHARE`, `FOR KEY SHARE`) are written into the tuple itself, in `t_xmax`, so PostgreSQL can lock any number of rows without memory limits.
On top of them, **NOWAIT** and **SKIP LOCKED** let a worker refuse to wait, which turns a plain table into a concurrent job queue, while **advisory locks** lock ideas that are not rows at all.

visualizer.title: Three queue workers, two locking clauses
visualizer.caption: Step through three workers claiming jobs with SKIP LOCKED, then switch to plain FOR UPDATE and watch them line up. Below, test any pair of row-lock modes.

presets.label: Claim a job
presets.note: Only job 1 gets `xmax` = our xid. `pg_locks` shows a **RowShareLock** on the table and nothing per row: the row lock lives in the tuple.

presets.label: Lock bits in the tuple
presets.note: Both rows carry our xid in `t_xmax`, with `HEAP_XMAX_LOCK_ONLY` (a lock, not a delete). The strength is in the flags: `HEAP_XMAX_EXCL_LOCK` vs `HEAP_XMAX_KEYSHR_LOCK`.

presets.label: Claim and start in one statement
presets.sql:
UPDATE jobs SET status = 'running'
WHERE id = (
  SELECT id FROM jobs WHERE status = 'queued'
  ORDER BY id LIMIT 1
  FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED)
RETURNING id, payload, status;
presets.note: The production pattern: the subquery picks and locks one unclaimed row, the UPDATE marks it, all in one round trip. Run it repeatedly: ids 1, 2, 3 …

presets.label: MultiXact: two lockers
presets.note: `t_xmax` has room for one xid. With two lockers (here our xid and the savepoint's subxid) it holds a **MultiXact id** instead, whose members are listed in `pg_multixact`.

presets.label: Foreign keys take KEY SHARE
presets.note: Inserting a child row locks the **referenced** customer `FOR KEY SHARE`. That blocks deleting the customer or changing its key, but not an ordinary UPDATE of its name.

presets.label: A hot counter row
presets.note: The trigger updated the single `job_stats` row, so its current version carries **our xid** as `xmin`, and the old one has it as `xmax`. Until COMMIT, any other session inserting a job must update the same row and waits on our xid: all inserts into `jobs` now run one at a time.

presets.label: Advisory locks
presets.note: Session locks stack (two locks need two unlocks) and **ignore ROLLBACK**: after it, the xact lock 7 is gone but the session lock from `pg_try_advisory_lock` is still held.

production.title: A job queue that stopped scaling at one worker
production.context: An email service stores outgoing messages in a `jobs` table. Workers poll with `SELECT … WHERE status = 'queued' ORDER BY id LIMIT 1 FOR UPDATE`.
production.problem: Every worker's query targets the same oldest row. All but one block on its row lock, then re-check, then block on the next row. Adding workers added lock waits, not throughput, and `pg_stat_activity` showed most workers in `Lock: transactionid`.
production.solution: Claim with `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` in the same statement that marks the job, and keep the claiming transaction short. Index the queue predicate so the scan does not walk finished jobs.
production.outcome: Each worker claims a different row without waiting, so throughput grows with the number of workers until the database itself is the bottleneck. The order of processing becomes approximate, which a queue can accept.

pitfalls.title: SKIP LOCKED for general reads
pitfalls.symptom: A report occasionally shows wrong totals with no error.
pitfalls.cause: SKIP LOCKED silently drops locked rows from the result. It gives an **inconsistent view** by design.
pitfalls.fix: Use it only for queue-style claiming. Ordinary reads need no row locks at all under MVCC.

pitfalls.title: LIMIT and locking functions
pitfalls.symptom: `pg_locks` shows many more advisory locks than the query returned.
pitfalls.cause: In `SELECT pg_advisory_lock(id) FROM t WHERE … LIMIT 100`, the LIMIT is not guaranteed to apply before the function runs.
pitfalls.fix: Apply the LIMIT in a subquery, then lock in the outer query.
pitfalls.sql: SELECT pg_advisory_lock(q.id) FROM (SELECT id FROM foo WHERE id > 12345 LIMIT 100) q;

pitfalls.title: Session advisory locks behind a pooler
pitfalls.symptom: A "singleton" job runs twice, or a lock is never released.
pitfalls.cause: Session-level advisory locks belong to the server connection. A transaction-mode pooler hands that connection to other clients.
pitfalls.fix: Behind transaction pooling use `pg_advisory_xact_lock`, which ends with the transaction.

pitfalls.title: A trigger-maintained counter row
pitfalls.symptom: Inserts into a busy table stop scaling with more clients, and `pg_stat_activity` shows them waiting on `Lock: transactionid` behind each other.
pitfalls.cause: An AFTER INSERT trigger keeps a running total by updating one summary row. That row lock is held until each inserting transaction commits, so every insert queues behind the previous one. A BEFORE trigger that reads the count and inserts the summary row when missing is worse: two sessions both see none and both insert.
pitfalls.fix: Compute the total on read, or spread the counter over several rows (`id = pid % 16`) and sum them, or append deltas and fold them in periodically. Create the summary row once with `INSERT … ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING`.

pitfalls.title: MultiXact growth from FK-heavy workloads
pitfalls.symptom: `pg_multixact` grows and anti-wraparound vacuums for multixacts appear.
pitfalls.cause: Many concurrent child inserts lock the same parent row `FOR KEY SHARE`, so its `t_xmax` becomes a MultiXact each time the locker set changes.
pitfalls.fix: Monitor `mxid_age(datminmxid)`, keep autovacuum healthy, and avoid hot parent rows when you can.

pointers: Four row modes: **FOR UPDATE** > **FOR NO KEY UPDATE** > **FOR SHARE** > **FOR KEY SHARE**. A plain UPDATE takes NO KEY UPDATE unless it changes a key.
Row locks are stored in **`t_xmax` + infomask** (a **MultiXact** when shared); they appear in `pg_locks` only while someone waits.
**NOWAIT** errors at once (55P03); **SKIP LOCKED** silently skips. Both still take the ROW SHARE table lock normally.
Job queue: `UPDATE … WHERE id = (SELECT … FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED LIMIT 1) RETURNING …`.
Advisory locks: **session** level (survive rollback, stack) vs **transaction** level (`pg_advisory_xact_lock`).

lessons.title: LWLocks, spinlocks and deadlock detection
tldr: PostgreSQL stacks three kinds of locks: **spinlocks** for a few instructions, **LWLocks** for shared-memory structures, and **heavyweight locks** for SQL objects, and only the last kind is checked for deadlocks.
Deadlock detection is deferred until a waiter has slept for **deadlock_timeout**, because walking the waits-for graph is expensive and real deadlocks are rare.

visualizer.title: Two transfers, one deadlock
visualizer.caption: Step through the classic two-account deadlock on a millisecond clock and watch the waits-for graph close. Switch to consistent lock order to see it disappear. Below, explore the lock hierarchy.

playground.setup:
CREATE TABLE accounts (acctnum int PRIMARY KEY, balance numeric NOT NULL);
INSERT INTO accounts VALUES (11111, 500), (22222, 500), (33333, 500);

presets.label: Deadlock settings
presets.note: `deadlock_timeout` = **1s**: a waiter sleeps that long before checking for a cycle. `pg_stat_database.deadlocks` counts every 40P01 in this database.

presets.label: Wait event families
presets.sql:
SELECT type, count(*) AS events
FROM pg_wait_events GROUP BY type ORDER BY events DESC;
presets.note: Every wait a backend can report is listed. **LWLock** (84 names in 18) and **Lock** (12 heavyweight lock types) are the two lock families; `SpinDelay` hides under **Timeout**.

presets.label: The LWLocks you will meet
presets.note: Hot LWLocks map to subsystems: buffer pages, WAL, the lock manager, snapshots (`ProcArray`), and the SLRU caches for commit status, subtransactions and MultiXacts.

presets.label: Heavyweight lock types
presets.sql: SELECT name, description FROM pg_wait_events WHERE type = 'Lock' ORDER BY name;
presets.note: These are the `locktype` values of `pg_locks`. Row-lock waits show up as **transactionid** (waiting for the holder to finish) and **tuple** (queuing behind other waiters).

presets.label: Lock in a consistent order
presets.note: Locking both rows up front in **acctnum order** means every transfer acquires its row locks in the same sequence, so no waits-for cycle can form, whatever order the UPDATEs run in.

presets.label: A transfer procedure that cannot deadlock
presets.note: Without the `PERFORM … FOR UPDATE`, two opposite transfers running at once lock their sender first and deadlock. With it, both lock 11111 before 22222, so the second simply waits. Balances end at **630** and **370**.

presets.label: Tune detection for a session
presets.note: Superusers can lower `deadlock_timeout` (fewer ms lost per real deadlock, more needless checks). The `pg_stat_activity` query is the one to run when sessions hang: look for `Lock` waits and their blockers.

production.title: Deadlocks between concurrent transfers
production.context: A wallet service moves money with two UPDATEs: debit the sender, then credit the receiver. Two users often pay each other at the same moment.
production.problem: Transfer X locks Alice then Bob; transfer Y locks Bob then Alice. Under load the logs fill with `ERROR: deadlock detected`, each one costing a retry and about **1 s** (`deadlock_timeout`) of latency for the surviving transaction.
production.solution: Acquire the row locks in a canonical order: lock both accounts in ascending id order before updating either. Keep a retry on 40P01 for other paths.
production.outcome: With one lock order a waits-for cycle between transfers is impossible, so this path produces zero 40P01 errors; conflicting transfers now simply queue for a few milliseconds instead of stalling 1 s and retrying. Track `pg_stat_database.deadlocks` to confirm.

pitfalls.title: Opposite lock order in different code paths
pitfalls.symptom: Sporadic `40P01 deadlock detected` errors, often in pairs of the same two statements.
pitfalls.cause: Two transactions lock the same rows or tables in opposite orders. Also common: UPDATE … WHERE id IN (…) without a stable order, or foreign-key checks interleaved with parent updates.
pitfalls.fix: Sort keys before locking, take the strongest lock first, and retry on 40P01. The DETAIL line names both processes and lock targets.

pitfalls.title: Raising deadlock_timeout to "fix" deadlocks
pitfalls.symptom: Fewer deadlock errors in logs, but more latency spikes.
pitfalls.cause: The timeout only delays **detection**. A real deadlock still ends in an abort, just later.
pitfalls.fix: Leave it around 1 s (ideally above typical transaction time) and fix the lock order. Use `log_lock_waits = on` to log any wait longer than `deadlock_timeout`.

pitfalls.title: Treating LWLock waits as blocking
pitfalls.symptom: Many sessions show `wait_event_type = LWLock` (for example `BufferMapping` or `WALInsert`), but `pg_locks` shows nothing waiting.
pitfalls.cause: LWLocks are short internal locks, not visible in `pg_locks`. Heavy LWLock waiting means **contention on a shared structure**, not one blocking session.
pitfalls.fix: Treat it as a capacity problem: reduce connections (pooling), add RAM for `shared_buffers`, batch WAL-heavy writes, or reduce subtransaction / MultiXact churn depending on the lock name.

pointers: Hierarchy: **spinlock** (instructions) → **LWLock** (shared memory structures, shared/exclusive) → **heavyweight lock** (SQL objects, 8 modes).
Only heavyweight locks have **deadlock detection**; LWLocks avoid deadlock by coding rules.
A waiter checks for deadlock after **deadlock_timeout** (default 1 s); a cycle aborts one transaction with **40P01**.
Prevent deadlocks with a **consistent lock order** (`ORDER BY id FOR UPDATE`) and retry the rare remainder.
Diagnose with `pg_stat_activity.wait_event_type` (`Lock` vs `LWLock`) and `pg_blocking_pids()`.

lessons.title: Views and materialized views
tldr: A **view** is a stored query that the rewriter splices into your query tree through an `ON SELECT DO INSTEAD` rule named `_RETURN`, while a **materialized view** runs that query once and keeps the result in a real heap.
Views give you reusable, permission-controlled abstractions at zero runtime cost, and materialized views trade freshness for speed when the query is too expensive to run on every read.

visualizer.title: From view name to plan, and from matview to refresh
visualizer.caption: Step through the rewriter expanding a view, then switch to **Materialized view** and watch REFRESH swap files while CONCURRENTLY patches one row. The numbers match what the playground presets print.

presets.label: The _RETURN rule
presets.note: The view is a relation with `relkind = v` and `relfilenode = 0` (no file). Its query lives in `pg_rewrite` as the `_RETURN` rule, `ev_type = 1` (SELECT), `is_instead = t`.

presets.label: View vs subquery plan
presets.note: Both plans are identical (`Hash Join cost=8.32..12.86`). The `id = 42` filter was pushed through the view down to `Index Scan using orders_pkey`.

presets.label: Matview goes stale
presets.note: The matview still reports 2919.00 from 56 orders. The live view already sees 3084.00 from 57.

presets.label: REFRESH swaps the file
presets.note: A plain REFRESH writes a brand new heap, so `relfilenode` changes. CONCURRENTLY is refused until the matview has a unique index. A matview created `WITH NO DATA` exists (`ispopulated = f`) but cannot be read at all until its first plain REFRESH.

presets.label: CONCURRENTLY patches rows
presets.note: Run after the previous preset. The relfilenode does not change, and only **1 of 360** rows has the new xmin: the diff touched just the changed group.

presets.label: Updatable view + CHECK OPTION
presets.note: `cheap_products` reads one table with a plain WHERE, so it is **automatically updatable**; `order_lines` (a join) is not. The second insert fails `WITH CHECK OPTION` because the row would be invisible through the view.

presets.label: Stacked views: LOCAL vs CASCADED
presets.note: Without a check option, John Snow is inserted through `fte` and becomes invisible in it. **LOCAL** on `fte_1` rejects department 2 but lets contractor Mia in, because `fte`'s own filter is not checked. **CASCADED** (the default for a bare `WITH CHECK OPTION`) checks `fte` too: `new row violates check option for view "fte"`. `DELETE … WHERE id = 3` removes nothing: Bob is a contractor, so he is not a row of `fte`.

presets.label: Recursive view: org chart
presets.note: `CREATE RECURSIVE VIEW` is shorthand for a view over `WITH RECURSIVE`; the column list is mandatory. Each pass joins the previous level: 1, 4, 10, then 5 people, then an empty working table ends it. The plan shows `Recursive Union` under a `CTE Scan` with `Filter: (employee_id = 10)` on top: the filter is applied **after** the whole tree is built, not pushed into the recursion.

production.title: A revenue dashboard that stopped melting the primary
production.context: An e-commerce analytics page showed revenue per day and category. Its query joined `orders` (tens of millions of rows) to `products` and grouped by day, and ran on every page load.
production.problem: Each load scanned and aggregated the whole orders table. With dozens of viewers refreshing, the database spent most of its CPU on identical aggregates, and order inserts slowed down.
production.solution: Move the aggregate into a **materialized view** keyed by `(day, category)`. Add the **unique index** that `REFRESH … CONCURRENTLY` requires, and refresh every five minutes from a scheduler. Readers keep reading during each refresh, and each refresh rewrites only the groups that changed.
production.outcome: Dashboard reads became an index lookup on a table of a few thousand rows instead of a full aggregate. The trade-off is explicit: numbers can be up to five minutes old, and the page shows when the last refresh ran. In the playground, a concurrent refresh after one new order rewrote 1 of 360 rows.

pitfalls.title: CONCURRENTLY without a usable unique index
pitfalls.symptom: `ERROR: cannot refresh materialized view "public.daily_revenue" concurrently`, or the refresh job falls back to a plain REFRESH that blocks every reader.
pitfalls.cause: CONCURRENTLY diffs old and new contents by a key. It needs at least one **UNIQUE** index on plain columns, with no WHERE clause and no expressions, and the matview must already be populated.
pitfalls.fix: Create a unique index on the natural grouping key. Populate once with a plain REFRESH if the matview was created `WITH NO DATA`.
pitfalls.sql: CREATE UNIQUE INDEX ON daily_revenue (day, category);

pitfalls.title: `SELECT *` in a view freezes the column list
pitfalls.symptom: A column added to the base table never shows up through the view, and nobody notices for months.
pitfalls.cause: The `*` is expanded when the view is created. The stored query tree points at the columns that existed then, by number, not by name. So renaming a base column is followed silently (the view keeps its old column name: `title AS t`), and dropping one the view uses fails with `cannot drop column … because other objects depend on it`.
pitfalls.fix: List columns explicitly. After altering the base table, run `CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW` with the new column added **at the end** (replacing may add columns but not reorder, rename or drop them: `cannot drop columns from view`). To remove a column, drop and recreate the view, or `DROP … CASCADE` knowing which dependants go with it.

pitfalls.title: A view that hides rows leaks them anyway
pitfalls.symptom: Users with access only to `public_phones` (a view filtering out private rows) can still learn private values.
pitfalls.cause: The planner may run a **cheap user function** in the outer WHERE before the view's own filter. A function that raises a NOTICE with its arguments sees every row. Views hide columns reliably, but not rows.
pitfalls.fix: Declare the view `WITH (security_barrier)` so its quals run first, or use row-level security. Only **LEAKPROOF** functions may then be pushed below the barrier.
pitfalls.sql:
CREATE VIEW public_phones WITH (security_barrier) AS
  SELECT person, phone FROM phone_data WHERE NOT private;

pitfalls.title: Base-table privileges checked as the view owner
pitfalls.symptom: A role with no rights on `orders` can read it through a view, or row-level security policies on the base table seem to be ignored.
pitfalls.cause: By default, relations inside a view are accessed with the **view owner's** privileges and policies. If the owner is the table owner, RLS does not apply to them.
pitfalls.fix: Set `security_invoker = true` on views that should run with the caller's rights and policies.
pitfalls.sql: ALTER VIEW order_lines SET (security_invoker = true);

pitfalls.title: Blaming REFRESH for blocked order writes
pitfalls.symptom: Refreshes are moved to 3 a.m. "because REFRESH locks the orders table", yet the dashboard still hangs for the length of every daytime refresh.
pitfalls.cause: A common claim is that REFRESH locks the underlying tables. It does not: the base tables get only **ACCESS SHARE**, the lock any SELECT takes, so writes to them continue. The lock that hurts is on the **matview**: a plain REFRESH holds **ACCESS EXCLUSIVE** on it, so every reader of the dashboard waits. CONCURRENTLY holds **EXCLUSIVE** instead, which blocks only other refreshes and writes to the matview, and its diff applies inserts, updates **and** deletes.
pitfalls.fix: Use `REFRESH … CONCURRENTLY` with a unique index for matviews that are read during the day. Check the locks yourself inside a transaction.

pitfalls.title: Relying on the ORDER BY inside a matview
pitfalls.symptom: A "top 10 products" widget runs `SELECT * FROM top_products LIMIT 10` and starts showing the wrong products after a few refreshes.
pitfalls.cause: The ORDER BY in the defining query only orders the rows as they are first written. A matview is a heap: CONCURRENTLY applies its diff as row changes, so new versions land wherever there is free space, and a plain SELECT returns rows in physical order.
pitfalls.fix: Put the ORDER BY in the query that reads the matview, and index the sort column if the list is long.
pitfalls.sql: SELECT * FROM daily_revenue ORDER BY revenue DESC LIMIT 10;

pointers: A view is `relkind = v` plus a `_RETURN` rule in `pg_rewrite`. The rewriter substitutes it as a subquery before planning, and the planner usually flattens it away.

Auto-updatable views: **one FROM item**, no aggregates, DISTINCT, GROUP BY, LIMIT or set operations. Add `WITH CHECK OPTION` (CASCADED by default; LOCAL checks only the top view) so writes stay visible through the view.
A **materialized view** is a real heap filled by its query. It is stale until you REFRESH it.
**REFRESH** rewrites the whole file under ACCESS EXCLUSIVE. **REFRESH CONCURRENTLY** needs a unique index, diffs rows, and lets readers continue.
Use `security_barrier` for row-filtering views and `security_invoker` when the caller's privileges and policies must apply.

lessons.title: Triggers
tldr: A **trigger** binds a function returning `trigger` to INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE or TRUNCATE on a table or view, firing BEFORE, AFTER or INSTEAD OF the change, once per row or once per statement.
Triggers let the database itself enforce rules, stamp columns, write audit trails and maintain derived data, so every client gets the same behaviour no matter which code path issued the write.

visualizer.title: Every trigger for one UPDATE, in firing order
visualizer.caption: Step through one UPDATE on three rows. Flip the toggles to skip a row, drop the WHEN clause, rename a trigger or change the statement, and watch the order change. With the default toggles the steps match, line for line, the `trigger_log` the first preset writes.

presets.label: Firing order log
presets.note: Ten log lines: statement BEFORE, then b_touch and c_guard per row (alphabetical), the two queued `d_audit` events at the end, and finally `e_summary` with `old_rows=2 new_rows=2 delta=-10`. B-2 was skipped, so it keeps qty 3 and no `updated_at`.

presets.label: No-op and zero-row updates
presets.note: The no-op update runs both BEFORE ROW triggers but `d_audit` never fires: its **WHEN** is false, so nothing was queued. The `WHERE false` update still fires both **statement** triggers, with empty transition tables.

presets.label: Trigger calls in EXPLAIN
presets.sql:
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, COSTS OFF, TIMING OFF, SUMMARY OFF)
UPDATE inventory SET qty = qty + 1;
presets.note: EXPLAIN ANALYZE ends with one `Trigger …: calls=N` line per trigger. Row triggers show calls=3; statement triggers show calls=1.

presets.label: Catalog: pg_trigger
presets.sql:
SELECT tgname, tgtype, pg_get_triggerdef(oid) AS definition
FROM pg_trigger
WHERE tgrelid = 'inventory'::regclass
ORDER BY tgname;
presets.note: `tgtype` is a bitmask: 1 = ROW, 2 = BEFORE, 16 = UPDATE. So 19 = BEFORE UPDATE FOR EACH ROW, 17 = AFTER ROW, 18 = BEFORE STATEMENT, 16 = AFTER STATEMENT.

presets.label: INSTEAD OF on a join view
presets.note: A join view is not auto-updatable, so the **INSTEAD OF** row trigger decides what an INSERT means. Version 1 does the work but returns NULL: the insert reports **0 rows** and `RETURNING` comes back empty. Version 2 returns NEW (with the new id filled in), so the row counts and `RETURNING` shows it. Both moves landed in the view, and the UPDATE inside also fired every inventory trigger.

presets.label: Gatekeeper: soft delete, no TRUNCATE
presets.note: A BEFORE ROW trigger is a **gatekeeper**: raise to abort, edit NEW to transform, or return NULL to skip. Here the DELETE returns **no rows** and Kettle stays, marked inactive. TRUNCATE never visits rows, so it fires no DELETE triggers; only a **statement-level** TRUNCATE trigger (BEFORE or AFTER) can stop it.

presets.label: Catalog peek: hidden FK triggers
presets.sql:
SELECT c.relname AS on_table, t.tgname, t.tgfoid::regproc AS function, t.tgisinternal, t.tgenabled
FROM pg_trigger t JOIN pg_class c ON c.oid = t.tgrelid
WHERE c.relname IN ('inventory', 'stock_moves', 'products')
ORDER BY t.tgisinternal, c.relname, t.tgname;

SELECT event_object_table, trigger_name, event_manipulation
FROM information_schema.triggers
WHERE event_object_table = 'products';
presets.note: The `stock_moves.sku` foreign key is enforced by four internal **RI_ConstraintTrigger** rows (`tgisinternal = true`), two on each table. `ALTER TABLE … DISABLE TRIGGER ALL` switches those off too; `DISABLE TRIGGER USER` leaves them on. `information_schema.triggers` has one row per event and does not list TRUNCATE triggers at all.

presets.label: Event trigger on DDL
presets.note: Event triggers are per database and fire on **DDL**, not DML. `ddl_command_end` sees the finished command through `pg_event_trigger_ddl_commands()`.

production.title: Auditing a bulk price update without one call per row
production.context: A catalogue team logged every price change through an `AFTER UPDATE … FOR EACH ROW` trigger that inserted one audit row per product.
production.problem: A nightly job updated millions of prices in one statement. The row trigger queued one AFTER event per row in memory, then ran its INSERT once per row, one function call and one plan execution each. The job time grew far beyond the UPDATE itself.
production.solution: Replace the row trigger with a **statement-level AFTER trigger with transition tables**. It runs once and writes the whole audit set with one `INSERT … SELECT` joining `old_rows` to `new_rows`. Keep a `WHEN`-style filter in that join so unchanged prices produce no audit rows.
production.outcome: On 100,000 rows the bare UPDATE took 386 ms, with the row trigger 937 ms, with the statement trigger 527 ms, writing the same 100,000 audit rows. EXPLAIN ANALYZE shows why: `Trigger audit_prices: calls=1` instead of `calls=100000`. Single-row updates from the app are still audited by the same trigger.

pitfalls.title: An AFTER trigger that updates its own table
pitfalls.symptom: `ERROR: stack depth limit exceeded`, or a statement that never finishes, after adding a trigger that "fixes up" a column.
pitfalls.cause: The trigger's UPDATE fires the same trigger again. PostgreSQL puts **no limit on cascade depth**: recursion is the trigger author's problem.
pitfalls.fix: Change the row in a **BEFORE** trigger by editing NEW (no extra UPDATE at all). If you must cascade, guard with `pg_trigger_depth()` or a WHEN clause that becomes false after the first pass.
pitfalls.sql:
CREATE TRIGGER fixup BEFORE UPDATE ON inventory FOR EACH ROW
  WHEN (pg_trigger_depth() = 0) EXECUTE FUNCTION touch();

pitfalls.title: A BEFORE trigger that forgets to return NEW
pitfalls.symptom: Inserts report `INSERT 0 0` and rows silently vanish, with no error anywhere.
pitfalls.cause: A row-level BEFORE trigger that falls off the end, or returns NULL, **skips the operation** for that row. In PL/pgSQL a missing RETURN is an error, but an early `RETURN NULL` in a branch is not.
pitfalls.fix: Return NEW for INSERT/UPDATE and OLD for DELETE on every path. Reserve `RETURN NULL` for rows you really mean to drop, and log when you do.

pitfalls.title: Relying on creation order
pitfalls.symptom: After a migration recreates triggers, a validation trigger starts running before the trigger that normalises data, and valid rows are rejected.
pitfalls.cause: Triggers for the same event on the same table fire in **alphabetical order by name**, not creation order (the SQL standard says creation order).
pitfalls.fix: Encode the order in the names, for example `10_normalize`, `20_validate`, `90_audit`.

pitfalls.title: Row triggers on bulk loads
pitfalls.symptom: A `COPY` or `INSERT … SELECT` of millions of rows runs many times slower than expected.
pitfalls.cause: Each row fires the function. AFTER ROW events are also held in memory until the end of the statement, and without WHEN each one re-fetches its row.
pitfalls.fix: Use statement triggers with transition tables, add `WHEN` to AFTER ROW triggers, or disable non-essential triggers for the load with `ALTER TABLE … DISABLE TRIGGER name` or `DISABLE TRIGGER USER`. `DISABLE TRIGGER ALL` also switches off the internal foreign-key triggers, so rows that break the FK load silently.

pitfalls.title: An INSTEAD OF trigger that returns NULL
pitfalls.symptom: Inserting through a join view works (the base tables change), but the client sees `INSERT 0 0`, `RETURNING` is empty, and an ORM reports that the save failed.
pitfalls.cause: For an INSTEAD OF row trigger, the return value says whether the row was processed. NULL means "nothing happened", so the command tag counts zero rows and RETURNING has nothing to return.
pitfalls.fix: Return NEW for INSERT and UPDATE (fill generated keys into NEW first) and OLD for DELETE. Also match the full key in UPDATE and DELETE branches, or one view row changes several base rows.

pitfalls.title: A per-row trigger that maintains a summary row
pitfalls.symptom: A customer's second order fails with `duplicate key value violates unique constraint "customer_stats_pkey"`. A "check, then insert or update" version instead creates duplicates or drifts under concurrent inserts.
pitfalls.cause: An AFTER INSERT trigger that blindly INSERTs one summary row per parent works only for the first child. A read-then-write version (`SELECT count(*)`, then INSERT or UPDATE) races, because two transactions can both see zero rows.
pitfalls.fix: Make the write a single upsert, and gate repeat work with WHEN so re-running the same UPDATE does not double-count. Every writer then serialises on that one summary row, so keep the trigger short.
pitfalls.sql:
INSERT INTO customer_stats (customer_id, total_spent)
VALUES (NEW.customer_id, NEW.total)
ON CONFLICT (customer_id)
DO UPDATE SET total_spent = customer_stats.total_spent + EXCLUDED.total_spent;

pointers: Order for one statement: **BEFORE STATEMENT → per row (BEFORE ROW in name order → write → queue AFTER) → AFTER ROW queue → AFTER STATEMENT**.
BEFORE ROW can **edit NEW** or **return NULL to skip** the row. AFTER return values are ignored.
Statement triggers fire **once per SQL statement** (not per transaction), **even when zero rows match**. The default granularity is FOR EACH STATEMENT.
AFTER-trigger **WHEN** runs at write time and decides whether an event is queued at all: free filtering for bulk statements.
**Transition tables** (`REFERENCING OLD TABLE … NEW TABLE …`) give AFTER triggers the whole changed set for set-based work.

lessons.title: PL/pgSQL functions and procedures
tldr: **PL/pgSQL** is the built-in procedural language: blocks of variables, loops and conditionals around embedded SQL, compiled on first call and run inside the server next to the data.
It exists so logic that needs many dependent queries runs without a network round trip per statement, and so triggers, checks and batch jobs can live in the database itself.

visualizer.title: An EXCEPTION block is a subtransaction
visualizer.caption: Step through one call and watch xids, row versions and variables. Switch to **Without EXCEPTION clause** to see the same error abort everything.

presets.label: Run demo()
presets.note: The function reports its xid and the caught error (x = 2: variables keep their values). Both audit rows have that same xmin, and account 1 is still alice. `pageinspect` shows the rolled-back `Joe` version at lp 3 with the **subtransaction's own xid** (top xid + 1) as `t_xmin`.

presets.label: Error kata: INTO, FOUND, CASE, ASSERT
presets.sql:
SELECT
  try_sql($q$DO $$ DECLARE r accounts; BEGIN SELECT * INTO STRICT r FROM accounts WHERE id = 99; END $$$q$) AS strict_no_row,
  try_sql($q$DO $$ DECLARE r accounts; BEGIN SELECT * INTO STRICT r FROM accounts WHERE balance > 0; END $$$q$) AS strict_two_rows,
  try_sql($q$DO $$ DECLARE r accounts; BEGIN SELECT * INTO r FROM accounts ORDER BY id; RAISE EXCEPTION 'kept %', r.owner; END $$$q$) AS plain_into;

SELECT
  try_sql($q$DO $$ DECLARE t numeric; BEGIN
    SELECT sum(balance) INTO t FROM accounts WHERE id = 99;
    IF FOUND THEN RAISE EXCEPTION 'FOUND = true, total = %', t; END IF; END $$$q$) AS sum_into_found,
  try_sql($q$DO $$ DECLARE x int := 3; BEGIN CASE x WHEN 1 THEN NULL; WHEN 2 THEN NULL; END CASE; END $$$q$) AS case_no_else,
  try_sql($q$DO $$ DECLARE n int; BEGIN SELECT count(*) INTO n FROM accounts; ASSERT n > 10, 'only ' || n || ' accounts'; END $$$q$) AS assert_false,
  try_sql($q$DO $$ DECLARE vat constant numeric := 0.1; BEGIN vat := 0.05; END $$$q$) AS assign_constant;

SELECT
  try_sql($q$DO $$ DECLARE t text := 'Brooklyn Desert'; BEGIN RAISE EXCEPTION 'title: %s', t; END $$$q$) AS percent_s,
  try_sql($q$DO $$ BEGIN RAISE NOTICE 'a % b %', 1; END $$$q$) AS too_few_args,
  try_sql($q$DO $$ BEGIN PERFORM 1/0; EXCEPTION WHEN division_by_zero THEN RAISE EXCEPTION 'wrapped: %', SQLERRM; END $$$q$) AS reraise_new,
  try_sql($q$DO $$ BEGIN PERFORM 1/0; EXCEPTION WHEN division_by_zero THEN RAISE; END $$$q$) AS reraise_bare;
presets.note: `INTO STRICT` raises **P0002** for no row and **P0003** for two; plain `INTO` silently keeps the first row. `SELECT sum(…) INTO` always returns one row, so **FOUND is true** even with no match and total NULL. A CASE statement with no match and no ELSE raises **20000**. ASSERT raises **P0004**, which `WHEN OTHERS` does not catch. RAISE uses a bare `%`, so `%s` prints "Brooklyn Desert**s**". A new RAISE EXCEPTION in a handler reports **P0001**; a bare `RAISE;` keeps the original **22012**.

presets.label: Cost of EXCEPTION blocks
presets.note: Same loop, same work. Entering and leaving a block with an EXCEPTION clause costs a subtransaction every iteration, several times slower even when no error ever happens.

presets.label: One subxid per block
presets.note: Plain inserts share the transaction's one xid. Each guarded insert ran in its own subtransaction, so 1000 rows carry **1000 different xmins**. Each one also consumed a transaction id.

presets.label: Procedure with COMMIT
presets.note: A **procedure** called with CALL can end transactions. Only the even batches survive, each with its own xmin, because every COMMIT starts a new transaction. Called from inside a SELECT, or inside an explicit `BEGIN … COMMIT` block, the first COMMIT fails with **2D000 invalid transaction termination**.

presets.label: Overloads, defaults, OUT and INOUT
presets.note: Overloads are chosen by their **IN argument types**; defaults are not part of the signature. `balance_of(1)` matches both functions, so it fails with **42725 is not unique**. `SELECT swap(…)` returns one **composite** value `(20,10)`; `SELECT * FROM swap(…)` expands it into columns. Procedures accept **OUT** parameters (since PostgreSQL 14); pass NULL for them in CALL. `$t$` does not close a `$T$` string.

presets.label: Dynamic SQL done safely
presets.note: `regclass` validates the table name, `%I` quotes identifiers, `%L` quotes literals, and `USING` passes values as parameters. EXECUTE is re-planned on every call.

presets.label: STABLE now() vs VOLATILE clock
presets.note: `now()` is **STABLE**: one value for the whole statement (in fact the whole transaction). `clock_timestamp()` is **VOLATILE** and changes per row. `provolatile` is `i`, `s` or `v`.

production.title: An upsert loop that burned through transaction ids
production.context: A sync worker copied rows from a partner feed with a PL/pgSQL function modelled on the classic retry loop: try UPDATE, and if no row was found, INSERT inside `BEGIN … EXCEPTION WHEN unique_violation`.
production.problem: Each call opened a subtransaction and, because it wrote, consumed its own transaction id. Batches of thousands of rows in one transaction overflowed the per-backend subtransaction cache (64 entries), so other sessions taking snapshots had to look subtransactions up in `pg_subtrans`. Xid consumption also brought anti-wraparound vacuums forward.
production.solution: Replace the loop with a single `INSERT … ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE`, which is atomic without any subtransaction, and keep EXCEPTION blocks for genuinely exceptional errors at the edge of a batch.
production.outcome: The batch now uses one xid instead of one per row (the "One subxid per block" preset shows 1000 xmins for 1000 guarded inserts versus 1 for plain ones), no subtransaction cache overflow, and one set-based statement instead of a per-row loop.

pitfalls.title: EXCEPTION blocks inside hot loops
pitfalls.symptom: A function is several times slower than expected, xid age climbs fast, and monitoring shows backends with overflowed subtransaction caches.
pitfalls.cause: Every entry into a block with an EXCEPTION clause starts a subtransaction. Such a block is significantly more expensive to enter and exit than one without, even when no error is ever raised. Each one that writes also consumes an xid.
pitfalls.fix: Put the EXCEPTION clause around the whole loop, not inside it, or avoid it: `ON CONFLICT`, `IF NOT FOUND`, and constraint checks before the write usually remove the need.

pitfalls.title: SQL injection through EXECUTE
pitfalls.symptom: A dynamic report function lets a caller drop tables by passing `orders; DROP TABLE users` as a table name.
pitfalls.cause: Concatenating strings into `EXECUTE` makes the input part of the SQL text. PL/pgSQL variables are only substituted as parameters in **static** SQL, never inside EXECUTE strings.
