pitfalls.fix: Take identifiers as `regclass`, quote with `format('%I')` and `%L`, and pass values with `EXECUTE … USING`.
pitfalls.sql: EXECUTE format('SELECT count(*) FROM %I WHERE owner = $1', tbl) INTO n USING who;

pitfalls.title: A variable with the same name as a column
pitfalls.symptom: `ERROR: column reference "owner" is ambiguous` the first time the function runs, not when it is created.
pitfalls.cause: Variables are substituted into SQL as parameters. When a name could be both, PL/pgSQL raises an error by default (`plpgsql.variable_conflict = error`). SQL inside a function is only analysed when first executed.
pitfalls.fix: Prefix variables (`v_owner`, `p_id`) or qualify (`accounts.owner`, `fn_name.param`). Turn on `plpgsql.extra_warnings = all` in development.

pitfalls.title: Marking a function IMMUTABLE when it is not
pitfalls.symptom: An expression index or a cached plan returns stale results after a lookup table or setting changes.
pitfalls.cause: IMMUTABLE promises the same result for the same arguments forever. The planner may pre-evaluate it at plan time, and indexes store its results. A function that reads tables or `now()` breaks that promise.
pitfalls.fix: Use **STABLE** for functions that read the database or settings within one statement, **VOLATILE** (the default) for anything with side effects or changing results.

pitfalls.title: Testing FOUND after an aggregate
pitfalls.symptom: A "customer not found" branch never runs. Unknown ids return a NULL total instead of the error the function was written to raise.
pitfalls.cause: `SELECT sum(amount) INTO total … WHERE customer_id = p_id` always produces exactly **one row**, even when no row matches, so FOUND is always true. The same applies to `count(*)`, `max()` and every other aggregate without GROUP BY. Plain `INTO` is also silent about extra rows: it keeps the first one.
pitfalls.fix: Test the value (`IF total IS NULL`), or check existence first with a non-aggregate query. Use `INTO STRICT` when exactly one row must exist: it raises `no_data_found` (P0002) or `too_many_rows` (P0003).

pitfalls.title: Re-raising an error under a new code
pitfalls.symptom: The application retries on serialization failures (40001) and handles unique violations (23505), but after a refactor every database error arrives as **P0001** and the retry logic never fires.
pitfalls.cause: A handler that does `RAISE EXCEPTION 'failed: %', SQLERRM` raises a **new** error with the default condition `raise_exception` (P0001). The original SQLSTATE is lost.
pitfalls.fix: Use a bare `RAISE;` to re-throw the caught error unchanged, or keep the code explicitly with `USING ERRCODE = SQLSTATE`. Add context with `DETAIL` or `HINT` instead of rewriting the message.

pointers: Block = `[DECLARE] BEGIN … [EXCEPTION WHEN … THEN …] END`. An EXCEPTION clause turns the block into a **subtransaction**.
On a caught error, **database changes in the block roll back** but **local variables keep their values**.
Code is compiled on first call; each SQL statement is **prepared on first execution** and may get a cached generic plan. `EXECUTE` re-plans every time.
**Procedures** (`CALL`) can `COMMIT`/`ROLLBACK`; functions cannot. Neither can end a transaction inside an EXCEPTION block.
Volatility: **IMMUTABLE** (pure), **STABLE** (fixed within a statement), **VOLATILE** (default, re-evaluated every call).

lessons.title: The rule system
tldr: The **rule system** is a query rewriter between the parser and the planner that turns one query tree into zero or more trees, using rules stored in `pg_rewrite`: it is how views work and how `CREATE RULE` adds or replaces commands.
It exists to transform whole statements at once, which is powerful for views but surprising for data changes, so nearly all custom write logic today belongs in triggers instead.

visualizer.title: Rewriting an UPDATE with log_shoelace, step by step
visualizer.caption: Follow the rewriter through its five steps for the `log_shoelace` rule. Switch statements to see a colour-only update log nothing and a multi-row update log 3 of 4 rows.

presets.label: Rules in pg_rewrite
presets.note: The view `shoelace` has its `_RETURN` rule (ev_type 1 = SELECT, INSTEAD). `log_shoelace` is ev_type 2 = UPDATE and `is_instead = f`: an ALSO rule.

presets.label: One UPDATE, two plans
presets.sql:
EXPLAIN (COSTS OFF)
UPDATE shoelace_data SET sl_avail = 6 WHERE sl_name = 'sl7';
presets.note: EXPLAIN prints **two plans**: first the rule's INSERT, with the substituted qual `Filter: (6 <> sl_avail)`, then the original UPDATE.

presets.label: Log a change
presets.sql:
UPDATE shoelace_data SET sl_avail = 6 WHERE sl_name = 'sl7';
SELECT sl_name, sl_avail, log_who FROM shoelace_log;
presets.note: One log row, written by the extra INSERT that the rewriter generated.

presets.label: Colour change: no log
presets.sql:
UPDATE shoelace_data SET sl_color = 'green' WHERE sl_name = 'sl7';
SELECT count(*) AS log_rows FROM shoelace_log;
presets.note: Still one log row. `NEW.sl_avail` was not assigned, so it was replaced by `shoelace_data.sl_avail` and the qual compared the column with itself.

presets.label: Multi-row: 4 updated, 3 logged
presets.sql:
UPDATE shoelace_data SET sl_avail = 0 WHERE sl_color = 'black';
SELECT sl_name, sl_avail FROM shoelace_log ORDER BY sl_name;
presets.note: sl1, sl2 and sl4 are logged with one INSERT … SELECT; sl3 already had 0. The action ran **before** the UPDATE, so it still saw the old values.

presets.label: Volatile functions run twice
presets.note: The copies have ids 3 and 4, not 1 and 2. `NEW.id` was replaced by the column default `nextval(…)`, which the rule action evaluated **again**. A trigger would see the real values.

presets.label: DO INSTEAD NOTHING
presets.note: The rewriter returned **zero** query trees: the DELETE silently became nothing (`DELETE 0`), with no error. That silence is why rules make poor constraints.

production.title: Retiring an audit rule that logged the wrong ids
production.context: A legacy schema mirrored every insert into `orders` to `orders_archive` with `CREATE RULE … ON INSERT … DO ALSO INSERT INTO orders_archive VALUES (NEW.id, …)`. The `id` column was a serial.
production.problem: Archive rows had ids that did not match any order: every insert consumed two sequence values and the archive got the second one. Bulk loads with `COPY` were not archived at all, because COPY does not invoke the rule system.
production.solution: Drop the rule and use an **AFTER INSERT trigger**. A trigger receives the row after defaults are evaluated, so it sees the real `id`, and triggers fire for COPY too. For bulk inserts, a statement trigger with a `NEW TABLE` transition table archives the whole batch in one statement.
production.outcome: Archive ids match the source again, sequences advance once per row, and COPY loads are archived. The "Volatile functions run twice" preset reproduces the original bug: ids 1 and 2 in the table, 3 and 4 in the copy.

pitfalls.title: Volatile expressions evaluated more than once
pitfalls.symptom: Rows copied by a rule have different serial ids, timestamps or random values than the originals.
pitfalls.cause: A rule rewrites the statement: each `NEW.col` is replaced by the **expression** from the original target list (or the column default), and the action evaluates it again.
pitfalls.fix: Use a trigger, which sees the final row values. Rules give surprising results with volatile functions, because each action re-evaluates the NEW expressions.

pitfalls.title: INSTEAD NOTHING hides failures
pitfalls.symptom: An application believes it deleted or updated rows, but nothing changed and no error was raised.
pitfalls.cause: An unconditional `DO INSTEAD NOTHING` produces zero query trees, and the command reports zero rows. A qualified INSTEAD rule silently discards rows that match its qual.
pitfalls.fix: To block writes, revoke privileges or use a BEFORE trigger that raises an exception, so callers see an error.

pitfalls.title: Rules and features they do not cover
pitfalls.symptom: `ERROR: WITH cannot be used in a query that is rewritten by rules into multiple queries`, or COPY into the table skips the rule's side effects.
pitfalls.cause: Rules work on query trees. Statements with `WITH` clauses and multiple-assignment sub-SELECTs are not supported, MERGE does not use non-SELECT rules, and COPY bypasses rules entirely.
pitfalls.fix: Move the logic to triggers, which run for INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, MERGE actions and COPY.

pointers: The rewriter runs **between parser and planner** and returns **zero or more** query trees. Views are `_RETURN` rules.
A rule action is a template: **NEW** becomes the original target-list expression (or OLD for unassigned UPDATE columns, NULL for INSERT), **OLD** becomes the result relation.
**ALSO** keeps the original query; **INSTEAD** replaces it; a qualified INSTEAD also adds the original with the negated qual.
For **ON UPDATE/DELETE** the actions run **before** the original; for **ON INSERT** after it.
Prefer **triggers** for data changes: rules re-evaluate volatile expressions, cannot raise errors, and skip COPY.

lessons.title: Foreign data wrappers
tldr: A **foreign data wrapper** is a C handler that lets a local table name stand in for data elsewhere, configured through a chain of SQL/MED objects: wrapper, server, user mapping and foreign table.

It exists so you can query another database or a file with plain SQL, while the wrapper decides how much of each query (filters, joins, sorts, aggregates) to **push down** to the remote side instead of dragging every row across the network.

visualizer.title: What does postgres_fdw ship to the remote server?
visualizer.caption: Click **Next scenario** or toggle clauses yourself. Watch the Remote SQL, the local Filter and the rows on the wire change. The remote table holds 1,000,000 orders.

presets.label: The SQL/MED chain
presets.note: Wrapper → server → user mapping. `fdwhandler = -` (0): this wrapper has no handler. Connection details live on the server; credentials live on the **user mapping**, per local role.

presets.label: Foreign tables
presets.note: `relkind = f` and **0 local bytes**: a foreign table is only a definition. The `column_name` option maps local `amount` to remote `total`; matching is by name, not position.

presets.label: Scanning needs a handler
presets.sql:
SELECT try_sql('SELECT * FROM orders_remote') AS scan,
       try_sql('IMPORT FOREIGN SCHEMA public LIMIT TO (invoices) FROM SERVER warehouse INTO public') AS import;
presets.note: Planning a scan calls the handler's `FdwRoutine` (GetForeignRelSize, GetForeignPaths, …), and IMPORT FOREIGN SCHEMA calls `ImportForeignSchema`. Without a handler both fail.

presets.label: What postgres_fdw would ship
presets.sql:
SELECT p.proname, p.provolatile,
       p.oid < 10000 AS built_in,
       p.provolatile = 'i' AND p.oid < 10000 AS shippable
FROM pg_proc p
WHERE p.proname IN ('texteq', 'textlike', 'lower', 'now', 'random', 'risk_score')
ORDER BY shippable DESC, p.proname;
presets.note: postgres_fdw ships a clause only if every function in it is **built-in and IMMUTABLE** (or belongs to an extension listed in the server's `extensions` option). `now()` is STABLE; `risk_score` is IMMUTABLE but user-defined.

presets.label: No validator, no checks
presets.note: The typo `fetch_sizee` is accepted because this wrapper has **no validator** function. postgres_fdw's validator would reject it at ALTER time.

presets.label: Tune options in place
presets.note: Options are text key/value pairs on each object. For postgres_fdw, a table-level option overrides the server-level one.

production.title: A reporting query that copied a whole remote table
production.context: A reporting database read `orders` from the OLTP primary through postgres_fdw. A dashboard asked for the last week of shipped orders: `WHERE status = 'shipped' AND created_at >= now() - interval '7 days' ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 50`.
production.problem: `EXPLAIN VERBOSE` showed the Remote SQL carrying only `status = 'shipped'`. Because `now()` is STABLE, the date filter ran locally, and with a local filter present the LIMIT could not be shipped either. Every shipped order ever recorded crossed the network, 100 rows per FETCH, for each dashboard refresh.
production.solution: Compute the cutoff in the application (or in a CTE materialised as a parameter) and pass a **literal**, so every clause is built-in and immutable and ships. Raise `fetch_size` for the remaining bulk reads, and turn on `use_remote_estimate` so the planner costs remote scans with real statistics.
production.sql:
-- before (date filter + LIMIT run locally):
--   Remote SQL: SELECT ... FROM public.orders WHERE ((status = 'shipped'::text))
-- after: the app binds the cutoff as a constant
SELECT * FROM orders_remote
WHERE status = 'shipped' AND created_at >= $1
ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 50;
ALTER SERVER warehouse OPTIONS (ADD fetch_size '1000', ADD use_remote_estimate 'true');
production.outcome: The Remote SQL now contains both predicates, the ORDER BY and `LIMIT 50::bigint`, so 50 rows cross the network instead of every shipped order. In the visualizer, scenario 3 against scenario 4 shows the same effect on a 1,000,000-row remote table: 250,000 rows against 10.

pitfalls.title: Mutable functions block pushdown
pitfalls.symptom: A selective query over a foreign table is slow, and EXPLAIN VERBOSE shows a local `Filter:` above the Foreign Scan.
pitfalls.cause: postgres_fdw only ships clauses whose functions and operators are **built-in and IMMUTABLE**. `now()`, `current_date`, user functions and casts that depend on settings are evaluated locally.
pitfalls.fix: Pass constants from the application, rewrite with immutable built-ins, or list a shared extension in the server's `extensions` option. Always read the `Remote SQL:` line.

pitfalls.title: Type or collation mismatch with the remote column
pitfalls.symptom: Results differ between querying the remote table directly and through the foreign table, especially for text comparisons and sorting.
pitfalls.cause: Shipped clauses are evaluated by the **remote** server with its own types and collations. A foreign table column declared with a different type or collation gives "surprising semantic anomalies".
pitfalls.fix: Declare columns with exactly the remote types and collations, or use `IMPORT FOREIGN SCHEMA`, which copies them.

pitfalls.title: Repeatable reads in a READ COMMITTED transaction
pitfalls.symptom: Inside one local transaction, repeated queries against a foreign table keep returning the same data even though the remote side committed changes.
pitfalls.cause: postgres_fdw opens the remote transaction as **REPEATABLE READ** (SERIALIZABLE if the local one is), so every scan in the local transaction shares one remote snapshot. There is no two-phase commit across servers.
pitfalls.fix: Keep transactions that read foreign tables short, and do not rely on atomic commit across servers.

pitfalls.title: Tiny fetch batches over a slow link
pitfalls.symptom: A large foreign scan is dominated by network latency, not by either server's CPU.
pitfalls.cause: `fetch_size` defaults to **100** rows per round trip, and inserts default to `batch_size` **1**.
pitfalls.fix: Raise them per server or per table.
pitfalls.sql: ALTER SERVER warehouse OPTIONS (ADD fetch_size '1000', ADD batch_size '100');

pointers: SQL/MED chain: **wrapper** (handler + validator) → **server** (where) → **user mapping** (who) → **foreign table** (what).
The handler returns an **FdwRoutine** of callbacks: plan with GetForeignRelSize/Paths/Plan, execute with Begin/Iterate/ReScan/EndForeignScan.
postgres_fdw ships WHERE clauses only with **built-in, IMMUTABLE** functions and operators; joins only between tables on the **same server**.
Read pushdown in `EXPLAIN VERBOSE`: the `Remote SQL:` line is what the other server actually runs.
Remote transactions run at **REPEATABLE READ** or SERIALIZABLE, without two-phase commit.

lessons.title: Extensions everyone runs
tldr: An **extension** is a versioned package of SQL objects (types, functions, operators, index classes, often backed by a C library) that `CREATE EXTENSION` installs as one unit and `DROP EXTENSION` removes as one unit.
Extensions are how PostgreSQL grows new capabilities, from query statistics to fuzzy text search to vector similarity, without forking the server or waiting for a core release.

visualizer.title: Inside two favourite extensions
visualizer.caption: Type two strings and watch pg_trgm split them into trigrams and score their overlap. Then switch to **pgvector** and step through an HNSW search descending three graph layers.

presets.label: What is installed
presets.note: Each row in `pg_extension` is one installed package and version. `plpgsql` itself is an extension, installed by default in `pg_catalog`.

presets.label: Trusted, versions, members
presets.sql:
SELECT name, version, superuser, trusted FROM pg_available_extension_versions
WHERE name IN ('pg_trgm', 'pgcrypto', 'pg_stat_statements', 'pageinspect') AND installed;

SELECT count(*) AS member_objects
FROM pg_depend
WHERE refclassid = 'pg_extension'::regclass AND deptype = 'e'
  AND refobjid = (SELECT oid FROM pg_extension WHERE extname = 'pg_trgm');

SELECT pg_describe_object(classid, objid, objsubid) AS member
FROM pg_depend
WHERE refclassid = 'pg_extension'::regclass AND deptype = 'e'
  AND refobjid = (SELECT oid FROM pg_extension WHERE extname = 'pg_trgm')
ORDER BY 1 LIMIT 8;
presets.note: `trusted = t` (pg_trgm, pgcrypto) lets any role with CREATE on the database install it. pg_trgm 1.6 owns **47** member objects, tracked by `deptype = e` in `pg_depend`; that is how DROP EXTENSION finds them.

presets.label: Trigrams & similarity
presets.note: 5 shared trigrams out of 12 distinct ones gives **0.416667**, above the 0.3 threshold, so `%` is true. `word_similarity` scores the best matching extent inside the second string.

presets.label: Trigram index for %…% search
presets.note: A B-tree cannot help with an unanchored pattern; the trigram GIN index can. The plan switches from a Seq Scan to a **Bitmap Index Scan on products_name_trgm**, followed by a recheck of each candidate row.

presets.label: pgvector: HNSW index
presets.note: `<=>` is cosine distance (`<->` is L2, `<#>` negative inner product). The plan is an **Index Scan … Order By**: an approximate nearest-neighbour search, not a sort of all 2000 rows.

presets.label: pg_stat_statements
presets.note: Constants are replaced by `$1`, so both LIKE queries collapse into **one** normalized entry with `calls = 2`. The ranking query puts `pg_sleep($1)` on top with almost all of the execution time, while it used no CPU at all: `total_exec_time` is wall time, waits included. On a server the module must be in `shared_preload_libraries`.

presets.label: pgcrypto
presets.note: `crypt` with a Blowfish salt produces a `$2a$08$…` hash. To check a password, hash the attempt using the stored hash as the salt and compare. New in PostgreSQL 18: `fips_mode()` reports whether OpenSSL runs in FIPS mode, and `pgcrypto.builtin_crypto_enabled` (`on`, `off` or `fips`) controls whether the built-in `gen_salt()` and `crypt()` work (`fips` disables them when OpenSSL is in FIPS mode).

presets.label: hstore: key/value in one column
presets.note: **hstore** adds a type with operators: `->` (value), `?` (has key), `@>` (contains pair), `||` (add or overwrite), plus functions such as `each` and `akeys`. Keys and values are **text only** and there is no nesting, which is why new designs mostly use jsonb. `@>`, `?`, `?&` and `?|` are GIN-indexable, just like their jsonb counterparts.

production.title: Typo-tolerant product search without a search engine
production.context: A storefront with a few million product names ran search as `WHERE name ILIKE '%' || $1 || '%'`. Users typed partial words and misspellings.
production.problem: Every search was a sequential scan of the whole table, and misspellings such as "caterpiler" found nothing at all.
production.solution: Install **pg_trgm** (a trusted extension, so the app owner can do it) and add one GIN trigram index. Use `ILIKE` for substring search, now index-assisted, and the `%` operator with `similarity()` ordering for "did you mean" results.
production.outcome: In the playground the same change turns `Seq Scan on products` into `Bitmap Index Scan on products_name_trgm` for `ILIKE '%gres 12%'`, and `similarity('caterpillar', 'caterpiler')` scores well above the 0.3 threshold, so the misspelling now matches.

pitfalls.title: pg_stat_statements created but empty
pitfalls.symptom: `CREATE EXTENSION pg_stat_statements` succeeds, but querying the view fails with "pg_stat_statements must be loaded via shared_preload_libraries".
pitfalls.cause: The module needs shared memory allocated at server start. CREATE EXTENSION only creates the SQL view and functions.
pitfalls.fix: Add it to `shared_preload_libraries` and restart, then check that `compute_query_id` is `auto` or `on`.

pitfalls.title: Trigram search on very short patterns
pitfalls.symptom: A trigram-indexed `ILIKE '%ab%'` is as slow as a sequential scan.
pitfalls.cause: Patterns that yield no complete trigram give the index nothing to look up, so it degenerates into a **full index scan** plus a recheck of every row.
pitfalls.fix: Require at least 3 characters before searching, or route very short inputs to a prefix B-tree index (`text_pattern_ops`).

pitfalls.title: Approximate vector search with filters returns too few rows
pitfalls.symptom: `ORDER BY embedding <-> $1 LIMIT 10` with an extra `WHERE category = 'x'` returns only 3 rows, or misses obvious matches.
pitfalls.cause: HNSW gathers `hnsw.ef_search` candidates (default **40**) first, then the filter removes most of them. The index is approximate by design.
pitfalls.fix: Raise `hnsw.ef_search` for filtered queries, use pgvector's iterative scans if available in your version, or partition / partially index by the filter column.

pitfalls.title: Upgrading the package but not the extension
pitfalls.symptom: After installing a newer extension package, new functions are missing and `pg_extension.extversion` still shows the old version.
pitfalls.cause: Installing files only makes new versions *available*. Each database keeps the version it installed until you run the update scripts.
pitfalls.fix: Run `ALTER EXTENSION name UPDATE;` in every database, and check `pg_available_extensions` for `installed_version` versus `default_version`.

pitfalls.title: Reading execution-time share as CPU
pitfalls.symptom: A "top queries by CPU" report built on pg_stat_statements points at a query that barely uses the processor, and tuning it changes nothing.
pitfalls.cause: `total_exec_time` is elapsed time inside the executor, including lock waits, I/O and sleeps. A share of `sum(total_exec_time) OVER ()` is a share of **execution time**, not CPU. A cast such as `numeric(6,3)` on the average also overflows once an average passes 999.999 ms.
pitfalls.fix: Call the column what it is, read `mean_exec_time` next to `calls`, and compare `shared_blks_read` and `shared_blks_hit` (plus I/O timing columns when `track_io_timing` is on) to tell waiting from computing. Then EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) the top entries.
pitfalls.sql:
SELECT calls, round(mean_exec_time::numeric, 2) AS mean_ms,
       round((100 * total_exec_time / sum(total_exec_time) OVER ())::numeric, 1) AS pct_exec_time,
       shared_blks_hit, shared_blks_read, left(query, 60) AS query
FROM pg_stat_statements ORDER BY total_exec_time DESC LIMIT 10;

pointers: An extension is a **control file + versioned SQL scripts** (+ shared library). Members are tracked in `pg_depend` with deptype `e`, and pg_dump emits only `CREATE EXTENSION`.
**Trusted** extensions can be installed by non-superusers with CREATE on the database. Check with `pg_available_extension_versions`.
**pg_stat_statements** needs `shared_preload_libraries`; it groups queries by normalized text into one row per query id, user and database.
**pg_trgm**: similarity = shared trigrams / union, threshold 0.3. GIN or GiST `*_trgm_ops` indexes speed up `%`, `LIKE`, `ILIKE` and regex, even unanchored.
**pgvector**: `<->` L2, `<=>` cosine, `<#>` inner product. HNSW (m=16, ef_construction=64, ef_search=40) gives approximate nearest neighbours.

lessons.title: Full-text search
tldr: **Full-text search** turns documents into a `tsvector` of normalized, positioned **lexemes** and queries into a `tsquery` of lexemes joined by AND, OR, NOT and FOLLOWED BY, then matches them with `@@`.
It exists because `LIKE` and regular expressions know nothing about language: they cannot match "indexes" to "index", skip stop words, rank results, or use an index for word searches.

visualizer.title: From words to lexemes to a GIN lookup
visualizer.caption: Pick a document to see the parser and dictionary at work, then click **Next query** to watch GIN combine posting lists. Every token, lexeme and position is exactly what `ts_debug` and `to_tsvector` return for these documents.

presets.label: Document → tsvector
presets.note: `ts_debug` shows each token, its type, the dictionary that handled it and the lexemes produced. `{}` means **stop word**: `on` and `up` are dropped, yet positions skip them. `ts_stat` counts documents and occurrences per lexeme: `page` and `row` lead with 3 documents each, and `search` counts "Search", "searching" and "Searching" as one lexeme.

presets.label: Four ways to build a tsquery
presets.sql:
SELECT to_tsquery('english', 'dead & rows') AS to_tsquery,
       plainto_tsquery('english', 'dead rows') AS plainto,
       phraseto_tsquery('english', 'dead rows') AS phraseto,
       websearch_to_tsquery('english', '"dead rows" or vacuum -index') AS websearch;
presets.note: `to_tsquery` needs operator syntax; `plainto` ANDs words; `phraseto` uses `<->`; `websearch_to_tsquery` understands quotes, `or` and `-` and never raises a syntax error.

presets.label: tsquery operators, and two that do not exist
presets.note: `:*` is a **prefix** match (`plan` finds "planner"), `<->` is FOLLOWED BY, `!` is NOT. Double quotes and a leading `-` are **websearch** syntax only: `to_tsquery` rejects both with a syntax error.

presets.label: Match with the GIN index
presets.note: A **Bitmap Index Scan on docs_tsv_gin** finds candidate rows; the `Recheck Cond` verifies them on the heap (needed here for the phrase positions).

presets.label: Ranking with weights
presets.sql:
SELECT id, title,
       ts_rank(tsv, q) AS rank,
       ts_rank_cd(tsv, q) AS rank_cd
FROM docs, websearch_to_tsquery('english', 'indexes') q
WHERE tsv @@ q
ORDER BY rank DESC;
presets.note: Both docs contain `index`, but doc 3 also has it in its **title** (weight A = 1.0 versus D = 0.1), so it ranks higher. Ranking reads every matching tsvector, so rank only what you filtered.

presets.label: Highlighting
presets.note: `ts_headline` re-parses the **original text**, not the tsvector, so it is slow on long documents. Its output is not HTML-escaped.

presets.label: Expression index: error, then fix
presets.note: The one-argument `to_tsvector` is only STABLE, so indexing it fails: **functions in index expression must be marked IMMUTABLE**. With `'english'` it builds, but a query written with the one-argument form still runs a **Seq Scan**; only the identical expression gets the Bitmap Index Scan. An expression index saves the stored column but makes every query repeat the expression.

presets.label: Cast vs to_tsvector
presets.sql:
SELECT 'fat cats ate fat rats'::tsvector AS cast_value,
       to_tsvector('english', 'fat cats ate fat rats') AS parsed,
       'fat cats ate fat rats'::tsvector @@ to_tsquery('english', 'fat & rat') AS cast_matches,
       to_tsvector('english', 'fat cats ate fat rats') @@ to_tsquery('english', 'fat & rat') AS parsed_matches;
presets.note: A cast only splits on spaces: no stemming, so `rats` never equals `rat`. Always build tsvectors with `to_tsvector`.

production.title: Replacing ILIKE search in a help-center
production.context: A help-center searched 400,000 articles with `WHERE body ILIKE '%' || $1 || '%'`, sorted by date.
production.problem: Every search scanned the whole table. A search for "indexes" missed articles that only said "index", and results came back in date order, not by relevance.
production.solution: Add a **stored generated tsvector column** that weights the title above the body, index it with **GIN**, query with `websearch_to_tsquery` (safe for raw user input) and order by `ts_rank`. Highlight snippets only for the page of results shown.
production.outcome: Searches use a Bitmap Index Scan on the GIN index instead of a full scan, stemming connects word forms, and title hits rank first. In the playground, the same pattern over 5,000 rows plans as `Bitmap Index Scan on docs_tsv_gin`, and the title-weighted doc 3 outranks doc 5 for "indexes".

pitfalls.title: The index is never used
pitfalls.symptom: `WHERE to_tsvector(body) @@ q` runs a Seq Scan even though an expression GIN index exists.
pitfalls.cause: An expression index must use the **two-argument** form with an explicit configuration, and the query must use the same expression. The one-argument form depends on `default_text_search_config`, which can change, so it cannot be indexed.
pitfalls.fix: Write `to_tsvector('english', body)` in both the index and the query, or index a generated tsvector column and query that column.

pitfalls.title: Casting text to tsvector
pitfalls.symptom: Searches for "rat" do not find documents that contain "rats".
pitfalls.cause: `'…'::tsvector` takes the text as already-normalized lexemes. It does no stemming and no stop-word removal.
pitfalls.fix: Build documents with `to_tsvector(config, text)` and queries with `websearch_to_tsquery` or `to_tsquery`.

pitfalls.title: Ranking every match
pitfalls.symptom: A broad search ("the product") with `ORDER BY ts_rank(...)` is slow even with a GIN index.
pitfalls.cause: GIN finds matches quickly, but **ranking has to read the tsvector of every matching row** before it can sort.
pitfalls.fix: Narrow first (date range, category), cap the candidate set in a subquery with LIMIT, or accept GIN order for very broad queries.

pitfalls.title: Language-specific stemming of names and codes
pitfalls.symptom: Product codes and names match too much or too little, for example "Pari" matching "Paris".
pitfalls.cause: The `english` Snowball stemmer stems everything it recognizes, including proper nouns.
pitfalls.fix: Use the `simple` configuration for codes and names, or put a synonym dictionary before the stemmer for protected words.

pitfalls.title: Writing web-search syntax into to_tsquery
pitfalls.symptom: `ERROR: syntax error in tsquery` as soon as a user types a quoted phrase, or a search for `pages -vacuum` fails instead of excluding vacuum.
pitfalls.cause: A common claim is that tsquery uses double quotes for phrases, a trailing `:` for prefixes and `-` for NOT. In `to_tsquery` the phrase operator is `<->` (or `<N>`), the prefix marker is `:*`, and negation is `!`. Quotes, `or` and `-` exist only in `websearch_to_tsquery`.
pitfalls.fix: Pass raw user input to `websearch_to_tsquery`, which never raises. Use `to_tsquery` only for queries your code builds, with `&`, `|`, `!`, `<->` and `:*`.
pitfalls.sql:
SELECT websearch_to_tsquery('english', '"dead rows" -vacuum'),
       to_tsquery('english', 'dead <-> row & !vacuum & plan:*');

pitfalls.title: Leaving out STORED on the tsvector column
pitfalls.symptom: `CREATE INDEX … USING gin (tsv)` fails with `indexes on virtual generated columns are not supported`.
pitfalls.cause: In PostgreSQL 18 a generated column is **VIRTUAL** by default: computed on every read, never written to disk (`attgenerated = v`). Virtual columns cannot be indexed, so the GIN index has nothing to store.
pitfalls.fix: Write `GENERATED ALWAYS AS (…) STORED` for a search column, or skip the column and index the expression `to_tsvector('english', body)` directly.
pitfalls.sql:
ALTER TABLE articles ADD COLUMN tsv tsvector
  GENERATED ALWAYS AS (to_tsvector('english', coalesce(body, ''))) STORED;

pointers: Pipeline: **parser** splits tokens → **dictionaries** normalize to lexemes and drop stop words → **tsvector** of sorted lexemes with positions.
Build queries with `websearch_to_tsquery` for user input: quotes → `<->`, `or` → `|`, `-` → `!`, no syntax errors.
Index with **GIN** (one entry per lexeme, posting lists) on a **stored generated tsvector column**, or on `to_tsvector('config', col)` with the same expression in queries.
**Weights** A–D (default 1.0, 0.4, 0.2, 0.1) let titles outrank bodies in `ts_rank` and `ts_rank_cd`.
Phrase (`<->`) and weighted queries need the row's tsvector, so GIN results are **rechecked**.

lessons.title: Row-level security
tldr: **Row-level security** attaches policies to a table, boolean expressions that PostgreSQL adds to every query so each role sees and changes only the rows the policies allow.
It exists so tenant or user isolation is enforced by the database for every query and code path, instead of trusting each application query to remember its `WHERE tenant_id = …`.

visualizer.title: How policies combine into one filter
visualizer.caption: Click **Next scenario**, or toggle policies, switch roles and change session settings. Watch the effective filter and each row's verdict, plus whether an INSERT passes WITH CHECK.

presets.label: Default deny
presets.note: RLS is on and no policy exists, so `app_user` sees **0 rows** and gets no error. The playground runs as a superuser, which is why every preset switches with `SET ROLE`.

presets.label: Tenant isolation
presets.note: One permissive policy, keyed on a **session setting** the application sets per connection or transaction. Tenant 1 sees tickets 1, 2 and 3.

presets.label: Add a restrictive policy
presets.note: Restrictive policies are **ANDed**: ticket 3 disappears. The plan shows the policy quals placed **before** the user's `title ~~ 'L%'`, so non-leakproof user functions never see hidden rows.

presets.label: Permissive policies OR
presets.note: `(tenant_isolation OR own_rows) AND hide_archived`: cho's open ticket 4 from tenant 2 now appears alongside tenant 1's open tickets.

presets.label: WITH CHECK and silent filtering
presets.note: A new row that fails the policy is an **error** (WITH CHECK, here implied by USING). An UPDATE of a row you cannot see is **silently filtered**: 0 rows, no error.

presets.label: Owner bypass and FORCE
presets.note: The **owner** bypasses policies (6 rows) until `FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY` (2 rows). Superusers and roles with **BYPASSRLS** bypass even FORCE.

presets.label: row_security = off for dumps
presets.note: `row_security = off` does not bypass anything: a query that policies would filter **raises an error** instead, so a backup never silently misses rows. `pg_policies` lists every policy.

presets.label: Per-command policies (CRM)
presets.note: `FOR INSERT … USING` is rejected: **only WITH CHECK expression allowed for INSERT**. With per-command policies, LexCorp's contacts are visible, the LEFT JOIN still lists Wayne and Queen with NULL contacts (RLS filters only `contacts`), the Joker insert fails WITH CHECK, and `DELETE` with no DELETE policy removes **0 rows** without an error. `set_config(…, true)` lasts only for the transaction; afterwards the setting reads as an **empty string**, which a bare `::int` cast turns into an error. `NULLIF(…, '')` makes it NULL, so the policy denies instead.

production.title: Multi-tenant isolation that does not depend on every query
production.context: A SaaS app kept all tenants in shared tables with a `tenant_id` column. Every query was supposed to include `WHERE tenant_id = $1`.
production.problem: A new reporting endpoint forgot the predicate and showed one customer another customer's tickets. Code review could not guarantee that no other query would ever forget it.
production.solution: Enable RLS with a **tenant policy** keyed on a transaction-local setting. The app connects as a non-owner role without BYPASSRLS and runs `SET LOCAL app.tenant_id = …` at the start of every transaction (safe with transaction pooling). `FORCE` covers the owner too, so migrations and jobs that run as the owner must set a tenant or use a dedicated BYPASSRLS role.
production.outcome: A query that forgets the predicate now returns only the current tenant's rows, and a write tagged with another tenant fails with `new row violates row-level security policy`. The policy is just a qual, so the `tenant_id` index keeps it cheap. The presets reproduce each behaviour.

pitfalls.title: Testing as a superuser or the table owner
pitfalls.symptom: Policies "work in staging" but every row is visible in production, or the reverse.
pitfalls.cause: Superusers and BYPASSRLS roles **always** bypass RLS, and the table owner bypasses it unless FORCE is set. Tests that connect as the owner never exercise the policies.
pitfalls.fix: Run the application and its tests as a dedicated non-owner role, and use `ALTER TABLE … FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY` when the owner role also serves traffic.

pitfalls.title: A missing setting breaks every query
pitfalls.symptom: `ERROR: unrecognized configuration parameter "app.tenant_id"` on connections that did not set it.
pitfalls.cause: `current_setting(name)` errors if the parameter was never set in the session. The `missing_ok` form has its own trap: once a `SET LOCAL` or `set_config(…, true)` has ended, the parameter still exists and reads as an **empty string**, so `::int` fails with `invalid input syntax for type integer: ""`.
pitfalls.fix: Use `NULLIF(current_setting('app.tenant_id', true), '')`. An unset tenant then becomes NULL, the policy evaluates to NULL, which counts as false: no rows instead of an error.
pitfalls.sql: USING (tenant_id = NULLIF(current_setting('app.tenant_id', true), '')::int)

pitfalls.title: Leaks through constraints and errors
pitfalls.symptom: A user can probe for other tenants' data, for example by trying INSERTs and watching for unique violations.
pitfalls.cause: **Unique, primary key and foreign key checks bypass RLS.** Their errors reveal whether a hidden row exists. Non-leakproof functions in queries can also leak values through error messages.
pitfalls.fix: Include `tenant_id` in unique keys, use non-guessable ids, and do not expose raw constraint errors to end users.

pitfalls.title: Only restrictive policies
pitfalls.symptom: After adding a carefully written restrictive policy, the application sees nothing at all.
pitfalls.cause: Restrictive policies only narrow what permissive policies allow. With **no permissive policy**, nothing is allowed: default deny.
pitfalls.fix: Always have at least one permissive policy (even `USING (true)` for a role) and layer restrictive ones on top.

pitfalls.title: Writing an INSERT policy with USING
pitfalls.symptom: `ERROR: only WITH CHECK expression allowed for INSERT` while creating per-command policies, or a migration that stops halfway through its policy list.
pitfalls.cause: USING filters rows that already exist. An INSERT has no existing row, so an INSERT policy accepts only **WITH CHECK**. The reverse also holds: a SELECT or DELETE policy takes only USING. A command with no policy at all is denied, and for DELETE that looks like success: `DELETE 0`.
pitfalls.fix: Write `FOR INSERT … WITH CHECK (…)`, `FOR SELECT` and `FOR DELETE … USING (…)`, and `FOR UPDATE` with both. Check the result in `pg_policies`.
pitfalls.sql:
CREATE POLICY c_ins ON contacts FOR INSERT TO app_user
  WITH CHECK (account_id = NULLIF(current_setting('rls.account_id', true), '')::int);

pitfalls.title: A session setting that outlives its request
pitfalls.symptom: Behind a connection pooler, a request occasionally sees another tenant's rows.
pitfalls.cause: A plain `SET app.tenant_id` lasts for the whole **session**. When the pooler hands that connection to the next request, which forgets to set its own tenant, the old value still applies. The setting is also no security boundary if clients can run arbitrary SQL: anyone can `SET` it.
pitfalls.fix: Set the tenant with `SET LOCAL` or `set_config('app.tenant_id', $1, true)` inside each transaction, so it ends at COMMIT. Only let trusted application code issue the SET; untrusted users need their own database roles.

pointers: `ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY` with no policy = **default deny**. Owners bypass unless **FORCE**; superusers and **BYPASSRLS** always bypass.
Filter = **(permissive OR permissive …) AND restrictive AND …**. No permissive policy means no rows.
**USING** silently filters existing rows; **WITH CHECK** raises an error for new or updated rows. FOR ALL without WITH CHECK reuses USING.
Policy quals run **before** user quals (except leakproof functions), so hidden rows never reach user code.
Key multi-tenant policies on `NULLIF(current_setting('app.tenant_id', true), '')` set with **SET LOCAL** per transaction. INSERT policies take only WITH CHECK.

lessons.title: Write-ahead logging and LSNs
tldr: The **write-ahead log** is an append-only stream of change records, and every byte in it has an address called a **Log Sequence Number** (LSN).
A change may reach a data file only after its WAL record is safely on disk, so a commit needs just one sequential WAL flush and a crash can always be repaired by replaying the log.

visualizer.title: Watch statements turn into WAL records
visualizer.caption: Step through eight statements and watch the insert and flush pointers move. Click any record to decode its LSN into a segment file and offset. Then pick a `synchronous_commit` level below.

presets.label: Where is the WAL now?
presets.sql:
SELECT pg_current_wal_lsn()                                 AS lsn,
       pg_walfile_name(pg_current_wal_lsn())                AS segment_file,
       (pg_walfile_name_offset(pg_current_wal_lsn())).file_offset AS offset_in_file,
       pg_current_wal_lsn() - '0/0'                         AS bytes_since_initdb,
       current_setting('wal_level')                         AS wal_level,
       current_setting('wal_segment_size')                  AS segment_size;
presets.note: An LSN is a byte offset. The file name is timeline (8 hex digits) + segment number, and the offset is the LSN modulo 16 MB.

presets.label: One INSERT, record by record
presets.note: `Heap INSERT`, `Btree INSERT_LEAF` for the primary key and a 34-byte `Transaction COMMIT`. The first `Sequence LOG` appears because the identity sequence logs 32 values ahead. `end_lsn - start_lsn` is the length rounded up to 8 bytes.

presets.label: ROLLBACK, UPDATE and DELETE
presets.note: The rolled-back INSERT is still in the WAL, followed by an `ABORT` record. The UPDATE is a single `HOT_UPDATE` with no index record. DELETE is just 54 bytes.

presets.label: LSN arithmetic
presets.sql:
SELECT '0/1769D18'::pg_lsn - '0/1769C60'::pg_lsn     AS bytes_between,
       '0/1769C60'::pg_lsn + 16777216                     AS one_segment_later,
       pg_walfile_name('0/1769C60')                       AS file_a,
       pg_walfile_name('0/1769C60'::pg_lsn + 16777216)   AS file_b,
       '0/9'::pg_lsn < '0/10'::pg_lsn                     AS lsn_compare,
       '0/9' < '0/10'                                     AS text_compare;
presets.note: Subtracting LSNs gives bytes. Adding 16 MB moves exactly one segment file. Compare LSNs as `pg_lsn`, never as text: as text, `0/9` sorts after `0/10`.

presets.label: Async commit: the loss window
presets.note: With `off`, COMMIT returns while its record is still only in WAL buffers. The next synchronous commit flushes everything. This single-process playground has no WAL writer, so the gap stays open until then; a server with a WAL writer closes it within about 600 ms.

presets.label: WAL volume by resource manager
presets.note: About one Heap and one Btree record per row, a `Sequence LOG` every 32 ids, but a **single COMMIT** for the whole statement. The flush cost is paid once per transaction, not once per row.

presets.label: Sequences log 32 values ahead
presets.note: 100 `nextval` calls wrote only **4** `Sequence LOG` records (at 1, 33, 65 and 97). Each record reserves the next 32 values, and `log_cnt` counts how many are left. After a crash the sequence restarts after the last reserved value, so up to 32 numbers are skipped.

presets.label: What skips the WAL: UNLOGGED and TEMP
presets.note: The same 1,000 rows cost about **96 kB** of WAL in a normal table and **40 bytes** (just the COMMIT record) in an unlogged or temp table. `relpersistence` is `p`, `u` or `t`. No WAL also means no crash safety and no replication.

production.title: Ingesting telemetry without fsync-bound commits
production.context: An IoT platform writes one small row per device reading, each in its own transaction, from 40 application threads. Billing rows go through the same database.
production.problem: Write throughput flattened as threads were added. `pg_stat_io` showed WAL `fsyncs` climbing in step with commits: every reading waited for its own WAL flush, so the commit rate was bounded by flush latency, not CPU.
production.solution: Make durability a per-transaction choice. Telemetry transactions run `SET LOCAL synchronous_commit = off`, so COMMIT returns as soon as the record is in WAL buffers. Billing transactions keep the default `on`. Both share one WAL, so a billing commit also flushes any telemetry before it. Do not touch `fsync`.
production.outcome: Telemetry commits stop waiting on flushes, so throughput is limited by CPU and WAL insertion instead. The risk is bounded: after a crash at most about 3 × `wal_writer_delay` (600 ms by default) of telemetry is missing, and the database is never corrupted. Billing durability is unchanged.

pitfalls.title: Turning off fsync to "speed up commits"
pitfalls.symptom: After a power cut the server will not start, or indexes and tables disagree. Data is corrupted, not merely missing.
pitfalls.cause: `fsync = off` removes every write barrier, so data pages can hit disk before their WAL and WAL order is lost. Async commit only skips the wait; the WAL rule still holds.
pitfalls.fix: Leave `fsync = on`. Use `synchronous_commit = off` per transaction (or per role) where losing the last fraction of a second is acceptable.
pitfalls.sql:
ALTER ROLE telemetry_writer SET synchronous_commit = off;  -- safe
-- never in production: fsync = off

pitfalls.title: Comparing LSNs as text
pitfalls.symptom: A lag monitor reports that a replica is "ahead" of the primary, or alerts flap when the low half of the LSN gains a digit.
pitfalls.cause: LSNs are two hex numbers. As text, `0/9` sorts after `0/10` and `0/FFFFFFFF` after `1/0`.
pitfalls.fix: Cast to `pg_lsn` and subtract to get bytes, or use `pg_wal_lsn_diff()`.
pitfalls.sql: SELECT pg_current_wal_lsn() - '0/1769C60'::pg_lsn AS bytes_since;

pitfalls.title: Expecting remote_apply without a synchronous standby
pitfalls.symptom: An application sets `synchronous_commit = remote_apply` for read-your-writes on a replica, yet reads on the replica still miss fresh rows.
pitfalls.cause: With `synchronous_standby_names` empty, `remote_write`, `remote_apply` and `local` all behave like `on`: the primary waits only for its own flush.
pitfalls.fix: Name the standby in `synchronous_standby_names` (it must be streaming), or route read-your-writes queries to the primary.

pitfalls.title: UNLOGGED tables for data you cannot rebuild
pitfalls.symptom: After a crash or a failover, a staging table is empty, and on the replicas it was never readable at all.
pitfalls.cause: An unlogged table writes no WAL for its rows. Crash recovery cannot replay it, so it is reset to empty, and streaming replicas never receive it.
pitfalls.fix: Use UNLOGGED only for data you can regenerate (caches, bulk-load staging). Make it durable with `ALTER TABLE … SET LOGGED`, which rewrites it through the WAL.
pitfalls.sql: ALTER TABLE t_unlogged SET LOGGED;

pitfalls.title: Expecting gapless sequence numbers
pitfalls.symptom: Invoice numbers jump from 1041 to 1073 after a server restart, or skip a value after a failed insert.
pitfalls.cause: A sequence logs 32 values ahead, so recovery resumes after the last reserved value. `nextval` is also never rolled back.
pitfalls.fix: Treat sequence values as unique, not consecutive. If gapless numbering is a legal requirement, keep a counter row updated inside the same transaction and accept that it serializes writers.

pointers: **WAL rule**: the WAL record must be flushed before the data page it describes may be written.
An **LSN** is a byte position; `lsn_a - lsn_b` is bytes; segment files are **16 MB**, named timeline + segment number.
COMMIT costs **one sequential flush**, and concurrent commits share it (**group commit**).
`synchronous_commit` is **per transaction**: `off` risks losing recent commits after a crash, never corruption.
Inspect real records with **`pg_walinspect`**: `pg_get_wal_records_info` and `pg_get_wal_stats`.

lessons.title: Checkpoints and full page writes
tldr: A **checkpoint** flushes every dirty page to the data files and records a **redo point** in `pg_control`, so crash recovery only has to replay WAL written after it.

Because a page write can be torn by a power failure, the first change to each page after a checkpoint logs a **full page image**, which makes recovery safe and makes WAL volume spike after every checkpoint.

visualizer.title: One checkpoint cycle, then a crash
visualizer.caption: Step through a checkpoint, three UPDATEs, a torn page and replay. Flip `wal_compression` to see the image sizes shrink.

presets.label: pg_control and the knobs
presets.note: Defaults: a checkpoint every 300 s or before 1 GB of WAL, writes spread over 90% of the interval. `redo_lsn` is where crash recovery would start right now.

presets.label: CHECKPOINT and its records
presets.note: `CHECKPOINT_REDO` marks the redo point, `RUNNING_XACTS` snapshots open transactions for standbys, and `CHECKPOINT_ONLINE` names the redo LSN in its description.

presets.label: First change after a checkpoint
presets.note: The `HOT_UPDATE` is about 14.8 kB: `(FPW)` images of heap block 0 (8192 minus the free-space hole) and of the visibility-map page, whose all-visible bit the UPDATE cleared.

presets.label: Same page, next change
presets.note: id 11 is on block 0, already imaged since the checkpoint: about 77 bytes. id 500 is on block 5: a new image of about 6.6 kB.

presets.label: Compress the page images
presets.note: `block_ref` now reports `compression saved: … method: pglz`. Here the image rides in an `FPI_FOR_HINT` record: reading the page set hint bits first, and with data checksums on that change is imaged too. `lz4` and `zstd` work only on servers built with those libraries; this one has pglz only.

presets.label: A whole-table UPDATE, twice
presets.note: The same statement writes far more WAL the first time after a checkpoint, because every page it touches is imaged once. Longer checkpoint intervals mean fewer images per hour.

production.title: Taming WAL spikes on a write-heavy IoT database
production.context: An IoT platform updates the latest reading of 2 million devices continuously. The primary ships WAL to two standbys and to an archive bucket.
production.problem: WAL generation, network to replicas and archive cost all spiked right after each checkpoint. The server log showed `checkpoints are occurring too frequently` because `max_wal_size` (1 GB) was reached in under the 30 s `checkpoint_warning` window, so almost every update after a checkpoint paid for a full page image.
production.solution: Space checkpoints out so each hot page is imaged less often, keep the writes spread, and compress what remains. Then watch the counters to confirm checkpoints are timed, not requested.
production.outcome: With one checkpoint per 15 minutes instead of one every few seconds, each hot page is imaged at most four times an hour. The FPI share of WAL (`wal_fpi` vs `wal_records`) dropped sharply, and so did replication and archive volume. The cost is longer crash recovery: up to one 15-minute cycle of WAL to replay, which the team measured and accepted.

pitfalls.title: Checkpoints driven by max_wal_size
pitfalls.symptom: The log repeats `checkpoints are occurring too frequently (N seconds apart)` and `pg_stat_checkpointer.num_requested` grows faster than `num_timed`.
pitfalls.cause: `max_wal_size` is too small for the write rate, so checkpoints are forced early. Each one flushes all dirty pages and restarts the full-page-image cycle.
pitfalls.fix: Raise `max_wal_size` until checkpoints are mostly timed. It is a soft limit, so leave disk headroom.
pitfalls.sql: SELECT num_timed, num_requested, write_time, sync_time FROM pg_stat_checkpointer;

pitfalls.title: Turning off full_page_writes on ordinary storage
pitfalls.symptom: After a power failure, recovery completes but some pages are silently corrupt, or the server cannot start.
pitfalls.cause: Without page images, a torn 8 kB write cannot be repaired from row-level WAL. A battery-backed cache alone does not guarantee atomic 8 kB writes.
pitfalls.fix: Keep `full_page_writes = on` unless the storage guarantees atomic page writes (for example ZFS). Reduce the cost with longer checkpoint intervals and `wal_compression` instead.

pitfalls.title: checkpoint_completion_target = 1.0
pitfalls.symptom: Checkpoints regularly overrun into the next one and I/O latency gets bursty.
pitfalls.cause: A checkpoint also does work besides buffer writes. Targeting 100% of the interval leaves no slack, so the next checkpoint starts late.
pitfalls.fix: Keep the default 0.9. Spread writes further by lengthening `checkpoint_timeout`, not by raising the target.

pointers: Checkpoint = **redo record → flush all dirty pages → checkpoint record → pg_control**.
Triggered by **`checkpoint_timeout`** (5 min) or **`max_wal_size`** (1 GB, soft), writes spread by `checkpoint_completion_target` 0.9.
The **first change to a page after a checkpoint logs its full image**; later changes to that page log only the delta.
Recovery: read **pg_control**, jump to the checkpoint, **replay from the redo point** to the end of WAL.
Fewer checkpoints = less WAL but longer recovery; **`wal_compression`** shrinks the images.

lessons.title: VACUUM vs VACUUM FULL
tldr: **VACUUM** removes dead row versions so their space can be reused, updates the visibility and free space maps, and runs alongside normal reads and writes.
**VACUUM FULL** instead rewrites the whole table into a new file to give space back to the operating system, at the price of an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock for the entire run.

visualizer.title: Vacuum a real table, phase by phase
visualizer.caption: Step through the seven phases of `pg_stat_progress_vacuum` on 106 pages, then switch to **VACUUM FULL** and compare locks, files and results. All counts are from VACUUM VERBOSE on the playground table.

presets.label: Make dead rows
presets.note: All 2,500 updates were **HOT** (fillfactor 70 left room). The table is still 106 pages: DELETE frees nothing by itself.

presets.label: Before VACUUM: maps
presets.sql:
SELECT * FROM pg_visibility_map_summary('orders');
SELECT count(*) AS pages, sum(avail) AS fsm_free_bytes FROM pg_freespace('orders');
presets.note: No page is all-visible: every page was modified. The FSM still reports only the fillfactor headroom, because the FSM is updated by VACUUM, not by DELETE.

presets.label: Run VACUUM
presets.note: The 16 empty pages at the end were truncated: **106 → 90**. All remaining pages are all-visible, and `n_dead_tup` is back to 0.

presets.label: Free space after VACUUM
presets.note: Each page now advertises its free bytes to the FSM, so the next INSERTs and non-HOT UPDATEs reuse them instead of growing the file.

presets.label: How VACUUM reads: its own ring
presets.sql:
SELECT backend_type, context, reads, hits, writes
FROM pg_stat_io
WHERE object = 'relation' AND context IN ('normal', 'vacuum') AND reads + hits > 0
ORDER BY context;

SELECT name, setting FROM pg_settings
WHERE name IN ('io_method', 'maintenance_io_concurrency', 'vacuum_buffer_usage_limit')
ORDER BY name;
presets.note: VACUUM's page accesses are counted under context **vacuum**: it reads through a small ring of buffers (`vacuum_buffer_usage_limit`, 2 MB) so a big table does not evict the hot working set. In 18, `io_method = worker` (the server default) lets VACUUM issue its reads ahead asynchronously; writes stay synchronous. This single-process build reports `sync`.

presets.label: TRUNCATE false keeps the tail
presets.note: With `TRUNCATE false` the emptied tail pages stay (no ACCESS EXCLUSIVE needed). A later plain VACUUM gives them back.

presets.label: VACUUM FULL rewrites the file
presets.note: A new `relfilenode` means a brand-new file. The index is rebuilt and smaller. In production this whole step holds ACCESS EXCLUSIVE.

presets.label: Emptying a table: DELETE vs TRUNCATE
presets.note: DELETE left **5,000 dead rows** in 64 pages for VACUUM. TRUNCATE swapped in a new empty file (new filenode, 0 bytes) and left nothing to clean, but it holds **AccessExclusiveLock** until COMMIT. Roll it back and the old file comes back.

production.title: An audit table that was "fixed" nightly with VACUUM FULL
production.context: A SaaS team keeps 90 days of audit events in one 120 GB table. A nightly job deletes rows older than 90 days, then runs `VACUUM FULL audit_events` to "reclaim space".
production.problem: VACUUM FULL took over 40 minutes and held ACCESS EXCLUSIVE the whole time, so every API call that wrote an audit row queued behind it and timed out. It also needed about 120 GB of free disk for the copy.
production.solution: Stop rewriting. The deleted space is reused by the next day's inserts, so a plain VACUUM after the purge keeps the table at a steady size. For the long term, partition by day and drop old partitions, which removes data without dead tuples at all.
production.outcome: The table settles at its steady-state size (about 90 days of data plus one day of churn) without ever going offline. Plain VACUUM runs alongside writes, needs no extra disk, and with partitions the nightly purge becomes a metadata change.

pitfalls.title: Running VACUUM FULL in business hours
pitfalls.symptom: Every query on the table hangs; `pg_locks` shows a granted AccessExclusiveLock and a queue of waiters.
pitfalls.cause: VACUUM FULL holds ACCESS EXCLUSIVE until the new file and all indexes are built. Even a plain SELECT must wait.
pitfalls.fix: Use plain VACUUM for routine work. If only the indexes are bloated, `REINDEX INDEX CONCURRENTLY` rebuilds one online under SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE (if it fails, it leaves an INVALID index to drop). To shrink the table itself online, use an extension such as pg_repack, or rebuild into a new table and swap.
pitfalls.sql: SELECT pid, mode, granted FROM pg_locks WHERE relation = 'orders'::regclass;

pitfalls.title: A long transaction makes VACUUM useless
pitfalls.symptom: VACUUM VERBOSE says `N are dead but not yet removable` and `n_dead_tup` never drops.
pitfalls.cause: VACUUM may remove a row version only when no snapshot can still see it. One old transaction, an idle-in-transaction session, or a stale replication slot holds the horizon back for the whole cluster.
pitfalls.fix: Find and end the oldest snapshot holders; set `idle_in_transaction_session_timeout`.
pitfalls.sql:
SELECT pid, state, xact_start, age(backend_xmin) AS xmin_age
FROM pg_stat_activity WHERE backend_xmin IS NOT NULL ORDER BY xmin_age DESC;

pitfalls.title: Expecting plain VACUUM to shrink the file
pitfalls.symptom: After deleting most rows and vacuuming, `pg_relation_size` barely moves.
pitfalls.cause: Plain VACUUM only truncates empty pages at the end of the file. Space freed in the middle is kept for reuse.
pitfalls.fix: That is usually what you want. If the table will stay small, rewrite it once in a maintenance window, or partition so you can drop whole chunks.

pitfalls.title: VACUUM from application code fails
pitfalls.symptom: A maintenance job gets `VACUUM cannot run inside a transaction block` (or `cannot be executed from a function`), while the same command works in psql.
pitfalls.cause: Many drivers open a transaction implicitly before the first statement, and VACUUM manages its own transactions, so it refuses to run inside one.
pitfalls.fix: Switch that connection to autocommit before sending VACUUM, and never wrap it in BEGIN, a function or a DO block.

pitfalls.title: Treating TRUNCATE as a cheap DELETE
pitfalls.symptom: A nightly `TRUNCATE staging` stalls every query on the table, and a report running at the same time sees the table as empty.
pitfalls.cause: A common claim is that TRUNCATE is fast because it locks lightly. It takes **ACCESS EXCLUSIVE**, the strongest lock, and swaps in a new file. It is not MVCC-safe: a REPEATABLE READ snapshot taken before it sees no rows afterwards.
pitfalls.fix: Use TRUNCATE for tables nobody else is reading at that moment. Keep its transaction short, and set `lock_timeout` so it gives up instead of queueing everyone behind it.
pitfalls.sql:
SET lock_timeout = '2s';
TRUNCATE staging;

pointers: Plain VACUUM: **SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE**, runs online, space is **reused**, only the empty tail goes back to the OS.
Phases: **scan heap (prune, collect dead TIDs) → vacuum indexes → vacuum heap → clean up indexes → truncate → final cleanup**.
Dead TIDs must fit in **`maintenance_work_mem`**, or indexes are scanned more than once.
VACUUM sets **all-visible / all-frozen** bits and fills the **FSM**; DELETE does neither.
VACUUM FULL: **ACCESS EXCLUSIVE**, new relfilenode, rebuilt indexes, needs disk for a full copy.

lessons.title: Tuning autovacuum
tldr: **Autovacuum** is a launcher plus a few worker processes that vacuum and analyze each table once its counts of dead, inserted or changed rows cross a threshold computed from the table size.
The defaults suit small tables, so big or hot tables need per-table thresholds and a larger I/O budget, or dead rows pile up faster than the throttled workers can remove them.

visualizer.title: When autovacuum fires, and how fast it can work
visualizer.caption: Pick a scenario or drag the sliders: the trigger formulas update, and a 24-hour simulation shows dead rows and runs. Switch to **How fast can it go?** for the cost-based throttle.

playground.setup:
CREATE TABLE sessions (id int PRIMARY KEY, user_id int NOT NULL, last_seen timestamptz NOT NULL, data text);
INSERT INTO sessions SELECT g, g % 5000, timestamptz '2026-11-01' + g * interval '1 second', md5(g::text)
FROM generate_series(1, 20000) g;
ANALYZE sessions;

CREATE FUNCTION av_opt(opts text[], name text) RETURNS float LANGUAGE sql STABLE AS $$
  SELECT coalesce((SELECT option_value FROM pg_options_to_table(opts) WHERE option_name = name),
                  current_setting(name))::float $$;

CREATE VIEW av_status AS
SELECT c.relname,
       greatest(c.reltuples, 0)::bigint AS reltuples,
       s.n_dead_tup,
       CASE WHEN o.vmax < 0 THEN o.vthr + o.vsf * greatest(c.reltuples, 0)
            ELSE least(o.vmax, o.vthr + o.vsf * greatest(c.reltuples, 0)) END::bigint AS vacuum_trigger,
       s.n_ins_since_vacuum,
       (o.ithr + o.isf * greatest(c.reltuples, 0)
          * (1 - CASE WHEN c.relpages > 0 THEN c.relallfrozen::float / c.relpages ELSE 0 END))::bigint AS insert_trigger,
       s.n_mod_since_analyze,
       (o.athr + o.asf * greatest(c.reltuples, 0))::bigint AS analyze_trigger
FROM pg_class c
JOIN pg_stat_user_tables s ON s.relid = c.oid
CROSS JOIN LATERAL (SELECT
  av_opt(c.reloptions, 'autovacuum_vacuum_threshold')           AS vthr,
  av_opt(c.reloptions, 'autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor')        AS vsf,
  av_opt(c.reloptions, 'autovacuum_vacuum_max_threshold')       AS vmax,
  av_opt(c.reloptions, 'autovacuum_vacuum_insert_threshold')    AS ithr,
  av_opt(c.reloptions, 'autovacuum_vacuum_insert_scale_factor') AS isf,
  av_opt(c.reloptions, 'autovacuum_analyze_threshold')          AS athr,
  av_opt(c.reloptions, 'autovacuum_analyze_scale_factor')       AS asf) o;

presets.label: The global knobs
presets.sql:
SELECT name, setting, unit FROM pg_settings
WHERE name LIKE 'autovacuum%' OR name IN ('vacuum_cost_limit', 'vacuum_cost_page_miss',
      'vacuum_cost_page_dirty', 'vacuum_cost_page_hit', 'track_counts', 'track_cost_delay_timing')
ORDER BY name;
presets.note: New in 18: `autovacuum_vacuum_max_threshold` (100 M), and `autovacuum_worker_slots` (16) next to `autovacuum_max_workers` (3). Slots reserve shared memory and need a restart; `max_workers` is reloadable up to the slot count. `autovacuum_vacuum_cost_limit = -1` means "use `vacuum_cost_limit`" (200).

presets.label: When will this table be vacuumed?
presets.sql:
SELECT pg_stat_force_next_flush();
SELECT * FROM av_status WHERE relname = 'sessions';
presets.note: With 20,000 rows the dead-row trigger is 50 + 0.2 × 20,000 = **4,050**. The `av_status` view in the setup applies the trigger formulas, including per-table overrides.

presets.label: Churn rows past the trigger
presets.note: 3,000 dead rows: not yet. 5,000: due. On a server the launcher would start a worker within `autovacuum_naptime` (1 min). This playground runs no autovacuum, so nothing happens by itself here.

presets.label: Per-table override
presets.note: Now 1000 + 0.01 × 20,000 = **1,200**. Storage parameters beat the global settings for this table only.

presets.label: Insert-only tables and freezing
presets.note: The insert trigger scales with the **unfrozen** share of the table. After VACUUM FREEZE every page is all-frozen, so the trigger falls to the base **1,000** instead of 1000 + 0.2 × 30,000 = 7,000. (`relpages` and `relallfrozen` refresh only at the next VACUUM or ANALYZE.)

presets.label: Throttle arithmetic
presets.sql:
SELECT current_setting('autovacuum_vacuum_cost_delay') AS delay,
       current_setting('vacuum_cost_limit')::int AS cost_limit,
       round(current_setting('vacuum_cost_limit')::int / current_setting('vacuum_cost_page_miss')::numeric
             / 0.002 * 8192 / 1048576, 1) AS max_mb_per_s_reading,
       round(current_setting('vacuum_cost_limit')::int
             / (current_setting('vacuum_cost_page_miss')::numeric + current_setting('vacuum_cost_page_dirty')::int)
             / 0.002 * 8192 / 1048576, 1) AS max_mb_per_s_read_and_dirty;
presets.note: At defaults one worker can read about 390 MB/s from disk but only about 35 MB/s when it also dirties every page. That budget is shared by all running workers.

presets.label: Health check and 18's timing columns
presets.note: The dead-row share uses `NULLIF` so an empty table does not divide by zero. The `total_*_time` columns (milliseconds, new in 18) show where vacuum time goes; `autovacuum_ms` stays 0 here because nothing runs automatically. A per-table `autovacuum_vacuum_max_threshold = 500` caps the trigger at **500** dead rows.

production.title: A 200 M-row orders table that bloated between vacuums
production.context: An e-commerce team runs a 200 M-row `orders` table. Each order is updated several times during fulfilment, about 40,000 updates a minute at peak.
production.problem: With the default scale factor, autovacuum waited for 50 + 0.2 × 200 M = **40 M** dead rows. That took about 17 hours of updates to reach, so heap and indexes carried up to 20% dead rows between runs, and every run had 40 M index entries to remove. Queries slowed as scans read through dead rows.
production.solution: Set per-table thresholds so the table is vacuumed after about 2 M dead rows, give autovacuum a bigger I/O budget, and monitor dead rows against the trigger.
production.outcome: The trigger drops from 40 M to about 2 M dead rows: roughly one run every 50 minutes at peak instead of one every 17 hours, and each run has 20× less to clean. Dead rows stay near 1% of the table.

pitfalls.title: Big tables wait for 20% of their rows to die
pitfalls.symptom: A large table shows millions of `n_dead_tup` and `last_autovacuum` days ago, while small tables are vacuumed constantly.
pitfalls.cause: The trigger is `50 + 0.2 × reltuples`. PostgreSQL 18 caps it at `autovacuum_vacuum_max_threshold` (100 M), which still allows huge backlogs.
pitfalls.fix: Lower `autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor` per table (0.01 to 0.05 for big, hot tables), or lower `autovacuum_vacuum_max_threshold`.
pitfalls.sql: ALTER TABLE orders SET (autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor = 0.01);

pitfalls.title: Autovacuum keeps getting cancelled
pitfalls.symptom: The log shows `canceling autovacuum task` again and again and the table is never fully vacuumed.
pitfalls.cause: Autovacuum yields to any conflicting lock request, such as frequent `ALTER TABLE`, `LOCK`, or manual ANALYZE on the same table. Only anti-wraparound runs refuse to yield.
pitfalls.fix: Stop the frequent conflicting command, or run a manual `VACUUM` in a quiet window. Check `pg_stat_user_tables.autovacuum_count` to confirm runs complete.

pitfalls.title: Adding workers does not make vacuum faster
pitfalls.symptom: After raising `autovacuum_max_workers` from 3 to 10, each table takes longer to vacuum.
pitfalls.cause: The cost limit is shared: total I/O stays at `autovacuum_vacuum_cost_limit` per `autovacuum_vacuum_cost_delay`, split among busy workers.
pitfalls.fix: Raise `autovacuum_vacuum_cost_limit` (or lower the delay) together with the worker count, within what the disks can sustain.

pitfalls.title: Partitioned parents are never auto-analyzed
pitfalls.symptom: Queries on a partitioned table get poor plans even though every partition has fresh statistics.
pitfalls.cause: Autovacuum processes partitions, but a partitioned table stores no rows, so it never triggers ANALYZE on the parent.
pitfalls.fix: Run `ANALYZE parent_table` after large loads and on a schedule.

pitfalls.title: Hunting autovacuum workers by query text
pitfalls.symptom: A script meant to cancel the autovacuum that blocks a migration kills the wrong session, or finds nothing, and the migration keeps waiting.
pitfalls.cause: Matching `query LIKE '%autovacuum%'` also matches the monitoring query itself. A worker's `query` reads `autovacuum: VACUUM public.orders`, and only `backend_type` identifies it reliably. Signalling it needs superuser unless the role has `pg_signal_autovacuum_worker` (new in 18).
pitfalls.fix: Filter on `backend_type`, grant the predefined role to the migration user, and remember that an anti-wraparound run will simply restart.

pointers: Vacuum when dead rows > **min(max_threshold, 50 + 0.2 × reltuples)**; max_threshold (100 M) is **new in 18**.
Insert-only tables: **1000 + 0.2 × reltuples × unfrozen share**; analyze: **50 + 0.1 × reltuples**.
Override per table with **storage parameters** (`ALTER TABLE … SET (autovacuum_…)`).
Throttle: **cost_limit 200** per **2 ms** delay, page hit 1 / miss 2 / dirty 20, **shared by all workers**.
Watch **`pg_stat_user_tables`**: `n_dead_tup`, `n_ins_since_vacuum`, `last_autovacuum`, `autovacuum_count`.

lessons.title: XID wraparound, freezing and MultiXacts
tldr: Transaction IDs are 32-bit counters compared modulo 2^32, so any row whose `xmin` falls more than about 2 billion transactions behind would suddenly look like it came from the future.

VACUUM prevents that by **freezing** old rows, marking them older than every XID, and PostgreSQL escalates from aggressive vacuums to forced autovacuums to refusing new XIDs as a table approaches the limit.

visualizer.title: The XID circle
visualizer.caption: Advance through each threshold and watch what the server does. Run VACUUM to freeze and pull `relfrozenxid` forward, then switch to **What if nothing froze?** and push past 2^31.

presets.label: How old is everything?
presets.note: The three ages to monitor: per table, including its TOAST table, and per database. `pg_current_xact_id()` returns a 64-bit `xid8` (epoch + xid); the on-disk xmin is the low 32 bits.

presets.label: Which statements use an XID?
presets.note: A transaction gets an XID only when it first **writes**: reads alone leave it NULL, so read traffic never ages the cluster. `txid_current()` and `pg_current_xact_id()` force one, so each probe call burns an XID (they differ by 1).

presets.label: Burn 100,000 XIDs
presets.note: Each loop commits once, so each consumes one XID. `relfrozenxid` stays put and its age grows. Busy servers burn this many in seconds to minutes.

presets.label: Not frozen yet
presets.note: Rows still carry their original xmin and no `HEAP_XMIN_FROZEN` flag. No page is all-frozen.

presets.label: VACUUM (FREEZE)
presets.note: `relfrozenxid` jumps forward and its age drops to almost 0. Each tuple shows `HEAP_XMIN_FROZEN`, yet `t_xmin` keeps its original value: freezing sets flag bits, it no longer overwrites xmin.

presets.label: The freeze settings
presets.sql:
SELECT name, to_char(setting::bigint, 'FM9,999,999,999') AS value
FROM pg_settings
WHERE name IN ('vacuum_freeze_min_age', 'vacuum_freeze_table_age', 'autovacuum_freeze_max_age',
               'vacuum_failsafe_age', 'vacuum_multixact_freeze_min_age',
               'vacuum_multixact_freeze_table_age', 'autovacuum_multixact_freeze_max_age')
ORDER BY setting::bigint;
presets.note: 50 M, 150 M, 200 M and 1.6 B for XIDs; multixacts have their own, larger limits (5 M, 150 M, 400 M).

presets.label: Make a MultiXact
presets.note: Two lockers on one row do not fit in `xmax`, so `xmax` holds a **MultiXact ID** (`HEAP_XMAX_IS_MULTI`) and its members live in `pg_multixact`. MultiXact IDs wrap around too.

production.title: A forgotten replication slot and the wraparound countdown
production.context: A logistics company runs about 3,000 write transactions per second on its primary. Months ago a team created a logical replication slot for a CDC pilot and abandoned it.
production.problem: Monitoring showed `age(datfrozenxid)` climbing past 1 billion although autovacuum ran constantly. The slot's `catalog_xmin` pinned the oldest XID that VACUUM could freeze past. At 3,000 XIDs/s, about 1.1 billion remaining XIDs is roughly 4 days until the 40 M warning zone.
production.solution: Follow the recovery order: find what holds the horizon back (prepared transactions, long sessions, slots), remove it, then plain VACUUM the oldest tables. No single-user mode, no VACUUM FULL, no FREEZE.
production.outcome: Once the slot was dropped, the next aggressive vacuums advanced `relfrozenxid`, and `age(datfrozenxid)` fell back to around the 200 M `autovacuum_freeze_max_age` range. An alert on `age(datfrozenxid) > 500 M` and on inactive slots now catches this weeks earlier.

pitfalls.title: Panicking into single-user mode
pitfalls.symptom: The server refuses new XIDs with "database is not accepting commands that assign new transaction IDs".
pitfalls.cause: A common belief is that you must stop the server and vacuum in single-user mode. In PostgreSQL 18 that is neither necessary nor desirable, and single-user mode disables the wraparound safeguards.
pitfalls.fix: Stay online. Clear prepared transactions, long transactions and stale slots, then run a plain database-wide `VACUUM` as superuser. Do not use VACUUM FULL (it needs an XID) or VACUUM FREEZE (more work than needed).

pitfalls.title: An idle-in-transaction session blocks freezing
pitfalls.symptom: `age(datfrozenxid)` keeps growing even though aggressive autovacuums finish.
pitfalls.cause: VACUUM cannot freeze past the oldest snapshot still running anywhere in the cluster. One forgotten `BEGIN` in a pooled connection holds it back.
pitfalls.fix: Set `idle_in_transaction_session_timeout` and alert on old `backend_xmin`.
pitfalls.sql:
SELECT pid, now() - xact_start AS open_for, age(backend_xmin)
FROM pg_stat_activity WHERE backend_xmin IS NOT NULL ORDER BY 3 DESC;

pitfalls.title: Insert-only tables surprise you with a huge vacuum
pitfalls.symptom: An append-only table that never had dead rows suddenly gets a long, unstoppable `(to prevent wraparound)` autovacuum that reads every page.
pitfalls.cause: Without dead rows, normal vacuums skipped its all-visible pages, so nothing was frozen until `autovacuum_freeze_max_age` forced a full aggressive scan.
pitfalls.fix: Let insert-triggered autovacuum freeze as you go (keep `autovacuum_vacuum_insert_threshold` enabled, consider a lower per-table `autovacuum_freeze_min_age`), or run `VACUUM (FREEZE)` after bulk loads.

pitfalls.title: A health check that burns XIDs
pitfalls.symptom: `age(datfrozenxid)` grows quickly on a database that is mostly read, and the XID rate tracks the monitoring interval.
pitfalls.cause: A probe such as `SELECT txid_current()` assigns a new XID on every call, even though it writes nothing. Thousands of probes per minute from load balancers add up to millions of XIDs a day.
pitfalls.fix: Probe with `SELECT 1`, or read the current value without assigning one: `pg_current_snapshot()` or `pg_current_xact_id_if_assigned()`.
pitfalls.sql: SELECT pg_snapshot_xmax(pg_current_snapshot()) AS next_xid;  -- assigns nothing

pointers: XIDs are **32-bit, compared modulo 2^32**: 2 billion in the past, 2 billion in the future.
**Freezing** marks a row older than every XID; `relfrozenxid` / `datfrozenxid` track the oldest unfrozen XID.
Ladder: **150 M** aggressive · **200 M** forced autovacuum · **1.6 B** failsafe · **40 M before wrap** warnings · **3 M before wrap** no new XIDs.
Recovery: end prepared/long transactions, drop stale slots, plain **VACUUM** as superuser; never single-user mode, FULL or FREEZE.
**MultiXacts** (several lockers in one `xmax`) age and wrap the same way: watch `mxid_age(relminmxid)`.

lessons.title: Physical streaming replication
tldr: A **standby** is a copy of the primary that stays in permanent recovery, receiving the primary's WAL over a replication connection and replaying it byte for byte.
Streaming gives a second server for failover and read queries, and **synchronous replication** lets a COMMIT wait until a standby has written, flushed or replayed its WAL.

visualizer.title: A primary streaming to a hot standby
visualizer.caption: Press **COMMIT** and watch WAL travel out and replies come back. Change the `synchronous_commit` level, the latency, cut the network, or start a long standby query. The standby is simulated: the playground database is a single process.

playground.setup:
CREATE TABLE orders (id bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY, total numeric(10,2) NOT NULL, created_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now());
INSERT INTO orders (total) SELECT (random() * 100)::numeric(10,2) FROM generate_series(1, 1000);

presets.label: Replication settings
presets.sql:
SELECT pg_is_in_recovery() AS is_standby;

SELECT name, setting FROM pg_settings
WHERE name IN ('wal_level', 'max_wal_senders', 'max_replication_slots', 'wal_keep_size',
               'max_slot_wal_keep_size', 'synchronous_standby_names', 'synchronous_commit',
               'hot_standby', 'hot_standby_feedback', 'max_standby_streaming_delay',
               'wal_receiver_status_interval')
ORDER BY name;
presets.note: `wal_level = replica` is enough for physical standbys. `max_slot_wal_keep_size = -1` means a slot may retain unlimited WAL. The standby-side settings are listed too; they only matter on a standby.

presets.label: Create a physical slot
presets.sql:
SELECT * FROM pg_create_physical_replication_slot('standby_a', true);

SELECT slot_name, slot_type, active, restart_lsn, wal_status FROM pg_replication_slots;
presets.note: The second argument reserves WAL immediately. A standby would use it with `primary_slot_name = 'standby_a'`.

presets.label: Write WAL nobody consumes
presets.note: With no standby attached, `restart_lsn` never moves, so every byte written since is pinned in `pg_wal`. `safe_wal_size` is NULL because `max_slot_wal_keep_size` is unlimited.
