presets.label: What a lag query computes
presets.sql:
-- the shape of pg_stat_replication on a real primary (one row per walsender):
SELECT column_name FROM information_schema.columns
WHERE table_name = 'pg_stat_replication' AND column_name ~ '(lsn|lag|state)$' ORDER BY ordinal_position;

-- the standard lag query, applied to a sample row
WITH r(application_name, sent_lsn, write_lsn, flush_lsn, replay_lsn) AS (
  VALUES ('standby_a', '0/3A00148'::pg_lsn, '0/3A00148'::pg_lsn, '0/3A00060'::pg_lsn, '0/39F2000'::pg_lsn))
SELECT application_name,
       sent_lsn - write_lsn   AS network_or_write_bytes,
       write_lsn - flush_lsn  AS awaiting_fsync_bytes,
       flush_lsn - replay_lsn AS replay_backlog_bytes
FROM r;
presets.note: Each gap points at a different bottleneck: network, standby disk, or replay (often a query conflict). `write_lag`, `flush_lag` and `replay_lag` give the same stages as time.

presets.label: Recovery functions on a primary
presets.sql:
SELECT pg_is_in_recovery()          AS in_recovery,
       pg_last_wal_receive_lsn()     AS last_received,
       pg_last_wal_replay_lsn()      AS last_replayed,
       pg_last_xact_replay_timestamp() AS last_replay_time,
       pg_current_wal_lsn()          AS current_lsn;
presets.note: On a primary the standby-side functions return NULL. On a standby, `now() - pg_last_xact_replay_timestamp()` is a common lag-in-time check.

presets.label: Drop the slot
presets.sql:
SELECT pg_drop_replication_slot('standby_a');
SELECT count(*) AS slots_left FROM pg_replication_slots;
presets.note: Dropping an unused slot releases the retained WAL at the next checkpoint. Forgotten slots are the classic cause of a full `pg_wal`.

production.title: Synchronous replication without single-standby hangs
production.context: A payments team runs a primary and two standbys in different zones and must not lose an acknowledged payment if the primary's zone fails.
production.problem: They started with `synchronous_standby_names = 's1'`. During a routine restart of s1, every write transaction on the primary hung at COMMIT for the whole maintenance window, because the only synchronous standby was gone.
production.solution: Use a quorum: any one of two standbys must confirm. Keep `synchronous_commit = on` for payments and let bulk jobs opt out per transaction. Monitor `sync_state` and lag.
production.outcome: Either standby can now confirm a commit, so restarting one no longer blocks writes, and an acknowledged payment is still on durable storage in a second zone. Commit latency is one round trip to the nearest healthy standby plus its fsync.

pitfalls.title: An inactive slot fills pg_wal
pitfalls.symptom: Disk usage of `pg_wal` grows for days; eventually the primary hits a full disk and PANICs.
pitfalls.cause: A replication slot whose standby is gone keeps `restart_lsn` in place, so no WAL after it can be recycled. `max_slot_wal_keep_size` defaults to -1 (unlimited).
pitfalls.fix: Alert on inactive slots and retained bytes, drop slots you no longer need, and set `max_slot_wal_keep_size` so a dead standby is invalidated instead of taking the primary down.
pitfalls.sql:
SELECT slot_name, active, pg_size_pretty(pg_current_wal_lsn() - restart_lsn) AS retained
FROM pg_replication_slots ORDER BY pg_current_wal_lsn() - restart_lsn DESC;

pitfalls.title: Standby queries cancelled with "conflict with recovery"
pitfalls.symptom: Reports on the standby fail with `canceling statement due to conflict with recovery`.
pitfalls.cause: Replay must apply a VACUUM cleanup record that removes rows a standby query still needs. Replay waits at most `max_standby_streaming_delay` (30 s), then cancels the query.
pitfalls.fix: Enable `hot_standby_feedback` (costs some bloat on the primary), raise `max_standby_streaming_delay` on reporting standbys, or move long reports to a dedicated delayed replica.

pitfalls.title: Both nodes think they are primary
pitfalls.symptom: After a failover, the old primary comes back and accepts writes; the two histories diverge.
pitfalls.cause: PostgreSQL does not detect failures or fence nodes. Promotion of the standby does not stop the old primary.
pitfalls.fix: Fence the old primary (STONITH) before promoting, and use a cluster manager. Rejoin the old primary as a standby with `pg_rewind` instead of a full re-clone.

pointers: **walsender** (primary) streams WAL to the **walreceiver** (standby); the **startup process** replays it.
Positions: **sent → write → flush → replay**; `pg_stat_replication` shows each LSN and the matching **lag**.
Slots keep WAL (and with feedback, old rows) until the standby has it; cap with **`max_slot_wal_keep_size`**.
`synchronous_standby_names` = `FIRST n (…)` or `ANY n (…)`; `synchronous_commit` picks **remote_write / on / remote_apply**.
Hot standby is read-only; conflicts are resolved by **delaying replay** up to `max_standby_streaming_delay`, then cancelling.

lessons.title: Logical replication
tldr: **Logical replication** decodes the WAL back into row-level INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE messages and streams them, per table, from a **publication** to a **subscription** on another server.
Unlike physical streaming it can replicate a subset of tables, rows and columns, across major versions and platforms, into a database that stays writable.

visualizer.title: From WAL records to filtered row changes
visualizer.caption: Step through four interleaved transactions: decoding, the reorder buffer, commit order, an abort, and a publication with a row filter and column list. Then flip old and new values below.

presets.label: Publication with a row filter and column list
presets.note: An INSERT-only publication may filter on any column. `total` and `card_last4` are not in the column list, so they never leave the publisher (but a column list is not a security boundary).

presets.label: Replica identity
presets.sql:
SELECT relname, relreplident,
       CASE relreplident WHEN 'd' THEN 'default: primary key, if any' WHEN 'f' THEN 'full row'
                         WHEN 'n' THEN 'nothing' WHEN 'i' THEN 'index' END AS meaning
FROM pg_class WHERE relname IN ('orders', 'products', 'clicks');
presets.note: UPDATE and DELETE messages identify the old row by its replica identity. `clicks` has no primary key, so its default identity is empty.

presets.label: Publishing UPDATEs needs an identity
presets.note: The error is raised **on the publisher**, even with no subscriber attached. `FULL` fixes it, at the cost of logging whole old rows and slow row lookups on the subscriber.

presets.label: Row filters must use identity columns
presets.note: A publication that sends UPDATEs must evaluate the filter on the old row, so it may only reference replica identity columns. Filtering on the primary key works.

presets.label: Generated columns (new in 18)
presets.note: With `publish_generated_columns = stored` the stored `price_with_vat` is sent; the **virtual** `label` never is, because it has no stored value. Listing a stored generated column in a column list publishes it even with the default `none`. On the subscriber the target column must be an ordinary column.

presets.label: DDL is not replicated
presets.sql:
ALTER TABLE orders ADD COLUMN coupon text;
SELECT pubname, attnames FROM pg_publication_tables WHERE tablename = 'orders' ORDER BY pubname;
presets.note: The new column joins publications without a column list automatically, but the ALTER itself is not sent: the subscriber must add `coupon` first, or apply errors start.

presets.label: The WAL is the source
presets.note: Logical decoding reads the same WAL as everything else; `pg_logical_emit_message` writes a record decoders pass through. Creating a logical slot needs `wal_level = logical`, which this playground runs without (it reports `replica`).

production.title: Upgrading a major version with near-zero downtime
production.context: A marketplace runs PostgreSQL 16 with a 2 TB database and wants to move to 18. `pg_upgrade --link` would need a maintenance window it cannot get.
production.problem: Physical replication cannot cross major versions, and a dump and restore of 2 TB takes many hours of read-only time.
production.solution: Stand up an 18 cluster, copy the schema, and replicate logically. After the initial sync and catch-up, freeze writes for a minute, sync sequences (they are not replicated), and switch the application.
production.outcome: The write freeze lasts as long as the final catch-up and the sequence sync, typically seconds to minutes instead of hours. Tables without a primary key were given one (or `REPLICA IDENTITY FULL`) beforehand, because their UPDATEs would otherwise fail on the publisher.

pitfalls.title: UPDATE fails: "does not have a replica identity"
pitfalls.symptom: After adding a table to a publication, application UPDATEs and DELETEs on it fail on the **publisher**.
pitfalls.cause: The table has no primary key, so its default replica identity is empty, and a publication that publishes UPDATE/DELETE needs one.
pitfalls.fix: Add a primary key, or `REPLICA IDENTITY USING INDEX` on a unique non-null index, or as a last resort `REPLICA IDENTITY FULL`.
pitfalls.sql: ALTER TABLE clicks ADD COLUMN id bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY;

pitfalls.title: Replication stops on a conflict
pitfalls.symptom: The subscriber log repeats `conflict detected on relation ...: conflict=insert_exists` and lag grows.
pitfalls.cause: Incoming changes apply like normal DML. A row written locally on the subscriber violates a unique constraint, so the apply worker errors and retries forever.
pitfalls.fix: Fix the local data, or skip the remote transaction with `ALTER SUBSCRIPTION ... SKIP (lsn = ...)` using the finish LSN from the log (with the default `streaming = parallel` it can be missing; set streaming to `on` and let the error repeat). Skipping drops the whole transaction. In 18, per-type conflict counters show what keeps happening; the `*_origin_differs` ones need `track_commit_timestamp = on` on the subscriber.

pitfalls.title: A dropped subscription leaves its slot behind
pitfalls.symptom: The publisher's `pg_wal` keeps growing after a subscriber was decommissioned.
pitfalls.cause: If the publisher was unreachable during `DROP SUBSCRIPTION`, or the slot was disassociated, the logical slot stays and retains WAL and catalog rows.
pitfalls.fix: Check `pg_replication_slots` on the publisher and drop orphaned slots; cap retention with `max_slot_wal_keep_size`.
pitfalls.sql:
SELECT slot_name, plugin, active, pg_size_pretty(pg_current_wal_lsn() - restart_lsn)
FROM pg_replication_slots WHERE slot_type = 'logical';

pitfalls.title: Sequences and DDL silently drift
pitfalls.symptom: After failing over to the subscriber, inserts fail with duplicate keys, or apply breaks after a schema change.
pitfalls.cause: Logical replication does not replicate DDL or sequence state.
pitfalls.fix: Apply schema changes to the subscriber first (additive changes), and run `setval` for every sequence before a switchover.

pitfalls.title: Publishing a generated column into a generated column
pitfalls.symptom: After enabling `publish_generated_columns = stored`, the subscriber's apply worker errors on every change to the table.
pitfalls.cause: The publisher now sends a value for `price_with_vat`, but on the subscriber that column is also `GENERATED`, and a generated column cannot accept a supplied value.
pitfalls.fix: Either leave the option at `none` and let the subscriber compute the column itself, or make the subscriber column an ordinary column. Virtual generated columns are never published.

pointers: **Publication** (what to send) on the publisher, **subscription** (where from) on the subscriber, one logical **slot** per subscription.
Decoding is in **commit order**; rolled-back transactions are **never sent**.
**Replica identity** (default: primary key) identifies old rows; without one, published UPDATE/DELETE fail on the publisher.
**Row filters** turn UPDATEs into INSERT/DELETE when rows cross the filter; **column lists** limit columns but are not security.
Not replicated: **DDL, sequences, large objects**. Initial data is copied by table-sync workers, then changes stream.

lessons.title: Declarative partitioning and pruning
tldr: A **partitioned table** has no storage of its own: each row is routed by its partition key to one partition, an ordinary table with its own heap, indexes and statistics.
Queries that constrain the key touch only the relevant partitions through **partition pruning**, and old data leaves by dropping a whole partition instead of deleting rows.

visualizer.title: Which partitions does a query touch?
visualizer.caption: Pick a query and see where pruning happens (plan time, executor start, or run time), next to its EXPLAIN output. Then route a few rows and compare DELETE with DROP for retention.

presets.label: Partitions and routing
presets.note: The parent stores nothing (0 bytes). `tableoid` shows which partition each row was routed to.

presets.label: Plan-time pruning
presets.note: With pruning only `events_2026_10` appears. Turn it off and the plan becomes an Append over all five partitions.

presets.label: Pruning at executor start
presets.note: Look for **Subplans Removed: 4**: the generic plan kept every partition, and pruning ran when the parameter became known.

presets.label: Pruning during execution
presets.note: Four subplans say **(never executed)**: the value came from an InitPlan, so the Append pruned at run time.

presets.label: Unique keys must include the partition key
presets.note: Each partition enforces uniqueness only inside itself, so a primary key on `id` alone is rejected. With `created_at` added it works, and the parent's key creates one index per partition.

presets.label: Retention: DELETE vs DROP
presets.note: DELETE logged every row (about 1.2 MB) and left 22,320 dead rows for VACUUM. DROP removed a month in a few kB of WAL and left nothing to clean.

presets.label: Add next month with ATTACH
presets.note: ATTACH takes only SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE on the parent. The matching CHECK constraint lets it skip the validation scan; the DEFAULT partition is still checked for December rows.

presets.label: DEFAULT partition traps
presets.note: A late row lands in the DEFAULT partition, and then creating January **fails**: the new bounds would make that row belong elsewhere. Moving the rows out and attaching in one transaction fixes it. As long as `partdefid` is set, `DETACH … CONCURRENTLY` is refused too.

production.title: Monthly partitions for a 3-year event log
production.context: An analytics product keeps 36 months of click events, about 1.5 billion rows, and deletes the oldest month every month. Most queries look at the last 7 days.
production.problem: The monthly `DELETE` produced tens of GB of WAL, saturated the replica link, and left a month of dead rows that autovacuum took days to clear. Recent-data queries still walked indexes covering three years.
production.solution: Range-partition by `created_at` per month. Create next month's partition ahead of time, and retire the oldest month with `DETACH PARTITION … CONCURRENTLY` and `DROP TABLE`. Queries filter on `created_at`, so they prune to one or two partitions.
production.outcome: Retention became a metadata operation of a few kB of WAL (dropping a 22,000-row month writes about 6 kB, deleting it about 1.2 MB), with no dead rows. Recent-data queries touch one month instead of 36, so their indexes are 36 times smaller and stay in cache.

pitfalls.title: Queries that do not mention the partition key
pitfalls.symptom: A lookup by `user_id` on a partitioned table is slower than before partitioning; EXPLAIN shows an Append over every partition.
pitfalls.cause: Pruning uses only conditions on the partition key. Without one, every partition and every partition index is searched.
pitfalls.fix: Partition by the column most queries filter on, add the key to hot queries, or accept the fan-out for rare queries.

pitfalls.title: DETACH CONCURRENTLY refused
pitfalls.symptom: `ERROR: cannot detach partitions concurrently when a default partition exists`.
pitfalls.cause: A popular rotation recipe adds a DEFAULT partition as a safety net and later detaches old partitions with CONCURRENTLY. The two do not mix: concurrent detach is refused while a DEFAULT partition exists, and it cannot run inside a transaction block either.
pitfalls.fix: Avoid a DEFAULT partition on tables you rotate (create future partitions ahead of time instead), or use a plain DETACH in a short maintenance window.
pitfalls.sql: ALTER TABLE events DETACH PARTITION events_2026_08;  -- takes ACCESS EXCLUSIVE on the parent

pitfalls.title: Too many partitions
pitfalls.symptom: Planning time and backend memory grow; simple queries that cannot prune become slow to plan.
pitfalls.cause: Every partition a session touches loads metadata into its local memory, and planning considers each one that is not pruned.
pitfalls.fix: Keep partition counts in the hundreds to low thousands, choose coarser ranges, and make sure common queries prune.

pitfalls.title: A DEFAULT partition that quietly fills up
pitfalls.symptom: `CREATE TABLE … PARTITION OF` for next month fails with `updated partition constraint for default partition would be violated by some row`, and every new partition takes longer to add.
pitfalls.cause: Rows with no matching range were routed to the DEFAULT partition. Adding a range scans the default for rows that would now belong to it, and refuses if any exist.
pitfalls.fix: Create partitions ahead of time and alert when the default holds any rows. To add a range, move its rows out of the default and ATTACH in one transaction (the last playground preset).
pitfalls.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM events_default;  -- should stay 0

pointers: RANGE / LIST / HASH; range bounds are **inclusive below, exclusive above**; the parent has **no storage**.
Pruning at **plan time** (constants), **executor start** (`Subplans Removed`), and **run time** (`(never executed)`).
PRIMARY KEY / UNIQUE must **include the partition key**; an index on the parent is created on every partition.
Retention: **DROP / DETACH a partition**, not DELETE; ATTACH with a matching CHECK to skip validation.
Autovacuum handles partitions, but **ANALYZE the parent** yourself.

lessons.title: Backups and point-in-time recovery
tldr: PostgreSQL backs up either **logically** with `pg_dump` (SQL or an archive of one database) or **physically** with a base backup of the whole cluster plus the continuous stream of archived WAL.
Physical backups enable **point-in-time recovery**: restore the base backup and replay archived WAL up to any moment after it, such as one second before a destructive mistake.

visualizer.title: Recover to one minute before the mistake
visualizer.caption: Step through a day with a base backup, archived WAL and a bad DROP, then recovery. Drag `recovery_target_time` to before 01:20, before 14:05, or after it and step again.

playground.setup:
CREATE TABLE invoices (id int PRIMARY KEY, customer text NOT NULL, amount numeric(10,2) NOT NULL, paid boolean NOT NULL DEFAULT false);
INSERT INTO invoices SELECT g, 'cust_' || (g % 40), (g % 300) + 0.5, g % 3 = 0 FROM generate_series(1, 2000) g;

presets.label: What pg_dump does inside the server
presets.note: A dump is one **REPEATABLE READ** transaction: every table is read in the same snapshot, so the output is consistent. It holds **AccessShareLock** on each table it dumps until the end, and no XID. `pg_export_snapshot()` is how `pg_dump -j` workers share that one snapshot.

presets.label: Archiving settings
presets.note: This playground runs with archiving off. A PITR-ready server needs `wal_level` replica or higher, `archive_mode = on` and a working `archive_command` or `archive_library`.

presets.label: A low-level base backup
presets.note: `labelfile` is the `backup_label` you must save with the copy: START WAL LOCATION and CHECKPOINT LOCATION tell recovery where to begin.

presets.label: Segment files and switches
presets.note: `pg_switch_wal` closes the current segment so it can be archived now (what `archive_timeout` does on a timer). Every file is a full 16 MB.

presets.label: A named restore point
presets.note: A `RESTORE_POINT` record sits in the WAL before the purge. Recovery could stop exactly there with `recovery_target_name = 'before_invoice_purge'`.

presets.label: Write the recovery settings
presets.sql:
SELECT format($f$restore_command = 'cp /mnt/archive/%%f "%%p"'
recovery_target_time = %L
recovery_target_inclusive = off
recovery_target_action = 'pause'
-- then: touch $PGDATA/recovery.signal and start the server$f$,
  now() - interval '1 minute') AS postgresql_conf_lines;

SELECT now() AS time, pg_current_wal_lsn() AS lsn, pg_current_xact_id() AS xid;
presets.note: Targets can be a time, a restore point name, an LSN or an XID (one at a time). `pause` lets you check the data before ending recovery.

presets.label: Incremental backups need WAL summaries
presets.note: `pg_basebackup --incremental` (17+) copies only blocks changed since a previous backup, using summaries written by the WAL summarizer. With `summarize_wal = off` there are none.

production.title: Undoing a bad migration with PITR
production.context: A billing service takes a nightly `pg_basebackup` at 01:00 and archives WAL to object storage. At 14:05 a migration meant for staging dropped the `invoices` table in production.
production.problem: A nightly `pg_dump` would restore last night's state and lose 13 hours of invoices. Restoring the base backup alone would do the same.
production.solution: Restore the 01:00 base backup on a new host, replay archived WAL to 14:04, inspect, then copy the table back to production (or promote the recovered host). The old timeline stays intact in the archive.
production.sql:
# postgresql.conf on the recovery host
restore_command = 'aws s3 cp s3://wal-archive/%f %p'
recovery_target_time = '2026-11-10 14:04:00+00'
recovery_target_action = 'pause'
# touch $PGDATA/recovery.signal ; pg_ctl start
# once paused at the target:
#   psql -c "SELECT count(*) FROM invoices"
#   pg_dump -t invoices | psql -h prod billing
production.outcome: Data loss is bounded by the recovery target, one minute here, instead of 13 hours. Recovery time is dominated by replaying 13 hours of WAL; newer incremental backups (`pg_basebackup --incremental` + `pg_combinebackup`) or a more recent base backup shorten it.

pitfalls.title: An archive_command that lies
pitfalls.symptom: Recovery stops early with `could not open file` for a segment that the archiver reported as done.
pitfalls.cause: The command returned 0 without storing the file (for example `cp -i` or a script that ignores errors), so PostgreSQL recycled the segment.
pitfalls.fix: Return 0 only after the file is durably stored, refuse to overwrite existing files, and test restores regularly. `pg_stat_archiver.failed_count` must stay flat.
pitfalls.sql: SELECT archived_count, failed_count, last_failed_wal, last_failed_time FROM pg_stat_archiver;

pitfalls.title: Archiving silently stopped and pg_wal filled
pitfalls.symptom: Disk usage of `pg_wal` grows until the server PANICs with a full disk.
pitfalls.cause: If `archive_command` keeps failing, segments cannot be recycled. PostgreSQL keeps retrying forever.
pitfalls.fix: Alert on `failed_count` and on `pg_wal` size; fix the archive target. Never delete files from `pg_wal` by hand.

pitfalls.title: Treating pg_dump as the only backup
pitfalls.symptom: After an incident the newest recoverable state is last night's dump.
pitfalls.cause: `pg_dump` is a logical snapshot of one database at one moment; it cannot be combined with WAL for PITR.
pitfalls.fix: Use base backups plus WAL archiving for recovery, and keep `pg_dump` for migrations, partial restores and cross-version moves. Verify base backups with `pg_verifybackup`.

pitfalls.title: pg_restore refuses the dump file
pitfalls.symptom: `pg_restore: error: input file appears to be a text format dump. Please use psql.`
pitfalls.cause: Plain format (the `pg_dump` default) and all `pg_dumpall` output are SQL scripts for `psql`. Only the custom, directory and tar archives are read by `pg_restore`, which is also what enables `-j` parallel restore and `-l` / `-L` to restore selected objects.
pitfalls.fix: Dump with `-Fc` or `-Fd` for anything you may restore selectively. Repeat `-t` / `-n` once per object (they do not take comma lists), use `-O` (`--no-owner`) when roles differ, and dump roles and tablespaces separately with `pg_dumpall --globals-only`, because `pg_dump` never includes them.
pitfalls.sql:
pg_dump -Fd -j 4 -t invoices -t customers -f /backups/billing.dir billing
pg_dumpall --globals-only > /backups/globals.sql
psql -f /backups/globals.sql postgres
pg_restore -j 4 -O -d billing_copy /backups/billing.dir

pitfalls.title: A long pg_dump blocks a migration and VACUUM
pitfalls.symptom: During the nightly dump an `ALTER TABLE` hangs, every query behind it queues, and dead rows pile up across the cluster.
pitfalls.cause: The dump holds ACCESS SHARE on every table until it finishes, which conflicts with the ACCESS EXCLUSIVE an ALTER needs. Its snapshot also stops VACUUM from removing rows deleted after the dump began.
pitfalls.fix: Schedule DDL outside dump windows and set `lock_timeout` on migrations. Take large dumps from a standby, or rely on base backups and use `pg_dump` for smaller, targeted exports.

pointers: **pg_dump**: one database in one snapshot; plain SQL goes to **psql**, custom/directory archives to **pg_restore** (`-j`, `-L`); roles need **pg_dumpall --globals-only**.
**Base backup + archived WAL** = PITR; replay must start at the backup's `START WAL LOCATION`.
`restore_command` + `recovery.signal` + one **recovery_target_*** (time, name, lsn, xid, immediate).
Ending recovery starts a **new timeline**; `.history` files record branch points.
Incremental backups (17+) need **`summarize_wal`** and are rebuilt with **`pg_combinebackup`**.

lessons.title: Connection pooling
tldr: Every PostgreSQL connection is a separate backend process with its own memory and session state, so thousands of mostly idle connections waste RAM and slots up to `max_connections`.

A **pooler** such as PgBouncer lets many clients share a few server connections, and its pooling mode decides which session features, such as `SET`, prepared statements, advisory locks and `LISTEN`, still behave correctly.

visualizer.title: Four clients, two server connections
visualizer.caption: Step through the same client script in **transaction**, **session** and **statement** mode and watch where session state lands and what breaks.

presets.label: Session state a pooler can leak
presets.note: All five live in **this backend**, not in the client. Under transaction pooling the next client on this server connection would inherit them, including the tenant_a search_path.

presets.label: DISCARD ALL wipes it
presets.note: `DISCARD ALL` resets settings to their defaults, drops prepared statements and temp tables, releases session advisory locks and stops listening: every count is back to 0. Session-mode poolers run it between clients.

presets.label: Transaction-scoped alternatives
presets.note: `SET LOCAL` and `pg_advisory_xact_lock` end with the transaction, so nothing survives COMMIT. This is what is safe under transaction pooling.

presets.label: Per-request context: set_config(…, true)
presets.note: The third argument `true` makes the value transaction-local, like `SET LOCAL`, so a tenant id used by row-level security policies cannot leak to the next client on the connection. Afterwards the value is an **empty string**, not NULL. Without `missing_ok = true`, reading a name that was never set raises an error.

presets.label: What one connection costs
presets.note: Even this idle backend holds about 2 MB in memory contexts (caches, plans), before any query runs, and each query can add `work_mem` per sort or hash node. The playground has one standalone backend; a server forks one process per connection.

presets.label: Timeouts that protect a pool
presets.note: All are off (0) by default. `idle_in_transaction_session_timeout` kills sessions that sit in an open transaction holding locks and an old snapshot; `idle_session_timeout` is dangerous behind a pooler, which keeps idle server connections on purpose.

presets.label: Idle in transaction holds an XID
presets.note: While a transaction stays open its `backend_xid` and snapshot hold back VACUUM cluster-wide. A pooled client that forgets COMMIT pins a server connection and the cleanup horizon.

presets.label: Find the sessions that hog the pool
presets.sql:
SELECT pid, usename, application_name, state,
       now() - xact_start  AS xact_open_for,
       now() - state_change AS in_state_for,
       left(query, 40)     AS last_query
FROM pg_stat_activity
WHERE backend_type = 'client backend' OR backend_type = 'standalone backend'
ORDER BY xact_start NULLS LAST;

SELECT pg_get_function_arguments('pg_terminate_backend'::regproc) AS terminate_signature;
presets.note: On a server, sort `idle in transaction` sessions by `xact_open_for` to find the ones holding connections and snapshots. `pg_terminate_backend(pid)` returns true once the signal is **sent**; with a `timeout` in ms it returns true only if the backend actually exited.

production.title: From 4,000 connections to 60
production.context: A Kubernetes deployment runs 200 pods, each with a client-side pool of 20 connections, against one primary: 4,000 connections, almost all idle.
production.problem: The server needed `max_connections = 5000`; each backend kept its own caches and memory even when idle, connection storms during deploys forked hundreds of processes at once, and snapshot work grows with the number of backends.
production.solution: Put PgBouncer in transaction mode in front of the primary with a small server pool, shrink the per-pod pools, and remove session state from the application: `SET LOCAL` instead of `SET`, transaction-level advisory locks, schema-qualified names, protocol-level prepared statements with `max_prepared_statements` enabled.
production.sql:
; pgbouncer.ini
[databases]
app = host=10.0.0.5 dbname=app
[pgbouncer]
pool_mode = transaction
default_pool_size = 60
max_client_conn = 5000
max_prepared_statements = 200

-- server side
ALTER SYSTEM SET max_connections = 200;
ALTER ROLE app SET idle_in_transaction_session_timeout = '30s';
production.outcome: The primary serves the same traffic with about 60 busy backends instead of 4,000 mostly idle ones, deploys no longer cause fork storms, and memory goes to `shared_buffers` and `work_mem` instead of idle processes. A sensible pool size is a small multiple of CPU cores, measured under load.

pitfalls.title: Session SET under transaction pooling
pitfalls.symptom: Requests intermittently see another tenant's data, the wrong time zone, or a stray `statement_timeout`.
pitfalls.cause: A plain `SET` sticks to the server connection, which the pooler hands to the next client.
pitfalls.fix: Use `SET LOCAL` inside a transaction, or pass settings per role/database (`ALTER ROLE … SET`). Schema-qualify names instead of relying on `search_path`.
pitfalls.sql: BEGIN; SET LOCAL search_path = tenant_b; SELECT …; COMMIT;

pitfalls.title: Session advisory locks that never unlock
pitfalls.symptom: A job scheduler using `pg_advisory_lock` stops running jobs; `pg_locks` shows advisory locks held by idle connections.
pitfalls.cause: Lock and unlock ran on different server connections, so the unlock returned false and the lock stayed with the first backend.
pitfalls.fix: Use `pg_advisory_xact_lock` (released at COMMIT) or route lock holders through a session-mode pool.

pitfalls.title: Prepared statements "do not exist"
pitfalls.symptom: `ERROR: prepared statement "S_1" does not exist` after enabling transaction pooling.
pitfalls.cause: The driver prepared on one server connection and executed on another.
pitfalls.fix: Enable the pooler's prepared-statement support (PgBouncer 1.21+ `max_prepared_statements`) for protocol-level statements, or disable server-side prepares in the driver. SQL-level `PREPARE` is never safe in transaction mode.

pitfalls.title: A new connection for every query
pitfalls.symptom: Latency is dominated by connection setup, CPU shows constant process creation, and with `log_connections` on the log records one new connection per request.
pitfalls.cause: Helper functions open and close their own connection on every call. Each one is a fork of a new backend plus authentication and cache warm-up, often several milliseconds before the first query runs.
pitfalls.fix: Create one pool per application process (the driver's built-in pool or a pool library) and borrow from it per request; add a server-side pooler when many processes connect.

pitfalls.title: Drivers that leave transactions open
pitfalls.symptom: `pg_stat_activity` shows many `idle in transaction` sessions whose last query is a plain SELECT, and VACUUM stops removing dead rows.
pitfalls.cause: With autocommit off, many drivers send BEGIN before the first statement. A read-only request that never commits keeps its transaction, snapshot and server connection open.
pitfalls.fix: Use autocommit for read paths, always end transactions (commit or rollback in a `finally`), and set `idle_in_transaction_session_timeout` as a backstop.
pitfalls.sql: ALTER ROLE app SET idle_in_transaction_session_timeout = '30s';

pointers: One connection = **one backend process** with private memory; `max_connections` (100) sizes shared memory and slots.
**Session** mode: safe but no multiplexing. **Transaction** mode: multiplexes, breaks session state. **Statement** mode: autocommit only.
Session state lives in the backend: **SET, PREPARE, session advisory locks, LISTEN, temp tables**; `DISCARD ALL` resets it.
Transaction-safe forms: **`SET LOCAL`**, **`pg_advisory_xact_lock`**, schema-qualified names.
Guard the pool with **`idle_in_transaction_session_timeout`**; avoid `idle_session_timeout` behind a pooler.
